name: Adept-2
baseline: CppAD (measured in the benchmark); autodiff (autodiff/autodiff, measured); ADOL-C and Sacado (named in the user guide, qualitative)
workload: Time to compute all sensitivities (reverse-mode adjoint AD) for four quant-finance workloads: Heston Monte Carlo (8 sensitivities), SABR calibration (15), XVA CVA (40), LIBOR swaption (161).
claimed_speedup: Xcelerit ad-benchmarks (GCC 13.3, Xeon 8488C, run by the XAD vendor): Adept 2 beats CppAD on all 4 rows (e.g. Heston 91 vs 268 ms) and loses to XAD on all 4; ADBench (OMS 2018, Adept 1.1) showed gains over ADOL-C on GMM (1.8x unsplit).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma on all libraries, median of 10 measured iterations after warmup (ad-benchmarks README)
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Ubuntu 24.04
license: Apache-2.0 (library); GNU all-permissive license for test and benchmark code
stars_or_usage: 189 stars; used in climate and weather codes (ECMWF)
tradeoffs: Operator-overloading AD with expression templates; Adept 2 adds array classes and optimizers; autotools build; reverse mode records a tape; optimized BLAS recommended for matrix work.
caveats: The ADBench paper used the newest tool versions available in July-August 2015, i.e. Adept 1.1 (June 2015 per the Adept-2 ChangeLog), not Adept 2.x (2.0 released September 2017); the Adept-2 README claims it is as fast as Adept 1.1 but that is first-party. Compiler and flags are not stated. On GMM without manual splitting ADOL-C was faster than Adept at some sizes (330 parameters: 8.79e-02 vs 9.61e-02; 3,300: 8.49e-01 vs 9.76e-01; 10,700: 1.90 vs 3.11), unsplit Adept crashed at 429k parameters and unsplit ADOL-C crashed from 21.5k parameters up. Ceres is forward-mode only in this test, which disadvantages it. Tapenade (C source transformation) was faster than Adept on both GMM and BA. The table captions do not restate the time unit. Adept is not the incumbent in this category's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor). ADBench repository is archived (July 2024). [retier] Two sources were mixed in the original record (ad-benchmarks for workload/hardware, ADBench for the speedup); ad-benchmarks is vendor-run by XAD's maker.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): ADBench (microsoft/ADBench) paper source Documents/ms.tex, surfaced by the query 'C++ automatic differentiation library benchmark comparison Adept CppAD ADOL-C Stan Math autodiff Sacado fastest'
WebSearch 'C++ automatic differentiation library benchmark faster than CppAD ADOL-C Adept' surfaced the ad-benchmarks repo; vcpkg has cppad but no adept port, conan has neither (config.yml 404).

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed comparison (ADBench paper; the source says shorter versions appeared at AD2016 and in Optimization Methods and Software, Feb 2018) with absolute-runtime tables for BA and GMM where Adept beats ADOL-C and Ceres; benchmark code is public in microsoft/ADBench and the CPU (Xeon E5-1620 @ 3.60GHz, Windows 10) is stated, but no compiler or flags, so not A.
verification.notes: Every cited number is in the ms.tex tables (tab:ba-abs, tab:gmm-10k-abs); fixed 'Ceres did not finish' to 'crashed' (bullet = crash per caption) and added the much smaller unsplit GMM ratio. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0 core (test/ and benchmark/ under GNU all-permissive), 189 stars, not archived, last commit 2025-10-05.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Gradient time, Adept vs CppAD: Heston MC 91 ms vs 268 ms; SABR calibration 19 ms vs 32 ms (autodiff 38 ms); XVA CVA 7.1 s vs 8.0 s; LIBOR swaption 1.15 s vs 4.57 s (about 2.9x, 1.7x, 1.1x, 4.0x, derived from page data). autodiff did not finish (DNF) on three of four workloads. XAD, the benchmark owner's own library, is faster than Adept in every row, so Adept is the second-fastest tape library there. The Adept user guide says reverse-mode differentiation 'tends to be significantly faster and use less memory' than ADOL-C, CppAD and Sacado, and usually only a little slower than a hand-written adjoint (no numbers in the guide; numbers are in Hogan 2014, ACM TOMS 40, 26).
corrected_fields.caveats: The A-tier benchmark is run and published by Xcelerit, the vendor of XAD (a competing library that wins every row), so it is a competitor's benchmark of Adept; ADOL-C and Sacado are not in it. The original claim is in the peer-reviewed Hogan 2014 ACM TOMS paper, which I could not open here (the user guide at doc/adept_documentation.tex only states it qualitatively); verifiers should open that paper for the 2014 numbers. The Adept margin over CppAD is small on XVA CVA (7.1 s vs 8.0 s). Last upstream commits are small additions (Oct 2025).

name: bare-metal (hand-optimized SASS/CUDA ML kernels for RTX 3070 Ti Laptop)
baseline: cuBLAS (local reference harness; cuDNN and cuSPARSELt rows also measured and lost)
workload: FP16 tensor-core HGEMM (16-warp kernel) on square 2048^3 and 4096^3 problems, against cuBLAS measured on the same RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU under a no-throttle fair-run policy (median of 11 runs after 5 warmups).
claimed_speedup: docs/comparison_to_sota.md: HGEMM 16-warp 2048^3 31,875 GFLOPS vs cuBLAS 28,631 GFLOPS (111.3%); 4096^3 31,765 vs 29,708 GFLOPS (106.9%). Losing rows on the same page: IGEMM pipelined cp.async 4096^3 20.23 vs 29.44 TOPS cuBLAS (68.7%); sparse IGEMM tiled 31.59 vs 124.28 TOPS (25.4%) at 2048^3 and 30.89 vs 170.11 TOPS (18.2%) at 4096^3 vs cuSPARSELt; conv2d implicit GEMM 7,150 vs 16,910 GFLOPS cuDNN (42.3%). The project's current data/baselines.json replaces the HGEMM 'Ours' readings with clock-locked (1605 MHz) medians of 29,174 GFLOPS at 2048^3 and 30,401 at 4096^3, about 1.02x the cuBLAS reference (derived from page data). Its notes record native-boost re-measurements of 28,090 and 27,307 GFLOPS, about 0.98x and 0.92x of cuBLAS (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -arch=sm_86 -O2 (kernels via --cubin, bench harnesses use the CUDA Driver API; reference benches add -std=c++17 and link cublas, cublasLt, cudnn, cusparseLt); CUDA 13.2 (nvcc V13.2.78) per AGENTS.md
hardware: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU (GA104, sm_86, 46 SMs) under a 150 W VBIOS cap, WSL2 on a Windows host; current project HGEMM baselines were measured under a host-side 1605 MHz SM clock lock (nvidia-smi -lgc), while the cuBLAS reference (recorded 2026-05-18) carries no clock-lock note; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: sm_86 (Ampere GA104) only; kernels are compiled to cubin and some are hand-edited at SASS level through the project's R package cuasmR, so they are not portable C++ source; reproduction needs CUDA, Nsight and R (make reproduce).
caveats: The win over cuBLAS is not settled. The two HGEMM rows that beat cuBLAS use native-boost readings that the repo itself disputes: the docs/inventory.md footnote says 'Do not quote it as a settled result', and issue #167 is titled 'hgemm_16warp has two canonical numbers'. Issue #158 records the kernel running slower at native boost than under a clock lock, and #159 records a 4.9% swing between two locked sessions. With the current locked baselines the margin is about 2%, inside that spread. At native boost the kernel measures below the cuBLAS reference. Project and cuBLAS numbers were taken on different dates and under different clock regimes. Every other row on the page loses: dense INT8 68.7% of cuBLAS, sparse INT8 25.4% and 18.2% of cuSPARSELt, conv2d 42.3% of cuDNN. This is a single laptop GPU with a power cap, the README says several results are n=1, and host CPU is not stated. Flash Attention and GroupNorm have no local reference ('not measured locally'). The like-for-like part holds: both sides take FP16 inputs and accumulate and write FP32.
found_via: github.com/topics/flash-attention?l=cuda and github.com/topics/gemm?l=cuda listings ('hand-tuned NVIDIA SASS kernels ... no cuBLAS / cuDNN / PyTorch'), then opened README, docs/comparison_to_sota.md, AGENTS.md, Makefile and data/reference_baselines.json

verification.tier_reason: The mechanics meet A: the harness is public (kernels/reference/cublas_hgemm/bench.cu runs cublasGemmEx, FP16 in, FP32 out, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F_FAST_16F; kernels/gemm/hgemm/bench for the project kernel). Makefile flags are -arch=sm_86 -O2, the toolchain is CUDA 13.2 and the GPU is named. But the only winning rows pair stale native-boost project readings (31,875 / 31,765 GFLOPS) with a cuBLAS reading taken on another date. The repo's own docs/inventory.md footnote and issue #167 say that HGEMM figure is disputed and not reproducible, and the current data/baselines.json puts the kernel at about 1.02x cuBLAS under a 1605 MHz clock lock and below cuBLAS at native boost. So the faster-than-cuBLAS claim is first-party and unsettled: C.
verification.notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup match comparison_to_sota.md exactly, but the repo's own data/baselines.json, the docs/inventory.md footnote and issue #167 (closed by PR #206, opened on github.com) contradict the headline. Recordable shortcoming: claim not reproducible per the project's own tracker; margin at most about 2% under a clock lock and negative at native boost. Metadata on github.com: MIT, 2 stars, 2 forks, not a fork, 320 commits, last commit 2026-08-17 (active), 29 open issues.

name: fast.cu (H100 BF16 matmul and sum-reduction kernels)
baseline: cuBLAS (cublasGemmEx, BF16 inputs, FP32 compute, CUBLAS_GEMM_DEFAULT) for matmul; CUB for sum reduction
workload: Square bf16 matrix multiplication with fp32 accumulation at N=4096 and N=8192, plus a sum over 2^30 elements, all on an H100.
claimed_speedup: Matmul N=4096: 763 TFLOPs vs cuBLAS 716 TFLOPs (about 1.07x, derived from page data); N=8192: 808 vs 795 TFLOPs (about 1.02x, derived from page data). Sum of 2^30 elements: 3240.11 GB/s vs CUB 3193 GB/s (about 1.01x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -DNDEBUG -w --expt-relaxed-constexpr --expt-extended-lambda --use_fast_math -Xcompiler=-fPIE -Xcompiler=-Wno-psabi -Xcompiler=-fno-strict-aliasing -gencode arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a -lineinfo, linked with -lcublas -lcuda (Makefile); CUDA toolkit 12.6 per a search-result snippet of the worklog post (post not opened, egress blocked)
hardware: NVIDIA H100 SXM 80GB (132 SMs, 3.35 TB/s HBM) per a search-result snippet of the worklog post; the README says only H100. Clocks and host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Hopper-only (sm_90a); BF16 square matrices with FP32 accumulation; orchestration in h100/matmul.cu with example kernels in h100/matmul/, tuned for specific sizes rather than a general GEMM API. The repo also carries GB300 NVFP4 GEMM kernels that need CUDA 13.1 and a GB300/B300.
caveats: Margins over cuBLAS are small (about 7% at N=4096, about 2% at N=8192) and only two sizes are reported; the sum-reduction win over CUB is about 1.5% on 2^30 int32 elements. The README does not say which of the 13 kernels in h100/matmul.cu produced 763/808 TFLOPs. The harness averages 8 timed repeats after one correctness/warm-up run. The CUDA 12.6 and H100 SXM details come from a search snippet of the substack worklog, which could not be opened; a newer cuBLAS may close the gap. The GB300 NVFP4 section (gb300/nvfp4, cuBLASLt baseline, run_bench_modes.sh) publishes no numbers in the repo.

name: FastGEMV (fp16/int8/int4 GEMV CUDA kernels)
baseline: PyTorch fp16 matrix-vector product (torch.matmul on a size x size fp16 matrix and size x 1 vector, baseline.py, kernel time via Nsight Systems)
workload: GEMV of an n x n fp16 matrix with an n x 1 fp16 vector for n=512..16384, plus int8 and int4 quantized-matrix variants that PyTorch cannot run directly; kernel runtime and estimated memory bandwidth.
claimed_speedup: README: max 2.7x speedup vs PyTorch on P100 and 1.4x on 3090 Ti. method_and_result.md, P100 fp16: 1.441x (n=512), 1.627x (1024), 1.551x (2048), 1.599x (4096), 2.695x (8192), 1.781x (16384); estimated bandwidth 602.0 GB/s vs PyTorch 320.8 GB/s at n=16384 (peak 732 GB/s). RTX 3090 fp16 kernel: 4372.4 ns vs PyTorch 6106.2 ns at n=1024 (about 1.40x, derived from page data); 609235 ns vs 691660.6 ns at n=16384 (about 1.14x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -m64 -std=c++17 with -gencode sm_60/sm_70/sm_75/sm_86 (Makefile); README requirements list CUDA 11.7 and Nsight Systems 2023.1.2; PyTorch version not stated
hardware: NVIDIA P100 and RTX 3090 (README says 3090 Ti, results doc says 3090); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Square power-of-two sizes only (512..16384); per-tensor scale and zero point for int8/int4; blockDim must be tuned per size and GPU; no batching; tested on Pascal and Ampere only.
caveats: Benchmarks date from May-June 2023 against the PyTorch (and the cuBLAS it dispatches to) of that time; the PyTorch version is not stated and newer releases may have closed the gap. The 2.7x peak is a single size (n=8192 on a P100), where the PyTorch baseline dips to 202 GB/s against 333 GB/s at n=4096. On the 3090 the fp16 gain is 1.02x at n=8192 (156448.3 vs 159163.1 ns) and 1.13x at n=2048 (12395.4 vs 13971.8 ns), both derived from page data, peaking at 1.40x at n=1024. Launch configurations are hand-tuned per size and per GPU. The int8/int4 columns move far fewer bytes than the fp16 PyTorch baseline, so they are not like-for-like. The README names a 3090 Ti while the results document says 3090. Timings are Nsight Systems kernel averages, not end-to-end wall clock. Host CPU not stated.
found_via: github.com/topics/cuda-kernels?l=cuda listing (description 'at most 2.7x speedup compared to pytorch baseline'), then opened repo, README, Makefile, baseline.py and method_and_result.md

name: HipKittens (AMD) / ThunderKittens sibling
baseline: AITER (AMD hand-tuned assembly attention kernels); also Composable Kernel, PyTorch SDPA, Triton and hipBLASLt in other plots
workload: GQA non-causal attention backward pass on one AMD Instinct MI355X: batch 16, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, sequence length 1024 to 16384, TFLOPS (repo's analysis/attn/bkwd plot).
claimed_speedup: GQA non-causal backward (B=16, 64 Q heads, 8 KV heads, D=128) on MI355X, from benchmark/mi355x_gqa_bkwd_non_causal.json and plot.py: HipKittens 881 / 1007 / 1106 / 1155 / 1176 TFLOPS at N = 1024 / 2048 / 4096 / 8192 / 16384 vs AITER 300 / 351 / 375 / 384 / 389, Composable Kernel 368 / 428 / 447 / 463 / 465 and PyTorch SDPA 220 / 273 / 301 / 309 / 312; 2.93x to 3.02x over AITER (derived from page data). GQA causal backward: 2.98x to 4.33x over AITER (588 vs 151 TFLOPS at N=1024, 995 vs 334 at 16384; derived from page data). The win is GQA-specific: for MHA (B=16, H=16, D=128) HipKittens is at parity or slower than AITER beyond short sequences: non-causal 734 vs 590 (1.24x) at N=1024, 1027 vs 1056 (0.97x) at 4096, 1119 vs 1201 (0.93x) at 16384; causal 462 vs 389 (1.19x) at 1024, 941 vs 1034 (0.91x) at 8192, 1028 vs 1109 (0.93x) at 16384 (derived from benchmark/mi355x_mha_bkwd_*.json).
compiler_and_flags: hipcc ($ROCM_PATH/bin/hipcc) inside the ROCm 7.0 preview image the README names (rocm/7.0-preview:rocm7.0_preview_pytorch_training_mi35x_beta); analysis/attn/bkwd/benchmark/Makefile builds the kernels as pybind11 extensions with -DKITTENS_CDNA4 --offload-arch=gfx950 -DHIP_ENABLE_WARP_SYNC_BUILTINS -ffast-math -std=c++20 -w -shared -fPIC (no explicit -O level in that Makefile; the newer kernels/common.mk adds -O3). test_python.py: 500 warmup and 100 timed iterations with torch.cuda events, BF16. CK baselines from ck_tile tile_example_fmha_bwd with -warmup=500 -repeat=100 (analysis/baselines/README.md).
hardware: AMD Instinct MI355X (gfx950, CDNA4); host CPU not stated; CDNA3 branch also covers MI300X/MI325X
stars_or_usage: 472 stars, 81 forks; MLSys 2026 paper; README says HK kernels landed in AMD AITER (March 2026) and AMD Transformer Engine (June 2026) as backends
tradeoffs: AMD CDNA3/CDNA4 GPUs only (MI355X/MI350X on main, MI300X/MI325X on the cdna3 branch), needs ROCm and hipcc. A tile-primitive DSL in C++ rather than a drop-in library: kernels are written per operation and shape configuration (matrix sizes are Makefile constants). Covers BF16/FP8/FP6 GEMM, MHA/GQA attention forward and backward, rotary and layernorm.
caveats: Baselines are AMD libraries (AITER, hipBLASLt, Composable Kernel) plus Triton and PyTorch, none of which are in the category's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor), and this is a GPU kernel library, so it fits the category only loosely. The roughly 3x attention-backward win holds only for GQA; on MHA backward the same harness shows HipKittens 3-9% slower than AITER from N=2048-4096 upward (benchmark/mi355x_mha_bkwd_non_causal.json and mi355x_mha_bkwd_causal.json), which suggests AITER's GQA backward path, not its tuned MHA path, is what HipKittens beats by 3x. Timing is not symmetric: AITER is timed as one autograd out.backward(dO) call through PyTorch (dispatch overhead and any GQA dK/dV reduction included), while HipKittens times its three kernels (prep, combined backward, dQ shuffle) directly. In plot.py the PyTorch SDPA values for the GQA plots are identical to the MHA values (220.27 / 273.06 / ... non-causal, 109.51 / 156.71 / ... causal), so the PyTorch bars in the GQA figures were copied, not measured on GQA shapes. The GQA N=16384 lines in mi355x_benchmark.sh are commented out (with ATTN_B=15), so how that JSON row was produced is not shown. HipKittens gradients differ from AITER within BF16 rounding (max abs error 0.0039; 103 dK and 1452 dV elements outside a 0.001 + 5% tolerance at N=1024). The BF16 GEMM plot (analysis/bf16_gemm) shows parity with AMD's libraries rather than a win (numbers from the search record, not re-checked here). Baseline numbers were collected by the authors in October/November 2025 and the README warns the frameworks keep evolving; AITER now includes HipKittens kernels (March 2026), so a re-run may differ. The paper (arXiv 2511.08083, MLSys 2026) and the Hazy Research and AMD blogs could not be opened (hosts blocked).

name: fbfft / fbcunn (FFT-based convolution for Torch7)
baseline: NVIDIA cuDNN R2 (layer-wise table); cuDNN R4 appears in the full-network tables where fbfft is slower
workload: Spatial convolution layer forward+backward (fprop, bprop, accGrad) timing from the convnet-benchmarks layer-wise table, last updated April 2015.
claimed_speedup: convnet-benchmarks layer-wise table (last updated April 2015): fbfft SpatialConvolutionCuFFT 256 ms (forward 101, backward 155) vs CuDNN R2 1019 ms (forward 269, backward 750), about 4x (derived from page data). In the full-network tables fbfft also beats CuDNN R2 (AlexNet 104 vs 231 ms, Overfeat-fast 342 vs 810 ms, OxfordNet 1092 vs 1099 ms) but loses to CuDNN R4 fp32 (81, 268, 529 ms). fbcunn README: temporal convolutions '1.5x to 10x faster compared to Torch's cunn implementations'. Paper (arXiv 1412.7580, via WebSearch summary only): faster than cuDNN for many common layers, up to 23.5x for a synthetic kernel configuration, and fbfft over 1.5x faster than cuFFT.
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-5930K CPU @ 3.50GHz + NVIDIA Titan X + Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64 (README header; the layer-wise section is marked last updated April 2015 and a legacy table was run on Titan Black)
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars, 242 forks; Facebook AI Research; repository moved to facebookarchive/fbcunn and archived 2022-01-13; independent suite convnet-benchmarks has 2.7k stars

name: FlashAttention-4 (CuTeDSL, Hopper/Blackwell)
baseline: cuDNN 9.13.0 fused attention (also benchmarked: cuDNN 9.19.1.2, Triton 3.6.0, Gluon 3.6.0, FlashAttention 2.8.3)
workload: Attention forward (and backward) in BF16 on B200: head dim 64, 128 and (192,128), causal and non-causal, sequence 1K to 32K with total tokens fixed at 32K, hidden dimension 2048 (32 or 16 heads); TFLOPs/s from 4 * seqlen^2 * head_dim * heads (halved for causal, backward = 2.5x forward).
claimed_speedup: Paper abstract: 'up to 1.3x speedup over cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7x over Triton on B200 GPUs with BF16, reaching up to 1613 TFLOPs/s (71% utilization)'. Figure 4 (forward, head dim 128, TFLOPs/s, seq 1K/2K/4K/8K/16K/32K): non-causal FA4 1355, 1468, 1532, 1579, 1601, 1613; cuDNN 9.13.0 1157, 1328, 1413, 1460, 1488, 1517 (FA4 1.06-1.17x, derived from page data); cuDNN 9.19.1.2 1346, 1474, 1552, 1585, 1609, 1613 (0.99-1.01x, derived); Triton 3.6.0 507 to 703 (FA4 2.29-2.67x, derived); FA2 383 to 432. Causal FA4 744, 1053, 1279, 1426, 1526, 1576; cuDNN 9.13.0 717, 929, 1076, 1168, 1285, 1266 (1.04-1.24x, derived); cuDNN 9.19.1 822, 1103, 1295, 1430, 1509, 1540 (0.91-1.02x, derived: cuDNN ahead up to 8K); Triton 351 to 670 (2.12-2.36x, derived). Figure 5 (forward causal, head dim 192/128): FA4 812, 1121, 1357, 1506, 1600, 1654 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 769, 999, 1167, 1276, 1375, 1382 (1.06-1.20x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1.2 860, 1133, 1311, 1415, 1515, 1563 (0.94-1.06x, derived). Figure 6 (backward, head dim 128): non-causal FA4 936, 1166, 1331, 1430, 1457, 1412 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 857, 1016, 1116, 1171, 1212, 1107 (1.09-1.28x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1.2 928, 1108, 1231, 1300, 1280, 1274 (1.01-1.14x, derived); causal FA4 614, 887, 1102, 1284, 1402, 1446 vs cuDNN 9.13.0 543, 732, 893, 1008, 1085, 1142 (1.13-1.29x, derived) vs cuDNN 9.19.1 651, 894, 1090, 1218, 1293, 1337 (0.94-1.08x, derived). So the 'up to 1.3x over cuDNN 9.13' is reached only in the backward pass (forward peaks at 1.24x), and the only remaining lead over current cuDNN 9.19 is in the backward pass at long sequences (up to about 1.14x).
compiler_and_flags: Paper Appendix A.1: CUDA 13.1, CuTe-DSL 4.4.1, PyTorch 2.10.0, Triton 3.6, FlashAttention 2.8.3, cuDNN 9.13 and 9.19.1.2; 5 warmup runs then 10 repeats averaged. CuTe-DSL kernels are JIT compiled; compile options are fixed in flash_attn/cute/interface.py (cute.compile options '--enable-tvm-ffi', plus a kernel's ptxas_options where set). HEAD's flash_attn/cute/pyproject.toml now requires nvidia-cutlass-dsl>=4.6.2, so a HEAD build does not match the paper's CuTe-DSL 4.4.1.
hardware: NVIDIA B200 (the main text says B200; Appendix A.1 writes 'B100 180GB SXM6 (1000W)', apparently a typo); CPU model not stated.
stars_or_usage: 25.1k stars (whole flash-attention repository, shared with FlashAttention-2 and -3); pip package flash-attn-4; paper by Princeton, Meta, Colfax, NVIDIA, Georgia Tech and Together AI authors, listed in MLSys 2026 proceedings per a WebSearch result
tradeoffs: Written in CuTe-DSL embedded in Python (paper claims 20-30x faster compile than C++ templates), so no C++ build step but a Python/CUTLASS-DSL dependency and JIT compile at first use; Hopper (sm90) and Blackwell (sm100/sm120) only, CUDA 13 recommended for best performance (cu13 extra). Forward and backward, GQA, varlen, paged KV, block sparsity and MLA kernels live in flash_attn/cute. Uses software-emulated exponentials and conditional softmax rescaling (paper abstract), which a numerics-sensitive user should check against a reference softmax.
caveats: Paper read from the PDF checked into the repo (assets/fa4_paper.pdf); arXiv, the MLSys proceedings page, the Together AI blog and the Colfax post were not opened (egress-blocked), so the peer-review status rests on a search result and was not checked by me. The Figure 4 caption itself says 'newer versions of cuDNN have incorporated many of the techniques described in this paper, yielding similar performance to FA4', and Appendix A.1 says the authors worked with the cuDNN team to fold FA4 techniques into cuDNN from 9.13/9.14 on: in the forward pass FA4 is at parity with cuDNN 9.19.1.2 (and behind it at short causal sequences, e.g. 744 vs 822 TFLOPs/s at 1K causal), and the 1.1-1.3x lead holds only against cuDNN 9.13.0; in the backward pass FA4 still leads cuDNN 9.19 by up to about 1.14x at long sequences (derived from page data). The forward figures alone peak at 1.24x over cuDNN 9.13, so the abstract's 'up to 1.3x' comes from the backward pass. Figure 5 shows 1654 TFLOPs/s at head dim 192/128, above the abstract's 'up to 1613'. Appendix inconsistencies: it names a 'B100 180GB SXM6 (1000W)' while the text and every figure say B200 (180 GB and 1000 W match B200), and it dates the library versions to 'March 2025', which cannot be right for CUDA 13.1. The public harness covers FA2, FA3, FA4, cuDNN and PyTorch standard attention but not the Triton or Gluon baselines, and no tag marks the commit used for the paper's figures. FlashAttention-3 'does not run on B200' (paper footnote), so there is no FA4 vs FA3 comparison, and the paper has no H100 FA4 numbers. Several authors are from NVIDIA and Colfax, and the cuDNN team is thanked for feedback. Shares the Dao-AILab/flash-attention repository with FlashAttention-3 (use id paper:flashattention-4).

name: FlashTP (SNU-ARC)
baseline: e3nn o3.TensorProduct (uvu, with torch_scatter) and NVIDIA cuEquivariance
workload: Channelwise (uvu) tensor-product layer of equivariant MLIPs (NequIP, SevenNet-type irreps configs in ir_config/), kernel microbenchmarks and end-to-end SevenNet-l3i5 inference and training.
claimed_speedup: Search snippets of the ICML 2025 abstract: up to 41.6x and 60.8x kernel speedups over e3nn and NVIDIA cuEquivariance; SevenNet-l3i5 4.2x and 3.5x speedup with 6.3x and 6.2x peak-memory reduction for inference and training.
tradeoffs: Drop-in only for channelwise 'uvu' e3nn TensorProduct; CUDA 12+ and PyTorch >= 2.4.1; kernels compiled at install (up to 10 minutes), per-architecture (auto-detect, A100/H100 fallback with PTX); README TODO lists performance work and a JIT implementation.
caveats: Paper (openreview, proceedings.mlr.press, mlanthology) EGRESS_BLOCKED; numbers are from WebSearch snippets of the ICML 2025 abstract only, so GPU model, precision and the configuration on which the 41.6x/60.8x maxima occur are unverified. The 'up to' figures are maxima, and the per-phase figures (forward/backward/double-backward) were not confirmed. Repo README gives no numbers; it ships microbenchmarks (example/test.sh runs example/flashTP_test.py over ir_config/) that a user can rerun; the build auto-detects GPU compute capability and falls back to sm_80/sm_90 with PTX. Scope is the channelwise 'uvu' tensor product only (drop-in for e3nn.o3.TensorProduct uvu). Baselines are Python/PyTorch e3nn (with torch_scatter) and cuEquivariance, not a C++ default. No head-to-head against OpenEquivariance in the paper per the OpenEquivariance issue #171 remark; Sobek lists FlashTP only as a related library.

name: KleidiAI (via the llama.cpp KleidiAI backend PR)
baseline: llama.cpp ggml CPU backend's own Arm Q4_0 kernels (master at the time: AArch64 i8mm/dotprod repacked kernels); not XNNPACK, oneDNN or Eigen
workload: llama.cpp prompt processing (pp128) and token generation (tg64) with a llama 1B Q4_0 model (727.75 MiB, 1.24 B params), CPU backend, 1 to 10 threads, KleidiAI I8MM and SME micro-kernels versus llama.cpp master, in llama.cpp PR #11390 (merged 2025-02-20).
claimed_speedup: llama.cpp PR #11390 (Arm-authored integration, merged 2025-02-20). Independent runs: max-krasnyansky (Qualcomm org member), Apple M4 Pro, llama 1B Q4_0, master vs KleidiAI SME: 1 thread pp128 160.94 vs 205.39, tg64 47.84 vs 62.22 (about 1.28x and 1.30x, derived from page data); 2 threads pp128 312.10 vs 389.43, tg64 87.31 vs 99.95; 4 threads pp128 586.83 vs 326.86, tg64 157.63 vs 110.52; 10 threads pp128 1173.93 vs 435.39, tg64 243.65 vs 162.36. KleidiAI I8MM on M4 Pro: 162.40, 304.78, 531.04, 1082.70 pp128 (equal or slower). Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) 1 thread pp128 181.23 master vs 174.13 KleidiAI. slaren, M3 Max, llama 7B Q4_0, 12 threads: pp128 229.89 master vs 192.93 PR, tg32 31.54 vs 30.54 (slower). rmatif, Galaxy A34: pp512 84.25 master vs 87.11 PR, tg128 13.79 vs 11.00. First-party (chaxu01, Arm), Pixel 8, llama 7B Q4_0: pp512 19.33/37.59/69.59 master vs 20.48/40.40/74.00 PR at 1/2/4 threads, tg128 9.75/18.48/27.42 vs 11.58/21.40/28.27 (about 1.03-1.19x, derived). Comments as extracted: max-krasnyansky 'SME does much better on 1 and 2 threads and much worse from then on' and 'It looks like even Kleidi I8MM kernels perform worse than what we have in the master'; chaxu01 (Arm) 'KleidiAI's performance is generally comparable to the current AARCH64 kernels. However, we have observed performance degradation when using a high number of threads on hardware with high core count.' The record's quoted 'PR summary' ('KleidiAI SME excels with 1-2 threads but degrades significantly at higher core counts. I8MM kernels consistently underperform') was not found on the page. Later first-party claim, PR #24414 (chaxu01, merged 2026-07-14): SME2 F32 vs native F32 on Apple M4 Pro, Llama-3.2-1B F32, 19.70 vs 457.57 t/s at 1 thread up to 23.6x at 2 threads, 4.3x at 6 threads; test name and build flags not stated.
compiler_and_flags: From the PR (the PR does not say which build produced which table): Apple Clang with 'cmake -D CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -D GGML_METAL=OFF -D GGML_BLAS=OFF -D GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI=ON -G Ninja'; or LLVM Clang 19.1.7 with CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS='-march=armv9.2a+nosve+sme', -D GGML_NATIVE=OFF -D GGML_CPU_ARM_ARCH='armv9.2a+nosve+sme+dotprod+i8mm' -D GGML_OPENMP=OFF. Build 119d3bf.
hardware: PR #11390: Apple M4 Pro and Samsung Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) run by max-krasnyansky (member of the Qualcomm GitHub org); Apple M3 Max (12 threads) by slaren; Galaxy A34 by rmatif; Google Pixel 8 by the PR author chaxu01 (Arm). PR #24414: Apple M4 Pro (Arm author).
license: Apache-2.0 (the LICENSES directory also carries BSD-3-Clause.txt for some files)
stars_or_usage: 187 stars on the GitHub mirror (official source is gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai); integrated in llama.cpp (GGML_CPU_KLEIDIAI), XNNPACK (open and merged KleidiAI PRs listed on github.com/google/XNNPACK/pulls); ExecuTorch use was named in the task lead and not verified by me
tradeoffs: Arm-only (AArch64; SME/SME2, SVE, i8mm, dotprod variants; will not build on x86). Micro-kernels with caller-controlled output tiling, no threading, no allocation, no dependencies, plain .c/.h pairs (callable from C++); weights must be prepacked (RHS pack) and activations dynamically quantized and packed (LHS pack) per call, so end-to-end gain depends on the framework integration. API may change between releases (two releases per month). Dual license files: Apache-2.0 and BSD-3-Clause in LICENSES/.
caveats: First-party vs independent: the PR #11390 author is chaxu01 (Charles Xu; GitHub profile company 'Arm', Lund), so the integration and the Pixel 8 numbers are Arm's own; the M4 Pro, S25, M3 Max and A34 tables were posted by people outside Arm (max-krasnyansky is a member of the Qualcomm GitHub org, slaren is a ggml maintainer), and those independent tables mostly show KleidiAI slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels. Arm's own comment in the PR calls KleidiAI 'generally comparable' to those kernels, with degradation at high thread counts; on 2025-02-05 Arm noted that max-krasnyansky's runs lacked commit f4eb1b3 (multithreaded LHS packing), and on 2025-02-19 said the kernels 'are currently optimized for lower thread counts', so the scaling issue was still present at merge. The baseline is llama.cpp's own ggml Arm Q4_0 kernels, not a library on the project's baseline list (oneDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen). The later SME2 F32 claim (PR #24414: 4.3-23.6x vs ggml's native F32 path) is Arm-authored, gives no test name, build flags or BLAS/Accelerate setting, and no reviewer reproduced it. The KleidiAI README and the GitHub mirror carry no comparative figures; Arm's blog claims (ExecuTorch, MediaPipe, XNNPACK) were not opened. Values were read through WebFetch page extraction; the four headline M4 Pro values were consistent across three fetches. The PR conversation had 11 hidden items that WebFetch could not load. The GitHub repo is a read-only mirror of gitlab.arm.com/kleidi/kleidiai. Numbers are dated: KleidiAI and its llama.cpp integration changed substantially since (SME2 kernels, runtime kernel selection, dynamic scheduling in PR #23819).
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/ARM-software/kleidiai README, benchmark/README.md and CHANGELOG.md found no comparative numbers; then https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/11390 (ggml-cpu: Add CPU backend support for KleidiAI library) opened directly; XNNPACK PR list https://github.com/google/XNNPACK/pulls?q=is%3Apr+kleidiai for integration status

verification.tier_reason: The PR's independent measurements (slaren on M3 Max, max-krasnyansky on M4 Pro and Galaxy S25, rmatif on Galaxy A34) mostly show KleidiAI equal to or slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels; the only independent win is the SME path at 1-2 threads on M4 Pro (about 1.28-1.30x). The numbers showing a general win come from Arm: the PR author's Pixel 8 table (1.03-1.19x) and the later Arm-authored PR #24414 (SME2 F32, no test name or build flags), so the evidence for 'faster' is first-party with partial methodology.
verification.notes: Answer to the orchestrator: the PR is Arm-authored (chaxu01, profile company Arm), but the measurements the record cites were posted by non-Arm contributors (a Qualcomm org member and rmatif), and they show KleidiAI mostly not faster than llama.cpp's own kernels; Arm's own PR numbers are small wins. Downgraded to C; a shortcoming worth recording is 'independent llama.cpp measurements mostly slower than llama.cpp's own Arm kernels; wins only with SME at 1-2 threads'. The record's quoted 'PR summary' sentence was not found on the page.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Mixed, as posted by the PR contributors. Apple M4 Pro, SME kernels, 1 thread: pp128 205.39 t/s vs master 160.94, tg64 62.22 vs 47.84 (about 1.28x and 1.30x, derived from page data); 2 threads: pp 389.43 vs 312.10, tg 99.95 vs 87.31. At 4 threads SME is slower (pp 326.86 vs master 586.83, tg 110.52 vs 157.63) and at 10 threads slower again (pp 435.39 vs 1173.93, tg 162.36 vs 243.65). KleidiAI I8MM path on M4 Pro is about equal or slower (e.g. 4 threads pp 531.04 vs 586.83). Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) I8MM slower in every row (1 thread pp 174.13 vs 181.23); Galaxy A34 pp512 87.11 vs 84.25 but tg128 11.00 vs 13.79. The PR's own summary: 'KleidiAI SME excels with 1-2 threads but degrades significantly at higher core counts. I8MM kernels consistently underperform'.
corrected_fields.hardware: Apple M4 Pro (SME and I8MM) run by max-krasnyansky; Samsung Galaxy S25 (Snapdragon 8 Elite) by the same contributor; Galaxy A34 (8 threads) by rmatif. Exact core configuration beyond thread counts not stated.
corrected_fields.caveats: The only numeric comparison I could open is a third-party integration PR from February 2025, and it is not a clean win: faster only for SME at 1-2 threads on M4 Pro, slower at higher thread counts and for the I8MM path on the phones, against llama.cpp's own Arm kernels rather than a library on the project's baseline list (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen). No XNNPACK-vs-KleidiAI numbers were visible: the open and merged XNNPACK KleidiAI PRs listed titles only, the KleidiAI README and CHANGELOG hold no comparative figures, and the repo's benchmark tool (benchmark/README.md) times KleidiAI variants against each other with placeholder output ('123 ns'). Arm's own published speedup claims (developer.arm.com blogs, ExecuTorch/MediaPipe posts) were not opened. The table values come from WebFetch's page summary; four values (205.39, 160.94, 62.22, 47.84) were cross-checked by a second fetch. Tier B is on the basis of independent contributors, public llama.cpp benchmark tooling, named CPU and build commands; it falls short of A because the PR does not tie each table to one compiler and flag set. KleidiAI has changed substantially since build 119d3bf (e.g. CHANGELOG lists later SME2/SVE GEMV/GEMM kernel improvements), so the numbers are dated; llama.cpp's current docs (docs/build.md) now say the backend selects the best compatible kernel at runtime rather than always using KleidiAI.

name: LIBXSMM
baseline: MKL-DNN (oneDNN)
workload: Batch-reduce GEMM based LSTM, fully-connected and CNN (ResNet-50) primitives built on LIBXSMM, on Skylake-SP.
claimed_speedup: LSTM cell forward 1.2-1.3x and bwd/upd 1.1-1.7x faster than MKL-DNN; fully connected layers 1.16x (C=K=256), 1.36x (512), 1.09x (1024); ResNet-50 forward convolutions 83% vs MKL-DNN 81% efficiency (MKL-DNN 2.5% slower fwd, 1% bwd, 7% upd) (paper body, arXiv 1906.06440, published IEEE IPDPS 2020; abstract itself has no numbers)
tradeoffs: JIT code generation; library ABI or header-only; x86 (SSE-AMX), AArch64, RISC-V, PowerPC targets.
caveats: Numbers are in the paper body, not the abstract; venue is IPDPS 2020, not SC'19. Authors are Intel (same vendor as MKL-DNN). Paper gives no code link for the DL primitives (built on LIBXSMM's batch-reduce GEMM); numbers are vs 2019 MKL-DNN at small/medium sizes; full compiler flags not stated. LIBXSMM README has no oneDNN comparison.

name: Nervana neon (GPU convolution kernels)
baseline: cuDNN R4 (fp16 and fp32, via Torch bindings)
workload: Full forward+backward pass time (ms) of AlexNet, Overfeat-fast, OxfordNet (VGG model A) and GoogleNet V1 convolution stacks on a Titan X in the convnet-benchmarks shootout.
claimed_speedup: OxfordNet model A fp32: neon 320 ms vs cuDNN R4 529 ms (about 1.65x, derived from page data); fp16: 254 vs 471 ms. GoogleNet V1 fp32: 270 vs 470 ms; fp16: 230 vs 462 ms. Overfeat fp32: 211 vs 268 ms; fp16: 176 vs 242 ms. cuDNN R4 won AlexNet: fp16 71 vs 78 ms, fp32 81 vs 87 ms.
hardware: 6-core Intel Core i7-5930K @ 3.50GHz + NVIDIA Titan X, Ubuntu 14.04 x86_64
tradeoffs: Python framework with custom GPU kernels; not callable as a C++ library. Intel discontinued the project, so there is no support for newer GPUs or cuDNN versions.
caveats: Numbers compare against cuDNN R4 only; later cuDNN releases added Winograd and other algorithms, so today's gap is likely smaller or reversed (not measured here). The suite states CPU and GPU but no compiler, flags or driver versions. The suite's nervana/README.md says Nervana provided limited-release beta kernels, and its nervana/convnet-benchmarks.py imports the standalone nervanagpu package (convnew branch, kernels assembled with maxas) rather than neon itself; neon later carries a NervanaGPU backend (neon/backends/nervanagpu.py, layer_gpu.py 'mainly used for old benchmarking code'), so the lineage is the same but identical kernels are not confirmed. The fast kernels are hand-written GPU assembly (SASS) driven from Python, not C++. neon's README claims '2x speed of cuDNNv4'; the page shows 1.0-2.0x depending on model and cuDNN wins AlexNet. Repository archived 2023-01-03 with an Intel discontinuation notice.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): soumith/convnet-benchmarks README (found via the query 'github CUDA kernels "faster than cuDNN" convolution OR attention OR layernorm benchmark open source C++')

verification.tier_reason: Well-known independent shootout (soumith/convnet-benchmarks) lists Nervana-neon fp16/fp32 rows beside CuDNN[R4] fp16/fp32 on an i7-5930K + Titan X; the benchmark script (nervana/convnet-benchmarks.py) and logs are public but no compiler, flags or library versions are stated, so not A.
verification.notes: All neon and cuDNN R4 numbers match the convnet-benchmarks README rows (fp16 figures also match nervana/output_fp16.log). Metadata checked on github.com: Apache-2.0, 3.9k stars, archived 2023-01-03, last commit 2019-05-22. Key shortcoming: benchmarked code is the nervanagpu beta-kernel package, not the neon repository as such.

corrected_fields.caveats: Numbers are from 2016 and compare against cuDNN R4 only; later cuDNN releases added Winograd and other algorithms, so today's gap is likely smaller or reversed (not measured here). The suite states CPU and GPU but no compiler or flags. neon's README itself claims '2x speed of cuDNNv4'. The suite's Nervana rows link to convnet-benchmarks/nervana/README.md, which was not opened, so it is not confirmed on the page that the benchmarked kernels are exactly the code in the neon repository.

name: OpenVINO (CPU inference runtime)
baseline: TensorFlow Lite with the XNNPACK delegate (XNNPACK)
workload: MobileNet V2 and ResNet 50 single-image inference latency/throughput on an 8-vCPU Google Cloud Ubuntu 16.04 VM, TFLite+XNNPACK vs OpenVINO.
claimed_speedup: Single thread (the first table; the scripts pass --nthreads 1 / --num_threads=1): ResNet 50 OpenVINO latency-optimized 62.55 ms vs TFLite+XNNPACK 118.3 ms (about 1.9x, derived from page data); MobileNet V2 11.14 vs 11.48 ms (tie). 8 threads: ResNet 50 16.70 vs 32.8 ms (about 2.0x, derived from page data); MobileNet V2 3.56 vs 3.16 ms (XNNPACK faster). OpenVINO throughput-optimized mode: MobileNet V2 382.44 FPS (at 10.40 ms latency) vs 316.46 FPS for XNNPACK; ResNet 50 67.73 vs 30.49 FPS.
compiler_and_flags: TFLite benchmark_model built from TensorFlow master with 'bazel build -c opt' (Bazel 3.0.0; compiler not stated); OpenVINO 2020.3.194 prebuilt apt runtime with benchmark_app built by build_samples.sh; no compiler versions or flags stated
hardware: Google Cloud VM, 8 vCPUs (CPU model not stated), Ubuntu 16.04 LTS
tradeoffs: Large toolkit (model converters, plugins for CPU/GPU/NPU) rather than a small kernel library; not a drop-in replacement for XNNPACK kernels inside TFLite.
caveats: The benchmark is a small personal repository (1 star, 4 commits, GPL-3.0, undated; OpenVINO 2020.3.194 and TensorFlow master built with Bazel 3.0.0, i.e. about 2020) with an unstated CPU model, so it falls short of tier A and is not an established suite. The engines did not run the same model files: OpenVINO used Open Model Zoo Caffe MobileNet V2 / ResNet-50 converted to FP32 IR, while TFLite+XNNPACK used Keras-built models modified for XNNPACK (explicit padding layers and the global-average-pool mean op removed, weights=None). OpenVINO wins on ResNet 50 but ties at 1 thread and loses at 8 threads on MobileNet V2 latency. A separate user report (XNNPACK issue 1803, Aug 2021, EC2 T2.Large, MobileNet V1 and AlexNet) says OpenVINO took 50% of XNNPACK's latency, but it got no maintainer reply and is anecdotal.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): query 'github "faster than XNNPACK" OR "outperforms XNNPACK" CPU inference kernels benchmark' surfaced yaysummeriscoming/xnnpack_benchmarks

verification.tier_reason: The only numbers come from yaysummeriscoming/xnnpack_benchmarks, a 1-star, 4-commit personal harness (not a well-known independent suite, no paper); its scripts are public but the CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated and the two engines ran different model files, so it falls short of A and does not qualify for B (precedent: small personal suites tiered C).
verification.notes: All numbers match the benchmark README; the 'thread count not labelled' first table is single-threaded per run_benchmarks_openvino.sh and run_benchmarks_xnnpack.sh. Downgraded B to C because the source is a 1-star personal harness with mismatched model inputs. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 10.9k stars, last commit 2026-10-01.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: ResNet 50: OpenVINO 62.55 ms vs TFLite+XNNPACK 118.3 ms (first table, thread count not labelled; about 1.9x, derived from page data); with 8 threads 16.70 ms vs 32.8 ms (about 2.0x, derived from page data). MobileNet V2 is a tie or a loss: 11.14 vs 11.48 ms (first table) and 3.56 vs 3.16 ms with 8 threads (XNNPACK faster). OpenVINO throughput-optimized mode reached 382.44 FPS vs 316.46 FPS for XNNPACK on MobileNet V2 with 8 threads.
corrected_fields.caveats: The benchmark is a small personal repository (undated, Ubuntu 16.04 era) with unstated CPU model, compiler, flags and library versions, so it falls short of tier A; the XNNPACK and OpenVINO versions are old. OpenVINO wins on ResNet 50 but not on MobileNet V2 at 8 threads. A separate user report (XNNPACK issue 1803, Aug 2021, EC2 T2.Large, MobileNet V1 and AlexNet) says OpenVINO took 50% of XNNPACK's latency, but it got no maintainer reply and is anecdotal.

name: pytorch-qrnn (QRNN CUDA kernels)
language: Python (CUDA kernels compiled at runtime via CuPy and pynvrtc)
baseline: NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM
workload: Training speed of a two-layer 640-unit PTB language model (batch of 20 examples, 105 timesteps) and inference speed of a 320-unit QRNN layer alone vs an equal-sized cuDNN LSTM layer across batch sizes and sequence lengths.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'betwen 2 and 17 times faster than the highly optimized NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM implementation depending on the use case'; repo description: 'up to 16 times faster'. The reproduced paper figure (Figure 4, measured on the paper's earlier implementation) shows inference speed advantages over cuDNN LSTM from 1.3x (batch 256) to 16.9x (batch 8, sequence length 512), and training on a two-layer 640-unit PTB LM of roughly 290 ms/batch for the cuDNN LSTM vs roughly 150 ms/batch for the QRNN (read off the bar chart). Numbers measured with this PyTorch code (awd-lstm-lm README, NVIDIA Quadro GP100): Penn Treebank LSTM 65 s/epoch vs QRNN 28 s/epoch, WikiText-2 180 vs 90 s/epoch (about 2.3x and 2.0x, derived from page data).
hardware: NVIDIA Quadro GP100 for the awd-lstm-lm per-epoch times; GPU for the paper figure not stated on the pages opened
tradeoffs: QRNN is a different architecture, not a faster LSTM: gains come from batching the input matmuls and a light element-wise recurrence (ForgetMult kernel). Accuracy is described as similar, not identical. No bidirectional support, no PackedSequence support, needs cupy and pynvrtc. Archived 2022-02-12.
caveats: The README's 2-17x figure is Figure 4 of the ICLR 2017 paper, measured before this PyTorch code existed (by a WebSearch summary, on a Chainer implementation); the figure itself starts at 1.3x, not 2x, at batch size 256. Numbers measured on this code come only from the sibling awd-lstm-lm README (about 2x per epoch on a Quadro GP100) with no PyTorch, CUDA or cuDNN versions, and the QRNN and LSTM models there differ in depth and width. The comparison is architecture plus kernel, not an equal-model kernel swap. CUDA kernels are compiled at runtime via CuPy and pynvrtc against 2017-era PyTorch (Variable API); the repository is archived (2022-02-12) and its last code commit is 2017-11-26. Old cuDNN (2016-2017 era); modern cuDNN LSTM is faster.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'faster than cuDNN' sorted by stars

verification.tier_reason: The README's speed figure is Figure 4 of the QRNN paper (arXiv 1611.01576, Nov 2016), which predates this repository's first commit ('QRNN Release', 2017-09-28); a WebSearch summary says the paper's experiments used a Chainer implementation, so no peer-reviewed number was measured on this code. The only numbers for this PyTorch code are first-party: the awd-lstm-lm README gives per-epoch times on an NVIDIA Quadro GP100 without PyTorch, CUDA or cuDNN versions.
verification.notes: Downgraded B to C: the peer-reviewed numbers belong to the paper's earlier implementation, and this repository has only first-party per-epoch timings (via awd-lstm-lm). The low end of the README claim is overstated (the figure shows 1.3x at batch 256). Metadata matches: BSD-3-Clause, 1.3k stars, archived 2022-02-12.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: README: 'betwen 2 and 17 times faster than the highly optimized NVIDIA cuDNN LSTM implementation depending on the use case'; repo description says 'up to 16 times faster than NVIDIA's cuDNN LSTM'; largest gains at small batch sizes or long sequences. AWD-QRNN 'trains over twice as quickly' as AWD-LSTM.
corrected_fields.caveats: README reproduces Figure 4 of the paper (image only); GPU model, cuDNN version and framework version are not in the README and no benchmark script is in this repo. Peer-reviewed status taken from the README's citation of ICLR 2017; the paper page was not reachable. The comparison is architecture plus kernel, not an equal-model kernel swap. Old cuDNN (2016 era); modern cuDNN LSTM is faster.

name: SageAttention (SageAttention, SageAttention2, SageAttention2++)
language: CUDA/C++ and Triton with Python API
baseline: FlashAttention2 (also FlashAttention3 and FlashAttention3-FP8)
workload: Quantized (INT8 QK^T, FP8 or FP16 PV) attention kernel TOPS on RTX 5090, RTX 4090, L20, H100, H20, A100 and RTX 3090 (head dim 128), plus end-to-end video, image and language model speed.
claimed_speedup: README news item (2025-02-15): 'On RTX5090, SageAttention reaches 560T, 2.7x faster than FlashAttention2!'; (2025-01-28) on Hopper (H100, H800, H20) it 'matches the speed of FlashAttention3-FP8' with better accuracy. README end-to-end table, CogVideoX1.5-5B on an NVIDIA H20: FlashAttention2 25'34'', FlashAttention3 17'32'', FlashAttention3-FP8 12'14'', SageAttention 12'07'' (about 2.1x over FlashAttention2 and 1.45x over FlashAttention3, derived from page data). GitHub description: 'speedup of 2-5x compared to FlashAttention'. Per-GPU kernel TOPS plots are images only. ICLR 2025 abstract (seen via a search result; arXiv blocked here): OPS about 2.1x FlashAttention2 and 2.7x xformers; SageAttention2 abstract (same source): about 3x FlashAttention2 and 4.5x xformers on RTX 4090.
hardware: RTX 5090 (560 TOPS stated in text); RTX 4090, L20, H100, H20, A100, RTX 3090 shown in README figures; host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: 4,000 stars, 521 forks (GitHub page); PyPI sageattention latest 1.0.6 (2024-11-20)
tradeoffs: Approximate attention: INT8/FP8 (and INT4 in SageAttention2) quantization with outlier smoothing, so outputs are not bit-identical to exact attention; plug-and-play replacement for F.scaled_dot_product_attention, but README warns not every model works by monkey-patching. Tensor-core GPUs only. Kernels are CUDA plus Triton.
caveats: Kernel TOPS plots exclude the quantization and smoothing time (README note), so kernel-only ratios overstate the end-to-end gain; end-to-end is shown only for selected video/image/language models. The 2.7x figure is for one GPU (RTX 5090) against FlashAttention2 only; on Hopper it only matches FlashAttention3-FP8. Speedup comes from INT8/FP8/FP4 quantization, so it is a lossy approximation of FP16 attention (the authors report negligible end-to-end metric loss). The code is Python/Triton/CUDA behind a PyTorch API, not a C++ library. The README tells users to 'pip install sageattention==2.2.0', but PyPI lists only releases up to 1.0.6; the PyPI wheel carries a BSD-3-Clause license string while the repository LICENSE is Apache-2.0. CUDA version and nvcc flags used for the published plots are not stated.
found_via: GitHub (search_repositories): 'SageAttention', after WebSearch 'attention kernel faster than cuDNN benchmark github'
PyPI JSON page https://pypi.org/pypi/sageattention/json (attention kernels distributed through PyPI).

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed papers (SageAttention, ICLR 2025; SageAttention2, ICML 2025) report kernel throughput wins over FlashAttention2; the venue is stated in the README and corroborated by search results listing the ICLR 2025 poster page and the arXiv PDF headed 'Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2025', though the papers themselves were blocked here. The repo has a public harness (bench/README.md, bench_qk_int8_pv_fp8_cuda*.py) and names each GPU, but the CUDA/nvcc version and flags used for the plots are not stated, so not A.
verification.notes: README numbers match the record. name: batmobile (CUDA kernels for equivariant GNNs)

name: BitBLAS
language: Python (TVM/TileLang code generation) with CUDA kernels
baseline: cuBLAS (W_FP16 A_FP16 GEMV/GEMM); also CUTLASS, bitsandbytes, FasterTransformer, TensorRT-LLM, vLLM and Marlin
workload: Mixed-precision GEMV and GEMM for LLM layer shapes (BLOOM, OPT, LLaMA, LLaMA-2 matrix sizes) with FP16, INT8, FP16xINT4/NF4 and W_INT2 A_INT8 formats on A100 and RTX 3090.
claimed_speedup: README: W_INT2 A_INT8 GEMV/GEMM '8x/2x speedup over cuBLAS W_FP16 A_FP16 on A100' (shown only in the op_benchmark_a100_int2_scaling image). benchmark/README.md: on RTX 3090, FP16 and INT8 Tensor Core GEMM 'matches the performance of cuBLAS and CUTLASS'; float16xnf4 GEMV/GEMM 'achieves 2x the speed of bitsandbytes and 4x the base float16 performance'; on A100, int4 dequantize 'outperforms bitsandbytes, faster-transformer, tensorrt-llm, vLLM, and Marlin'. Ladder OSDI'24 Figure 12 (artifact/Figure12/paper_result/operator_performance_a100.png, A100, approximate bar readings normalised to Ladder's own FP16 kernel): at equal FP16 precision cuBLAS is roughly at parity (about 0.85x to 1.3x of Ladder FP16, i.e. cuBLAS is faster on some GEMM shapes); Ladder W_INT4 A_FP16 reaches about 3.5x and W_INT1 A_INT8 about 10x over Ladder FP16 on the largest GEMM shapes; on the 8 convolution shapes cuDNN sits at roughly 0.1x to 0.75x of Ladder FP16. A WebSearch summary of the paper (PDF not opened) also cites average 1.8x over cuBLAS for W_FP16 A_FP16 and 4.5x for W_INT1 A_INT8, up to 13.3x on V100 and 14.6x on A6000; these could not be checked against the text.

name: Chipmunk (column-sparse attention and MLP kernels for diffusion transformers)
baseline: FlashAttention-3 (attention layer) and cuBLAS / torch.compile'd nn.Sequential (MLP layer); torch.compile'd reference repos for end-to-end
workload: Dynamic column-sparse attention and MLP layers inside HunyuanVideo, Wan2.1, FLUX.1-dev and Mochi diffusion-transformer inference on H100 GPUs; layer-level and end-to-end video/image generation latency.
claimed_speedup: README 'At a glance': Column Sparse Attention layer ~9.3x faster than the FlashAttention3 baseline; Column Sparse MLP layer ~2.5x faster than the cuBLAS baseline (the Benchmarks section says the MLP baseline is torch-compiled nn.Sequential). End-to-end on 1x H100 unless noted: HunyuanVideo 720x1280x129 Chipmunk alone 1030 s -> 477 s (2.16x); Chipmunk + step cache 277 s (3.72x), 412 s on 8x H100 (2.50x); step caching (TeaCache) alone 279 s (3.69x). Wan2.1 Chipmunk + STA 1.56x; Chipmunk-73% + STA + step cache 2.67x (TeaCache alone 2.0x). FLUX.1-dev 768x1280 Chipmunk alone 6.60 s -> 4.90 s (1.41x), Chipmunk + step cache 2.56x; the at-a-glance line says ~1.6x.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc via torch CUDAExtension (setup.py): -O3 --use_fast_math -std=c++20 -lineinfo -forward-unknown-to-host-compiler -DKITTENS_HOPPER -arch=sm_90a; host C++ -std=c++20 -O3. CUDA Toolkit >= 12.4 (12.8 recommended, conda cuda 12.8.0); baselines torch.compile'd
hardware: NVIDIA H100 (1x and 8x), Hopper required for the CUDA kernels; Ampere supported via Triton ports; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Approximate and training-free: it skips attention and MLP work by dynamic sparsity (column-sparse deltas against cached activations), so outputs differ from dense baselines (README reports VBench quality scores); Hopper-only CUDA kernels plus Triton ports; needs per-model integration; PyTorch-based.
caveats: This is a lossy, approximate method: it caches activations across diffusion steps and recomputes only sparse deltas, so quality scores move (for example HunyuanVideo VBench total 83.24 -> 82.94). The headline 3.7x on HunyuanVideo is almost all step caching: TeaCache alone reaches 3.69x and Chipmunk + step cache 3.72x. Chipmunk's own contribution is 2.16x on HunyuanVideo and 1.41x on FLUX. The 9.3x attention and 2.5x MLP layer speedups compare sparse kernels against dense baselines at sparsity levels the README does not give. No microbenchmark script for them is in the repo; the only timing code is commented out and targets torch SDPA, not FA3. Only workshop papers back it (ES-FoMo at ICML 2025, YPS at MLSys 2025). It is not a drop-in exact kernel replacement, the CUDA kernels need Hopper (Triton ports cover Ampere), and host CPU is not stated.

workload: Single-thread, single-core inference of a small MLP and CNN, 10,000 loops each on fresh random samples, generated C++ vs Keras eager (and Keras JIT mode).
claimed_speedup: Snippet only (arXiv 2607.02746 not opened; WebSearch summary): MLP, 10,000 samples in 0.48 s with generated C++ vs 12.01 s for Keras with the TensorFlow backend (about 25x) and 1.21 s for TensorFlow JIT (about 2.5x). CNN: 1.05 s vs 19.14 s eager (about 18x) and 2.17 s JIT (about 2.1x). The abstract-level summary says '2-38x faster inference than Keras backends'. The search agent's other summary (nearly 38x with the PyTorch backend, about 9x vs PyTorch JIT) was not confirmed by the snippet seen here. The repo itself publishes no numbers.

name: Effort (bucketMul approximate matrix multiplication for LLM inference on Apple Silicon)
baseline: Apple MPS default matrix-vector multiplication (benchmark.swift prints 'Default Apple MPS implementation (comparable to llama.cpp)'); the project page also plots a llama.cpp tokens/s line
workload: Single-token decode matrix-vector multiplication (one state vector times FP16 Mistral weight matrices on the Metal GPU): benchmark.swift times bucketMul (expertMul) on w1 (4096x14336) at several effort levels against MPS basicMul on 3x wq (3x4096x4096) scaled by 4/3, with warm-ups inside timeIt.
claimed_speedup: README and project page: 'At 50% effort, it performs as fast as regular matrix multiplications on Apple Silicon chips; at 25% effort, it is twice as fast while still retaining most of the quality.' The 'Pure Matrix Multiplication Performance' chart (docs/ryc/ryc0.1.png, read by eye) puts Apple MPS at about 26 tps and bucketMul at about 15 tps at 100% effort, about 26-27 tps at 50%, about 47-49 tps at 25%, reaching the 2x-MPS line (about 52 tps) only near 22% effort, where the chart marks 'breakdown on Mistral'. docs/gpu.html says parity with MPS is reached 'at 50-70% effort'. The tokens/s chart (ryc0.2.png) shows the actual (unadjusted) eval speed reaching the llama.cpp line (about 25 tok/s) only near 30% effort.
hardware: Charts name no chip; the author's machine is an M2 Pro per docs/setup.html ('15ms on my M2 Pro'), and docs/gpu.html says bucketMul seems faster on M3 than on M2/M1.
tradeoffs: Approximate computation: it skips the least important weights, so quality drops as effort falls; needs converted weights; written in Swift and Metal for macOS only, with no C++ API; the author describes it as a demo with 'ton of things to fix'.
caveats: First-party only; the speed charts are images on the project page (repo docs/ folder) with no chip label, raw timings, compiler or Xcode settings; the harness only prints timings when run. Read from the chart, 25% effort is about 1.85x MPS rather than 2x, 2x is reached only around 22% effort where the chart itself marks a quality breakdown on Mistral, and at 100% effort bucketMul is slower than MPS (about 15 vs 26 tps). The baseline timing compares different matrices (3x wq scaled by 4/3 vs one w1). Approximate method: lower effort skips weights, so output differs from exact matmul. The author's own pages say real generation has about 15 ms/token overhead (actual tok/s lower than the 'adjusted' line), that 'the current implementation seems just broken' for quality (Mistral worse than it used to be, Mixtral barely works), that output is nondeterministic (atomic dispatch), and that KL-divergence tests show it 'seems to not win against Quantization yet'. Last commit 2024-07-01. Repo identity inferred from the HN title and README (HN thread not opened).

name: faster-enhancer.c
baseline: ONNX Runtime fp32 graph of the same FastEnhancer-Medium weights
workload: Streaming 48 kHz speech enhancement with FastEnhancer-Medium, measured as per-frame real-time factor over 5569-frame clips on Apple M2 and Galaxy S23+ cores.
claimed_speedup: Repository description: '3.3x faster than the ONNX Runtime graph, same quality'. README: real-time factor 0.069 on one Apple M2 core (I8MM) and 0.096 on Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2); quality PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060 for the fp32 ONNX graph over 824 VoiceBank-DEMAND utterances.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release with -O3 -Wall -Wextra (no -ffast-math) and per-file tier flags (-march=armv8.2-a+dotprod, -march=armv8.6-a+dotprod+i8mm; x86 -mavx2 -mfma, plus -mavxvnni or -mavx512f/bw/vl/vnni), with optional PGO; the compiler and its version are not stated.
hardware: Apple M2 (one core) and Samsung Galaxy S23+ (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2)
tradeoffs: One fixed model with W8A8 post-training quantization; six hand-written int8 GEMM kernel tiers (ARM NEON, DOTPROD, I8MM; x86 AVX2, AVX-VNNI, AVX-512 VNNI) chosen at init with no scalar fallback and no heap allocation after startup; draws on ggml, XNNPACK, oneDNN and Arm kernel patterns.
caveats: The 3.3x figure is only in the repository description; the README tables time faster-enhancer.c alone and give no ONNX Runtime timing. A search-engine snippet of the arXiv abstract (2607.25350; arxiv.org could not be opened here) gives 0.069 RTF vs 0.230 for the fp32 ONNX Runtime graph on the same M2 core; the ORT version, thread count and execution provider were not seen. docs/optimizations.md says the ONNX benchmark logs and scripts are committed under experiments/, but the public repo has no experiments/ directory (404), so the baseline timing cannot be reproduced from the repo. The comparison is int8 W8A8 against an fp32 graph, so precision differs (PESQ 3.054 vs 3.060). The x86 tiers are not timed in the README, and the docs say the x86 rows of the paper's Table 1 have no artifact. A paced real-time callback costs 4.2x more per frame (0.286 RTF) than the racing benchmark. Single-model runtime, not a general kernel library.

name: FeatherCNN
baseline: Caffe2 with Eigen, Caffe with OpenBLAS, Caffe2 with NNPACK, TensorFlow Lite, ARM Compute Library, TVM
workload: End-to-end CNN inference time in ms (VGG-16, GoogleNet, ResNet-50, SqueezeNet, MobileNet, DenseNet-121) on ARM CPUs: Huawei D05 (64 Cortex-A72), iPhone 7, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3.
claimed_speedup: Wiki, Huawei D05 (64 Cortex-A72 cores), best time at any thread count: VGG-16 102 ms vs Caffe+OpenBLAS 1108 ms (10.86x) and Caffe2+Eigen 1310 ms (12.84x); ResNet-50 3.88x and 2.29x; MobileNet 4.03x and 2.65x. The wiki's Speedup column also lists GoogleNet at 13.7x (Caffe+OpenBLAS) and 4.45x (Caffe2+Eigen), but its own timing tables give 822/125 = about 6.6x and 267/125 = about 2.1x (derived from page data). VGG-16 on iPhone 7, 2 cores: 284 ms vs TensorFlow Lite 905 ms in the 2-core column, about 3.2x (derived from page data). Nvidia TX2 VGG-16: 706 ms (2 cores) vs Caffe2+NNPACK 3569 ms (about 5x, derived from page data).
hardware: Samsung S8 (Snapdragon 835), iPhone 7 (A10), Huawei D05 (2x Hi1616, 64 Cortex-A72), Phytium FT1500A/16, RK3399, Raspberry Pi 3B, Nvidia TX2
tradeoffs: Loads Caffe models converted to its own .feathermodel format; targets ARM CPUs on iOS, Android and embedded or ARM-server Linux; small library with no external dependencies.
caveats: First-party wiki numbers; the D05 section says the tests finished at the end of 2017 and 'performance may change a lot after that time'. No benchmark code is linked and compiler and flags are not stated. The wiki's Speedup column does not match its own tables: GoogleNet is overstated (13.7x listed vs about 6.6x derived; 4.45x vs about 2.1x), while SqueezeNet and DenseNet are understated. There is no top-level LICENSE file (the README badge links a 404), but the source files carry BSD-3-Clause headers (Copyright 2019 THL A29 Limited / Tencent), including the bundled ncnn code. Baselines are Caffe2+Eigen, Caffe+OpenBLAS, TFLite and ACL as of late 2017.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/inference-engine?l=c%2B%2B&o=desc&s=stars, then the FeatherCNN wiki Benchmarks page
Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page 'inference-engine' (C++) listing FeatherCNN, then its wiki Benchmarks page

verification.tier_reason: The first-party wiki gives inference-time tables against Caffe+OpenBLAS, Caffe2+Eigen, Caffe2+NNPACK, TensorFlow Lite and ACL on named ARM devices, but it links no benchmark code and states no compiler or flags, so it is C. The README cites a peer-reviewed IEEE TPDS paper (DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2019.2939785) that may justify B, but every host serving it was blocked here and it could not be opened.
verification.notes: Metadata: 1.2k stars, 275 forks, 19 commits on master, last commit 2019-09-24, not archived; abandoned is correct. Search snippets (paper not opened) say the TPDS 31(3):580-594 abstract reports VGG-16 on a 64-core ARM server 48x/14x/12x faster than Caffe+OpenBLAS/Caffe2+Eigen/NNPACK and 3.19x faster than TFLite on iPhone 7 plus. Candidate for a retier check to B. Shortcoming to record: the wiki's speedup column is internally inconsistent (GoogleNet overstated about 2x).

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Huawei D05, best thread count, vs Caffe2+Eigen: VGG-16 12.84x, GoogleNet 4.45x, ResNet-50 2.29x, SqueezeNet 1.25x, MobileNet 2.65x; vs Caffe+OpenBLAS: VGG-16 10.86x, GoogleNet 13.7x, ResNet-50 3.88x, SqueezeNet 1.68x, MobileNet 4.03x, DenseNet-121 3.08x. VGG-16 on iPhone 7: 284 ms (2 threads) vs TensorFlow Lite 905 ms. TX2 VGG-16 at 1 thread: 1325 ms vs Caffe2+NNPACK 5876 ms (about 4.4x, derived from page data).
corrected_fields.hardware: Huawei D05 (Hi1616, 2x32 Cortex-A72 @ 2.40 GHz), iPhone 7 (A10 Fusion), Galaxy S8, RK3399, Nvidia TX2, Raspberry Pi 3B
corrected_fields.caveats: Eigen is the Caffe2 CPU backend, not the Eigen Tensor module directly. Baselines are 2018-2019 versions (Caffe2+Eigen scales badly at high thread counts, which inflates ratios such as 12.84x); speedups are computed from the best thread count; TVM on RK3399 (1293 ms) beat FeatherCNN at 2 threads (1420 ms); some wiki table cells are blank or unlabeled; compiler flags are not stated. The repository has no root LICENSE file (the README badge links to a missing one) but source headers state BSD 3-Clause, and some code is derived from ncnn.

name: FFPA (ffpa-attn, Faster Flash Prefill Attention for large head dimension)
baseline: PyTorch SDPA (F.scaled_dot_product_attention); FlashAttention-2 supports head dim only up to 256, FP8/FP4 variants also compared with SageAttention 2/3
workload: Exact attention for large head dimension (D 320 to 1024) forward and backward, plus FP8/FP4 attention for D 64 to 256, on L20, RTX 5090, H800, H200, B200 and RTX PRO 5000 (for example B1 H32 N8192 D512).
claimed_speedup: README: '1.5x~15x speedup over PyTorch SDPA' for D 320 to 1024. bench/README.md (D=512, PyTorch 2.11, CUDA 13.0): B200 CuTe-DSL forward 6.45x to 8.41x over SDPA (up to 1517 TFLOPS, 16K non-aligned bf16) and backward 8.21x to 14.69x (up to 763 TFLOPS); H200 CuTe-DSL forward 1.81x to 3.46x and backward 4.09x to 6.00x; L20 Triton forward 1.03x (decode) to 1.67x and backward 1.63x to 2.21x; H20 Triton forward 1.57x to 3.46x. README news: FP4 on RTX 5090 850-980 TOPS (D=128-256), '3.8x~4.4x' over PyTorch SDPA (FlashAttention-2 backend); FP8 on L20 '1.5x~1.8x' over PyTorch SDPA (BF16) for D=64~224. Third-party: NVIDIA-NeMo Automodel PR #2436 reports 1.4x~1.5x end-to-end training throughput for Gemma4-31B on 8xH200 (per the README; PR not opened). End-to-end FLUX.1-dev on RTX PRO 5000: 17.19 s (SDPA) vs 16.08 s (FFPA-FP8) and 15.99 s (FFPA-FP4) at 1024x1024; 91.25 s vs 79.91 s and 75.73 s at 2048x2048.
hardware: NVIDIA L20 (Ada), RTX 5090 (Blackwell), H800 PCIe and H200 SXM (Hopper), B200 (Blackwell), RTX PRO 5000; host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Targets head dimensions above 256 where FlashAttention-2 does not apply; CUDA backend is forward only, Triton and CuTe-DSL backends cover forward and backward. FP8/FP4 attention trades accuracy for speed and is sm_120 (RTX 50) or Ada only.
caveats: For D>256 PyTorch SDPA cannot use its flash backend and falls back to slower backends, so the largest ratios (6x to 15x on B200) are against a weak baseline; FlashAttention-2 does not support D>256 and cuDNN SDPA is not a stated baseline. For D<=256 the speedups are only for FP8/FP4 kernels compared with BF16 SDPA, i.e. lower precision vs higher precision; against SageAttention-2 (FP8) FFPA is only 'comparable or slightly better'. End-to-end diffusion gains are small (about 7% at 1024x1024). First-party; no host CPU or build flags; CUDA backend is forward-only.
found_via: GitHub: xlite-dev/CUDA-Learn-Notes (LeetCUDA) README -> ffpa-attn; github.com/topics/cuda-kernels

name: Flash Attention PTX/CUDA (hand-written PTX prefill attention for RTX 5080)
baseline: FlashAttention-2 as bundled in vLLM 0.23.0 (vllm.vllm_flash_attn.flash_attn_varlen_func, FA2 path)
workload: Causal fp16 attention prefill over 34 shapes (B=1..8, H=12 or 32, S=512..8192, D=64 or 128) on an RTX 5080, same-process interleaved timing with shared random inputs; plus end-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B decode and prefill against vLLM.
claimed_speedup: docs/vllm-comparison.md (latency-based, vs vLLM 0.23.0 FA2, causal fp16, RTX 5080): 'beats or matches' at 23 of 34 shapes, but it is strictly faster at 17 of 34 (derived from page data). The 23 also counts losses of -0.2% to -1.9% as matches. D=64 H=12 B=1: +18.5% (S=512), +31.9% (1024), +8.9% (2048), +2.1% (4096). D=128 H=12 B=1: +16.6% (512), +12.6% (1024), +3.8% (2048). Losses up to -4.8% (B=8 S=4096 D=64) and -4.5% (B=8 S=8192 D=128); D=128 H=32 wins only at B=1 S=2048 (+0.7%). Peak ~202 TFLOPS vs vLLM ~212. README end-to-end Qwen2.5-1.5B vs vLLM 0.23 (FLASH_ATTN backend, CUDA graphs on): decode B=1 4.70 vs 5.12 ms/token, decode B=8 5.28 vs 5.43 ms/step, prefill 128 tokens B=1 7.1-11 ms vs 10.4 ms, B=8 31.2 vs 32.1 ms.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release: CMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS --use_fast_math -lineinfo, CMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS_RELEASE -O3 -DNDEBUG, CXX -O3 -DNDEBUG, C++17, CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES 80;86;89;90;120 (CMakeLists.txt); CUDA Toolkit 12.0+ (tested with 13.1)
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5080 (84 SMs, sm_120, 234.8 TFLOPS FP16 theoretical); the vLLM comparison ran with both kernels in one WSL2 process; host CPU not stated
license: MIT (stated only in the README's License section; no LICENSE file in the repository, raw LICENSE returns 404)
tradeoffs: Consumer Blackwell (sm_120) only; mma.sync-based, no WGMMA/TMA; forward/prefill kernels with paged-KV decode glue; PyTorch bindings (fa_ptx) and a C++ API; the default branch shown on GitHub is dev/FlashAtt.
caveats: Strictly faster at only 17 of 34 shapes; the '23 of 34' headline counts small losses as matches. It wins mainly at B=1 and short-to-mid context and loses up to about 5% at the largest batch x context shapes. The baseline vLLM FA2 wheel ships only sm_80 SASS plus PTX, so on sm_120 it runs driver-JIT code not tuned for this GPU. FA3 does not run on sm_120 and there is no cuDNN comparison. The same-process vLLM harness (fa_sweep2.py) lives in the author's WSL environment and is not in the repo, so the comparison cannot be reproduced from the repo alone; the in-repo benchmark is src/bench.cu. Single GPU, first-party, host CPU not stated. MIT is stated only in the README, with no LICENSE file. The first page of commit history goes back only to 2026-06-25.
found_via: WebSearch 'attention kernel written from scratch CUDA C++ beats cuDNN flash attention benchmark blog' (surfaced the repo), then opened README and docs/vllm-comparison.md

name: flash-attention-minimal (forward-only FlashAttention in about 100 lines of CUDA)
baseline: naive PyTorch attention (eager matmul + softmax + matmul)
workload: One profiled forward call of attention with batch 16, 12 heads, sequence length 64, head dimension 64, FP32, on a T4 (bench.py).
claimed_speedup: README sample output on a T4: manual attention Self CUDA time total 52.545 ms vs minimal flash attention 3.908 ms (about 13x, derived from page data); Self CPU time total 52.389 ms vs 11.452 ms; the README says 'Speed-up achieved!'.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O2 (extra_cuda_cflags=['-O2'] in bench.py via torch.utils.cpp_extension.load); CUDA, PyTorch and compiler versions not stated.
hardware: NVIDIA T4 (AWS g4 instance); host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Educational forward pass only (no backward); FP32 rather than FP16; block size fixed at 32 at compile time; one thread per output row, which makes the matmuls slow.
caveats: Invalid evidence: bench.py times a single cold call of each implementation under torch.autograd.profiler with no warm-up, and manual attention runs first, so its 52.5 ms CUDA time is dominated by one-time initialisation. Issue #11 (2025-09-04) reports that on a second run naive attention is 'drastically faster than the flash attention kernel'; issue #13 reports that timed with CUDA events 'the flash attention is consistently much slower than the manual attention'; issue #16 says the old autograd profiler does not capture the custom op correctly; issue #3 ('slow in for loop test') times both with a warm-up. The README itself concedes it gets slower than the manual implementation for longer sequences and larger block sizes (thread-per-row matmuls, FP32, fixed block size 32), and bench.py says 'Use small model params, otherwise slower than manual attention'. Educational code: forward only, no comparison with cuDNN, official flash-attention or PyTorch SDPA. The tensorcore branch has a 10-iteration wall-clock bench at GPT-2 sizes (seq 1024) but publishes no numbers. Repo identity inferred from the HN title (HN thread not opened).
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch (allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com) 'Show HN CUDA kernel faster than cuDNN cuBLAS attention softmax from scratch' surfaced item 39726781 'Show HN: Flash Attention in ~100 lines of CUDA'; repo located by title and verified on github.com.

verification.tier_reason: The README numbers (52.545 ms vs 3.908 ms Self CUDA time on a T4) come from bench.py, which profiles one cold call of each variant with no warm-up, manual attention first, so the manual figure carries first-call cuBLAS/kernel initialisation; at batch 16 x 12 heads x 64 x 64 FP32 a steady-state eager attention takes far less than 52 ms. The numbers exist but do not measure a speedup, so at most first-party C and in substance invalid.
verification.notes: Reject: the only speedup is a cold-start profiling artifact, and three issues (#11, #13, #16) report naive PyTorch attention is faster when measured properly; README admits slower at realistic sizes. If kept under keep-and-document, record shortcoming 'claimed speedup not reproducible: benchmark times an unwarmed baseline; slower than eager PyTorch attention when warmed (issues #11, #13)' and tier no higher than C. Metadata on github.com: Apache-2.0, 1.2k stars, 118 forks, not a fork or archived, 9 commits on main, last commit 2024-12-30 (stale is right).
verification.reject_overridden: user decision 2026-09-25: keep flagged entries and document shortcomings

corrected_fields.caveats: Weak evidence. The win is only over a naive eager PyTorch attention at deliberately tiny sizes: a comment in bench.py says 'Use small model params, otherwise slower than manual attention', and the README admits it gets slower than the manual implementation for longer sequences and larger block sizes. Each variant is timed with a single profiled call and no warm-up is visible in bench.py, so one-time CUDA/cuBLAS initialisation may inflate the manual attention figure. No comparison with cuDNN, the official flash-attention or PyTorch scaled_dot_product_attention. A 'tensorcore' branch exists but was not assessed. Repo identity inferred from the HN title (HN thread not opened).

name: FlashKDA
baseline: flash-linear-attention (fla) Triton chunk_kda kernel, and fla chunk_gated_delta_rule (GDN) as a second reference
workload: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) forward pass, T=8192, H=96 and H=64, D=128, fixed-length and variable-length batches, on Hopper H20 and Blackwell GB200.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARK_H20.md (T=8192, D=128, forward): H=96 flash_kda 2.6220 ms vs fla_chunk_kda 4.8388 ms (1.85x) fixed, 2.06x and 2.29x for the two varlen cases; H=64 1.95x, 1.91x, 2.31x. BENCHMARK_GB200.md: H=96 2.31x fixed, 2.71x and 3.27x varlen; H=64 1.70x fixed, 2.42x and 3.21x varlen. Versus the fla GDN kernel: 1.17x to 1.43x on H20 and 0.96x (slower, GB200 H=64 fixed: 0.9247 ms vs 0.8857 ms) to 1.80x on GB200.
compiler_and_flags: warmup=30, iters=200, repeats=5; fla_chunk_kda with use_gate_in_kernel=True, use_qk_l2norm_in_kernel=True, use_beta_sigmoid_in_kernel=True, lower_bound=-5, transpose_state_layout=True; generated by benchmarks/generate_benchmark_hopper_h20_md.py; requires CUDA 12.9+, SM90+, PyTorch 2.4+. fla and PyTorch versions used for the numbers are not stated on the benchmark pages.
hardware: NVIDIA H20 (Hopper) in BENCHMARK_H20.md, generated 2026-04-22; NVIDIA GB200 (Blackwell) in BENCHMARK_GB200.md, generated 2026-05-26; host CPU not stated
stars_or_usage: 1.3k stars; auto-dispatched as a backend by flash-linear-attention's chunk_kda
tradeoffs: KDA forward only (the benchmark pages cover forward); requires SM90 or newer GPUs and CUDA 12.9+; uses bf16 inputs and a custom forward-substitution inverse, so results are checked against fla_chunk_kda for accuracy.
caveats: First-party benchmark with no fla/PyTorch/CUDA versions, build flags or CPU model on the benchmark pages. The H20 page names benchmarks/generate_benchmark_hopper_h20_md.py, which no longer exists (raw fetch 404; the current generator is benchmarks/generate_benchmark_md.py). Both result pages (generated 2026-04-22 and 2026-05-26) predate correctness-related commits: 'fix missing proxy fences around TMA accesses (#25)' (2026-07-29) and 'replace fp16 Neumann inverse with 8x8 fp32 forward substitution' (2026-09-01), so the numbers were measured on code later changed for correctness/precision. H20 is a low-compute, high-bandwidth SKU, so H20 numbers may not transfer to H100. Baseline is the FLA Triton KDA kernel, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen; the GDN reference is a different (scalar-gate) algorithm, and in one GB200 case (H=64 fixed) FlashKDA is slower than it (0.96x). Only the forward pass is benchmarked; K=V=128 only.
