name: FlashQLA
baseline: FLA Triton kernels (flash-linear-attention chunk_gated_delta_rule) and FlashInfer GDN prefill kernel
workload: Gated DeltaNet (GDN) chunked-prefill forward and backward kernels at Qwen3.5/Qwen3.6 head configurations (TP1 to TP8, d=128), single-sequence and varlen batches up to 32768 tokens, CUDA-graph timing on H200 and GB200.
claimed_speedup: README: '2-3x forward speedup and 2x backward speedup over the FLA Triton kernel'. benchmark_results_H200.txt, forward, 397B/122B TP8, 1x32768: FlashQLA 0.348 ms vs FLA 1.019 ms (2.93x) vs FlashInfer 1.645 ms (4.73x); 1x4096: 1.19x vs FLA; TP4 4096x8: 3.18x vs FLA but 0.64x vs FlashInfer. H200 across 171 forward rows: 1.18x to 3.32x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.07x, derived from page data), FlashInfer faster in 56 rows (as low as 0.62x); 32 backward rows: 1.38x to 5.47x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.56x, derived from page data). benchmark_results_GB200.txt (torch 2.11.0, fla 0.5.1, flashinfer 0.6.12, tilelang 0.1.12): 171 forward rows 1.07x to 3.58x vs FLA (geometric mean 2.17x, derived from page data), FlashInfer faster in 85 rows (as low as 0.48x; geometric mean vs FlashInfer 1.07x, derived from page data); 32 backward rows 1.94x to 6.44x vs FLA (geometric mean 3.24x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: H200 file: torch 2.8.0+cu128, fla 0.5.1, flashinfer 0.6.13, tilelang 0.1.12; GB200 file: torch 2.11.0, fla 0.5.1, flashinfer 0.6.12, tilelang 0.1.12; both Warmup=10, Repeats=100, Backend=cudagraph (README text names FLA 0.5.0, Triton 3.5.1, FlashInfer 0.6.9, TileLang 0.1.8). No compiler flags stated.
hardware: NVIDIA H200 (benchmark_results_H200.txt) and NVIDIA GB200 (benchmark_results_GB200.txt); host CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Specific to Gated DeltaNet chunked prefill (Qwen3.5/3.6 linear-attention layers), not general attention. Needs Hopper or Blackwell GPUs (SM120 forward only) and the TileLang toolchain. Uses an algebraic reformulation of the GDN forward/backward flow that the authors say keeps numerical precision.
caveats: First-party benchmark; host CPU and compiler flags not stated (benchmark script benchmark/bench_gated_delta_rule.py and the result files are public). Baselines are the FLA Triton and FlashInfer GDN kernels, not oneDNN/cuDNN/XNNPACK/Eigen. Speedup is shape dependent: on H200 FlashInfer is faster than FlashQLA in 56 of 171 forward rows (as low as 0.62x) and on GB200 in 85 of 171 (as low as 0.48x), mostly small-batch varlen rows, so against FlashInfer FlashQLA is roughly at parity on GB200 forward. Backward is compared only with FLA (FlashInfer has no backward in the table). The README's quoted library versions differ from those printed in the result files. Result files were updated on 2026-09-30.

name: Kaoken (baked-weight C code generation for CPU transformer inference)
baseline: PyTorch CPU layers (transformers GPT-2 building blocks)
workload: Per-layer CPU timings of GPT-2 blocks at batch 1 (LayerNorm [1,768], GELU [1,768], Linear [768,50257], Attention [1,768]), average of five runs, no GPU.
claimed_speedup: PyTorch vs Kaoken in ms: LayerNorm 0.052 vs 0.0052; GELU 0.174 vs 0.084; Linear 22.4 vs 2.378; Attention 14.484 vs 9.386 (about 10x, 2.1x, 9.4x and 1.5x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: clang -arch arm64 -O3 (generated/Makefile; NEON intrinsics in the generated code). The README does not say which build or machine produced the benchmark numbers.
tradeoffs: Weights are baked into generated source and matmuls are unrolled into straight-line code, so each model needs its own generated, very large C file; only GPT-2 layers implemented; CPU only; Python tooling required to generate.
caveats: CPU model, PyTorch version and thread count are not stated (generated/Makefile targets arm64 with clang -O3 and the README mentions a MacBook Air, so Apple Silicon is implied but not stated). Methodology is weak: validation/linear.py and validation/layer_normalization.py time a single cold first call of the PyTorch layer with time.time() (no warm-up), the generated C main() times one call with clock(), and 'average of five runs' means five such runs, so PyTorch's first-call overhead likely inflates the gap, especially for LayerNorm and GELU at [1,768]. The weights are synthetic patterns from the validation scripts (e.g. every Linear row is 0.1*(i+1)), not GPT-2 weights, and they are baked into the C source as constants. The README says baked layers with real GPT-2 weights could not be compiled on a MacBook Air, the MLP row has no Kaoken number, end-to-end model.generate() benchmarks were never done, and the headline still reads 'by X%'. About one month of commit history (Oct-Nov 2024, 17 commits); first-party.

name: Marlin (FP16xINT4 LLM matmul kernel)
baseline: FP16 PyTorch matmul (calls CUTLASS) and other 4-bit kernels: torch-nightly, exllamav2, AWQ, bitsandbytes
workload: 16-bit x 4-bit (group size 128) matrix multiplication on a 72k x 18k weight matrix on an NVIDIA A10 across batch sizes 1-128, plus the linear layers of Llama and Falcon models at batch size 16 on A10, 3090, A6000 and A100.
claimed_speedup: Approximate plot readings (derived from page data). Peak plot (A10, 72k x 18k matrix, group size 128): Marlin about 3.87x to 3.9x over FP16 PyTorch at batch 1 to 16, 3.8x at 32, 3.1x at 64 and 1.55x at 128, tracking the 'Ideal' line; at batch 16, torch-nightly about 1.4x, exllamav2 about 0.7x, AWQ about 0.3x, bitsandbytes about 0.4x. Model layers at batch 16: about 3.4x to 4.25x on A10, 3090 and A6000, and 2.2x to 3.65x on A100. Sustained plot (A10 at locked base clock): about 3.9x to batch 16, 3.3x at 32, 1.7x at 64 and 1.0x at 128. README text: 'close to ideal (4x)' up to batch 16-32, with a maximum of 3.87x after the group-scale overhead.
hardware: NVIDIA A10 with ECC disabled (peak and sustained plots); A10, RTX 3090, A6000 and A100 (model layers); host CPU not stated; CUDA >= 11.8, torch >= 2.0
tradeoffs: Weight-only FP16xINT4 inference kernel for Ampere/Ada GPUs (compute capability >= 8.0); the README says it is not yet optimised for Hopper; needs quantised, reshuffled weights; PyTorch extension.

name: metal-flash-attention
baseline: Dao-AILab FlashAttention-2 (A100) and FlashAttention-3 (H100), compared by utilization percentage, not wall time
workload: Single-headed attention forward, backward dQ and backward dK/dV kernels in FP16 on Apple GPUs (M1 Max, M4, M3 architecture) at head dimensions D = 64, 128, 256, measured as gigainstructions per second and ALU utilization against a hardware roofline.
claimed_speedup: No wall-clock ratio against any other library. README: a consistent 4400 gigainstructions per second on M1 Max (83% ALU utilization) at infinite sequence length and head dimension with BF16 emulation. Forward utilization on M1 architecture 86% (D=64), 85% (D=128), 86% (D=256); forward + backward 62%, 63%, 64%. M3 architecture forward 94%, 91%, 82%; forward + backward 71%, 69%, 61%. Quoted comparison tables: A100 Flash2 FP16 forward + backward 56% (D=64), 65% (D=128), 0% (D=256, no result reported); H100 Flash3 FP16 forward + backward 48%, 59%, 0%. README claims 'Apple hardware is training transformers faster than Nvidia hardware doing the same work' after normalizing for GPU size and utilization.
compiler_and_flags: swift build/test with -Xswiftc -Ounchecked (README); Metal kernels are JIT compiled at runtime.
hardware: Apple M1 Max (roofline 10616 GFLOPS, 5308 gigainstructions/s), M4 (3580 GFLOPS); NVIDIA A100 SXM and H100 SXM figures are taken from the FlashAttention papers, not re-measured.
stars_or_usage: 612 stars; a Draw Things blog post and the derived mps-flash-attention project build on it
tradeoffs: Single-headed attention only (no multi-head, masks or block sparsity yet). Backward pass avoids FP32 atomics by using 7 GEMMs instead of 5 (9D+15 versus 7D+10 work per N^2), which uses less memory than the official backward pass but more compute. Intentional register spilling with a third blocking dimension along D for large head dimensions. Needs Apple silicon and Swift/Metal; JIT compiles shaders at runtime. Not a drop-in C++ or Python library.
caveats: The only comparison is ALU utilization against FlashAttention-2 (A100) and FlashAttention-3 (H100) on different hardware, using the author's own gigainstruction metric; the NVIDIA side is the highest GFLOPS from each paper graph divided by 312000 (A100 SXM) or 989000 (H100 SXM), and D=256 backward entries are 0% because no result was reported. It is not a speed comparison and cannot show Apple hardware is faster in wall time; the README's 'faster than Nvidia hardware' sentence is normalized for GPU size. MFA's backward pass issues more work (7 GEMMs instead of 5), which the utilization figures partly account for via a 7/9 factor. The listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) and MLX/MPS/PyTorch MPS attention are not compared in the README. The derived project imperatormk/mps-flash-attention claims 1.1-4x over PyTorch SDPA on Apple Silicon; that is not evidence for this repo. name: OpenEquivariance
language: Python/C++ (JIT-generated CUDA, HIP and SYCL kernels)
baseline: e3nn (torch.compile max-autotune with CUDA graphs in the harness); also compared with NVIDIA cuEquivariance and FlashTP
workload: Clebsch-Gordan tensor products and fused equivariant graph convolutions for MACE, NequIP, DiffDock and e3nn tetris-poly problems, forward and backward, float32 and float64, run by tests/benchmark.py (uvu, uvw, roofline and conv suites; 100 warmup and 100 timed iterations, PRNG seed 11111).
claimed_speedup: README: 'We provide up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn' and performance 'on par with the latest version of NVIDIA cuEquivariance'; docs/index.rst: 'up to an order of magnitude speedup over e3nn and competitive performance with NVIDIA's cuEquivariance'. Docs (tests_and_benchmarks.rst) and CHANGELOG v0.4.0: 'up to 2x speedup over FlashTP's fused kernels'. Paper abstract (SIAM ACDA25, arXiv 2501.13986; WebSearch snippet only, paper not opened): fused kernels give up to 4.5x forward and 3x (another snippet says 3.5x) backward speedup over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn, and up to 5.3x (another snippet: 5.4x) MACE inference speedup over the original unoptimized version. One snippet also gives 5.3x over e3nn and 1.5x over cuEquivariance in FP32, and 6.6x and 1.43x in FP64. The snippet figures disagree between paper versions and need checking against the PDF.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (kernels are JIT-compiled at runtime; README asks for PyTorch and GCC 9+).
hardware: Paper benchmarks: NVIDIA A100-SXM-80GB at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst). The docs also list example invocations for an NVIDIA A5000 and note that the roofline slope and peak are only correct on an A100.
stars_or_usage: 170 stars, 17 forks (github.com page, 2026-10-03); pip package 'openequivariance'; works with MACE and NequIP
tradeoffs: Supports most 'uvu' and 'uvw' e3nn tensor products, not all of e3nn. Results equal e3nn up to rounding for many configurations; for 'uvw' connection modes the weights must be reordered (reorder_weights_from_e3nn/to_e3nn). Fused convolution has an atomics mode that is non-deterministic and a deterministic mode needing receiver-sorted indices plus a transpose permutation. JIT compile at first use; needs a CUDA, HIP or SYCL (beta) toolchain; PyTorch and JAX frontends.
caveats: The headline figures are first-party README statements with no per-problem numbers on the pages I could open, so tier C is a floor. The paper (SIAM ACDA25) is peer reviewed and the benchmark code is public with A100-SXM-80GB stated and exact reproduction commands in docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst, so a verifier with paper access may justify tier B, or A if the paper states compiler and flags. The README sentence is garbled ('up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn perform on par with...'), which is quoted as is. The harness removes e3nn's torch-compile variant for float64 'benzene' because it runs out of memory, and for 'limited-memory' GPUs drops expensive tests. The 2x claim over FlashTP is against FlashTP's fused kernels only. Opened: README, LICENSE, CHANGELOG.md, docs/tests_and_benchmarks.rst and tests/benchmark.py via raw.githubusercontent.com, plus the repo tree and commit pages on github.com. [retier] Paper not opened (arXiv, author site, SIAM, researchgate and alphaxiv all blocked from this container); every paper figure is from WebSearch snippets only, and the snippets disagree across paper versions: earlier snippets give up to 4.5x forward and 3x or 3.5x backward over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn and 5.3x or 5.4x MACE inference speedup, while a 2026-10-03 snippet gives up to 1.3x over cuEquivariance, >10x over e3nn and up to 6.2x MACE inference speedup. The README itself claims only 'up to an order of magnitude acceleration over e3nn' and performance 'on par with' cuEquivariance, which is consistent with the smaller cuEquivariance figure. The harness is public (tests/benchmark.py; the e3nn baseline is the torch.compile max-autotune plus CUDA-graphs variant, with an uncompiled variant also available), but the bench extra in openequivariance/pyproject.toml leaves e3nn, cuequivariance, cuequivariance-torch and cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12 unpinned, so a rerun compares against whatever versions are current, and no result tables are committed. Docs also claim up to 2x over FlashTP's fused kernels (first-party, no numbers in the repo); the FlashTP README does not mention OpenEquivariance.

name: PowerInfer
baseline: llama.cpp
workload: Single-request LLM generation on one RTX 4090 (24 GB) with FP16 ReLU models (Falcon(ReLU)-40B, Llama(ReLU)-2-70B; the paper abstract also covers OPT-175B) at input length 64, plus an RTX 2080Ti (11 GB) run with INT4 ReLU models at input length 8. Speed is reported as end-to-end tokens/s (prompt + generation time divided by tokens generated).
claimed_speedup: Outperforms llama.cpp by up to 11.69x on an RTX 4090 (README: up to 11x on Falcon 40B, up to 3x on Llama 2 70B); on an RTX 2080Ti with INT4 models up to 8x on Falcon 40B and 3x on Llama 2 70B. Average 13.20 tokens/s and peak 29.08 tokens/s on the RTX 4090, 18% below an A100.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24 GB) and RTX 2080Ti (11 GB); CPU model not given in the README
tradeoffs: GPU-CPU hybrid engine that exploits activation sparsity, so it needs ReLU-style sparse model variants (ReLU-fied Falcon and Llama 2, Bamboo, TurboSparse); dense models get no speedup; built on llama.cpp/ggml code and model format; x86-64 with AVX2.
caveats: The speedup depends on ReLU-sparsified models (ReLU/ReGLU/Squared-ReLU only). The README says standard llama.cpp weights run with no performance gain, and its FAQ admits the ReLU fine-tuned models (5B tokens of retraining) lose accuracy, especially the 70B. The llama.cpp baseline dates from late 2023. README charts are images, and the text gives only maxima (11x Falcon 40B, 3x Llama 2 70B on the 4090; 8x and 3x on the 2080Ti). The peer-reviewed paper (SOSP '24, DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695964) could not be opened from this container. CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated on pages opened. OPT support code and predictor-training code are still unreleased TODOs. The repo now lives at github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer (the SJTU-IPADS URL resolves there); Tiiny AI sells hardware built on it. It is derived from llama.cpp (LICENSE copyright Georgi Gerganov and SJTU-IPADS) but is not marked as a GitHub fork.
found_via: Named-candidate check of llama.cpp competitors; raw README fetched and repo page opened

verification.tier_reason: The README gives the paper's headline result (up to 11.69x over llama.cpp, 13.20 tokens/s average and 29.08 peak on one RTX 4090), and WebSearch results list the same paper in ACM DL (DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695964) as SOSP '24, with the authors' copy named song-sosp24.pdf. The work is peer-reviewed, so B. It cannot be A: the README charts are images, no CPU model, compiler or flags are given, and the evaluation scripts (OPT code, predictor training) are listed as unreleased TODOs.
verification.notes: Numbers match the README. Tier raised from C to B because the paper appeared at SOSP '24, but the venue was seen only in WebSearch result listings (arxiv.org, dl.acm.org and ipads.se.sjtu.edu.cn are blocked here); a retier check can confirm. The repo moved to Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer, so consider overriding repo_url. Metadata checked: MIT, 9.8k stars, last commit 2026-05-11, not archived, not a fork.

corrected_fields.caveats: Comparison uses ReLU-fied models chosen to exploit sparsity; the llama.cpp baseline dates from late 2023; speedup charts are images and the text gives maxima only; the README cites arXiv 2312.12456 (not opened) so peer-review status is not confirmed on pages opened. The repo is derived from llama.cpp but GitHub does not mark it as a fork. Compiler flags are not stated.

name: QuACK (CuTe-DSL memory-bound kernels)
baseline: cuDNN v9.10.1 (RMSNorm only), torch.compile (PyTorch 2.7.1, default mode) and Liger Kernel v0.5.10
workload: Memory-bound kernels (RMSNorm, softmax, cross-entropy; forward and backward), batch 8k to 32k rows, reduction dimension 256 to 262k, FP32 and BF16 inputs, measured as model memory throughput on H100.
claimed_speedup: Blog: 'achieves nearly 50% more throughput (e.g., 3.01 TB/s vs 1.89 TB/s for FP32 softmax)' than torch.compile at reduction dim 262k; about 3 TB/s (~90% of peak) for reduction dim larger than 4k; 'significantly outperforms all baselines when reduction dim >= 65k for all 3 kernels' (cuDNN baseline covers RMSNorm only).
compiler_and_flags: PyTorch 2.7.1 torch.compile default mode, Liger Kernel v0.5.10, cuDNN v9.10.1; QuACK requires CUDA toolkit 12.9+ and Python 3.12 (README). JIT-compiled CuTe-DSL kernels, no compiler flags stated.
hardware: 1x NVIDIA H100 80GB HBM3 (3.35 TB/s peak) with Intel Xeon Platinum 8468 CPU
tradeoffs: Needs H100, B200/B300 or RTX 50 series GPUs, CUDA 12.9+ and Python 3.12. The advantage comes from cluster reduction (thread-block clusters with distributed shared memory) on Hopper, so it targets very long reduction dimensions. Also ships Hopper/Blackwell GEMM-with-epilogue kernels.
caveats: First-party blog numbers; the per-size results are only in a figure (combined_kernel_benchmarks_final.png); the text gives the 262k FP32 softmax ratio (3.01 vs 1.89 TB/s, which the blog calls 'nearly 50% more' though it is about 1.59x (derived from page data)) and the >=65k claim. Liger is only benchmarked up to reduction dim 65k (larger sizes unsupported) and cuDNN only on RMSNorm. Harness is public (benchmarks/benchmark_softmax.py, benchmark_rmsnorm.py, benchmark_cross_entropy.py) but has evolved since the July 2025 blog, and the blog does not state the CuTe-DSL or CUDA versions. Baselines are 2025 versions. Below about 4k reduction dim no advantage is claimed. It is a Python CuTe-DSL kernel library for PyTorch/JAX on H100/B200/RTX 50, not a C++ library.
found_via: GitHub: Dao-AILab/quack README -> media/2025-07-10-membound-sol.md (checked while looking for kernel libraries that benchmark against cuDNN)

verification.tier_reason: The first-party blog (media/2025-07-10-membound-sol.md) states the baselines (torch.compile on PyTorch 2.7.1 default mode, Liger Kernel v0.5.10, cuDNN v9.10.1 for RMSNorm only), the hardware (1x H100 80GB HBM3 with Xeon Platinum 8468) and the quoted 3.01 vs 1.89 TB/s and >=65k sentences verbatim; the harness is public (benchmarks/benchmark_softmax.py times quack, torch.compile and liger with triton do_bench). The CuTe-DSL/CUTLASS and CUDA versions used for the blog run are not stated and the per-size numbers exist only as a figure, so it stays C rather than A.
verification.notes: Blog text, README, repo page (Apache-2.0, 1.2k stars, not archived) and commits page (latest 2026-09-13) all match the record. Possible A if a later retier accepts PyTorch/Liger/cuDNN versions plus the public harness as sufficient, but the blog lacks the CuTe-DSL compiler version.

The blog is dated 2025-07-10 and the baselines are older versions. Below about 4k reduction dim no advantage is claimed.

name: RTNeural
baseline: libtorch, ONNX Runtime 1.15.1, TensorFlow Lite 2.14.0
workload: Single-sample real-time-factor (48 kHz audio) of Dense, Conv1D, GRU, LSTM layers and activations at layer sizes 4 to 64, RTNeural compile-time and run-time APIs with Eigen, xsimd and STL backends vs libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite.
claimed_speedup: Exact values from RTNeural-compare results/bench_*.txt (real-time factor at 48 kHz, one sample per call, higher is better). LSTM size 4: RTNeural Eigen static 268.3x real time vs ONNX Runtime 1.42x and libtorch 0.375x (about 189x vs ONNX Runtime, derived from page data); size 64: Eigen static 6.46x vs ONNX Runtime 1.13x and libtorch 0.262x (about 5.7x, derived). GRU size 4: xsimd static 338.2x vs ONNX Runtime 1.46x and libtorch 0.370x; size 64: Eigen static 8.67x vs 1.23x and 0.273x. Dense size 4: xsimd static 6164x (STL static 5969x) vs TensorFlow Lite 151.5x, ONNX Runtime 7.51x, libtorch 2.33x (about 41x vs TensorFlow Lite, derived); size 64: Eigen static 76.8x (xsimd static 67.9x) vs TensorFlow Lite 40.7x (about 1.9x, derived), ONNX Runtime 6.84x, libtorch 1.75x. The STL backend at size 64 reaches only 1.01x (LSTM) and 1.37x (GRU) against ONNX Runtime's 1.13x and 1.23x, and 8.69x vs TensorFlow Lite's 40.7x on Dense, so it is slower there.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build (run_bench.sh: -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release), C++17; compiler and version not stated. Baselines: prebuilt onnxruntime-osx-x86_64 1.15.1 and tensorflowlite_c 2.14.0; libtorch version not stated.
hardware: 2018 Mac Mini, Intel Core i7-8700B @ 3.20 GHz
stars_or_usage: 848 stars; used in many audio plugins (BYOD, Chow Centaur, NeuralNote)
tradeoffs: Small fixed set of layer types (Dense, Conv1D/2D, GRU, LSTM, pooling, batch norm, common activations) and inference only; models are exported to JSON; header library with Eigen, xsimd or STL backends (Eigen best for larger networks, xsimd for small ones); designed for real-time audio, single-sample processing.
caveats: Benchmark by the RTNeural author on one x86 Mac (i7-8700B), one sample per call, so per-call framework overhead dominates the libtorch, ONNX Runtime and TensorFlow Lite figures; the advantage shrinks as layer size grows, and the STL backend falls below ONNX Runtime (LSTM size 64) and well below TensorFlow Lite (Dense size 64). Baselines were timed only in the STL-backend run; the Eigen and xsimd runs were RTNEURAL_ONLY builds, so those ratios compare separate runs. Compiler not stated, libtorch version not stated. The reference paper (arXiv:2106.03037) is a preprint.
found_via: WebSearch 'header-only C++ neural network inference library benchmark faster than TensorFlow Lite ONNX Runtime github README' (RTNeural-compare repo).

verification.tier_reason: First-party benchmark by the RTNeural author with public code (RTNeural-compare src/benchmark.cpp, run_bench.sh, raw logs in results/bench_{stl,eigen,xsimd}.txt) and a named CPU (Intel Core i7-8700B), built as CMake Release, but the compiler and its version are not stated, so not A. The arXiv paper 2106.03037 appears to be a preprint only (no venue seen), so not B.
verification.notes: Replaced plot readings with exact values from the raw result logs; the record's approximations were right except Dense size 64, where the about-75x figure belongs to the Eigen backend (xsimd static is 67.9x). Metadata confirmed: BSD-3-Clause, 848 stars, last commit 2026-08-20 (active).

Dense layer size 4: RTNeural xsimd (static) about 6000x vs TensorFlow Lite about 150x, ONNX Runtime about 7.5x, libtorch about 2.3x; at size 64: about 75x vs TensorFlow Lite about 41x (about 1.8x).

name: sgemm.cu (hand-tuned FP32 GEMM for NVIDIA GA102/Ampere GPUs)
baseline: cuBLAS SGEMM (CUDA 12.6)
workload: FP32 SGEMM, NN layout, square m=n=k from 1024 to about 12800 in steps of 128, RTX 3090, with clocks unlocked and with clocks locked at 1395 MHz, both at 350 W.
claimed_speedup: The README gives no text numbers, only two plots (assets/perf.png, perf_locked.png). Reading them by eye at m=n=k near 12800: about 25,300-25,500 GFLOP/s vs cuBLAS about 24,300 with unlocked clocks (about 4-5% faster), and about 23,000-23,500 vs about 21,800 with locked 1395 MHz clocks (about 6-7% faster); approximate, derived from page data. The HN title claims 'up to 24% faster than cuBLAS on a 4090' (snippet only, not on the repo page).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc V12.6.85 (CUDA Runtime 12.6, CUDA Driver 12.4), g++ 13.3, CMake 3.28.3; the build is fixed by CMakeLists.txt: CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86, CUDA_SEPARABLE_COMPILATION ON, -DGPUCC=86 -DCUBLAS=0/1, no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE and no explicit -O flags (the -O3 lines are commented out).
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090 (driver 550.120), Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS; host CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: FP32 SGEMM only, and the README documents only the NN case; tuned and tested for RTX 3090 (GA102), expected to be fast on Ada/Ampere/Volta/Turing; it is a benchmark and test harness rather than a packaged library.
caveats: Numbers exist only as two plot images (assets/perf.png unlocked clocks, assets/perf_locked.png at 1395 MHz, both 350 W); values are read by eye. Margins are single-digit percent at large sizes (about 4-5% unlocked, about 6-7% locked near m=n=k=12800), and sgemm.cu is slower than cuBLAS at several small sizes (near m=n=k=1280 about 17,000 vs about 19,300 GFLOP/s unlocked). Square FP32 NN only, tuned for the RTX 3090 (GA102); other GPUs untested in the repo. The host CPU is not stated (immaterial for a device-bound GEMM; A rests on the GPU-kernel precedent). The last commit (2025-01-21) swapped m and n in the cublasSgemm calls; for the square sizes plotted this does not change the cuBLAS work. The 'up to 24% faster than cuBLAS on a 4090' figure from the HN title is not on the repo page (snippet only); the project page salykova.github.io/sgemm-gpu was not opened (blocked). The plots also show a 'Simon Boehm | tinyBLAS' kernel well below cuBLAS. Repo identity inferred from the HN title and README (HN thread not opened).

name: Sobek (streaming equivariant tensor-product convolutions)
baseline: OpenEquivariance (primary), also cuEquivariance and e3nn
workload: Edge-conditioned equivariant tensor-product convolution (uvw and uvu operator families), forward, backward and double backward, on capacity-matched grids (16-profile UVW grid, 9-profile UVU grid); also peak memory.
claimed_speedup: Search snippet of arXiv 2607.18074 abstract: faster in all 75 capacity-matched comparisons across two operator families and all three differentiation orders, 1.2x to 49.7x, peak allocated memory reduced by up to 99%; at the last degree point shared with OpenEquivariance, OpenEquivariance allocates 24.1-27.1 GiB vs Sobek 0.1-0.4 GiB; runs workloads up to two orders of magnitude beyond OpenEquivariance capacity.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit 13.3 recommended (CUDA 12.9 builds about 25% slower per README); PyTorch >= 2.12 JIT extension builder; float32 with ieee or tf32 GEMMs; nvcc flags not stated
tradeoffs: CUDA/PyTorch only, float32 only; requires CUDA toolkit for JIT compile (first call per problem compiles specialised kernels). Supports uvw and homogeneous uvu contractions, fused radial projection so the caller must pass the compact radial embedding plus final projection weight. Deterministic, no atomics, bounded scratch (receiver_scratch_bytes).
caveats: The paper (arxiv.org abs/html/pdf, pith.science) was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the numbers are from WebSearch snippets of the abstract and could not be checked against tables; GPU model and per-case numbers unknown. Repo ships a benchmark CLI (suites minimal, scaling, throughput, uvu-throughput; 'matched' command for OpenEquivariance-capacity-matched timing; peak-memory re-measurement with --memory-only) but no checked-in results and no paper PDF (tree: sobek/, tests/, LICENSE, NOTICE, pyproject.toml). Preprint, not peer reviewed; authors are the repo owners (Cortex Discovery GmbH). Speedups are over a partly different formulation (Sobek fuses the final radial projection while baselines take precomputed per-edge weights), and comparisons are capacity-matched against OpenEquivariance, so 1.2x-49.7x is a range over cases, not a typical figure. Float32 only. No evidence of a benchmark against FlashTP (README only lists FlashTP among related libraries). Very young repo: 5 commits between 2026-07-20 and 2026-07-24, 12 stars, 0 forks.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Cortex-Discovery/sobek README plus WebSearch snippet of arXiv 2607.18074

name: tiny-cuda-nn
baseline: TensorFlow v2.5.0 with XLA (which uses cuDNN/cuBLAS)
workload: Training and inference throughput (elements per second) of fully fused multi-layer perceptrons 64 and 128 neurons wide, batch sizes 2^14 to 2^21.
claimed_speedup: The README chart (data/readme/fully-fused-vs-tensorflow.png) shows fully fused MLPs ahead of TensorFlow 2.5.0 with XLA at every batch size from 2^14 to 2^21 on an RTX 3090. Read from the chart (approximate, derived from page data), 64-neuron-wide training throughput is about 1.2e8 vs 0.12e8 elements/s at batch 2^14 (~10x), narrowing to about 2.0e8 vs 1.0e8 at 2^21 (~2x). 64-wide inference is about 1.08e9 vs 0.14e9 elements/s at 2^21 (~8x), with a larger gap at small batches. The 128-wide (dashed) gap is about 2x to 6x for training. Separately, the README claims JIT fusion gives 1.5x to 2.5x over tiny-cuda-nn's own earlier path (it can slow down RTX 3000-series or large models), and Instant NGP gets 5x by fusing its NeRF ray marcher into one kernel.
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3090
stars_or_usage: 4.5k stars; used by Instant NGP and NerfStudio
tradeoffs: Fully fused MLPs work for narrow layers only (up to about 128 neurons; JIT fusion can slow larger models and older GPUs); NVIDIA GPU, CUDA 10.2+ (Linux), C++17, CMake 3.21+; PyTorch bindings add overhead (about 2x slower at batch 64k than native CUDA).
caveats: The TensorFlow comparison is a chart with no numbers in the text, against a 2021 TensorFlow 2.5 plus XLA baseline. The README names benchmarks/bench_ours.cu and benchmarks/bench_tensorflow.py, but those paths 404; the files now live at benchmarks/image/bench_ours.cu and benchmarks/image/bench_tensorflow.py (an image-learning workload). CPU model, compiler and CUDA versions are not stated; the CMake defaults are Release and --use_fast_math. The 1.5x-2.5x and 5x figures are against the library's own earlier path or a non-fused application, not an external baseline. The fully fused MLP paper (Mueller et al. 2021, real-time neural radiance caching) could not be opened (tom94.net is blocked here).
found_via: Direct README lookup (PyPI tinycudann returned 404, so no registry hit); not in vcpkg or conan.
Named-candidate check of GPU neural-network kernel libraries; raw README fetched

name: tiny-ml-runtime
baseline: PyTorch 2.x (Python, batch size 1)
workload: Single-sample inference of a 4-8-3 Iris MLP and a 784-128-10 MNIST MLP, pure C engine versus PyTorch called from a single-threaded Python loop.
claimed_speedup: README: Iris (4-8-3), batch 1, 1M iterations: pure C 2,732,240 predictions/s (0.366 s) vs PyTorch from a single-threaded Python loop 10,596 predictions/s (94.374 s), stated as 258x; the README warns this measures Python plus PyTorch dispatch overhead, not compute throughput. MNIST (784-128-10), 100K iterations: pure C 4,244 predictions/s (23.563 s) vs PyTorch 22,502 (0.444 s), i.e. PyTorch about 5.3x faster (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -Wall -Wextra -O2 (Makefile); compiler version not stated
hardware: Apple M1 (ARM64)
tradeoffs: Naive C loops with no SIMD, tiling or threading; dense layers, ReLU and softmax only; weights exported from PyTorch to a binary file.
caveats: Educational project with 0 stars. The 258x win is Python-interpreter and PyTorch dispatch overhead on a 4-feature input (the README says so), not a like-for-like library comparison: the PyTorch side is a Python loop that calls .item() on every prediction and is timed with time.time() (wall clock), while the C side is timed with clock() (CPU time) and is not compared against libtorch or any C/C++ inference engine. The C predict() mallocs and frees two buffers per call and uses naive loops with no SIMD, so on the compute-bound MNIST case PyTorch wins by about 5x. Single Apple M1 run, compiler version unstated.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ library faster than XNNPACK OR oneDNN inference kernels benchmark GitHub' follow-up query for 'tiny-ml-runtime ... 258x faster than PyTorch'.

verification.tier_reason: First-party README table with public benchmark code (src/c/inference.c benchmark(), src/python/benchmark.py), Makefile flags (gcc -O2) and the hardware (Apple M1) named, but no compiler version, and the C and Python sides use different timers. The gain is over 50x against a Python-dispatch baseline, so it is capped at C.
verification.notes: README numbers match the record exactly. Metadata confirmed (MIT, 0 stars, last commit 2026-03-25, active). Keep only as a flagged toy: its single win is overhead-bound and it loses on the compute-bound workload.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Iris (4-8-3): pure C 2,732,240 predictions/s vs PyTorch 10,596 predictions/s (258x, as stated; 1M iterations 0.366 s vs 94.374 s). MNIST (784-128-10): pure C 4,244 vs PyTorch 22,502 predictions/s, i.e. PyTorch 5x faster.
corrected_fields.caveats: Educational project. The README itself says the 258x figure measures Python plus PyTorch dispatch overhead on a 4-feature input, not computational throughput, and that the gap disappears with batching, and on MNIST PyTorch wins by 5x. Included only because toy projects are in scope; likely a keep-with-shortcomings or reject for the verifier.

name: TTV (tlib tensor-times-vector library)
baseline: Eigen Tensor (sequential in-place tensor-times-vector); also TBLIS and TCL
workload: Mode-q tensor-times-vector products for symmetric (order 2-7, 324 cases) and asymmetric (order 2-10, 1296 cases) shapes in single and double precision.
claimed_speedup: The README has no speedups in text, only plots. Approximate values read from the README PNG plots (misc/*_speedup_*.png), per test case: over Eigen (sequential), about 3x to 300x on symmetric tensors and up to about 900x on asymmetric single-precision tensors; over TBLIS, about 1x to 17x, mostly 2-8x; over TCL, about 0.3x to 35x, so TTV is slower than TCL in some cases. On symmetric single-precision tensors TTV reaches about 20-35 Gflop/s, against up to about 31 for TCL, about 15 for TBLIS and about 8 for Eigen. The paper's abstract, seen only as a search-engine snippet because the paper itself could not be opened, says TTV is on average 6.1x and up to 12.6x faster than TCL's TTGT implementation and reaches 34.8 Gflop/s in single precision.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.3 with -Ofast -march=native -pthread -fopenmp; OpenBLAS 0.2.20 dot/gemv; OpenMP 4.5
hardware: Intel Core i9-7900X (10 cores, 20 threads, 3.3 GHz)
tradeoffs: Covers only the tensor-times-vector contraction (loops-over-GEMV/DOT), not general contractions; needs contiguous storage; relies on a BLAS (OpenBLAS, MKL or BLIS) for peak speed.
caveats: The repo has no benchmark harness for the TCL/TBLIS/Eigen comparison (test/ holds gtest unit tests only, misc/ holds PNG plots only), so the README plots cannot be reproduced from the repo. Speedups appear only as scatter plots, so the per-case values are approximate readings. In several cases TTV is slower than TCL (plotted speedup below 1). Eigen ran sequentially while TTV ran in parallel on 10 cores/20 threads, which inflates the Eigen ratios; the 100-900x Eigen points are not like for like. TTV calls OpenBLAS/MKL gemv/dot and is not faster than BLAS itself, so this is really a tensor-contraction entry rather than a BLAS replacement. The experiments date from 2019 and use GCC 7.3, OpenBLAS 0.2.20, TCL 0.1.1, TBLIS 1.0.0 and Eigen 3.3.90. LICENSE.txt is LGPL-3.0, while the README badge just says GPL. The verifier could not open the ICCS paper (Springer, iccs-meeting.org and Fraunhofer hosts are blocked).
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): GitHub topic page 'tensor-contraction' listing ttv, then the README Experiments section

verification.tier_reason: The measurements come from a peer-reviewed paper (Bassoy, ICCS 2019, Springer LNCS pp. 32-45) that compares TTV with Eigen, TCL and TBLIS; the README repeats its setup (i9-7900X, GCC 7.3, -Ofast -march=native -fopenmp, OpenBLAS 0.2.20) and its plots. Not A, because the harness that runs TCL/TBLIS/Eigen is not public: test/ holds only gtest unit tests, example/ holds interface demos and misc/ holds only PNG plots.
verification.notes: The repo exists and is not a fork or archived; it has 24 stars, 5 forks, the LGPL-3.0 license (LICENSE.txt) and a last commit on 2025-11-02. The B tier rests on the paper's ICCS 2019 venue and its abstract numbers (6.1x average, 12.6x maximum over TCL), which were seen only through search-engine snippets. The orchestrator might move this entry from blas-lapack to a tensor-contraction category.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: README plots (read from the single-precision speedup figures, approximate): TTV over Eigen is mostly about 3x to 15x with outliers into the hundreds (asymmetric cases reach several hundred x); over TBLIS typically about 3x to 5x; over TCL mostly 1x to 10x with some cases below 1x. README text: for large tensors it 'reaches peak matrix-times-vector performance'. (plot readings are derived from page data)

name: ZhiLight
baseline: vLLM and SGLang (versions not stated)
workload: LLM serving benchmark (QPS, TTFT, TPOT) with 3.7k-token prompts (DeepSeek-R1 AWQ: 2.8k prompt, 750 output tokens) on NVIDIA AD102 PCIe (x1, x2, x4), A800 (x4, x8) and H20 (x8), for models from MiniCPM-2B to DeepSeek-R1. Runs use the ZhiLight benchmark Docker tool, which sweeps offered QPS via --min_qps/--max_qps/--qps_step.
claimed_speedup: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct-GPTQ-INT4 on 4x AD102 PCIe: TTFT mean 1419.74 ms vs vLLM 4796.32 ms and SGLang 3962.99 ms, TPOT mean 30.97 vs 41.54 and 63.22 ms. Qwen1.5-110B-GPTQ-Int4 on 4x AD102: QPS 0.18 vs 0.09 for both vLLM and SGLang, TTFT mean 1671.38 vs 3085.74 ms (vLLM). DeepSeek-R1 AWQ on 8x A800: QPS 0.16 vs vLLM 0.08.
hardware: NVIDIA AD102 PCIe (1, 2 and 4 GPUs), A800 (x4, x8), H20 (x8); CPU not stated
tradeoffs: Targets PCIe-connected GPUs (dual-stream encode and all-reduce overlap, INT8 reduce); supports INT8, FP8, AWQ and GPTQ; OpenAI-compatible server; the repo is C++/CUDA with a Python server layer.
caveats: Results are mixed within the same document. Llama-3.1-8B on 2x AD102: ZhiLight QPS 0.4 vs vLLM 0.46 and SGLang 0.84, TTFT 1091.12 vs 915.58 ms (vLLM), TPOT 66.24 vs 18.68 ms (vLLM). Qwen2-72B on 4x A800: SGLang QPS 0.36 vs ZhiLight 0.18. Qwen1.5-110B on 4x A800: SGLang QPS 0.18 vs ZhiLight 0.1. ZhiLight TPOT is worse in several rows (DeepSeek-R1 AWQ 115.97 vs vLLM 109.86 ms; Qwen1.5-110B on AD102 39.68 vs 30.34 ms; MiniCPM-2B 26.1 vs 16.71 ms). The clearest wins are TTFT on PCIe AD102 multi-GPU runs. QPS values look like offered-load steps from the benchmark tool (many engines tie at exactly 0.09 or 0.18), so QPS ratios may reflect the highest load step sustained rather than measured throughput. The benchmark tool is distributed as a Docker image, with its source not found in the pages opened. vLLM/SGLang versions and compiler flags are not stated, and there is no H20 baseline. This is an LLM serving engine rather than a kernel library, and its baselines are not in the category list.

name: Clad (Clang-plugin source-transformation AD)
baseline: Enzyme (LLVM-level AD, run through Clad's own use_enzyme backend); Tapenade planned; none of the listed baselines (oneDNN, cuDNN, XNNPACK, Eigen tensor) apply
workload: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks in the repo comparing Clad-generated reverse-mode and vector-forward-mode gradients with Enzyme-generated gradients of small functions (array add and multiply, sum), plus Hessian, matrix, tape, multithreading, GPT-2 training (cladtorch) and LULESH and XSBench (CUDA) benchmarks. No results are published.
claimed_speedup: No numbers found: neither the README, the docs (CoreConcepts, FAQ, UsingEnzymeWithinClad, ReleaseNotes) nor the opened repo pages state any speedup or timing versus Adept, CppAD, CoDiPack or Enzyme.
compiler_and_flags: Benchmarks target is built in release mode; GPT2Training is built with -O3 -ffast-math (from benchmark/CMakeLists.txt); no results to attach flags to.
stars_or_usage: 421 stars, 212 forks; reported (search results) as used in ROOT/RooFit at CERN
tradeoffs: Compiler plugin: needs a matching Clang/LLVM (14.0.x to 23.2.x per README), differentiates only code visible to Clang at compile time (custom derivatives needed for external functions), and supports a growing but incomplete set of C++ features. Source transformation can expose optimizations to the compiler, but reverse mode stores intermediates on a tape (memory grows with operation count). LGPL-3.0.
caveats: Evidence-free record: the repo ships benchmark code (benchmark/EnzymeCladComparison.cpp, built only with CLAD_ENABLE_ENZYME_BACKEND, plus Hessians.cpp, VectorModeComparison.cpp, GPT2Training.cpp built with -O3 -ffast-math, LULESH_diff.patch, XSBench_diff.patch, benchmark_compare.py) but no committed results; the Clad-vs-Enzyme benchmark compares two backends of Clad itself. Issue #1764 and PR #1771 (benchmark::DoNotOptimize fix for 0 ns results) are cited from the search record and were not re-opened. The ACAT 2022 paper 'Automatic Differentiation of Binned Likelihoods With RooFit and Clad' (arXiv 2304.02650) and the ROOT blog 'Automatic differentiation in RooFit with Clad' report, per search-result snippets only (arXiv, root.cern and indico.cern.ch blocked), TFormula gradient speedups of about 10x to 29x and a HistFactory minimization speedup of about 5.5x versus ROOT 6.26's numerical (finite-difference) gradients; that baseline is numerical differentiation, not another AD tool or a listed baseline, and the gain comes from reverse mode needing one sweep instead of n function calls. Tier D kept although the repo has fewer than 1k stars because Clad is the AD engine integrated in ROOT/RooFit at CERN.

name: cuEquivariance
language: Python (frontends; CUDA kernels ship as separate pip packages)
baseline: e3nn (PyTorch equivariant tensor products for MACE, NequIP and similar models)
workload: The repo's PyTorch MACE tutorial (docs/tutorials/pytorch/MACE.rst) contains an executable timing cell comparing e3nn's channelwise tensor product plus scatter_add against cuEquivariance's fused uniform_1d kernel: multiplicity 128 (128x0e + 128x1o), 1000 nodes, 10000 edges, float32, CUDA, 10 throwaway and 1000 timed repetitions with torch.cuda.synchronize.
claimed_speedup: Independent study (arXiv 2510.23621, abstract seen via WebSearch snippets only, paper not opened): cuEquivariance 'reduces inference latency by about 3x' for MACE compared with the e3nn backend. Repo: no numbers. The MACE tutorial cell (docs/tutorials/pytorch/MACE.rst) prints 'Speedup: {e3nn_avg/cuet_avg}x' but stores no output; one WebSearch summary said the rendered docs.nvidia.com tutorial shows 5.6x for the channelwise tensor product, but a second targeted search did not confirm it and docs.nvidia.com is egress-blocked, so that figure is unverified. CHANGELOG '~3x' (JAX v0.3.0 vs Torch v0.2.0) and 'up to 2x' (uniform 1d kernel) compare cuEquivariance with its own earlier releases.
stars_or_usage: 441 stars, 43 forks (github.com page, 2026-10-03); NVIDIA library named in the README as accelerating DiffDock, MACE, Allegro and NequIP; a backend option in MACE
tradeoffs: Python library with PyTorch and JAX bindings. The repository files are Apache-2.0, but the CUDA kernels are installed from separate cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12/cu13 and cuequivariance-ops-jax-cu12/cu13 pip packages; OpenEquivariance's README calls cuEquivariance's kernel package 'closed-source', and I did not find the kernel source or the ops-package license in the repo. NVIDIA-GPU only; beta status per README. Uses the transpose of e3nn's mul_ir data layout and the tutorial warns that layout transposes can be expensive. Triton-based triangle kernels have optional ahead-of-time tuning that can take hours.
caveats: Numbers are snippet only: the independent arXiv 2510.23621 abstract (about 3x MACE inference latency versus e3nn) was read through WebSearch because arxiv.org is egress-blocked; methodology, GPU and precision were not visible. docs.nvidia.com was also egress-blocked, and the repo's MACE tutorial timing cell (1000 nodes, 10000 edges, multiplicity 128, float32, 1000 timed repetitions) stores no output. The tutorial itself notes 'our kernels tend to have best performance for very large input sizes'. The repo's Python frontends are Apache-2.0 ('All files hosted in this repository are subject to the Apache 2.0 license'), but the CUDA kernels ship as separate pip packages (cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12/-cu13, cuequivariance-ops-jax-*) under the proprietary 'NVIDIA Math Libraries SDK' license agreement (pypi.org metadata: 'Other/Proprietary License'), which forbids reverse engineering and derivative works, so usability is 'mixed'. Other independent measurements exist: OpenEquivariance's peer-reviewed ACDA25 paper and harness (tests/benchmark.py) time cuEquivariance against e3nn; per its abstract snippets, OpenEquivariance's fused kernels beat cuEquivariance by up to 4.5x forward. name: blip_mp
baseline: GMP 6.3.0 (mpz_t; built with assembly and with --disable-assembly)
workload: Own bench executable (blip_mp_bench) timing add/sub/mul/divMod/powm/invMod on pre-built pools of values at sizes from i64-range up to 98304 bits, e.g. 5M iterations of r = pool[i % 256] + pool[(i+1) % 256], against mpz_* in a C program using the same libc malloc.
claimed_speedup: Apple M4 vs GMP with assembly, from RESULTS.md. All i64-fitting adds are 1.95-2.66x faster (RESULTS.md: immediate add 2.06 ns vs 4.83 ns, 2.34x). Mul: 12 of 15 sizes from 128 to 8192 bits are faster, including RSA-1024 1.20x (210 vs 252 ns), RSA-2048 1.19x (673 vs 800 ns), RSA-3072 1.37x (1265 vs 1733 ns) and 1536 bits 1.45x; 16384 bits is 0.87x and 32768 bits 0.55x. Sub is 1.03-2.11x faster from 256 to 8192 bits (768 bits: 4.38 vs 9.23 ns). Add is 1.04-1.28x faster at 768 bits and above. powm is 13% faster at 2048 bits (3333 vs 3839 us), 3% at 1024 and 8% at 3072. The public Mp.divMod is 1.25-2.00x SLOWER than mpz_tdiv_qr from 256 to 8192 bits (2048: 526.7 vs 416.5 ns). The README's 'divMod 1.31x' is blip vs GMP-noasm on x86 (452.8 vs 593.2 ns), and its '24% faster long division' is a limb-only inner kernel (~470 vs 614 ns). invMod is 3.25-5.36x slower. On Zen 4 vs GMP with assembly, only i64-fitting adds win (immediate add 3.36 vs 4.44 ns); mul at 2048-32768 bits loses by 2.24-3.36x, powm at 2048 by 1.99x and divMod at 2048 by 2.09x.
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build bench -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (tests/benchmark/blip_mp_bench.zig); GMP harness tests/benchmark/gmp_bench.c compiled with -O3 -Wall -Wextra and linked against nixpkgs GMP (nixos-unstable pinned in flake.lock rev 1c3fe55a) and against a --disable-assembly GMP override; libc malloc on both sides; run via nix build .#bench; 3-run hand medians
hardware: Apple M4, aarch64-darwin (stated in RESULTS.md and BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 17); cross-check on an AMD Ryzen 9 7940HS (Zen 4) Framework laptop under NixOS (BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 18)
tradeoffs: Variable-length self-describing byte storage with small-buffer optimization instead of limb arrays; pure Zig, no inline assembly, C FFI exists. Integers only (no mpf/mpq/mpfr). FFT multiplication is implemented but disabled because Toom-3 still wins in the supported range, so it falls behind GMP past ~16K bits. Win is specific to Apple Silicon: on x86_64 GMP's hand-written assembly beats it by 1.5-4x on large operands.
caveats: First-party 3-run hand medians, and the author lists hyperfine aggregation as to-do. The README headline mixes runs and machines. Its RSA-2048 'trifecta' divMod win (1.31x) is not supported on Apple Silicon, where RESULTS.md's own table shows the full divMod 1.26x slower. The '24% faster' long-division figure is an inner-kernel microbenchmark against a GMP timing (614 ns) about 1.5x higher than the 400-417 ns mpz_tdiv_qr timings in other tables. The README's 'honest losses' list (128-256-bit mul 0.40-0.67x) is stale against RESULTS.md (128-bit mul 1.38x faster). BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md Run 17's sub table has raw timings that contradict its ratios (256 bits: 6.87 ns vs 5.49 ns is marked a 1.28x win). Cross-check counts differ between documents (8240, 12029, 13029). The wins are Apple Silicon only: on Zen 4, GMP's assembly is 1.65-3.88x faster than GMP-noasm, and blip_mp loses every tier-3 size to it by 1.5-4x. Modular inverse is 2.5-5x slower than GMP. There is no LICENSE file; the README says 'MIT or Apache-2.0 (TBD before tagging a release)', so usability is reference. The repo has 1 star, the project is research-grade, and the benchmark runs are dated 2026-05-02 to 2026-05-04.

name: CGBN (Cooperative Groups Big Numbers)
baseline: GMP 6.1.2 (OpenMP, 20-core Xeon)
workload: Batched fixed-size unsigned big-integer operations (add, sub, low multiply, Montgomery reduction, odd modular exponentiation, div/qr, sqrt, gcd, modular inverse) at 128 to 8192 bits, one CUDA cooperative group of 4/8/16/32 threads per number, versus GMP calls spread over 20 CPU cores with OpenMP.
claimed_speedup: README speed-up table, Tesla V100 vs Xeon E5-2698v4 (GMP+OpenMP), average over 128-8192 bits: add 77.4x, sub 77.1x, mul (low) 43.5x, mont_reduce 29.3x, powm_odd 21.4x, div_qr 14.4x, sqrt 11.3x, gcd 6.9x, mod inv 4.1x; per-size extremes: 128-bit add 174.3x, 128-bit mul (low) 172.9x, 8192-bit powm_odd 16.8x, 8192-bit mod inv 4.0x
compiler_and_flags: perf_tests/Makefile: nvcc -I../include -arch=sm_70 xmp_tester.cu -lgmp (no explicit -O; CUDA 10+ required for Volta, exact version not stated); GMP side: g++ gmp_tester.cc -o gmp_tester -lgmp -fopenmp (no -O flag, so the harness loop builds at g++'s default -O0; libgmp itself is built separately with its own ./configure); compiler versions and GMP configure flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 (Volta) GPU vs Intel Xeon E5-2698v4, 20 cores at 2.2 GHz
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA (Kepler through Ampere targets in the Makefile). Fixed-size unsigned integers only, 32 to 32K bits in 32-bit steps, 4/8/16/32 threads per number, written inside CUDA kernels with a fixed number of bits per kernel. It pays off for large batches of independent numbers, not for one big number. No floating point, no arbitrary-size operands.
caveats: Numbers are first-party, from the 2018 beta on a V100 against GMP 6.1.2 (current GMP is 6.3.x). This compares a GPU with a CPU, so it measures per-device throughput on large batches of independent operations, not a better algorithm; single-operand latency would lose to GMP. The GMP driver (perf_tests/gmp_tester.cc) is compiled with no optimisation flag, which inflates loop overhead around the cheapest calls and probably the 128-bit add/sub ratios (174x). Only libgmp's own code is optimised. Compiler versions are not stated. A third-party report (pscamillo/mr_blackwell README) says CGBN runs 'orders of magnitude slower than expected' on Blackwell (sm_120) GPUs, and the Makefile lists architectures only up to Ampere. steleman/nvidia-cgbn is a fork adding signed integers and Ada/Blackwell support (tested with CUDA 12.9/13.2); it is not reported separately. Supports fixed sizes only, up to 32K bits in multiples of 32.

name: ctbignum
baseline: GMP (mpn/mpz)
workload: Fixed-width multiplication of 2, 4 and 8 64-bit-limb integers (100-500 bit range), run time and compile time.
claimed_speedup: Table 3 (-march=native, forced inlining): 2 limbs 4 ns vs GMP mpn_mul 14 ns (3.5x); 4 limbs 18 vs 29 ns (1.6x); 8 limbs 85 vs 67 ns (GMP 1.27x faster). compiler_and_flags: Apple LLVM 9.0.0, -O3 -march=native with forced inlining of mul (Table 3); Table 1 uses -O3 without -march=native
hardware: 2017 MacBook Pro, quad-core 2.3 GHz Intel Core i5 (Kaby Lake), 16 GB, Turbo Boost disabled
tradeoffs: Fixed-width only (sizes known at compile time), C++20 header-only; wins only for small limb counts via inlining and unrolling.

name: dashu (dashu-int)
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate; gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 pinned in Cargo.lock)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add/sub/mul/div/gcd/pow/modular ops swept over 10 to 10^4 bits, plus small-value (<=128 bit) workloads and string round-trips, dashu-int 0.4.2 vs rug (GMP), ibig, num-bigint and malachite.
claimed_speedup: Small operands: ubig_add at 100 bits dashu 3.7 ns vs rug 21.9 ns; ubig_div at 100 bits 5.7 ns vs 32.4 ns; ubig_mul at 100 bits 22.6 ns vs 25.1 ns; ubig_gcd at 1000 bits 2.87 us vs 3.05 us; ubig_from_hex at 10^4 bits 2.56 us vs 6.60 us. Report summary: dashu faster than rug in 98 of 153 small-value cases and in 123 of 205 head-to-head cases overall; the page says rug/GMP is typically 2-6x slower on tiny values because of a fixed per-value heap allocation. rug/GMP is faster from about 1000 bits (ubig_mul at 10^4 bits: rug 4.52 us vs dashu 12.76 us).
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (ded5c06cf 2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp with the default bench profile (Cargo.toml sets no [profile] overrides, so opt-level 3, inherits release); criterion 0.5.1 run with --warm-up-time 1 --measurement-time 2 --sample-size 100; dashu-int 0.4.2, rug 1.30.0 with gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 (Cargo.lock)
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (arm64)
stars_or_usage: 142 stars, 20 forks; dashu-int 3,894,865 crates.io downloads (1,662,908 recent) as of 2026-10-01
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, inline storage for values up to two words, so no heap allocation for small integers. Slower than GMP from about 1000 bits upward (GMP has tuned assembly and asymptotically faster algorithms). Rust API, so usable from C++ only through FFI. Not an mpz-compatible API.
caveats: The report calls itself 'quick, machine-specific local numbers, not authoritative' (one laptop, 2 s measurement). It benchmarks dashu-int 0.4.2, while crates.io's current release is 0.6.1 (2026-09-25). Each bench op returns a new value, so rug pays a heap allocation per result while dashu stores up to two words inline; the small-value win is about allocation and inline storage, not GMP's mpn kernels. The ubig_div bench divides two operands of the same bit length (b = random + a), so the quotient is tiny and it measures overhead, not long division. The suite was written for (but not merged into) the dashu repo and generalises dashu's own primitive.rs bench, so it is not fully arm's-length. The bit-width sweep stops at 10^4 bits. A second suite by ibig's author (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1, dashu 0.4.2) shows GMP-backed rug far ahead on large workloads: digits of e at 10M rug 2.788 s vs dashu 19.943 s; Fibonacci at 100M rug 2.937 s vs dashu 26.224 s. The win is limited to small operands (about two words) and gcd near 1000 bits.

name: ECM-ELF (ECM stage 1, AVX-512 IFMA 8-curve batch backend)
language: C/C++ (GitHub lists C as primary; the AVX-512 kernels are .cpp; CUDA and OpenCL backends also exist)
baseline: GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (ecm-zen3.exe, built on GMP, curve family -param 0); the same table also compares Prime95 v31.04b05 (GWNUM FFT)
workload: Elliptic-curve-method stage 1 only (B2=0 or B2=B1), Suyama sigma Montgomery curves, one thread on one physical core, on Mersenne numbers 2^k-1 (M127 to M19701), per-curve seconds; the SIMD backend runs 8 curves per batch (time divided by 8). Directly measured case: N = M4001 = 2^4001-1 at B1 = 1e5, 1e6 and 2e6.
claimed_speedup: docs/ECM_Montgomery_STAGE1.md section 14.2, M4001, stage 1 only, one thread, per curve: B1=1e5 0.596 s vs GMP-ECM 1.787 s (3.00x faster); B1=1e6 6.264 s vs 15.008 s (2.40x); B1=2e6 13.455 s vs about 30 s (GMP-ECM value scaled, about 2.2x). Section 14.5 size sweep at B1=1e6 (README labels these rows measured, only M5755 and M8527 fitted): M1277 0.979 s vs 2.484 s (2.54x), M2203 2.285 s vs 5.804 s (2.54x), M3001 4.137 s vs 9.586 s (2.32x), M3500 5.164 s vs 11.656 s (2.26x), M4001 6.290 s vs 14.624 s (2.32x); about 1.7x at M5755 and M8527 and about 1.75x at M19701 (all columns fitted). Section 10.4 (earlier, before clock pinning), same-machine GMP-ECM ecm-zen3.exe, B2=B1: M1277 B1=1e5 0.135 vs 0.234 s per curve (1.74x), M1277 B1=1e6 1.418 vs 3.551 s (2.50x), M3001 B1=1e5 0.526 vs 1.148 s (2.18x). Against Prime95 v31.04b05 (a model calibrated on one measured M3001 point, 5.65 s, plus the M4001 B1=1e7 run; the 14.2 Prime95 values at B1 1e5-2e6 are scaled from 1e7): 32.7x at M127, 10.4x at M521, 3.94x at M1277, 1.37x at M3001, 0.90x at M4001, 0.17x at M19701 (fitted); the doc recommends the new code below about 3700 bits and Prime95 above about 6000 bits.
compiler_and_flags: Own code: MSVC Release build (build_vs18\Release\ecm.exe; README build section says 'Release build (MSVC /O2)'; the Visual Studio version is not stated, build_vs18 implies the VS 18 generator while the README dependency table recommends VS 2022). CMakeLists.txt gives /arch:AVX512 (or -mavx512f -mavx512ifma -mavx512dq on GCC/Clang) to src/cpu/simd_edwards.cpp, simd_mont_ifma.cpp and simd_mont_curve.cpp. Commands (section 14.4): echo (2^4001-1) | ecm.exe --mont --mont-backend simd --mont-threads 1 -gpucurves 8 --sigma 4242 <B1> 0, versus ecm-zen3.exe -param 0 -c 2 <B1> <B1> (the section 14.1 table writes -c 8). Baseline: GMP-ECM 7.0.6 ecm-zen3.exe from the prebuilt ecm-2025.10.28-win.multiarch package (--enable-asm-redc); a WebSearch snippet places that package on download.mersenne.ca/GMP-ECM (host blocked here); its compiler and flags are not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (Strix Point, Zen 5 plus Zen 5c, 256-bit FPU datapath so 512-bit IFMA runs as 2 x 256-bit); clocks pinned at 3990 MHz on the Zen 5 cores (logical CPUs 0-7) and 2995 MHz on Zen 5c; Windows (exe paths). Single-thread numbers stated reproducible to about +-3%.
tradeoffs: Stage 1 only (stage 2 is handed to Prime95 or GMP-ECM through compatible .save files). The fast path needs AVX-512 IFMA hardware (explicit error otherwise; auto falls back to a slow scalar mpn backend). Gains come from 8-lane batches, a Mersenne fold domain for N = 2^k-1 (about 2x faster than general N per the README) and affine differential ladder; general N uses Montgomery CIOS. Cost grows about n^1.66 in word count, so Prime95's FFT overtakes it above about 3700 bits. GPL-3.0 copyleft. Windows-first build; Chinese-language README (README.en.md exists). Renamed from OpenCL-ECM.
caveats: All GMP-ECM comparisons use Mersenne numbers 2^k-1, where this code switches to a folded-domain reduction that the README says makes 2^k-1 about 2x faster than a general integer of the same size; no comparison on general N is published, and the doc does not show whether GMP-ECM's own special 2^k+-1 arithmetic was active. One author, one laptop-class machine (Ryzen AI 9 HX 370, 256-bit FPU datapath) with hand-pinned clocks, and Prime95 was running on other cores during the section 14 measurements (doc says single-thread numbers reproduce to about +-3%). The section 14.5 footnote says the fit (about 2.98e-7*k^2 + 3.79e-4*k s) built from the measured 1277-4001-bit points extrapolates the larger sizes, and the README table marks only M5755 and M8527 as fitted, so the 1277-4001 rows read as measurements; the M4001 row (6.290/14.624 s) differs slightly from section 14.2 (6.264/15.008 s), suggesting a separate run. The 'about 30 s' GMP-ECM figure at B1=2e6 is scaled, not measured; the section 10.4 numbers predate clock pinning; the doc gives -c 8 in section 14.1 and -c 2 in section 14.4 for GMP-ECM. The prebuilt GMP-ECM binary's compiler and flags are unknown. Stage 1 only (stage 2 is handed to GMP-ECM or Prime95). The repo changes daily (2026-10-02 commits are on the GPU stage 2 path) and the numbers, dated 2026-09-24, were not re-run against HEAD. The scalar GMP mpn backend is only a cross-check (about 5.6 s/curve at M1277, B1=1e5, versus 0.135 s/curve for SIMD), so there is no win against raw GMP mpn arithmetic to claim. GPU backends (CUDA CGBN, OpenCL) are not covered by this entry. GPL-3.0.

name: libzahl
baseline: GMP (also TomsFastMath and LibTomMath)
workload: Per-function micro-benchmarks of integer operations (set, swap, neg, abs, bit operations, comparison, add, sub, multiply, square, string conversion, gcd and more) on operands of 1 to 4097 bits, run through translation layers in bench/ for each library.
claimed_speedup: STATUS (1-4097 bits): zset, zswap, zbtest, zsave, zload, zneg(a,b), zabs(a,b), ztrunc(a,b,c), znot, zbits and zcmpu are 'always fastest'; zsub is 'always fastest'; zadd is 'fastest after ~90 (clang), ~260 (gcc+musl), or ~840 (gcc+glibc)'; zand and zor are fastest only after ~400 and ~1150 bits. Losses: zlsh is 'not too fast anymore'; for zrsh 'gmp is almost always faster'; zmul, zsqr and zstr are 'slowest'; for zstr_length(a,10) 'gmp is faster'. The 'zgcd 21 % of gmp' row sits in the file's '[out of date legacy area]' (152-bit operands), and the file uses 'X % of Y' in rows that still need optimising, so it most likely means libzahl is slower than GMP there.
compiler_and_flags: libzahl built with gcc+glibc, gcc+musl and clang+glibc; other libraries with gcc+glibc; config.mk CFLAGS = -std=c99 -O3 -flto; no CPU extensions or assembly extensions used
hardware: Intel Core 2 Quad Q9300 (x86-64), Linux, 50 us timer slack, benchmark process pinned to one CPU
tradeoffs: C library with long-jump error handling, allocation caching and no thread safety. Wins on cheap and small-operand operations; multiplication, squaring and many derived operations (modular multiply, pow, primality test) were still the slowest, so it does not beat GMP on arithmetic-heavy work. Plain C code, no assembly.
caveats: Mixed result, not a general win over GMP. The STATUS file's own multiply, square and string-conversion rows say 'slowest', and GMP wins on right shift. Results are published only as per-function rankings and crossover sizes, with no timing tables. Measured on a 2008 Core 2 Quad with no CPU extensions, so modern GMP assembly paths (mulx, adx, AVX) are not represented. Compiler and GMP versions are not stated, and the GMP numbers come through the repo's translation layer (bench/libgmp.h). STATUS notes that GMP does no failure checking while libzahl does, that TomsFastMath has a compile-time size limit, and that the author flags some rows (zlsb, zcmp) as suspicious. The gcd figure comes from an out-of-date legacy section. Repository archived 2024-10-06; last commit 2022-07-20. The README itself gives no numbers.

name: VROOM (vectorized RNS modular multiplication, BoringSSL fork)
baseline: BoringSSL BN_mod_mul_montgomery / BN modular exponentiation and RSA (same binary, multiplication backend swapped), OpenSSL at commit 7a53925 including its AVX-512 IFMA almost-Montgomery routines ossl_rsaz_amm52x{20,30,40} (separate harness kevin-he-01/vroom-openssl), FLINT 3.2.1 (GMP-based mpn_mod_mul / fmpz_mod_mul), and Arkworks (Rust, modmul only)
workload: Modular multiplication versus modulus size, modular exponentiation (public e = 65537, secret exponent, RSA-CRT) and RSA sign/verify latency using AVX-512 IFMA with a residue number system, single core pinned with taskset, versus BoringSSL Montgomery, OpenSSL and FLINT.
claimed_speedup: The repository README gives no figures; it says 'the relative speedup of VROOM over each baseline is the paper's claim' and points to the paper (IACR ePrint 2026/393). A WebSearch result summarizing the paper abstract (the ePrint and USENIX pages themselves could not be opened, egress blocked) states that VROOM accelerates RSA-4096 signatures by 4.0x (verify) and 1.3x (sign) over OpenSSL, and BLS signature verification by 3.43x over the assembly-optimized BLST library (the BLS result is not covered by this repository). These figures are not verified from an opened page.
compiler_and_flags: Clang 21.1.8 (official LLVM prebuilt, installed by install_deps.sh); configure.sh runs 'cmake -GNinja -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release'; CMakeLists.txt adds -O3 to the Release flags and -mavx512f -mavx512ifma for the RNS path; FLINT 3.2.1; runs pinned with 'taskset -c 0 ./build/bssl_bench'
hardware: AWS c7i.metal-24xl, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C (Sapphire Rapids, AVX-512 IFMA required), Amazon Linux 2023; README says relative speedups also reproduce on c7i-flex.large

name: avxbls
baseline: blst (non-vectorized x64 assembly BLS12-381 pairing)
workload: Full optimal ate pairing on BLS12-381 (Miller loop plus final exponentiation), single pairing latency in CPU cycles, AVX-512 IFMA 52-bit limb arithmetic versus blst's mulx/adx scalar assembly.
claimed_speedup: Per the TCHES 2025(4):848-872 paper (abstract seen as a search snippet only): 1,265,314 cycles (Granger-Scott cyclotomic squaring) or 1,195,236 cycles (compressed cyclotomic squaring) for the full pairing versus blst at 2,351,615 cycles, i.e. blst is 1.86x (resp. 1.97x) slower.

Cycle counts use read_tsc via src/rdtsc64.S, 10000 iterations after cache warm-up (src/main.c timing_pairing). gcc version not stated in the repo.
hardware: Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake) per the paper abstract snippet; the repo itself does not state the CPU.
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 with IFMA (Ice Lake or newer Intel, Zen 4/5 class AMD with IFMA). Latency-optimized for a single pairing, not aggregate batch throughput. Built on and bundles blst sources (a baseline directory carries the scalar reference). The repo is pairing only; signatures are in a separate project.
caveats: Cycle counts and CPU (Intel Core i3-1005G1, Ice Lake) come from the TCHES/ePrint abstract seen as a WebSearch snippet; tches.iacr.org and eprint.iacr.org are blocked here (403), so the full paper (compiler version, turbo settings) was not read. name: ibig
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate; gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 pinned in Cargo.lock)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div at 10 to 10^4 bits, ibig 0.3.6 versus dashu, num-bigint, malachite-nz and rug (GMP).
claimed_speedup: At 10 bits: ubig_add ibig 1.8 ns vs rug 17.7 ns, ubig_sub 1.5 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_mul 2.1 ns vs 18.0 ns, ubig_div 1.5 ns vs 28.3 ns. Parsing beats rug at every size: ubig_from_hex at 10^4 bits 2.55 us vs 6.60 us, ubig_from_dec 10.17 us vs 11.51 us; ibig_from_str_small 34.1 ns vs 111.3 ns. Already at 100 bits rug wins add/sub/div (ubig_add 25.7 ns vs 21.9 ns), and at 10^4 bits GMP wins clearly: ubig_mul rug 4.52 us vs ibig 12.69 us.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 (ded5c06cf 2025-12-08); cargo bench --features gmp with the default bench profile (Cargo.toml sets no [profile] overrides, so opt-level 3, inherits release); criterion 0.5.1 run with --warm-up-time 1 --measurement-time 2 --sample-size 100; ibig 0.3.6, rug 1.30.0 with gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1 (Cargo.lock)
hardware: Apple M2 Max, macOS (Darwin 25.5.0, arm64)
stars_or_usage: 107 stars; ibig crate 875,051 crates.io downloads (118,046 recent) as of 2026-10-01; last crates.io release 0.3.6 (2022-09-17)
tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no_std, inline small-integer representation; no subquadratic gcd (10-13x slower than dashu/malachite/rug at 10^4 bits), no C API.
caveats: Win over GMP is confined to one-word integers (about 10 bits in the sweep) and to string parsing; from 100 bits rug is ahead on add/sub/div, and ibig's gcd is far slower than rug at every size from 100 bits (ubig_gcd at 10^4 bits 850.52 us vs 53.05 us). Each bench op returns a new value, so rug pays a heap allocation per result while ibig stores one word inline; the small-value win is about allocation, not GMP's kernels. The ubig_div bench divides equal-length operands (tiny quotient). The benchmarked crate is ibig 0.3.6, the last crates.io release (2022-09-17); the repository has since been restructured (ibig, ibig-core, ibig-old directories; rustc 1.95 MSRV), so current code may differ. In the second suite by ibig's own author (github.com/tczajka/bigint-benchmark-rs, rug 1.24.1) ibig is far behind rug on large workloads (digits of e at 10M: rug 2.788 s vs ibig 20.673 s). Dashu, a hard fork of ibig, is its own entry. The report calls itself non-authoritative (one laptop, 2 s measurement).

is_fork_of: https://bellard.org/libbf (mirror of Fabrice Bellard's libbf tar releases with fixes and CI; not a GitHub fork)
name: LibBF (Fabrice Bellard)
baseline: GNU MPFR (mpfr_mul, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate: GMP 6.3 / MPFR 4.2)
workload: Correctly rounded floating-point multiplication, addition, division and square root at 53 to 300,000 bits of precision, reported as ns per 64-bit limb.
claimed_speedup: Multiplication at 300,000-bit precision: libbf 51.2 ns/limb vs MPFR (rug) 78.9 ns/limb (about 1.5x, derived from page data), from two different harnesses. libbf is slower than MPFR everywhere else on the page: mul at 53 bits 43.4 vs 15.6, 3,000 bits 13.0 vs 9.4, 30,000 bits 43.0 vs 35.3; add, div and sqrt at every size; and exp/log/sin/cos/tan/atan/pow at 53-256 bits (for example exp at 53 bits 2985 vs 518).
compiler_and_flags: libbf 2025-06-03 bftest built locally with clang -O2 ('./bftest -S -p <prec> <op> <op>'); the report says the C harness timed with clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC), but the public bftest.c uses x86 rdtsc and prints cycles per limb, so the harness was modified (patch not published). MPFR side: rug 1.30.0 (gmp-mpfr-sys 1.7.1, GMP 6.3, MPFR 4.2) under rustc 1.96.1 --release in libbeef's tests/bftest.rs (BFTEST_SEED=1234, BFTEST_DURATION=200)
hardware: Apple M4, 32 GiB RAM, macOS 26.5
stars_or_usage: 19 stars (rurban/libbf mirror). It was QuickJS's BigInt/BigFloat backend until the QuickJS 2025-04-26 release removed the bignum extensions and added a new BigInt implementation; the current QuickJS Makefile no longer builds libbf.
tradeoffs: Small (about 90 KB compiled), no dependencies, SIMD-optimised NTT multiplication with near-linear running time, also decimal floats and IEEE semantics. Transcendental functions are much slower than MPFR (exp at 53 bits 2985 vs 518 ns/limb).
caveats: The only win over MPFR is multiplication at 300,000 bits on one Apple M4, and it is not a like-for-like measurement: libbf ran in its own C bftest (operands of uniform random length in [1, 2*prec] bits with run-length random bits, results printed per rounding mode including RNDF, where bf_mul truncates inputs to prec+2 bits; the report does not say which line it quoted) while MPFR ran via rug in libbeef's Rust harness with full-width operands. The public bftest.c already prints an MPFR column on identical operands, which the report did not quote, and it times with x86 rdtsc (cycles), so the report's C harness on Apple M4 was an unpublished modification. Measured by the author of libbeef, a competing Rust port. libbf's own README says it 'is not the fastest library' and is about 4x slower than TachusPI on pi. bellard.org/libbf was blocked, so the GitHub mirror (rurban/libbf, last commit 2025-08-19) is cited.

The public bftest.c (libbf 2025-06-03) times with x86 rdtsc, prints cycles per limb ('c/64bit') and has its own MPFR column on identical operands; the report says its C harness used clock_gettime on an Apple M4, so it was modified and the patch is not published, and the like-for-like MPFR column was not reported. name: Malachite
baseline: GNU GMP (mpz, via the Rust rug 1.30.0 crate)
workload: Criterion microbenchmarks of unsigned big-integer add, sub, mul, div, gcd, extended gcd and conversions for 10 to 10^4 bits, malachite-nz 0.9.1 versus dashu, ibig, num-bigint and rug (GMP).

name: avx-ecm
baseline: GMP-ECM (the ecm program, built on GMP)
workload: Elliptic Curve Method factoring: curves per second for stage 1 and stage 2 on general inputs up to about 1000 bits, AVX-512 8-way (52-bit digits) or 16-way (32-bit digits) vector arithmetic per thread.
claimed_speedup: about 1.5 to 2.5 times the throughput (curves/sec) of GMP-ECM, for numbers up to a thousand bits or so (README, 'has been observed'). README adds that large numbers are more efficient with GMP-ECM because AVX-ECM does not use sub-quadratic multiplication.
compiler_and_flags: README names icc or gcc 7.3.0 or newer, e.g. 'make COMPILER=gcc730 SKYLAKEX=1' (KNL=1 for Knights Landing). The Makefile uses -O3 plus -march=skylake-avx512 (SKYLAKEX=1), -march=icelake-client -DIFMA (ICELAKE=1) or -march=tigerlake -DIFMA (TIGERLAKE=1); the IFMA options were added in a November 2020 commit and are not in the README. No flags or build are tied to the quoted ratio.
tradeoffs: Needs AVX-512 (Skylake-X, Knights Landing, or IFMA on Ice Lake/Tiger Lake). Curves run in constant-time steps of 208 bits (128 bits with DIGITBITS=32), so 417-bit and 623-bit inputs cost the same. No sub-quadratic multiplier, so it loses to GMP-ECM on large inputs. Stage 2 is the standard continuation with pairing (B2 = 100 x B1 by default). It writes a stage 1 savefile that GMP-ECM stage 2 can resume. Multi-threaded with pthreads. Not a library: command-line program.
caveats: README ratio is a first-party 'has been observed' range with no table, CPU model, GMP-ECM version or flags, and no benchmark script in the README. The mersenneforum thread (www.mersenneforum.org is blocked here) was seen only as a search snippet, which says about 2x GMP-ECM throughput with 1 thread on a Xeon Gold 5122 and, for one input size, 16 simultaneous 512-bit curves in 18.7 s (1.17 s/curve) versus GMP-ECM at 1.72 s/curve (ratio about 1.47, derived from snippet data); the snippet could not be opened, so treat those as unverified. The comparator is GMP-ECM, not GMP itself, so it only loosely matches the listed GMP/MPFR baselines. Last commit 2021-03-09 (repo inactive for over 5 years). Newer GMP-ECM releases and AVX-512 downclocking were not measured.

name: avxbls-sig (AVX-512 BLS signatures on BLS12-381)
baseline: blst (supranational/blst x64 assembly: blst_sign_pk_in_g1/g2, hash_to_g1/g2, pairing aggregation)
workload: Per-operation cycle counts (rdtsc average over many iterations) in test.c, AVX-512 vector routines versus blst scalar calls for scalar multiplication, point add/double, sk_to_pk, subgroup checks, hash-to-curve, signing in G1 and G2, and pairing-based aggregate/verify; the BLS scheme operations keygen, signing, aggregation, verification.
claimed_speedup: Repository publishes no numbers (test.c prints scalar/baseline versus vec average cycles at run time). Paper 'Efficient SIMD Implementation of the BLS Signature Scheme Using Intel AVX-512' (TCHES 2026, ePrint 2026/947; abstract seen as a WebSearch snippet only): the vectorised BLS software using AVX-512 (AVX-512IFMA, 8-way 52x52-bit multiplies) is at least 1.57 times faster than an x64 assembly implementation of blst, benchmarked on an Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake). Per-operation figures not read.
compiler_and_flags: makefile: /opt/gcc-13.3/bin/gcc -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -m64 -mbmi2 -fwrapv -mtune=native -march=native -z noexecstack -w, linked against libblst.a built by build.sh (blst flags -O3 -fno-builtin -fPIC, -D__ADX__ when the CPU has ADX, -mno-avx).
hardware: Not stated in the repo; the paper snippet names an Intel Core i3-1005G1 (Ice Lake, AVX-512 IFMA).
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; sibling of the catalogued hchengv/avxbls (optimal ate pairing)
tradeoffs: Latency-optimised AVX-512 (IFMA-style 52-bit limb) code for x86-64 only, Linux oriented; built on blst (bundled in src_blst and a committed libblst.a) and links it for scalar fallbacks. Makefile hard-codes /opt/gcc-13.3/bin/gcc and -march=native. Covers keygen, signing, aggregation and verification on BLS12-381 (G1 and G2 variants). Research code with a cycle-count harness, no stable API documented.
caveats: Tier B rests on search snippets of the paper abstract (TCHES 2026, ePrint 2026/947), not on the paper itself: eprint.iacr.org and iacr.org are blocked here, so the per-operation cycle tables, the compiler version used and turbo settings were not read, and the 'at least 1.57x' lower bound cannot be mapped to specific operations. The repo README has no paper link; the link is inferred from the matching first author (Ganqin Liu, repo owner) and topic. test.c averages rdtsc (reference cycles, not core cycles) over 10,000-100,000 iterations after a 1,000-iteration warm-up, for scalar multiplication, point add/double, isogeny maps, sk_to_pk, subgroup checks, hash-to-curve, signing in G1 and G2, pairing aggregation (blst_pairing_chk_n_mul_n_aggr_pk_in_g1/g2), core verify and final verify. The baseline is the single-signature blst API built from a vendored blst copy (src_blst/server.c plus build_blst/assembly.S via build.sh: -O3 -fno-builtin -fPIC, -D__ADX__ when the CPU has ADX, -mno-avx), not blst's multi-threaded or batch-verification paths. The signing benchmarks hash with SwiftEC (blst_swiftec_* from src/swiftec_blst.c, the authors' addition, not part of upstream blst) when the SWIFTEC_ON switch is set and with standard blst_hash_to_g1/g2 otherwise; where SWIFTEC_ON is defined was not located. A prebuilt libblst.a binary is committed and the makefile hard-codes /opt/gcc-13.3/bin/gcc. The pairing code builds on hchengv/avxbls (already listed, tier B), so verification gains overlap that entry. Needs AVX-512 IFMA (Ice Lake or newer). Retier to A if the paper names the compiler and flags matching the makefile. [retier] Repo has bench code and public flags but no numbers; the 'at least 1.57x over blst on an i3-1005G1' claim is a search snippet of ePrint 2026/947 (blocked). The aggregation benches run vendored blst with the standard SSWU hash against *_vec paths using the cheaper SwiftEC hash (SWIFTEC_ON 1), and the sign rows compare the authors' scalar SwiftEC code, not stock blst; default SwiftEC signatures are not RFC 9380 interoperable. Reuses the catalogued avxbls pairing code; self-tests never fail on bad signatures.

claimed_speedup: vs math/big multiplication: 1 Mb 105237800 ns -> 28446400 ns (-72.97%), 10 Mb -89.43%, 100 Mb 147599836000 -> 5921594000 ns (-95.99%); decimal scan of 1e6 digits 1776707489 -> 144867502 ns (-91.85%). Versus GMP, bigfft is slower at every size (e.g. 1 Mb 12100000 ns GMP vs 22391830 ns bigfft; 100 Mb 2673000000 vs 5228991000 ns).

tradeoffs: Go package using FFT (Schonhage-Strassen) multiplication above about 200 kbits and plugging into math/big types; the README says it is a toy proof of concept that is not expected to be used in production. Go only.

Versus Go's math/big it only wins above roughly 1 Mbit (FFT switches on above 200 kbits; at 1 kb to 100 kb it is up to 4.9% slower), and decimal scanning is slower up to 1e4 digits. Old CPUs; Go version unstated; last commit 2023-01-29. Go library, not callable from C++ without cgo glue.
