name: GNU MPFR with CUDA/CGBN backend (gnu-mpfr-cgbn)
baseline: MPFR 4.2.1 scalar functions (GMP 6.3.0) on one CPU core
workload: Correctly rounded mpfr_mul, add, div, sqrt and fma on batches of 1 to 16384 operands at 128 to 65536 bits of precision, GPU batch interface (with PCIe transfer) and device-resident vectors, versus the plain scalar MPFR function in a loop.
claimed_speedup: Peak batch speedups at n = 1024: div 30.4x and sqrt 28.2x at 32768 bits, mul 21.2x at 49152 bits, fma 18.3x at 40960 bits. Device-resident at n = 16384: fma 284x at 8192 bits, mul 230x at 4096, div 157x at 16384, add 120x at 8192, sqrt 115x at 16384. A single operation is always slower on the GPU (launch floor about 6.5 us resident, 16 us with transfers); batch add never beats the CPU (<= 0.7x); div and sqrt above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 13.2 (driver 595.71.05) with NVCCFLAGS '-O3 -arch=$cuda_arch -Xcompiler -fPIC' (configure default arch 'native', sm_120 on the test GPU); host compiler GCC 14.3.1 per the design PDF's test-system table, but CFLAGS for the MPFR baseline are not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120, 82 SMs at 2.41 GHz), CUDA 13.2; CPU baseline is 'one core, the same machine' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Results are bit-identical to MPFR (same correctly rounded value, ternary value and flags for all five rounding modes); without --enable-cgbn the library is plain MPFR. Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA. Precision above 65536 bits runs on the CPU, all results in one batch must share a precision, device calls are serialized on a mutex, and only mul/add/sub/div/sqrt/fma are offloaded.
caveats: First-party measurements on a single machine; the CPU model is never given (README or design PDF), and the baseline is one core of scalar MPFR, so a multi-core MPFR run would shrink the ratios by up to the core count. A single operation (n = 1) is always a loss, about 3x to 1570x slower than the CPU (derived from page data); addition never wins in batch mode (every add batch cell is 0.7x or lower); the README's Limitations section says division and square root above 32768 bits are slower than the CPU. The repository is one 'Initial Github commit' (2026-09-12) of an MPFR 4.2.1 tree plus the GPU backend; no sign of upstream MPFR adoption was found, although the new source files carry the stock FSF/INRIA MPFR copyright header. The top-level LICENSE file is the GPL-3.0 text (as in upstream MPFR), while the library sources, including the new src/mpfr-cgbn.c and tests/cgbnbench.c, are LGPL-3.0-or-later. Uses CGBN beyond its documented maximum size (above 32768 bits), checked by tests/cgbn-verify.

name: mr_blackwell (native Miller-Rabin GPU kernel)
baseline: GMP (CPU Miller-Rabin probable-prime test with GMP modular exponentiation)
workload: Base-2 Miller-Rabin probable-prime tests (Montgomery CIOS modular exponentiation, 4-bit fixed window, PTX carry chains) on 65536 random 683-bit candidates, RTX 5070 GPU versus the CPU/GMP prime-gap test on a Ryzen 9 8800X3D.
claimed_speedup: README standalone table: v2d kernel 1,805,000 PRP/sec at 683 bits labelled 132x versus 'CPU (GMP) 13,700' on a Ryzen 9 8800X3D (as named in the README), and 295,000 PRP/sec = 21x at 1240 bits; but the benchmark program computes these ratios against a hard-coded 13,700 constant rather than timing GMP. Measured end to end in the prime-gap pipeline (P=503, 13K tests): CPU gap_test_simple 28.0 s versus GPU v2 3.1 s, about 9x (derived from page data), with kernel throughput about 1,800,000 versus 13,700 PRP/sec. CGBN on Blackwell is described as 'impractical' / 'orders of magnitude slower' with no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: nvcc -O3 -arch=sm_120 (Makefile), CUDA 12.9, Linux Mint; GMP version and CPU baseline build flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 5070 (SM 12.0 Blackwell) versus AMD Ryzen 9 8800X3D
stars_or_usage: 3 stars, 1 fork, 18 commits; the README says it produced 60 prime-gap world records (as of 2026-05-05) through the sethtroisi/prime-gap pipeline
tradeoffs: Specialised to Miller-Rabin / modular exponentiation of fixed-size odd moduli (template LIMBS dispatch, e.g. 22 limbs for 683 bits), not a general bigint library; NVIDIA GPUs only; drop-in replacement for the CGBN miller_rabin.h used by prime-gap.
caveats: First-party README numbers. The standalone benchmark's 'vs CPU' column divides by a hard-coded 13700 (printf '%.1fx vs CPU@13700' in mr_blackwell.cu); GMP is used there only as an untimed correctness check via mpz_probab_prime_p(n, 1), so the 132x/21x ratios are not reproduced by the published harness. The 13,700 PRP/sec figure comes from sethtroisi/prime-gap's gap_test_simple, whose main loop is single-threaded at HEAD (no OpenMP), so the ratio is a GPU against what appears to be one CPU core; GMP version and CPU build flags are not stated. 'Ryzen 9 8800X3D' is the README's name for the CPU and does not match a known AMD model name, possibly a typo. The source header says 5-bit window by default while the README says 4-bit. Only Blackwell (sm_120) is tested; other architectures are listed as 'should work (untested)'. The CGBN-on-Blackwell slowness claim is the author's own observation without numbers. last_commit 2026-05-05 confirmed on the master commits page.

name: MultiFloats.jl
baseline: MPFR (via Julia BigFloat)
workload: Extended-precision (128-256 bit, 30-60 digit) floating-point arithmetic, e.g. +, -, *, / and linear algebra such as 400x400 QR, versus Julia BigFloat (MPFR), Quadmath.jl and DoubleFloats.jl.
claimed_speedup: README: 'At 30-digit precision, MultiFloats.jl is 30x faster than BigFloat, 6x faster than Quadmath.jl, and 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl.'
tradeoffs: Fixed small number of Float64 limbs (Float64x2/x3/x4, Float32x2-4), so precision is limited to roughly 106-212 bits rather than arbitrary; no dynamic allocation, branch-free algorithms usable on CPU and GPU in Julia. Transcendental functions fall back to MPFR. Julia only, so C++ use means a port.
caveats: README gives bare ratios ('at 30-digit precision ... 30x faster than BigFloat, 6x faster than Quadmath.jl, 2x faster than DoubleFloats.jl') without a table, hardware, Julia version or version of the package measured. The current v3.0 README no longer links the benchmark gist (gist.github.com/dzhang314/3e10463843f4ab5f5a4a2206c877771b, MultiFloatsBenchmark.jl: QR of 400x400 and pseudoinverse of 250x400 at about 106 bits); the gist has code but no recorded output. Correctness history: the README says the v2.0 algorithms for Float64x5-Float64x8 were 'fundamentally broken' (types removed in v3.0), v2.0 had denormalization issues causing spurious accuracy losses, and prevfloat/nextfloat skipped values before v3.0. Treats +-Inf inputs as NaN; transcendental functions go through MPFR. Compared against MPFR only through Julia's allocating BigFloat. Pure Julia package, not callable from C++ without embedding Julia. The SC25 paper (Zhang and Aiken, doi 10.1145/3712285.3759876) reportedly measures a C++ prototype of the same algorithms against QD, CAMPARY, MPFR and FLINT, but it was not opened.

name: simd-f128
baseline: GCC __float128 (libquadmath)
workload: 10,000,000 iterations in latency mode of add, mul and div on a 128-bit double-double (about 31 digits) type with AVX2/NEON/WASM-SIMD backends versus GCC __float128.
claimed_speedup: The README has two inconsistent tables for the same 10M-iteration latency test against __float128 (GCC). The summary table gives __float128 add 152.31 ms, mul 189.81 ms, div 276.00 ms, and simd-f128 73.60, 56.15 and 159.70 ms; it claims '3.38x faster than GCC' on multiply and '1.7x to 3.3x faster' overall. The 'Comparative Speed' section with raw bench_compare console output gives __float128 153.37 / 193.23 / 325.37 ms and simd-f128 (AVX2) 99.44 / 74.46 / 207.98 ms, which it states as 'multiplication is 2.59x faster, addition is 1.54x faster, and division is 1.56x faster'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the published runs. CMakeLists.txt sets -Wall -Wextra -O3 for GCC/Clang, plus -mavx2 -mfma when SIMD_F128_AVX2 is on (inferred from the build files, not from the benchmark write-up).
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; published on PyPI (simd-f128 1.6.2), npm and crates.io
tradeoffs: Header-only C11/C++11 double-double arithmetic: about 31 digits, zero allocation, no dependencies, AVX2/SSE2/NEON/WASM-SIMD or scalar fallback. Not IEEE binary128 compliant and susceptible to catastrophic cancellation; no arbitrary precision.
caveats: Weak evidence. No CPU model or compiler version is given (the Google Benchmark output shows only 12 x 3266.69 MHz with a 16 MiB L3). The README's two benchmark tables disagree (multiply 3.38x vs 2.59x; division 1.73x vs 1.56x, derived from page data), so the headline '1.7x to 3.3x' comes from the more favourable run. The comparison is against __float128, not GMP or MPFR (the README only calls GMP/MPFR 'Very Slow', with no numbers). Double-double (~106-bit mantissa) is not IEEE binary128: it has a smaller exponent range and no correct rounding, and the README warns of catastrophic cancellation and says to use __float128 when binary128 compliance is needed. In the Google Benchmark mul loop (bench_arithmetic.cpp) the value is multiplied by about 2 every iteration, so it overflows to infinity quickly. The project is very new (first commits 2026-08-09) and has 2 stars.

name: TzdLanguage NTT BigInt multiplier
baseline: GNU GMP 6.3.0 (single-core mpz_mul)
workload: Multiplication of two 4,741,006-digit integers using a 3-prime NTT with Garner CRT on CPU (AVX2) and GPU (CUDA).
claimed_speedup: README/wiki, 4,741,006-digit operands on i7-4790 + P106-090: CPU AVX2 NTT convolution 54.02 ms vs single-core GMP 6.3.0 mpz_mul 111.78 ms (2.07x as stated); GPU NTT kernel 29.20 ms (3.83x as stated); 8-thread Karatsuba-wrapped GMP 84.58 ms. End-to-end decimal string in to decimal string out: CPU 175.41 ms and GPU 56.52 ms vs single-core GMP 2,549.30 ms (14.5x and 45.1x as stated). The wiki's own breakdown (parse 10.64 + ntt 54.02 + crt_carry 97.08 + format 13.67 ms) shows that the 54.02 ms leaves out CRT reconstruction and carry propagation. The complete CPU product is therefore 151.10 ms, which is 1.35x SLOWER than single-core GMP's 111.78 ms (derived from page data), even though the CPU engine uses OpenMP on all 8 threads. The complete GPU product (ntt=42.01 ms including CRT/carry/copy) is 2.66x faster than single-core GMP (derived from page data). Almost all of the end-to-end gain comes from base-10^9 storage avoiding GMP's binary/decimal conversion (686.85 ms parse + 1,750.67 ms mpz_get_str).
compiler_and_flags: GMP harness: MSVC cl /O2 /openmp /EHsc /std:c++17 (test/run_bench_gmp_mt.bat), linked against vcpkg x64-windows gmp.lib (whether GMP's assembly kernels were enabled is not stated). TzdTools: MSVC (Visual Studio 2026 / v145) Release via CMakeLists.txt with /arch:AVX2 /openmp; exact optimization flags for the timed build not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i7-4790 (4C/8T, 3.60 GHz); NVIDIA P106-090 GPU (Pascal, 192 GB/s)
license: MIT (stated only in the README and badge; there is no LICENSE file in the repository: raw main/LICENSE and github.com blob/main/LICENSE both 404)
tradeoffs: The NTT multiplier lives inside a programming-language interpreter (src files TzdExperimentalCompute.cpp for the CPU engine, TzdPyTorch.cpp for the GPU engine) and surfaces through language-level operations, not as a standalone library; extracting it takes work. Single operand size tested.
caveats: First-party numbers from a 17-day-old language project (first commit 2026-09-13, 81 commits, 10 stars). The NTT multiply is buried in a Windows/MSVC-only interpreter (Generated/TzdExperimentalCompute.cpp uses _umul128; GPU path in TzdPyTorch.cpp) and works on decimal strings. It is not a standalone library. The CPU 2.07x 'pure multiply' ratio compares a multi-threaded NTT convolution that excludes the 97.08 ms CRT/carry step with a complete single-threaded mpz_mul; the complete CPU multiply (151.10 ms) is slower than single-core GMP. The pages contradict each other: the README and CPU wiki give multi-threaded GMP end-to-end as ~519 ms in one place and 2,522.09 ms in the table, and the GPU wiki claims 'over 10x' over GMP for the 29.20 ms kernel (3.83x). GMP was a vcpkg MSVC build with unknown asm configuration. Each figure is a single run (iters=1 at 4.74M digits). No LICENSE file (MIT is declared only in the README).

name: libMetalFloat64 (philipturner/metal-float64; emulated FP64 on Apple GPUs)
baseline: Native hardware FP64 on the Apple Silicon CPU (NEON) in the README table, and OpenCL FP64 in the precision table; the listed baselines GMP and MPFR are not compared
workload: Theoretical maximum scalar giga-operations per second per operation (FFMA, FADD, FMUL, FCMPSEL, FCMP, FRECIP, FDIV, FRSQRT, FSQRT) for a reference system with an 8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU (four 128-bit vector ALUs per core) and a 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU, computed from instruction counts and not measured.
claimed_speedup: README 'Performance' table of maximum theoretical scalar Gops (not measured), CPU FP64 vs GPU FP32x2 (double-single, 1+47-bit mantissa): FFMA 392 vs 590, FADD 196 vs 482, FMUL 196 vs 758, FCMPSEL 196 vs 2123, FCMP 196 vs 1769, FRECIP 49 vs 196, FDIV 49 vs 183, FRSQRT 49 vs 171, FSQRT 49 vs 189 (ratios 1.5x to 10.8x, derived from page data). The 'GPU eFP64' column (float64_t with edge-case checking disabled) is empty. Text: 'Based on theoretical estimates, additions and multiplications will have 1/32-1/64 the throughput of their 32-bit counterparts.'
hardware: README reference system: 8-core 3.064 GHz ARM CPU and 32-core 1.296 GHz Apple GPU; the chip is not named.
tradeoffs: Swift package that builds a Metal dynamic library and headers; needs an Apple6-family or newer GPU (A13 and later, Metal 3) and macOS Ventura on Intel Macs. Two precisions: float64_t is IEEE-compliant but the README gives no throughput for it, while float32x2_t has 1+47 mantissa bits, flushes denormals and has undefined INF/NaN results. Larger functions are called through the dynamic library, so inlining is partial. The planned 64-bit atomics use a lock buffer and the README warns that a missing useResource call can freeze half the GPU. Matrix types, division, square root and transcendentals were still planned; the README states the library is 'not a finished library'.
caveats: The README says 'Still in the planning stage - this is not a finished library!'. The only numbers are theoretical peaks from instruction counts (the README's own 'maximum theoretical performance'); no workload was timed anywhere I could open, the eFP64 column (float64_t with edge-case checks disabled) is blank and the precision table is mostly '???'. The comparison is not like-for-like: the CPU column is full IEEE FP64, while the filled GPU column is FP32x2 double-single with an 8-bit exponent and 1+47-bit mantissa that flushes denormals and gives undefined results for INF/NAN. The comparison is against the CPU's hardware double, not the category baselines GMP or MPFR (software arbitrary precision), so the entry does not fit big-integer-arbitrary-precision; it would sit better with floating-point emulation or GPU numerics. The README credits GPT-4 for much of the work. Archived (read-only) on 2024-08-11; last commit 2023-05-17. [retier] HEAD contains no FP64 arithmetic: float64_t/float59_t/float43_t are empty ulong wrappers with no operators; the only MetalFloat64 source is a placeholder increment(uint) marked 'TODO: Remove this entire file'; the README's float32x2_t does not exist in the code. MetalAtomic64 fetch_add ignores the type id (an f64 add would be an integer add) and the device store has no lock. The header copies Apple Metal stdlib code under Apple copyright, so MIT does not cover all of it. The README Performance table is theoretical peak from instruction counts, not a measurement; archived 2024-08-11.

name: libQD3 (double-double, triple-double, quad-double, extended-double)
baseline: MPFR (the MPLAPACK manual's Rgemm numbers for upstream QD against MPFR and GMP at their 512-bit default); libQD3's own docs/qd.tex also carries the original QD paper's per-operation timing table against Bailey's MPFUN
workload: No benchmark of libQD3 itself found. Indirect lead: MPLAPACK's Rgemm (dense matrix multiply) benchmark with the upstream QD library as the quad-double back end, against MPFR and GMP back ends, on one machine.
claimed_speedup: None for libQD3 itself. Lineage numbers: (1) MPLAPACK user manual (doc/manual/manual.pdf on master, titled 'MPLAPACK version 1.0.0 user manual', section 9 Benchmarks, upstream QD rather than libQD3): peak Rgemm, reference versions quad-double 33 MFlops, GMP 19 MFlops, MPFR 11 MFlops; OpenMP versions quad-double 1.3 GFlops, GMP 693 MFlops, MPFR 390 MFlops (about 3.0x MPFR single-threaded and 3.3x with OpenMP, derived from page data). (2) libQD3 docs/qd.tex timing table (original Hida/Li/Bailey QD, microseconds per operation, Pentium II 400 MHz): quad-double add 0.583, mul 1.965, sloppy mul 1.016, div 5.267 vs MPFUN add 5.729, mul 7.624, div 10.102 (about 9.8x, 3.9x and 1.9x, derived from page data); Power3 200 MHz: QD add 0.710, mul 1.131, div 6.699 vs MPFUN 4.651, 5.837, 9.180 (about 6.6x, 5.2x, 1.4x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: MPLAPACK run: GCC 9.3.0 inside Docker, flags not stated. docs/qd.tex table: g++ 2.95.2 -O3 -funroll-loops -finline-functions -mcpu=i686 -march=i686 (Pentium II, PowerPC 750 without the -m flags), Sun CC 5.0 -xO5 -native (UltraSparc), IBM xlC -O3 -qarch=pwr3 -qtune=pwr3 -qstrict (Power3).
hardware: MPLAPACK Rgemm run: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3970X, 256 GB DDR4-3200 (the manual says ECC is not enabled for the Rgemm runs and 'ECC Unbuffered' for the Raxpy runs), Docker. docs/qd.tex table: Intel Pentium II 400 MHz, Sun UltraSparc 333 MHz, PowerPC 750 266 MHz, IBM Power3 200 MHz.
stars_or_usage: 2 stars, 0 forks, 158 commits on main; MPLAPACK (same author, 108 stars) uses libQD3 as its QD back end per the MPLAPACK README
tradeoffs: Fixed-precision floating point built from 2 to 4 binary64 limbs (about 106, 159, 212 bits) or two binary80 limbs (EDD): binary64 exponent range, not correctly rounded, not arbitrary precision. Sloppy add, multiply and divide are on by default (a few bits of accuracy traded for speed); optional branch-free arithmetic (QD_ENABLE_BF*), FMA selection and x86-64-v3 or native code generation. C, C++ and Fortran interfaces. EDD needs binary80 long double (x87), with known MinGW/Wine trigonometry test failures.
caveats: Why only C: no measurement of libQD3 itself exists; both number sets cover the QD double-double/quad-double code that libQD3 inherited (the README says the fork 'keeps the original double-double and quad-double functionality'), not its new td_real, edd_real or binary32 types or the optional branch-free paths (CHANGES.1.2.0.md says those follow the Kouya/Zhang-Aiken algorithms; no timings given). The MPLAPACK manual numbers predate libQD3 (upstream QD), compare unequal precisions (quad-double about 212 bits vs MPFR and GMP at 512 bits), run through MPLAPACK's C++ wrappers (in the Raxpy section the author suspects the MPFR C++ binding makes needless copies, since MPFR ran at half of GMP's speed), and are not peer reviewed; the manual opened is titled version 1.0.0 (search results title arXiv 2109.13406 'MPLAPACK version 2.0.1 user manual'; arXiv is blocked here and was not opened). The docs/qd.tex table is from about 2000 (Pentium II, g++ 2.95.2), compares against MPFUN rather than MPFR, and the MPFUN harness is not in the repo; tests/qd_timer.cpp times QD only. docs/td.tex gives flop counts, not timings: TD add 41 flops vs QD 84, TD mul 116/206 (FMA/no FMA) vs QD 182/332, and states FMA gives about 1.8x for multiplication and 1.6x for division (the 2.7x figure is DD's 24/9 ratio, derived from page data). Licensing: LICENSE is BSD-3-Clause; COPYING (LBNL notice) asks commercial users to contact LBNL's Technology Transfer Department, and the td.tex abstract says 'BSD 2-clause', which does not match LICENSE. Related lineage evidence not opened (arXiv blocked): Kouya, arXiv 1510.08642, a table titled 'Computational times of QD and MPFR/GMP (212 bits) matrix multiplication' (equal precision, upstream QD); Kouya, arXiv 2603.14926 (ICCSA 2026 workshops), branch-free TD/QD with SIMD; a search summary says TD 1.2-1.5x and QD 1.4-2.0x 'compared to MPFR' for matrix multiplication, unverified and possibly branch-free vs conventional.

workload: Prime factorization of semiprimes: Pollard's rho on GPU (CUDA with the author's CGBN fork) against CPU ECM on the same number, 16-digit factor; CPU ECM wall clock on a 32-core box for 30-, 35- and 40-digit factors.
claimed_speedup: None: the project claims no speedup and says the opposite. README 'Performance reality': the GPU programs 'do not beat the CPU for hard inputs'; for integers below 2^64 they are 'much slower than their GMP-ECM equivalent'; on an RTX 4080 a 16-digit factor takes about 8.7 s with GPU rho versus about 2 s for CPU ECM on the same number (about 4x slower, derived from page data), and 19-digit and larger factors are impractical. CPU path wall clock (32-core box, equal-size prime semiprime): 30-digit factor about 10.5 s, 35-digit about 20.6 s, 40-digit about 5.7 min.
compiler_and_flags: CPU: /usr/bin/gcc -O3 -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -funroll-loops -ftree-vectorize -ftree-slp-vectorize -fopenmp, -D_GNU_SOURCE -D_XOPEN_SOURCE=700, link -lecm -lgmp -lm -flto=32 -O3. GPU: nvcc (/usr/local/cuda-12.9, also tested with CUDA 13.2) -O3 -arch=sm_89 (sm_120 on Blackwell), OpenMPI 5.0.5 via mpicxx --showme, GMP-ECM 7.0.6 (from the Makefile and README).
hardware: Tested on a laptop with RTX 4080 Ada (sm_89) and Core i9-14900HX, and an Intel NUC 13 Extreme with RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (sm_120) and Core i9-13900K, Fedora 41 and 44; the 32-core CPU box for the ECM timings is not identified.
tradeoffs: Hobby research code. primefactors.c is arbitrary precision through GMP mpz_t with trial division, Pollard's rho and GMP-ECM curves spread across cores by OpenMP (memory grows with threads times B1). The two CUDA programs (cgbnprimefactors.cu, ecmcgbnprimefactorsmpi.cu) need CUDA, the author's CGBN fork and OpenMPI; GPU rho gains only about sqrt(k) from k parallel walks. Single-machine ECM tops out around 45 digits per the README; MPI scaling was never tested beyond one node.
caveats: Does not qualify as faster than its baseline. The README ('Performance reality') and primefactors-design.pdf both say neither GPU program is meant to beat the CPU GMP-ECM path: GPU rho is about 4x slower on a 16-digit factor (8.7 s vs 2 s, derived from page data), 'much slower' below 2^64 because of CUDA/MPI start-up cost, and impractical at 19 or more digits. The CPU program wraps GMP and libecm with its own trial division, Pollard's rho and OpenMP curve-parallel ECM scheduling, but makes no comparison against the stock ecm binary or single-threaded GMP-ECM; its 30/35/40-digit wall-clock figures (about 10.5 s, 20.6 s, 5.7 min) come from an unidentified 32-core box. The design doc's ~37 s to ~8.65 s (~4.3x) is GPU-vs-GPU tuning; three further GPU 'optimizations' were reverted as net-slower (Brent batched gcd about 2.6x slower, per-instance ILP 2-4x slower, __launch_bounds__ capping). Kept as a record so the shortcoming is documented. The README says the author used Claude Opus 5.0 for the Pollard's rho code and for testing and bug finding. The author's CGBN fork (steleman/nvidia-cgbn) was not examined.

name: blackwell-tensorcore-kernels
baseline: cuBLAS FP16-in/FP32-accumulate tensor-core GEMM (cublasGemmEx, which dispatches cutlass_80_tensorop_s16816gemm_f16_128x64 on sm_120)
workload: Hand-written FP16-in/FP32-acc GEMM using raw mma.sync m16n8k16 + ldmatrix, XOR-swizzled shared memory, 16-byte vectorized cp.async with a 2-stage pipeline (sweep winner 2 > 3 > 4), 128x128 CTA and 64x64 per-warp register tiles, M=N=K=8192 on a power-capped (300 W) Blackwell workstation GPU; 10 timed calls after one warm-up, CUDA events.
claimed_speedup: 243.2 TFLOP/s vs 229.0 TFLOP/s for cuBLAS tensor-core GEMM at 8192^3 on sm_120 (106.1%, README Phase 2 table; five process runs 243.2-244.0 vs 229.0-229.5); the canonical results/bench.csv re-run after the cuBLAS handle-caching fix has 238.47 vs 225.75 TFLOP/s (about 1.056x, derived from page data); nsys per-kernel durations 4.52 ms vs 4.79 ms. The WMMA kernel in the same repo reaches only 44.4% of cuBLAS-TC, and a CUTLASS 3.x wgmma build reaches 85.5% of cuBLAS on H100 (641 TFLOP/s).
compiler_and_flags: nvcc from CUDA 12.8 via CMake (C++17; CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES 90 120; sm_120a for FP4 rows); no extra nvcc flags set in CMakeLists.txt
hardware: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q (sm_120, CUDA 12.8); cross-generation rows on an H100 80GB SXM5 (sm_90, CUDA 13.1)
tradeoffs: FP16-in/FP32-acc GEMM only; a teaching/measurement repo with an ablation ladder, not a drop-in library; sm_120 tuned; the Hopper path needs CUTLASS 3.x and sm_90a.
caveats: The 6% win is over the older cutlass_80 kernel that cuBLAS picks on this card (a dispatch gap), at one size (8192^3) and one shape, on a power-capped Max-Q part; the README says it is not a cuBLAS replacement and every other row is below cuBLAS (45% for WMMA, 85.5% for the H100 CUTLASS path); the cuBLAS harness originally created a cuBLAS handle on every timed call (fixed 2026-06-02, data re-run 2026-06-04; the post-fix 8192 result still shows the win); CMakeLists sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or extra nvcc flags; recent commits are co-authored by an AI assistant per the commit list; baseline cuBLAS is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.

name: emugemm-cdna
baseline: rocBLAS native FP32 sgemm on AMD MI250 (per-shape tuned solutions)
workload: FP32 GEMM emulated by splitting inputs into three BF16 slices (bf16x3) multiplied on the matrix cores, on one MI250 GCD, three shapes (8192x28672x8192, 16384x8192x8192, 12288^3), with the native rocBLAS FP32 side also tuned per shape; row-major, non-transposed, alpha=1, beta=0 only.
claimed_speedup: bf16x3 vs native FP32 rocBLAS, both sides per-shape solution-tuned, on one MI250 GCD: 45.33 vs 37.52 TFLOP/s at M=8192 N=28672 K=8192 (1.21x), 44.26 vs 37.03 at M=16384 N=8192 K=8192 (1.20x), 45.06 vs 37.02 at M=N=K=12288 (1.22x) (docs/RESULTS_ROUND8.md section C; README summarizes as 1.20-1.22x on every shape tested). Whole node, 8 GCDs at 8192^3: 325.1 vs 278.4 TF (1.17x).
compiler_and_flags: hipcc -O3 -Wno-deprecated-declarations --offload-arch=gfx90a, ROCm 7.2.3
hardware: AMD MI250 (gfx90a), 1 GCD, 104 CU
tradeoffs: Not bit-compatible with FP32: accuracy floor of 4.4355e-6 relative error with the bf16x3 scheme, with a request API (max_rel_err) that reports 'TARGET UNREACHABLE' instead of silently under-delivering; only gfx90a was tested; needs a tuning table per GPU and ROCm version; speed ceiling on MI250 is 1.33x.
caveats: GPU, not CPU. Only three shapes back the 1.20-1.22x; the harness that produced them (emu_tuned.cpp) is not published. bf16x3 has a relative-error floor of 4.4355e-6, so at the tested K (8192-12288) it is less accurate than native FP32 (4.49e-6 vs 1.62e-6 at K=8192 in the same docs): the speedup is at a lower accuracy tier, not like-for-like. The README records that an earlier 2.1x was really 1.21x because the baseline ran rocBLAS's default kernel, and ties the investigation to ROCm/rocm-libraries issue 9985, so the win depends on how well the native baseline is tuned; the tuning table is specific to gfx90a and ROCm 7.2.3. Timing-harness fixes landed 2026-08-13 ('Stop a failed HIP call from returning a plausible-looking timing'), after the Round 8 numbers (2026-07-25); the docs do not say whether the 1.20-1.22x table was re-measured. Last commit co-authored by an AI assistant. Baseline rocBLAS is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.

name: PureBLAS.jl
baseline: OpenBLAS (Julia's bundled build) and AOCL-BLIS (AMD's BLIS fork); the repo's gate is max(OpenBLAS, AOCL)
workload: Single-threaded Float64 and ComplexF64 BLAS 1-3 and LAPACK routines across sizes on three AMD microarchitectures (2619 op/size/machine cells), measured with ABBA-interleaved rounds at locked clock frequency and the median ratio reported.
claimed_speedup: README: about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL), single-threaded. Median PureBLAS/OpenBLAS ratios (Zen3/Zen4/Zen5) from bench/gen_table.md: gemm 1.17/1.08/1.23, potrf 1.11/1.46/1.49, geqrf 1.55/1.79/1.66, getrf 1.17/1.20/1.31, gesvd 1.30/1.27/1.30, syev 1.40/1.44/1.34. Versus AOCL (gen_table_aocl.md): gemm 1.06/1.08/1.07, potrf 1.72/1.37/1.20, geqrf 1.64/1.30/1.24. notes.md: gemm at n=4096 is 1.252/1.280/1.308 (Zen4/Zen3/Zen5) against the faster of OpenBLAS and AOCL.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.13: Project.toml compat julia = "1.13" and LinearAlgebra = "1.13.0", and CI tests only 1.13. The exact patch release, LLVM and OpenBLAS_jll versions used for the sweep are not stated. Default JIT optimization (no custom flags). The harness is bench/plots.jl with BLAS.set_num_threads(1), BLIS_NUM_THREADS/OMP_NUM_THREADS pinned to 1 before AOCL loads, and PureBLAS called through its native API against LinearAlgebra.BLAS. Frequency is locked with bench/fleet_freqlock.sh (boost off, base clock) and runs use ABBA-interleaved rounds with the median ratio reported. Reproduce: taskset -c N julia --project=bench bench/plots.jl bench. AOCL comes from AOCL_jll (amd-main).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X (Zen3), Ryzen 5 7640U (Zen4), Ryzen AI 5 340 (Zen5); measured 2026-09-23 (bench/provenance.md)
tradeoffs: Pure Julia BLAS and LAPACK (about 36k lines) that derives block sizes from detected cache and vector sizes. Inside Julia it reroutes LinearAlgebra through libblastrampoline with PureBLAS.activate(). It can also build libpureblas.so (ILP64 BLAS symbols, embedded Julia runtime) via juliac --trim, which the README calls experimental; that route makes it linkable from C/C++/Rust. Single-threaded only (multithreading deliberately on hold). Singular vectors only for Float64 and complex.
caveats: This is a very young project (9 stars). The benchmarks are the project's own and run only on three AMD Zen machines; the Zen5 box is a laptop whose worst cells move by several points between runs, and there are no Intel or Arm results in the table. The table shows a per-op median with the worst cell, so some cells lose: gemm worst 0.94 on Zen4 and 0.90 on Zen5, and docs/src/notes.md lists trmm on AVX2 at 0.84 as still open. That notes page also says gemm 'gates at every size on all three boxes', which conflicts with the table's worst cells. Above about min(m,n,k) >= 256, gemm uses Strassen-Winograd (notes.md, ROADMAP.md), so the gemm and BLAS-3 ratios compare a fast-matrix-multiplication algorithm with weaker error bounds against OpenBLAS's classical gemm. Some large ratios reflect weak reference implementations rather than kernel speed: nrm2 runs at 8-11x, and methodology.md itself warns about packed Cholesky and small-n AOCL. The README says about 87% of benchmarked cells are at or above max(OpenBLAS, AOCL). methodology.md gives per-cell drift of 1-6% and says about 30% of cells sit within +-5% of parity. notes.md compares potrf against BLASFEO as an MKL proxy (0.87-1.04x), not against MKL directly. All code is single-threaded. The C-callable shared library depends on experimental juliac --trim.

name: TCCG / GETT (Tensor Contraction Code Generator)
language: Python (generator that emits vectorized C code)
baseline: TTGT (transpose-transpose-GEMM-transpose) tensor contraction built on Intel MKL sgemm/dgemm (the repo's default BLAS in config.cfg is MKL); TTGT is TCCG's own backend, not a third-party tensor library
workload: Dense tensor contractions from the repo's benchmark v0.1 (CCSD, AO2MO and intensli test cases, up to 6-D tensors, largest tensor 200 MiB), single and double precision, GFLOPS on one core; GETT versus LoG versus TTGT, and TCCG versus the best of CTF/naive (single) or CTF/TT/naive (double).
claimed_speedup: No numeric table; values read by eye from the figures. benchmark/GETT_LoG_TTGT.png, single precision, one Haswell core: abcde-efbad-cf GETT about 20.5 GFLOPS vs TTGT about 15 (about 1.4x, derived from figure); abcdef-dfgb-geac GETT about 55.5 vs TTGT about 25 (about 2.2x, derived from figure); on compute-bound cases TTGT ties or beats GETT (abcd-aebf-fdec about 67 vs about 75 GFLOPS single precision; in double precision TTGT leads on the last four cases, about 31 vs 37). benchmark/benchmark.png (Fig. 11): TCCG about 55 GFLOPS vs max(CTF, naive) about 13 on abcdef-dfgb-geac, and about 20.5 vs about 2 on abcde-efbad-cf (roughly 10x, derived from figure); near parity with the best other tool on the compute-bound cases. README text only says GETT is 'especially outstanding' for bandwidth-bound contractions.
compiler_and_flags: Intel icpc 16.0.1 20151021, -O3 -xhost -mkl (benchmark/README.md)
hardware: Single core of an Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 (Haswell); ECC enabled, Intel SpeedStep and TurboBoost disabled
stars_or_usage: 40 stars; subject of ACM TOMS 2018 / arXiv 1607.00145. TCL uses TTGT, not GETT (GETT is planned there 'eventually').
tradeoffs: Generator written in Python 2.7 that emits C with AVX2 (AVX-512 experimental; CUDA only for TTGT and LoG); needs Intel icc 15+ (g++ 4.8+ experimental), a BLAS such as MKL, and the HPTT library. GETT has a stated limitation: the product of free-index sizes of each input tensor must be a multiple of 24. Auto-tuning explores up to N candidate implementations at generation time (--maxImplementations). Parallel GETT only on the v0.2.0 branch per the changelog; the published benchmark is single-core.
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repository (raw LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md and COPYING all returned 404 and GitHub shows none), so the code is reference-only even though the sibling HPTT is BSD-3-Clause. The TTGT baseline is the authors' own implementation (HPTT-style transposes plus MKL GEMM) rather than an independent library. Results are single-core, 2016-era hardware and compiler; figures are images, so values are read by eye and approximate. GETT does not win everywhere: on compute-bound contractions TTGT is on par or faster. benchmark.py also drives libtensor, TBLIS, CTF and Eigen scripts (with a hard-coded author path) but the README publishes only the GETT/LoG/TTGT and TCCG-vs-best-of-others figures. The peer-reviewed paper (Springer and Bientinesi, ACM TOMS 2018, arXiv 1607.00145) is not opened (arXiv, ACM and the author's PDF host are blocked); its abstract, seen only as search-engine snippets, reports up to 12.4x over existing approaches for bandwidth-bound contractions and up to 91.3% of peak on compute-bound ones; those numbers are not used above. Abandoned since 2017.

name: COSMA
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK pdgemm (also Cray LibSci, Cray LibSci_acc, CARMA, CTF)
workload: Distributed matrix-matrix multiplication (communication-optimal, with a ScaLAPACK pxgemm wrapper): CP2K RPA benchmark of 128 water molecules (46 tall-and-skinny pdgemm calls) and square matrices, on Piz Daint.
claimed_speedup: README text: 'speedups by factor of up to 8.3x over the second-fastest algorithm' (no supporting table on the README). CP2K RPA 128-H2O on 1024 Piz Daint GPU nodes: the 46 pdgemm calls took 75.26 s with COSMA-GPU vs 139.82 s with Cray LibSci_acc 19.10.1 (README 'approximately 2x faster'; 1.86x derived from page data). On 128 nodes: CPU-only COSMA 1723.62 s vs Intel MKL 19.0.1.144 ScaLAPACK 1836.85 s vs Cray LibSci 5896.45 s for the pdgemm calls (1.07x over MKL derived from page data; table annotation '~10% faster'; whole CP2K run 2238.94 s vs 2305.41 s), COSMA-GPU 257.99 s vs LibSci_acc 338.47 s (1.31x derived from page data; README '25-27% faster than the second best'). Square matrices on 128 nodes vs MKL ScaLAPACK: plot annotated '~2x faster on CPU' (about 300 vs 150 GFlop/s at n=20000, narrowing to about 740 vs 565 at n=120000, read from plot) and '~3x faster on GPU' (GPU COSMA vs CPU-only MKL).
hardware: Piz Daint: CP2K runs on Cray XC50 GPU-partition nodes (Intel Xeon E5-2690 v3 @ 2.60GHz 12 cores, NVIDIA Tesla P100 16GB), 128 and 1024 nodes; square-matrix runs on 128 XC50 (GPU) and XC40 (CPU-only) nodes
tradeoffs: MPI-based, needs a local BLAS (MKL, LibSci, OpenBLAS, BLIS, cuBLAS, rocBLAS) and optionally ScaLAPACK for the wrapper; distributed-memory only; speedups depend on matrix shape and node count; the ScaLAPACK-layout wrapper costs some throughput versus the native layout.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (SC19 Best Student Paper; ACM DL and arXiv:1908.09606 linked from README) but the paper could not be opened in this run (arxiv.org and mirrors blocked); its abstract, seen only as a web-search snippet, reports up to 12.8x (2.2x on average) over ScaLAPACK, CARMA and CTF, while the README says up to 8.3x over the second-fastest algorithm. Eigendecomposition is ahead of OpenBLAS around n=1000 (~2.2e9 vs ~1.2e9) but behind OpenBLAS, BLIS and MKL at n=10^4 (~2.9e9 vs ~3.7e9, ~4.0e9 and ~4.6e9). compiler_and_flags: Not stated beyond 'Eigen is compiled with the -fopenmp flag'. The paper gives no Rust toolchain, faer version, optimization flags or BLAS/MKL versions.

name: fast-matmul (Benson and Ballard)
baseline: Intel MKL dgemm
workload: Sequential square dgemm (N = 1000 to 7500) comparing MKL against Strassen and other fast matrix multiplication algorithms with 1 to 3 recursion levels; run times in ms, median of five trials, data checked into data/all_sequential_algs/square.all.big.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (median of five trials, sequential, ms): Strassen with 2 recursion levels 4836 ms vs MKL 5361 ms at N=4000 (1.11x) and 15790 vs 18075 ms at N=6000 (1.14x); 3 levels 15561 ms at N=6000 (1.16x); 1.04x at N=2000. Best exact-algorithm ratios in the file are 1.19x (<4,2,3> one level, N=1000) and 1.17x (<3,2,3> two levels, N=7500); the approximate Bini algorithm reaches 1.21x. Exact algorithms beat MKL in 329 of 756 (algorithm, N) data points. The PPoPP 2015 paper (cited in README) reports better performance than MKL dgemm; the paper itself was not opened here.
compiler_and_flags: Intel icpc (version not stated; Edison config loads gcc/4.8.0 module) with -O3 -std=c++11 -DNDEBUG -DBLAS_POST, sequential mode, Intel MKL from composer_xe_2013.5.192 (Makefile and make.incs/make.inc.edison)
hardware: NERSC Edison (data/README.md: 'Performance data collected on Edison'); data/all_sequential_algs/README.md says that because of Intel Turbo Boost the performance should be read relative to a 3.2 GHz processor instead of a 2.4 GHz processor; CPU model not stated in the files read
tradeoffs: Code-generated implementations of Strassen, Bini (approximate) and many other fast algorithms for sequential and shared-memory parallel use, calling MKL for base cases; requires MKL. Fast algorithms have weaker numerical stability (README reports errors about 1e-14 to 1e-15 for exact algorithms and larger for approximate ones) and only win for large matrices.
caveats: The 1.11-1.19x figures are derived from raw timing files and exclude the approximate (Bini) algorithm, which is faster still but numerically lossy; some rows in the data are noisy (for example one-level Strassen at N=1000 takes 405.8 ms vs 108.2 ms for MKL). Exact algorithms win in fewer than half of the data points, and the speedup is mainly at N of about 2000 and above. The baseline is a 2013 MKL on a 2014-era supercomputer node, so the ratio against current MKL on modern CPUs is unknown. The paper itself (arXiv 1409.2908) could not be opened here (arxiv.org blocked); the paper claim is from the README citation and search results. Last commit 2021-07-06 (APA algorithms added); core code from 2014-2017.

name: fmm-gen (Generating Families of Practical Fast Matrix Multiplication Algorithms)
baseline: Conventional GEMM. The public harness (the test driver emitted by meta/misc_gen.py) times the generated Strassen-like routine against the project's own BLIS-style dgemm (bl_dgemm in common/dgemm/my_dgemm.c, built on the same AVX 8x4 micro-kernel) and prints the effective GFLOPS of both. MKL is linked (-DUSE_BLAS, -mkl=parallel) only for bl_dgemm_ref. Whether the IPDPS 2017 paper also compared against BLIS or MKL dgemm could not be checked.
workload: Generated Strassen-like fast matrix multiplication (20+ algorithm variants, multi-level, arbitrary matrix sizes and shapes) with the matrix additions fused into GEMM packing and micro-kernels, run on single-core and multicore systems and compared with a performance model.
claimed_speedup: README abstract: 'Our implementations demonstrate a performance benefit over conventional GEMM on single core and multi-core systems.' No numeric speedup appears on any opened page.
compiler_and_flags: icc/icpc 15.0.3 with the GCC 4.9.3 standard library (fmm_artifact.pdf); -O3 -openmp -mavx -fPIC -DUSE_BLAS, linked with -mkl=parallel (common/make.inc.files/make.intel.inc with COMPILER_OPT_LEVEL=O3 from common/sourceme.sh)
hardware: Maverick supercomputer at TACC (fmm_artifact.pdf; CPU model not stated on any opened page)
tradeoffs: Python scripts generate and compile C code per algorithm and partition (OpenMP, config.py and SLURM scripts for cluster runs). Fast matrix multiplication trades numerical stability and extra additions for fewer multiplications, and only helps above some matrix size; no BLAS-compatible drop-in interface is shown.
caveats: No numbers were seen: the IPDPS 2017 paper (Huang, Rice, Matthews, van de Geijn), which holds all the measurements, is on egress-blocked hosts (cs.utexas.edu, arxiv.org 1611.01120). The repo's artifact description gives icc 15.0.3 and 'Maverick supercomputer at TACC' but no CPU model, and says only that relative effective-GFLOPS trends should match the paper's curves. The public test driver compares against the authors' own BLISlab-style dgemm, not against a vendor BLAS. It is a research code generator (Python 2.7 scripts emitting C with AVX inline assembly, SLURM/Maverick paths hard-coded in config.py and sourceme.sh). There have been no commits since 2017-07-07. arbenson/fast-matmul is catalogued separately and is a different code base.

name: TBLIS (Tensor-Based Library Instantiation Software)
baseline: BLAS-based tensor contraction (TTGT: transpose plus GEMM). In the independent tblis-rs benchmark this is NumPy einsum backed by Intel MKL, alongside PyTorch (CPU).
workload: Tensor contraction (a multi-dimensional generalisation of GEMM) done natively with BLIS-style micro-kernels, without the explicit tensor transpositions that a GEMM-based approach needs.
claimed_speedup: Independent tblis-rs README (AMD Ryzen 7945HX, 16 cores, FP64 tensors of shape 96^4), TBLIS vs NumPy (MKL) vs PyTorch CPU. Contiguous: abxy,xycd->abcd 1.90 s vs 2.13 s vs 1.98 s; axyz,ybzx->ab 120.7 vs 207.7 vs 211.1 ms; axby,yacx->abc 124.1 ms vs 29.7 s vs 179.2 ms. TBLIS loses on axyz,xyzb->ab (132.3 vs 63.1 vs 63.4 ms) and on SYRK-shaped axyz,bxyz->ab (96.9 vs 293.2 vs 37.4 ms). Strided (stride 128): abxy,xycd->abcd 2.02 s vs 7.30 s vs 2.10 s; axyz,xyzb->ab 133.1 vs 776.8 vs 204.4 ms. That is about 1.1x (contiguous GEMM-shaped) to 5.8x (strided) over NumPy/MKL and 1.0-1.8x over PyTorch where TBLIS wins (derived from page data). The TBLIS wiki itself claims only 'essentially zero overhead compared to matrix multiplication'.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7945HX, 16 cores (independent tblis-rs benchmark)
stars_or_usage: 145 stars, 39 forks; wrapped by tblis-rs (Rust) and pytblis (Python)
tradeoffs: C and C++ interfaces (tblis.h header in the repo); builds on BLIS-style kernels and its own threading; the wiki lists build/usage pages. Tensor operations only, not a drop-in BLAS replacement.
caveats: The project's own pages (README, wiki home and Research pages) give no benchmark numbers. The numbers come from an independent wrapper author's laptop run (tblis-rs README) that states no compiler, flags or thread settings. There, TBLIS is about 2x slower than MKL/PyTorch on plain GEMM-shaped contiguous contractions and 2.6x slower than PyTorch on a SYRK-shaped one. The wrapper author says TBLIS 'may probably not the best choice' for contractions that map to GEMM. The 200-1000x gaps on batched and trace contractions come from NumPy einsum falling back to a non-BLAS path, so they are not a fair TTGT comparison. The SISC 2018 paper (arXiv 1607.00291) could not be opened (arxiv.org and epubs.siam.org are egress-blocked), so its TTGT comparison numbers, CPU and compiler are unverified.

name: apple-bottom
baseline: Apple Accelerate DGEMM on AMX (and OpenBLAS 6-thread in a Quantum ESPRESSO run)
workload: DGEMM GFLOP/s using double-float (FP32 pair) arithmetic on Metal GPU kernels versus the CPU Accelerate AMX path, plus end-to-end Quantum ESPRESSO Si64 wall time.
claimed_speedup: M2 Max: DGEMM 2048^2 552 GFLOP/s vs Accelerate 468 (+18%), 4096^2 643 vs 566 (+14%). Quantum ESPRESSO Si64: 2:01 with apple-bottom vs 2:28 with OpenBLAS 6-thread (22% faster wall time, 47% less CPU usage); Si128 +12% wall.
compiler_and_flags: clang: -Wall -Wextra -O3 -std=c11 for C and -O3 -fobjc-arc for the Objective-C++ Metal sources (Makefile). The compiler and Xcode version are not stated; the README requires an Xcode 16+ SDK for MTLMathModeSafe.
hardware: Apple M2 Max (38-core GPU, 64 GB unified memory)
tradeoffs: Metal compute shaders with a C API (apple_bottom.h) and a Fortran bridge that routes calls under 100M FLOPs to OpenBLAS/Accelerate and large calls to the GPU; callable from C++. Not IEEE FP64: precision is about 1e-15 (double-float), so results are not bit-exact; ZHERK is slower than the CPU path; single calls under N=1024 are dominated by about 100 us GPU overhead; max dimension 46,340.
caveats: The numbers are first-party from one machine (M2 Max), with no compiler version. The README's DGEMM rows (552 vs 468 GFLOP/s at 2048^2, 643 vs 566 at 4096^2) are not in the committed results. benchmarks/results/2026-04-23-5cfcd52/bench_paper.csv shows 656 vs 560 (1.17x) and 672 vs 604 (1.11x). The README headline says 618 GFLOP/s, and its prior-art table lists Accelerate at 536. benchmarks/bench_dgemm.c times only ab_dgemm on matrices already uploaded to the GPU, so FP64-to-double-float conversion, upload and download fall outside the timed loop, while the Accelerate loop is timed whole. Only 5 iterations are run at N >= 2048, and Accelerate's thread count is left at its default. Per the repo's own results file, the GPU path loses to Accelerate below about N=1024-1536 (0.11x at 256, 0.95x at 1024) and on the Quantum ESPRESSO-like tall-skinny ZGEMM shapes (0.38-0.88x); ZHERK runs at 0.07-0.56x. The 22% Quantum ESPRESSO wall-time win is against 6-thread OpenBLAS, not Accelerate, and the Fortran bridge routes calls under 100M FLOPs to OpenBLAS/Accelerate. Double-float arithmetic gives a ~48-bit mantissa, not IEEE FP64. The normwise error is ~1e-14, but the same results file reports a maximum per-element relative error of up to 2.3e-7 (4096x150, K=150), and 'bit-identical energy' means agreement to the 8 printed decimals of the Ry energy. The project is Apple-GPU only (Metal) and has 3 stars.

name: cbk (Compact Batch Kernels)
baseline: Intel MKL compact kernels (mkl_dgeqrf_compact, mkl_dpotrf_compact, mkl_dtrsm_compact pipeline) and per-matrix LAPACKE (LAPACKE_dgels, LAPACKE_dposv, LAPACKE_dgeqrf)

claimed_speedup: QR solve (1000 matrices, n=10..120, 1 RHS): cbk gels 2.7x geometric mean over LAPACKE_dgels (1.5x at n=100) and cbk-batch 1.25x over MKL-batch; at 64 RHS the gels win drops to 1.3x and cbk-batch to 1.12x over MKL. SPD solve (512 matrices, 1 RHS): fused compact solve 2-9x over LAPACKE_dposv at orders 8-48, 1.4-2.2x at 60-105, geometric mean 1.7x, level with MKL's compact pipeline (0.9-1.0x geomean).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 -march=native (CMake Release); MKL compact paths linked against sequential MKL, all paths driven with the same thread count
hardware: '4-core AVX-512 container' (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Needs the compact (interleaved) layout and packing; many small matrices only; the win disappears for larger matrices; unpivoted LDL^T (no Bunch-Kaufman pivoting); optional MKL-compatible API layer; GCC/Clang vector extensions, OpenMP over groups of V matrices.
caveats: Hardware is not identified beyond '4-core AVX-512 container', so tier C; the benchmark page labels the runs 'indicative'; pack/unpack time is excluded from the timed region; per-matrix LAPACK wins from about n=128-168 (0.25x at n=256) and at nrhs=64 is level or ahead at several sizes (0.85-0.95x at n=80 and 120); SPD solve only matches MKL compact. name: COSTA (communication-optimal distributed matrix redistribution and transpose; ScaLAPACK pxgemr2d/pxtran replacement)
baseline: Intel MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 pdgemr2d (matrix redistribution between block-cyclic layouts)
workload: pdgemr2d redistribution of square double-precision matrices with n = 20000 to 100000 between block-cyclic layouts, once with identical layouts (128x128 blocks) and once with different block sizes (36x36 to 128x128), on 8 Piz Daint nodes of 36 cores each with 16 MPI ranks (4x4 grid); COSTA run without rank relabelling and without memory pools.
claimed_speedup: README chart data labels (docs/costa-same.svg and docs/costa-diff.svg, rendered locally; time in ms, COSTA vs MKL). Same layout: n=20000 14 vs 292; 40000 56 vs 1100; 60000 128 vs 2487; 80000 208 vs 4402; 100000 324 vs 6702 (chart caption '~20x faster'; ratios 19.4x to 21.2x derived from page data). Different layouts: n=20000 188 vs 406; 40000 702 vs 1987; 60000 1608 vs 4579; 80000 2900 vs 8012; 100000 4557 vs 12737 (chart caption 'up to 3x faster'; ratios 2.2x to 2.9x derived from page data). README overview text also says it 'outperforms other scalapack implementations by orders of magnitude in some cases'.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark. CMakeLists.txt adds -funroll-loops (or -Munroll) and a build_type.cmake default that was not read; MKL ScaLAPACK v19.1 is named as the baseline; the MPI implementation and compiler are not given.
hardware: Piz Daint (Cray XC40, CSCS), 8 nodes x 36 cores, 16 MPI ranks as a 4x4 grid; the CPU model is not stated on the page.
stars_or_usage: 14 stars, 8 forks; used by COSMA, which is used by CP2K (README)
tradeoffs: Needs MPI 3 and OpenMP and CMake 3.12 or newer. Drop-in ScaLAPACK wrappers (pdgemr2d, pstran, pdtran, pctranu/c and complex variants) take effect when COSTA is linked before ScaLAPACK. Handles arbitrary irregular layouts, not only block-cyclic, and can transform several layouts in one communication round at the cost of larger messages and more memory. Optional rank relabelling can remove communication entirely when layouts differ only by a rank permutation (not used in these charts).
caveats: The baseline is MKL's ScaLAPACK redistribution routine pdgemr2d, not a BLAS or LAPACK kernel, so it only loosely fits the blas-lapack baselines. The identical-layout case (about 20x) most likely reflects MKL's slow generic path when no data needs to move (my inference, not stated by the authors). The charts are first-party; MKL and MPI settings, the compiler, flags and CPU model are not stated, and the README does not say which repetition or statistic is plotted (the miniapp's n_rep default is 2 and it prints every repetition's time in ms for both COSTA and ScaLAPACK). The benchmark code is public (miniapps/pxgemr2d_miniapp.cpp, pxtran_miniapp.cpp). The peer-reviewed paper (Kabic, Pintarelli, Kozhevnikov, VandeVondele, ISC 2021, Springer LNCS pp. 217-236; arXiv 2106.06601) is cited in the README but could not be opened (Springer and arXiv are blocked in this session); a check that can open it should consider B and whether its numbers match the README charts. name: fast_matmul (NinjadenMu; didactic BLIS-style SGEMM for Apple M4)
baseline: OpenBLAS as called through NumPy (float32 A @ B in scripts/openblas.py)
workload: Square float32 matrix multiplication for n = 100, 200, 300, ... each run once until a cumulative 5 s budget is used (scripts/driver.py), custom BLIS-style code versus NumPy with OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 and with default threads.
claimed_speedup: README text: the single-threaded BLIS-style implementation is 'comparable to an OpenBLAS build targeting Apple Silicon (with the difference being too small for me to reliably measure)' and the multi-threaded one is 'noticeably faster (probably due to better load balancing on my particular M4 spec)'; '~200x faster (40x faster with just one thread)' is against the project's own naive loop, not OpenBLAS. Read by eye from plots/plot.png: single-threaded OpenBLAS reaches n=3100 at about 4.55 s cumulative versus single-threaded BLIS-style n=3000 at about 4.08 s, and the two curves overlap point for point (parity). Multi-threaded BLIS-style reaches n=4500 at about 4.08 s versus multi-threaded OpenBLAS n=4200 at about 4.7 s; cumulative time to reach n=4200 is about 3.1 s versus about 4.7 s, roughly 1.5x (derived from page data, read by eye). The per-step times at n=3000 (about 0.5 s) imply roughly 100-120 GFLOPS single-threaded for both sides (derived from page data, read by eye).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile: clang -O3 -ffast-math -march=native (commented alternative -mcpu=apple-m4), OpenMP via Homebrew libomp, -fno-vectorize on the early didactic versions. The clang version is not stated and neither are the NumPy or OpenBLAS versions.
hardware: Apple M4 (README: 'my Apple M4'); core configuration and RAM not stated.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks; same author as MuBLIS (which is already on the known list)
tradeoffs: Teaching code: float32 only, square matrices only, column-major, no transposes or alpha/beta and no BLAS interface. ARM NEON intrinsics (Apple Silicon only; the README says x86 needs retuned block sizes and AVX kernels). Fixed 12x8 register tile, cache block sizes tuned by scripts/tuner.py, OpenMP dynamic scheduling for the parallel version. No LICENSE file, so the code cannot be copied.
caveats: The benchmark treats the two sides unequally. The custom side runs ./bench with one untimed warm-up call and then one timed call on already-allocated, already-touched buffers (C is zeroed once before the warm-up and not re-zeroed; utils/bench.c). The baseline times a single NumPy A @ B call in a fresh Python process with no warm-up and with the result matrix allocated inside the timed region (scripts/openblas.py). There is one measurement per n, no repeats or variance, the metric is 'largest n within a cumulative time budget' rather than GFLOPS, and the custom code is built with -ffast-math. The README does not say which NumPy or OpenBLAS build was used; because OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 changes the baseline curve and the implied single-thread rate is about 110 GFLOPS, the baseline was evidently a NEON-path OpenBLAS rather than Apple Accelerate (inferred, not stated). OpenBLAS issue #6073 (2026-09-29, Apple M4 Pro, OpenBLAS develop 63d7f22) reports 707-766 GFLOPS single-thread OpenBLAS SGEMM and 1127-1185 GFLOPS for Accelerate, so the platform's fastest BLAS (Accelerate/SME) and SME-enabled OpenBLAS were not compared and would likely beat this NEON code by a wide margin. Parity is the only single-thread result, and the author attributes the multi-thread gap to load balancing on his particular M4, which may be a P/E-core scheduling artifact. Numbers are read by eye from the plot image. The author's deep-dive post on ninjadenmu.github.io is egress-blocked. No license (no LICENSE file, none in the GitHub sidebar).

name: LoopVectorization.jl
baseline: Intel MKL dgemm (single-threaded, via Julia LinearAlgebra.mul!)
workload: Float64 matrix multiply C = A*B with M=191, K=189, N=171, written as a plain triple loop under the @turbo macro, single thread, BenchmarkTools minimum time.
claimed_speedup: README example: @turbo triple-loop gemm minimum 111.722 microseconds (110.5 GFLOPS) vs MKL mul! (BLAS.set_num_threads(1), vendor :mkl) minimum 117.221 microseconds (105.3 GFLOPS) at M=191, K=189, N=171, about 5% faster (derived from page data); the same loop with only @inbounds @fastmath took 4.891 ms (about 44x slower than @turbo, derived from page data). The project's own docs (docs/src/examples/matrix_multiplication.md) say that for C = A*B LoopVectorization 'falls behind MKL's gemm beyond 70x70 or so', and for A'*B it is 'well behind MKL and OpenBLAS' because it does not pack.
compiler_and_flags: Julia (version not stated) with the @turbo macro; MKL selected with BLAS.set_num_threads(1) and BLAS.vendor() == :mkl.
tradeoffs: Julia only, not callable from C++ without embedding Julia. It is a loop-vectorizing macro, not a BLAS: @turbo reorders loops, does no bounds checking (misuse can segfault), supports only simple loop nests, and does no cache blocking or packing, so the README says parallelism and cache efficiency are left to the user and the gemm kernel suits small to medium matrices.
caveats: Single-shape, single-thread micro-benchmark with a margin of about 5%; the CPU is not named (README: 'the CPU I'm running these benchmarks on', Float64 SIMD width 8, which implies AVX-512) and the Julia version is not stated. The project's own documentation (docs/src/examples/matrix_multiplication.md, read from the repo source since JuliaSIMD.github.io is egress-blocked) says LoopVectorization falls behind MKL's gemm beyond about 70x70 for C = A*B and is well behind MKL and OpenBLAS for A'*B (no packing, no memory modelling), so the README win does not generalize to larger matrices; its main measured advantage is over compiled loops (Clang, gfortran, icc, ifort, Eigen). The benchmark harness in benchmark/ (loadsharedlibs.jl, looptests.c/.f90, looptestseigen.cpp) lists flags such as clang -Ofast -march=native and g++ -O3 -march=native for Eigen. @turbo performs no bounds checking and may reorder operations; misuse gives wrong results. The package is in maintenance mode under the SciML Small Grants programme. Julia-only, so it fits the 'then any' language filter rather than C++. Larger-size Julia work with this approach is Octavian.jl (already catalogued).

claimed_speedup: SNIPPET ONLY (search-engine summaries of the tables in arXiv 0811.1714 / ACM TOMS Algorithm 898; the paper itself could not be opened). M4RI-20080821 vs Magma, 64-bit 2.33 GHz Core 2 Duo: n=10,000 2.210 s vs 1.504 s; n=16,384 8.670 s vs 6.074 s; n=20,000 16.030 s vs 10.721 s; n=32,000 58.730 s vs 43.197 s (about 1.47x, 1.43x, 1.50x and 1.36x, derived from snippet data); GAP 4.4 takes 6.130 s at n=10,000. 64-bit 2.6 GHz Opteron: n=10,000 2.656 s vs 2.490 s (about 1.07x); n=16,384 10.260 s vs 10.490 s; n=20,000 18.156 s vs 17.730 s; n=32,000 67.237 s vs 67.840 s (parity, within about 2% either way). tradeoffs: C library for GF(2) only (GF(2^e) is the separate M4RIE library). GPL-2.0-or-later is copyleft. Algorithms: M4RM and Strassen-Winograd multiplication at O(n^log2(7)), PLE factorisation, and M4RI row echelon / inversion at O(n^3/log n).

name: NanoGEMM
baseline: OpenBLAS (through NumPy 2.2.x sgemm / matmul)
workload: Single-threaded float32 square matmul (16x16 to 128x128) called from Python through NumPy arrays. The README states 'median latency across 10,000 iterations with cache pre-warming', but benchmarks/bench_vs_numpy.py times the mean per-call latency of one loop (25,000 to 50 iterations depending on size) and notebooks/benchmark.ipynb takes the best of 3 loop means (10,000/3,000/1,000 iterations); NumPy's `A @ B` allocates a new output each call while NanoGEMM writes into a preallocated `out=` buffer.
claimed_speedup: NanoGEMM vs NumPy: 16x16 1.71 us vs 4.05 us (2.36x; 0.68 us for the C kernel, 5.5x); 24x24 2.67 us vs 19.39 us (7.26x); 32x32 4.21 us vs 7.14 us; 48x48 11.15 us vs 12.65 us; 64x64 13.89 us vs 19.69 us (1.42x); 128x128 115.90 us vs 89.44 us (0.77x, slower).
compiler_and_flags: GCC -O3 -mavx2 -mfma / MSVC /O2 /arch:AVX2; NumPy 2.2+ linked against OpenBLAS; single thread
hardware: Unnamed x86-64 CPU with AVX2+FMA (no model given); INT8 and batched tests on Google Colab CPU
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; packaged on PyPI, conda-forge and an APT PPA
tradeoffs: Static AVX2/FMA (6x16) and ARM NEON (4x8) register-tiled micro-kernels, no JIT, no threads, about 100 KB binary. Strongest only for matrices up to about 64x64; float32 and int8 only. The C kernel is in src/nanogemm_kernel.c/.h so it can be used from C or C++, but the project is packaged and documented as a Python extension.
caveats: First-party; CPU model not stated. Timed through Python, so NumPy per-call dispatch (README quotes 3-5 us fixed cost) dominates the small sizes; no direct cblas_sgemm call is compared. The README says 'median over 10,000 iterations' but the shipped benchmark code reports mean loop time (notebook: best of 3), and only the baseline pays for allocating its output (NanoGEMM uses a preallocated out= buffer). The headline 7.26x at 24x24 rests on a NumPy outlier (19.39 us at 24x24 vs 7.14 us at 32x32); 24 and 48 come from the Colab notebook, not bench_vs_numpy.py. NumPy/OpenBLAS thread count is not pinned. Slower than NumPy at 128x128 (0.77x). The INT8 table compares against NumPy int8 `@`, which does not use BLAS and returns int8 (wrapping) while NanoGEMM returns int32, so it is not a like-for-like baseline. name: ReLAPACK
baseline: reference LAPACK, OpenBLAS LAPACK routines and Intel MKL LAPACK routines
workload: Recursive implementations of LAPACK compute kernels (LU, Cholesky, triangular inversion, Sylvester and Lyapunov solvers and others) that call BLAS; README says they outperform LAPACK and improve on OpenBLAS and MKL.
claimed_speedup: README: 'ReLAPACK's routines not only outperform the reference LAPACK but also improve upon the performance of tuned implementations, such as OpenBLAS and MKL.' No numbers on the README page.
stars_or_usage: 44 stars; vendored in OpenBLAS (relapack/ directory, optional build); published as ACM TOMS Algorithm 979
tradeoffs: Drop-in LAPACK interface (links in front of LAPACK, replaces only the covered routines); needs a BLAS plus LAPACK unblocked kernels underneath; covers only routines where recursion helps (see coverage.md); C code with Fortran-style interfaces.
caveats: No numbers anywhere in the repo. The measurements are in Peise and Bientinesi, 'Recursive Algorithms for Dense Linear Algebra: The ReLAPACK Collection' (arXiv:1602.06763; web-search results give ACM TOMS 44(2), 16:1-16:19, 2017, as Algorithm 979), which this run could not open (arxiv.org, ar5iv, Semantic Scholar and the HPAC site are blocked); its abstract, seen in search snippets, says only that ReLAPACK 'clearly outperforms reference LAPACK, and even improves upon the performance of optimized libraries' in many scenarios. A check with access to the paper should raise the tier to B. Last commit is a 2022 typo fix; the code dates from 2016-2017 and was compared with OpenBLAS and MKL versions of that era. Linking with MKL requires COMPLEX_FUNCTIONS_AS_ROUTINES=1.
found_via: Candidate from domain knowledge (recursive LAPACK); opened github.com/HPAC/ReLAPACK, its README and commits page; WebSearch for the ReLAPACK paper title (paper itself not reachable).

verification.tier_reason: The README (and config.md, coverage.md, test/README.md, examples/README.md) state that ReLAPACK outperforms reference LAPACK and improves on OpenBLAS and MKL but give no numbers; the peer-reviewed paper that holds the measurements (arXiv:1602.06763, ACM TOMS Algorithm 979) could not be opened, so only a qualitative claim was seen.
verification.notes: Downgraded C to D because no numbers were visible on any reachable page; do not reject: it is notable (OpenBLAS ships a copy under relapack/, peer-reviewed TOMS algorithm). Recommend an Opus retier check against the arXiv paper, which likely yields B. Metadata verified: MIT, 44 stars, last commit 2022-02-20, abandoned.

corrected_fields.caveats: The README quantifies nothing. The numbers are in the cited paper, Peise and Bientinesi, 'Recursive Algorithms for Dense Linear Algebra: The ReLAPACK Collection' (arXiv:1602.06763; a search snippet reports publication as ACM TOMS Algorithm 979, vol 44(2), 2017), which this run could not open (arxiv.org, ACM and Semantic Scholar are blocked in this container), so the tier is set from the README claim alone and a verifier with access to the paper could raise it to B or A. Last commit is a typo fix; the code dates from 2016-2017 and compares against OpenBLAS and MKL versions of that era.

name: sme-gemm
baseline: Apple Accelerate (cblas_sgemm, which may use AMX); also candle and burn
workload: Unpacked strided GEMM TF/s on an Apple M5 for f32, f16 and f64 across 256^3 to 4096^3 and rectangular shapes, via examples/vs_accelerate, vs_candle and vs_burn.
claimed_speedup: Unpacked strided GEMM vs Accelerate on Apple M5, TF/s: f32 512^3 1.97 vs 1.61, 1024^3 2.34 vs 2.03, 4096^3 2.14 vs 2.07, 4096x512x512 2.29 vs 1.94, 16384x512x512 2.30 vs 2.00; Accelerate leads at 256^3 (1.50 vs 1.67) and 2048^3 (2.04 vs 2.14). f64 ahead at every shape: 256^3 0.46 vs 0.44, 512^3 0.58 vs 0.46, 1024^3-4096^3 0.55 vs 0.52, tall shapes 0.61 vs 0.52. f16 (Accelerate has no f16 path; compared with upcast + sgemm + downcast): 1024^3 3.83 vs 1.40, 2048^3 4.32 vs 1.70, 4096x11008x4096 3.32 vs 1.89. Dispatch latency (us/call, f32): Accelerate cblas_sgemm is faster at every square size 8^3-256^3 (e.g. 128^3 3.2 vs 7.9 packed SME); packed SME wins the 1x4096x4096 decode shape (634 vs 836).
compiler_and_flags: C kernels (csrc/, arm_sme.h) built by build.rs through the cc crate with -mcpu=apple-m4 -ffp-contract=fast -O3; M5-only TUs add +sme-f16f16/+sme-b16b16/+sme-f64f64/+sme-i16i64 target features behind a runtime probe. Rust release profile opt-level=3, lto="thin"; rust-version 1.97 (MSRV). Apple clang and rustc versions not stated. examples/vs_accelerate.rs: 3 warm-up calls each plus a 60-call clock warm-up, then 12 interleaved passes of 40 iterations (4 for large shapes), best per-call time kept for both backends.
hardware: Apple M5 (SVL=512, P- and E-cluster SME units), best-of-N
tradeoffs: Rust crate of hand-written SME kernels for Apple M4 and newer (f16/bf16/f32/f64, i8/i16, 4-bit weights), fused epilogues, batched and pre-packed GEMM, flash attention. Rust-only API, not a BLAS ABI. Native f16 accumulation changes numerical behavior (error grows about sqrt(K)).
caveats: Baseline is Apple Accelerate, not OpenBLAS/MKL/Eigen/BLIS, so it is off the category's usual incumbents (Accelerate may itself use the SME/AMX unit). Wins are small and mixed for f32 (Accelerate leads at 256^3 and 2048^3, and has lower per-call latency for every size up to 256^3); f64 margins are 5-26%; the large f16 margin is against an upcast-to-f32 path because Accelerate has no f16 GEMM. Some f16 cells come from the candle adapter or the inference_value example rather than vs_accelerate. Apple Silicon M4+ on macOS only (scalar reference fallback elsewhere); the kernels are C behind Rust bindings and use both the P- and E-cluster SME units via GCD. First-party, best-of-N timing, constant-valued inputs, brand-new repo (first commit 2026-08-03) with 0 stars.

name: tblis-strassen (Strassen's Algorithm for Tensor Contraction)
baseline: TBLIS regular tensor-contraction routine (Strassen level L=0 in the same code); TBLIS is itself the state-of-the-art non-BLAS contraction library
workload: Synthetic tensor contractions and the Tensor Contraction Benchmark (TCCG 'tcb' set) on single-core, multicore and distributed-memory systems, using Strassen's algorithm inside a transposition-free contraction.
claimed_speedup: README: 'achieving up to 1.3x speedup'.
compiler_and_flags: icc/icpc 15.0.3 with the GCC 4.9.3 standard library for single-node runs, mpicc/mpicxx from mvapich2 2.1 for distributed runs; configure --disable-shared --enable-config=sandybridge (artifact.pdf, README); other compiler flags not stated
hardware: Maverick supercomputer at TACC (artifact.pdf; CPU model not stated on any opened page)
tradeoffs: Research code built on a copy of TBLIS and BLIS; test_strassen driver and tcb_run_*.sh scripts; build and run steps are described in artifact.pdf in the repo. Strassen adds extra additions and workspace use, and only pays off for large enough contractions.
caveats: The 1.3x is a best case ('up to') from the authors' own runs, measured against the same code with Strassen turned off (L=0 runs the regular TBLIS contraction). Per-case numbers, the CPU model and the speedups on the Tensor Contraction Benchmark are in the SISC paper, which could not be opened (arxiv.org 1704.03092 and the publisher are egress-blocked). The code appears to be built on a 2016-era TBLIS code base: the LICENSE is TBLIS's BSD-3-Clause, copyright Devin Matthews 2015-2016. Build instructions configure only the Sandy Bridge AVX kernels, and the distributed scripts assume TACC Maverick SLURM queues. There have been no commits since 2017-07-07. This is a research artifact, not a maintained library; for production use the current TBLIS (MatthewsResearchGroup/tblis) is the maintained code base, but it has no Strassen path.
found_via: GitHub topic page https://github.com/topics/tensor-contraction (listing flame/tblis-strassen); README and commits page opened; the claim was cross-checked against the TBLIS wiki Research page.

name: Tiled-MM
baseline: NVIDIA cublasXt (vanilla and manually tuned with 4000 tile size and pinned memory)
workload: Double-precision square column-major GEMM (alpha=beta=1) on matrices stored in host memory, tiled and pipelined to one GPU (also ported to AMD via rocBLAS).
claimed_speedup: README chart docs/performance.svg (tables of numbers rendered as an image): DGEMM time Tiled-MM vs cublasXt vanilla 83 vs 167 ms at n=4000 up to 16205 vs 76882 ms at n=32000 (2.0x to 4.7x, derived from page data); throughput 4044.18 vs 852.42 GFlop/s at n=32000 (89.87% vs 18.94% of 4500 GFlop/s peak). Against tuned cublasXt: 83 vs 127 ms at n=4000 (1.5x, derived), 352 vs 412 ms at n=8000 (1.17x, derived), and parity within about 1% from n=12000 to 32000 (tuned cublasXt slightly faster at 20000: 4252 vs 4282 ms, and 28000: 11113 vs 11171 ms).
hardware: One Piz Daint (Cray XC50) node with an NVIDIA P100 GPU (chart states peak 4500 GFlop/s, CUDA toolkit 10.1); host CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Host-pointer tiled GEMM for CUDA or ROCm; user-selectable tile size per dimension and stream count; reusable context for repeated calls; templated over data types.
caveats: Numbers exist only inside the README's chart image (docs/performance.svg), not in text. The clear win is over vanilla cublasXt (2.0-4.7x); against a hand-tuned cublasXt (tile 4000, pinned memory) it is 1.5x at n=4000 and 1.17x at n=8000 and only on par from n=12000 upward. Compiler and flags for the run are not stated (README build example uses gcc-8; CMake defaults to Release); host CPU not stated. The chart sizes (4000-32000) do not match examples/compare.sh (4000-20000), so the exact run script is not published. Correctness bugs were fixed after the 2019 measurements ('Fixed the wrong results bug for certain tile sizes', Feb 2024; synchronization issue that 'would sometimes' return an incorrect result, Jun 2024). P100/CUDA 10.1-era data. Baseline cublasXt is not one of OpenBLAS, MKL, Eigen or BLIS.

name: batmat (batched small-matrix linear algebra)
baseline: Intel MKL and OpenBLAS (per-matrix BLAS/LAPACK calls via the BLAS interface), BLASFEO
workload: Batches (depth 8) of small dense matrices, sizes 1 to 1024, for gemm, syrk, trmm, trsm, trtri, potrf, syrk-potrf, QR and others, single-threaded (OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, taskset -c 0), batmat interleaved SIMD kernels versus per-matrix calls of BLAS libraries, BLASFEO and Eigen; benchmark source only, no published results.
claimed_speedup: README gives no numbers: 'Batmat performs exceptionally well on matrices smaller than around 100x100 (that fit in the L2 cache), where it outperforms traditional scalar linear algebra libraries such as Intel MKL, OpenBLAS, and BLASFEO (especially for triangular or symmetric matrices).'
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14 or later required (Clang and ICX supported); SIMD flags come from the user's Conan profile (scripts/dev/profiles); benchmark target run with Google Benchmark --benchmark_min_time=0.1s, 3 repetitions, random interleaving. Actual flags of the author's runs are not published.
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; linear-algebra backend of the Cyqlone optimal-control solver (kul-optec/cyqlone)
tradeoffs: Data must be stored in an interleaved 'compact' layout (one SIMD lane per matrix of the batch), so it helps only when many same-sized small matrices are processed together (for example stages of an optimal control problem) and is not a drop-in replacement for single-matrix BLAS. Needs GCC 14+ (or Clang with the GSI-HPC simd library, or ICX), Conan and the guanaqo dependency. LGPL-3.0 licence. Routines include gemm, syrk, trmm, trsm, potrf, trtri and fused variants.
caveats: The README states a win over MKL, OpenBLAS and BLASFEO but publishes no numbers, no CPU model and no result files (docs/ holds only logos and Doxygen config). The benchmark sources exist (benchmarks/*.cpp, including benchmarks/mkl/potrf-mkl.cpp) and run the baselines as ordinary per-matrix calls (MKL dpotrf, guanaqo BLAS xgemm) rather than MKL's compact or batched APIs, so the comparison is batched-SIMD against non-batched calls. The Cyqlone paper (Pas and Patrinos, arXiv 2512.09058), whose abstract per a search snippet says batched routines 'significantly outperform BLAS and BLASFEO for the small matrices that arise in optimal control', and a Zenodo benchmark record could not be opened (arXiv and Zenodo blocked), so no numbers are recorded. Very new, 3 stars.

name: Admiral
baseline: FFTW 3 (FFTW_MEASURE, single thread; version and build flags of the system fftw3 not stated in the admiral repo, while the author's separate fft_bench uses FFTW 3.3.11); also ducc0 (commit c4dda23)
workload: Complex and real 1-D (19 lengths for the FFTW comparison, 61 for ducc0) and N-D (9 shapes for FFTW, 27 for ducc0) FFTs in float and double on a 16-core AVX-512 Xeon, timed with nanobench (min across repetitions) after an accuracy gate against a reference DFT.
claimed_speedup: At 1 thread beats FFTW_MEASURE by 1.34x (1-D) and 1.43x (N-D), both precisions pooled; vs ducc0 at 1 thread 2.18x (f64) / 2.70x (f32) on 1-D, 1.12x / 1.41x on 2-D, 1.60x / 1.67x on 3-D; at 16 threads vs ducc0 2-D 1.27x / 1.58x and 3-D 2.67x / 3.53x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, CMake 'release' preset: CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's GCC default -O3 -DNDEBUG), ADM_TARGET_ARCH=native (-march=native), ADM_USE_FAST_MATH=ON (-ffast-math, the default), LTO off; sweep of 2026-08-24 per benchmark/README.md. FFTW is the system fftw3/fftw3f found via pkg-config, configure flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Xeon w5-3435X (16 physical cores, AVX-512)
stars_or_usage: 0 stars, 0 forks, 188 commits (oldest commit on the first commits page 2026-09-11; the README sweep is dated 2026-08-24, so the history goes back further)
tradeoffs: Needs C++20 (buildable at C++17 with -DADM_CXX_STANDARD=17); GCC 14+ or Clang 19+ recommended, older compilers generate worse code. Compile time is long (compiled codelets up to radix 64 via xsimd and poet). Default -march=native binaries are not portable. Three interfaces: C++, C and an FFTW-subset drop-in (<admiral/fftw3.h>). Any size and rank, float/double/long double; no wisdom files (cost model at effort::estimate, plan-time race at automatic). Threads stay serial below about 32k elements.
caveats: Benchmark is run by the library author, and the same author (DiamonDinoia) wrote the fft_bench shootout repo, so that repo is not independent evidence. Only pooled ratios are published (FFTW: 19 1-D lengths and 9 N-D shapes, both precisions pooled), no per-size times. Admiral is built with -ffast-math by default (relaxed IEEE, flushed denormals), though every timed size is accuracy-gated against a reference DFT; FFTW's version and build flags (e.g. whether AVX-512 codelets were enabled) are not stated for the w5-3435X sweep. In bench_fft.cpp the 1-D ducc0 arm calls ducc0_forward_fft, which allocates and zero-fills a fresh output std::vector inside the timed lambda while Admiral reuses a preallocated buffer, so the 1-D ducc0 ratios (2.18x/2.70x) carry allocation overhead that matters most at small N; the N-D ducc0 arm and the FFTW arm use preallocated buffers. In the fft_bench plots (images only) Admiral is roughly tied with MKL and FFTW over much of the 1-D range single-threaded on Xeon Platinum 8362 and EPYC 9474F, with MKL ahead at small sizes on Intel, FFTW ahead at small sizes on AMD, Sleef ahead at mid and large sizes on EPYC 9474F, and multi-threaded MKL clearly ahead for large 1-D on the Intel node; that README marks its MKL-omp numbers for rome and genoa as invalid. 16-thread 1-D vs threaded ducc0 is mixed per benchmark/README.md (geomean 0.33x to 1.82x by size). Very new project; the README says much of the code and cost-model tuning was done with Claude and that the author does not claim the fastest FFT. License is BSD-3-Clause-Attribution (adds an acknowledgment clause naming the Admiral FFT library), which the SPDX license list marks as not OSI-approved, hence usability reference.
