name: AppleSiliconFFT
baseline: Apple vDSP/Accelerate FFT (CPU)
workload: Batched single-precision complex FFT on the Apple M1 GPU (Metal kernels), N=4096, batch=256, GFLOPS vs vDSP on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: Apple M1, N=4096 batch=256 (README): radix-8 Stockham 138.45 GFLOPS (1.78 us/FFT) vs vDSP 107.0 GFLOPS (2.29 us/FFT), +29%; in-place Cooley-Tukey with simdgroup_matrix 128 GFLOPS (+20%); radix-4 Stockham 113.6 GFLOPS (+6%). Apple M6 (m6/README.md): one-pass N=8192/16384 kernels 2.2x / 1.85x faster than MPSGraph (4.4x with FP16 storage); per m6/results/stage3_onepass.stdout this holds at DRAM-resident batches (N=8192 batch 2048: 604.4 vs 257.4 GF hot; N=16384 batch 1024: 547.2 vs 296.0 GF cold), while at L2-resident N=16384 MPSGraph is faster (805.2 vs 220.4 GF). CPU SME2 radix-8 FFT 'up to 5.3x' vDSP is the column-FFT case (m6/results/stage5_col.stdout, N=512 x W=256 matrix, 1 thread: SME 263.4 GF vs vDSP transpose+fftm+transpose 49.6 GF); for contiguous batched FFTs (stage5_fft.stdout) SME-CG beats vDSP_fft by 1.21x to 3.52x, but only 0.51x to 1.76x once packing into the SME layout is counted, i.e. slower than vDSP at N>=512.
compiler_and_flags: M1: xcrun metal + metallib; host swiftc -O -framework Metal -framework Accelerate (Xcode and macOS versions not stated). M6: swift build -c release for the M6Bench harness; SME2 C kernels clang -O3 -mcpu=apple-m4 (build line recorded in each m6/results log header).
hardware: Apple M1 (main README; GPU core count and macOS version not stated); Apple M6, macOS 27.0 (m6/README.md; logs dated 2026-09-26)
tradeoffs: GPU-only Metal kernels, power-of-two sizes 256 to 16384 (four-step for larger), single precision; N=4096 batch workload; Apple Silicon only.
caveats: The M1 +29% compares the whole GPU against a single CPU core: GPU kernels are timed from the command buffer's gpuStartTime to gpuEndTime (GPU execution only, dispatch overhead excluded), while the vDSP baseline (benchmarks/Sources/vdsp_baseline_bench.swift) is one thread looping vDSP_fft_zop (radix-2 setup, split complex) and timing the wall clock; a multithreaded vDSP baseline was not measured. The M1 headline is for one size (N=4096, batch 256); the multi-size table (N=256 to 16384, batch 64) lists GFLOPS without vDSP columns. On M6 the one-pass kernels beat MPSGraph only at DRAM-resident batches (MPSGraph is 3.7x faster at L2-resident N=16384, derived from page data), and the SME2 'up to 5.3x' figure is for column FFTs of a matrix; for contiguous batches with packing counted the SME path is slower than vDSP at N>=512. Hot and cold runs differ by up to 3.7x per the m6 README. The M6 hardware and macOS 27.0 may be hard for a verifier to reproduce. Research code (Metal kernels, Swift host harnesses, C SME2 kernels), not a packaged C++ library. Results come from the author's own preprints (arXiv 2603.27569 for the M1 paper and 2609.32237 for the M6 paper per search results), not peer reviewed as far as could be checked. Baseline is Apple-specific (vDSP, MPSGraph), not FFTW, MKL or KissFFT. name: dft_simd (vertical-SIMD FFTW codelets)
baseline: FFTW 3 (planner/execute API with its SSE/AVX codelets, single and 8-transform advanced interface)
workload: Bulk transformation of short single-precision real-to-complex DFTs: 2^24 (16.8 million) transforms of 60 samples in the original test and of 1024 samples in the 2025 AVX2 test, and 2^25 transforms of 1024 samples in the 2025 AVX512 test (nvec=16), with codelets generated by FFTW's genfft and compiled for AVX/AVX2/AVX512 vector types so that 8 (or 16) transforms run side by side ('vertical' SIMD). FFTW cases use fftwf_plan_dft_r2c_1d or fftwf_plan_many_dft_r2c with FFTW_MEASURE.
claimed_speedup: 2025, AMD EPYC 9474F single core: 60-sample AVX2 codelet with fixed strides 79 ms vs FFTW aligned single-DFT plan 858 ms (10.8x per the README); 1024-sample AVX2 7,270 ms vs 12,136 ms (1.67x, derived from page data; README says about 1.6x) and AVX512 10,610 ms vs 24,657 ms (2.3x). 2018, MacBook Pro i5-5287U: 8-transform 60-sample codelet 379 ms vs best FFTW plan 1,912 ms (about 5x per the README) and 207 ms with compile-time strides. 2018, Xeon E5-2650 v4 with gcc 4.8.5: AVX codelet 220 ms vs best FFTW case 2,194 ms (a factor of 10 per the README).
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt adds -march=native and -O3 (also for RelWithDebInfo), C++11; README build uses -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo. Apple LLVM 9.0.0 (clang-900.0.39.2) for the 2018 MacBook run and gcc 4.8.5 (Red Hat 4.8.5-16) for the Xeon E5-2650 v4 run; compiler for the 2025 EPYC run not stated; FFTW from MacPorts for the 2018 run, FFTW version and build not stated otherwise
hardware: 2018: MacBook Pro, Intel Core i5-5287U 2.90GHz (AVX2+FMA), FFTW from MacPorts; 2025: AMD EPYC 9474F, single core.
tradeoffs: Not a drop-in library: demonstration of adapting FFTW's genfft scalar codelets to SIMD vector types so that 8 (AVX2) or 16 (AVX512) independent transforms are processed per call ('vertical' SIMD). Only tiny fixed sizes (60 and 1024 real-to-complex single-precision); callers must batch and interleave data into vector lanes; x86 AVX2/AVX512 only (OpenCL variant is experimental); fixed-stride version trades runtime flexibility; codelets must be generated with FFTW's OCaml genfft, so code is GPL.
caveats: Author's own benchmark of a bulk short-DFT workload where FFTW's horizontal SIMD is inefficient, so it does not show a win on single large transforms. The test code fills the input directly in the interleaved SIMD layout before the loop and re-transforms the same in-cache buffer, so packing into and out of that layout is not timed; when FFTW is given the same interleaved layout (FFTW_Aligned_TransposedEight) it is slower than its own contiguous plans. Times appear to be gtest per-test durations, which would also count FFTW_MEASURE planning in the FFTW cases (small next to the totals). The AVX512 column runs twice as many transforms (2^25) as the AVX2 columns, so compare ratios only within a column. The 2025 EPYC table names no compiler or FFTW build. It is a test and demonstration repository rather than a packaged library; users generate codelets for their own sizes with genfft. GPL-2.0-or-later (source headers; LICENSE holds the GPLv2 text) inherited from FFTW codelet generators; the author notes copyright on machine-generated code is unclear; README text is CC-BY-SA-4.0. [retier] AVX-512 path bug: lanes 8-15 use zero twiddle constants, so half the transforms are wrong; tests print only lane 0. Treat AVX-512 numbers as unverified.

name: go-fft
baseline: FFTW 3.3.11 (native C, FFTW_MEASURE, threads=1); also numpy.fft, scipy.fft (pocketfft) and gonum/dsp/fourier
workload: Steady-state (plan reused) complex 1-D, real 1-D and complex 2-D FFTs in float64 on an Apple M4 Max, ns/op and GFLOP/s, with go-fft's 2-D path using several goroutines and every reference single-threaded.
claimed_speedup: June snapshot tables (Apple M4 Max), go-fft vs FFTW: lags FFTW 1.17x to 3.28x on complex 1-D rows (e.g. N=1,024 3,395 ns vs 2,127 ns); faster only on the 2-D multicore rows: 256x256 208,437 ns vs 271,098 ns; 512x512 633,920 ns vs 1,247,215 ns; 1024x1024 2,784,623 ns vs 6,301,688 ns. Vs scipy.fft (pocketfft) complex 1-D: N=256 716 ns vs 2,302 ns; N=1,024 3,395 ns vs 4,470 ns; N=65,536 377,784 ns vs 499,500 ns (slower at N=1,048,576: 13.36 ms vs 8.04 ms). Summary of that snapshot: at or above parity with FFTW on 3 of 24 ops and with gonum on 19 of 19; 'typically 3-5x on composite N' faster than gonum. Fresh single-threaded 1-D runs of 2026-09-30 (go-fft time / FFTW time, below 1 = go-fft faster): complex 2^20 0.81 on M4 Max and 0.67 on Neoverse-N1; prime 1009 0.53 (M4 Max), 0.75 (EPYC 7773X), 0.54 (Neoverse-N1); RFFT 2^20 0.92 on Neoverse-N1; complex 65536 1.00 on Neoverse-N1; most other 1-D rows still lag 1.07x to 2.92x; 2-D 512^2/1024^2 multicore 0.43/0.45 (M4 Max), 1.63/0.87 (EPYC 7773X), 0.51/0.25 (Neoverse-N1).
compiler_and_flags: go1.26.4 (CGO=0 pure Go; cross-compiled for the Linux hosts), go test -benchtime=1s; FFTW 3.3.11 Homebrew arm64 bottle with NEON on the M4 Max and FFTW 3.3.10 built from source with SSE2/AVX/AVX2/FMA (Zen 3) or NEON (N1) on the Linux hosts, plans FFTW_MEASURE threads=1 from a C harness; numpy 2.5.0 and scipy 1.18.0 pinned single-threaded (2.5.3 / 1.18.1 on the Linux hosts)
hardware: Apple M4 Max (12P+4E), macOS 26.5, for the main tables; fresh 2026-09-30 runs also on AMD EPYC 7773X (Zen 3, GCC Compile Farm cfarm420, 128 threads) and ARM Neoverse-N1 (cfarm424, 64 cores)
tradeoffs: Pure Go with no cgo, so not callable from C++ without a wrapper. Arbitrary lengths: mixed radix for 13-smooth lengths, Rader for primes whose N-1 is 7-smooth, large-prime convolution otherwise (BENCHMARKS.md shows FFTW ahead at primes 1,009 and 10,007 by 1.26x and 2.15x). AVX2 and NEON SIMD butterflies. Plan creation is far cheaper than FFTW_MEASURE (e.g. 14,808 ns vs 3,434,000 ns at N=1,024).
caveats: Pure Go library, not callable from C++ without cgo; listed for the FFTW comparison. In the June M4 Max snapshot it does not beat FFTW on any single-threaded row; the fresh 2026-09-30 runs show single-threaded wins only at a few sizes (complex 2^20 on M4 Max and Neoverse-N1, prime N=1009 on all three hosts, RFFT 2^20 on N1), while most 1-D rows still lag FFTW by 1.07x to 2.92x and the M4 Max run was under background load (load average 3.4-5). The 2-D wins come from go-fft fanning rows and columns across goroutines while FFTW, numpy and scipy run single-threaded, so the 2-D comparison is not apples-to-apples; the 2-D fresh rows also predate a fan-out fix. FFT2/FFTN return a newly allocated slice, which the report says skews 2-D comparisons against FFTW on many-core hosts via GC cost. The README attributes part of the scipy gap at small N to Python FFI overhead, so the scipy comparison there is not like-for-like. The README tables still show the June snapshot. name: Auto-MPFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.5 (planning excluded from run time), Intel MKL (version not stated), PFT (snudatalab/PFT, KDD 2021) and FFTW's pruned FFT (fftw.org/pruned.html); all single precision, with tolerances set so every method keeps relative l2 error below 1e-6.
workload: 2-D real single-precision arrays: synthetic sets of 1,000 random matrices of size 2^n x 2^n for n = 8..15, and five image datasets (Cityscapes, ADE20K, DF2K, RiceLeaf, Bird) resized to one resolution per set; output is a centered 2^4 x 2^4 to 2^9 x 2^9 block of Fourier coefficients (synthetic: up to 2^13 x 2^13).
claimed_speedup: Paper, real-world datasets (Figure 4): up to 7.6x on Cityscapes, with per-dataset maxima annotated as 7.6x (Cityscapes), 5.7x (ADE20K), 6.9x (DF2K), 2.8x (RiceLeaf) and 2.6x (Bird) over the competitors. Synthetic data: up to 4.7x over the baselines when the input size varies (2^8 x 2^8 to 2^15 x 2^15, output 2^6 x 2^6), and up to 3.3x over PFT and Pruned FFT when the output size varies (input 2^15 x 2^15). The text does not name which competitor each annotated ratio is taken against. Relaxing the tolerance to 1e-4 or 1e-2 cuts Auto-MPFT's own time by up to 21.2% or 49.8% (Table 4; e.g. 133.7 ms at 1e-6 for a 2^5 x 2^5 output from a 2^15 x 2^15 input).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The paper says only that all methods are implemented in C++; the repo ships no Makefile or CMake file.
hardware: Intel Core i7-10700KF @ 3.80GHz, 32GB RAM (paper Section 4.1). Thread count not stated.
tradeoffs: Approximates only a chosen subset of coefficients (partial Fourier transform) and so wins only when the output is much smaller than the input; needs MKL, IPP and FFTW installed to build the comparison code. Hyperparameters chosen automatically by a convex solver.
caveats: Peer-reviewed (KDD 2024) but the README has no result table, hardware or compiler flags, and the 7.6x figure is a maximum over all datasets and baselines (the abstract groups partial-FT methods and optimized FFT libraries together, so the max ratio may not be against FFTW or MKL). The paper PDF (author site, ACM DL, OpenReview) could not be opened from this container, so per-baseline numbers were not read. The baseline file src/FFTW.cpp includes the Windows-only tchar.h, the repo ships no Makefile or CMake file, and the code depends on Intel MKL and Intel IPP (proprietary, free-to-use) for the core routines. Computes only a subset of 2-D Fourier coefficients, not a full FFT. The predecessor PFT (snudatalab/PFT, KDD 2021, C++, Apache-2.0, 16 stars) makes the same kind of claim against FFTW and MKL but its README states no numbers. [retier] The speedups hold only when the output window is much smaller than the input. The paper says that as M approaches N Auto-MPFT runs slightly slower than a full FFT, and Figure 3(a) shows it losing to the baselines in some cases. The 7.6x headline is the single best dataset (Cityscapes); the other datasets give 2.6x to 6.9x, and the paper does not say which competitor each ratio is measured against. Compiler, flags, threading and MKL version are not stated. The paper says code and datasets are at the GitHub repo, but the repo has no build files, src/FFTW.cpp includes the Windows-only tchar.h, and the core routines depend on Intel MKL and IPP. Only a 2-D subset of Fourier coefficients is computed, not a full FFT.

claimed_speedup: Per the authors' paper (arXiv 1412.7580; text seen only as a search snippet, not on any opened page): fbfft gives over 1.5x speedup over cuFFT for the FFT sizes of interest in whole CNNs (reported mean 1.51x, sd 0.21, geometric mean 1.49x). name: FFTW++ (implicit dealiased convolutions on FFTW3)
baseline: FFTW 3 with explicit zero-padded convolutions (and FFTW's MPI transpose for the distributed code)
workload: 2D and 3D dealiased (zero-padded) convolutions and FFTs built on FFTW3; implicit padding avoids transforming the padded zeros.
claimed_speedup: README: 'in 2D and 3D implicit zero-padding substantially reduces memory usage and computation time' (no numbers on the repository). Per a WebSearch summary of Bowman and Roberts, SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 33:1 (2011) / arXiv 1008.1366 (the paper itself was not opened): increased data locality 'significantly enhanced performance by as much as a factor of 2', and an implicit complex convolution needs one-half the memory of a zero-padded one in 2D and one-quarter in 3D (centered Hermitian: 2/3 in 2D, 4/9 in 3D).
tradeoffs: Header library and MPI transposes on top of FFTW3 (so FFTW's GPL licence applies unless a commercial FFTW licence is used); the gain is specific to dealiased convolutions in 2D/3D, plain FFTs are plain FFTW calls; C, Fortran and Python wrappers for the convolution routines; mpi/fftw directory benchmarks the adaptive transpose against FFTW's MPI transpose.
caveats: No numbers on the repository page; the speedup (up to about 2x over explicit zero-padded convolutions, plus 2-4x less memory in 2D/3D) comes from the peer-reviewed papers, seen here only through a WebSearch summary because arxiv.org, math.ualberta.ca, archive.org and doi.org are blocked in this container. The baseline is explicit zero padding implemented by the same authors on top of FFTW, so this is an algorithmic win for dealiased convolutions, not a faster FFT kernel. Timing scripts are public (tests/timing.py, tests/timing/timing) but no timing data, CPU, compiler or flags are committed. name: PFT (Partial Fourier Transform)
baseline: FFTW (real-to-complex 1D, FFTW_ESTIMATE), Intel MKL DFTI, FFTW pruned FFT, Goertzel algorithm
workload: Partial Fourier transform of length N up to 2^22 computing M output coefficients (Table 3 best 1.273 ms at M=2^9, N=2^22), single precision, relative L2 error below 1e-6, versus FFTW 3.3.5, MKL and pruned FFTW with planning time excluded (paper Section 5).
claimed_speedup: Per the authors' KDD 2021 paper (text seen only as a search snippet, not on any opened page): an order of magnitude speedup for sufficiently small output sizes without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming FFTW, MKL, pruned FFT and Goertzel. No number appears in the repo.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700HQ 2.60 GHz, 8 GB RAM (paper Section 5); compiler, flags and thread count not stated.
tradeoffs: Approximate, not exact: error is selectable from e-1 to e-7 through precomputed polynomial coefficient files (src/precomputed). The sample code is written for real-valued input and a target output range centered at zero (the file header says a small modification removes this limit). Single precision throughout. Needs Intel MKL and IPP (mkl.h, mkl_dfti.h, ipp.h, ipps.h) plus fftw3.h. Gains only when M is much smaller than N (O(N + M log M) instead of O(N log N)). Research sample code, not a packaged library.
caveats: (1) Snippet only: the paper (ACM DOI 10.1145/3447548.3467293, arXiv 2008.12559) could not be opened here (dl.acm.org, arXiv, openreview and yongchanpark.github.io are egress-blocked; the yongchanpark.github.io GitHub repo holds only an empty README), so CPU model, compiler, flags and the actual ratios are unknown. The KDD 2021 venue itself is confirmed by the repo README's citation. Retier to B if a session with ACM or arXiv access confirms the abstract and tables. (2) No timing harness in the repo: src/PFT.cpp prints the first and last coefficients and the relative L2 error against the MKL DFTI full FFT and has no timers; src/FFTW.cpp declares clock_t variables but never reads them; src/PrunedFFTW.cpp is the FFTW pruned-FFT web-page pseudocode and does not compile as is; src/goertzel.c is copied from pramasoul/jrand. (3) The FFTW baseline in src/FFTW.cpp is a 1,048,576-point float r2c transform on 4 threads planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE (FFTW_MEASURE only in a comment), weaker than a tuned FFTW; it includes the Windows-only tchar.h. (4) PFT.cpp's header says the example is designed for real-valued input with a target range centered at zero; other ranges need the modification described in the paper. (5) Building needs Intel MKL and IPP (proprietary but freely redistributable) in addition to the Apache-2.0 code. (6) Last commit 2025-08-19 is a README edit; the last source change is 'Update PFT.cpp' on 2021-06-03 (github.com commits page). (7) Follow-up multidimensional work (snudatalab/Auto-MPFT, KDD 2024) was not opened.

name: PhastFT
baseline: FFTW 3.3.8 (via the Rust fftw crate); also RustFFT
workload: Single-threaded complex-to-complex forward and inverse FFT, f32 and f64, power-of-two lengths 8 to 8,388,608, divan benchmark on an M1 MacBook Pro in a third-party benchmark repo (astral4/fft-benchmark).

It is a small personal repo from 2024 benchmarking phastft v0.2.1, while the crate is now v0.4.1 with the parallel feature on by default. RustFFT beats PhastFT at N=16 and 32 and at N>=2^22 for f32, and at N=16, 32, 65,536 and N>=2^21 for f64. Each timed call includes planning: FFTW builds a C2CPlan with FFTW_ESTIMATE | DESTROYINPUT and executes it; RustFFT calls plan_fft_forward/inverse on a fresh FftPlanner (created in untimed setup) and processes.
claimed_speedup: Table medians, forward / inverse, plan creation included in the timed region for both libraries. f32 N=8,388,608: RustFFT 103.9 / 103.6 ms vs FFTW 193.3 / 192.9 ms (about 1.86x, derived from page data); f32 N=16: 124.6 / 94.09 ns vs 1.405 / 1.416 us; f32 N=1,048,576: 12.49 / 12.58 ms vs 14.20 / 13.13 ms (about 1.14x forward, derived from page data); f64 N=65,536: 754.4 / 774.5 us vs 953.5 / 966.9 us (about 1.26x forward, derived from page data). RustFFT is SLOWER than this FFTW build at f32 N=1024 (7.707 vs 7.291 us), N=2048 (22.87 vs 11.74 us, FFTW about 1.95x faster, derived from page data), N=4096 (45.33 vs 21.20 us), N=8192 forward (84.08 vs 45.62 us), N=16384 both directions (156.7 / 225.2 vs 101.1 / 180.0 us), and at f64 N=1024 (8.624 vs 7.749 us), N=2048 (18.49 vs 12.54 us) and N=524,288 (9.427 vs 7.911 ms). The author's conclusion 'fftw was consistently slower than both rustfft and phastft' is contradicted by the page's own table for RustFFT.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.80.0-nightly (d2d24e395 2024-05-03); Cargo.toml [profile.bench] lto = true, strip = true (cargo bench default opt-level 3), no target-cpu or RUSTFLAGS stated; rustfft v6.2.0; fftw crate v0.8.0 default 'source' feature: fftw-src build.rs runs FFTW 3.3.8 './configure --with-pic --enable-static --disable-doc' (plus --enable-single for f32), no SIMD flag, compiled with Apple clang 15.0.0 (clang-1500.0.40.1)

tradeoffs: Pure Rust, no C API (C++ use needs an FFI wrapper). Any length including primes in O(n log n); AVX and SSE4.1 on x86_64, NEON on AArch64, optional wasm SIMD. baseline: FFTW (fftw_plan_dft_2d, full N x N 2D FFT recomputed after every event or event packet)

The README says FFTW3 'served as the benchmark for testing and evaluation' and benchmarks/efft_benchmark.cpp pairs BenchmarkFeedWithEvents/BenchmarkFeedWithPackets with FFTW versions; CI runs that target (ci.yaml 'Benchmark' step) but results are not committed. A TPAMI abstract snippet (not opened) gives absolute eFFT times only (< 1 microsecond per event for packets of more than 40 events at 128 x 128).

stars_or_usage: 23 stars, 2 forks; PyPI package efft; Docker image; TPAMI 2024 and JORS 2026 papers
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 on top of Eigen; frame size is a compile-time template parameter and must be a power of two (radix-2 tree); keeps a tree of intermediate matrices (about log2 N levels of N x N complex floats) so memory is well above one frame; single-precision complex (float) output; GPLv3 copyleft; Python bindings via nanobind. It is not a drop-in FFT: it only wins when the input changes by a few pixels between transforms (event streams) and needs one initial full transform.
caveats: (1) No benchmark numbers or CPU model appear in the repo, README, PyPI description or any page I could open; the TPAMI paper (doi 10.1109/TPAMI.2024.3422209), the JORS paper (doi 10.5334/jors.642, openresearchsoftware.metajnl.com) and Zenodo are egress-blocked. The abstract snippet gives absolute eFFT times only (PSNR > 55 dB, SSIM > 0.999; < 1 microsecond per event for packets > 40 events and < 0.5 microsecond for > 200 events at 128 x 128), not a ratio against FFTW. Retier to B if the TPAMI paper's FFTW comparison is read. (2) The in-repo FFTW baseline is deliberately weak: initializeGroundTruth plans fftw_plan_dft_2d with FFTW_ESTIMATE | FFTW_UNALIGNED | FFTW_NO_SIMD | FFTW_PRESERVE_INPUT, runs in double precision while eFFT uses float, and recomputes the whole N x N transform for every event (or packet); getGroundTruthFFT() also casts and transposes the row-major double result into a float Eigen matrix. Both benchmark sides copy the result into a new matrix (auto result = efft.getFFT() copies too), so the copy cost is roughly symmetric apart from the cast. In CI FFTW comes from the distro package, so the -O3 -march=native -ffast-math flags apply only to eFFT. (3) Different problem from a plain FFT: incremental exact update after sparse input changes versus a from-scratch transform, meaningful only for event-stream use. (4) Events are seeded from std::random_device, so runs are not bit-reproducible. (5) Last commit 2026-09-22 ('Update .gitignore'), read from the github.com commits page; PyPI efft 1.0.5 lists GPL-3.0-later while the header and GitHub say GPL v3.

Linux aarch64 6 x 1.73 GHz: 53.8 ns vs 95.3 ns at N=8, 0.778 vs 0.850 at N=64, 16.5 vs 21.7 at N=1024, 2238 vs 2735 at N=65536 (slightly slower at N=16: 0.161 vs 0.149).

name: GPU_FFT (Raspberry Pi VideoCore IV, hello_fft in raspberrypi/userland)
language: C with VideoCore QPU assembly kernels
baseline: FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE) running on the Raspberry Pi 1 ARM CPU

Per-transform milliseconds, GPU_FFT (batch 1) vs FFTW_MEASURE: 2^8 0.033 vs 0.092; 2^12 0.25 vs 3.0; 2^15 3.5 vs 31; 2^16 7.0 vs 83; 2^20 194 vs 1600; 2^22 786 vs 8800. name: heFFTe (Highly Efficient FFT for Exascale)
baseline: Distributed 3-D FFT libraries fftMPI, SWFFT, AccFFT and P3DFFT (FFTW-MPI-class); FFTW is heFFTe's own CPU backend
workload: Distributed-memory 2-D/3-D complex FFTs (e.g. 1024^3 on Summit nodes) with pencil or slab decomposition; the repo's speed3d benchmark reports heFFTe's own GFlops/s per backend.
claimed_speedup: Repo: no competitor numbers; benchmarks/speed3d.h prints only heFFTe's own 'Performance: <x> GFlops/s' for the chosen backend (stock, FFTW, MKL, cuFFT, rocFFT, oneMKL). Peer-reviewed ICCS 2020 paper (seen only through search-result summaries; every copy was EGRESS_BLOCKED): GPU local kernels more than 40x faster than CPU state-of-the-art local kernels and over 2x for the whole FFT; heFFTe GPU about 2x faster than fftMPI and SWFFT; heFFTe beats FFTE by more than a factor of 2 with better scalability; about 90% of roofline peak for a 1024^3 FFT on Summit (6 MPI ranks per node, one V100 per rank). The heFFTe CPU path is built on improved fftMPI/SWFFT kernels and is described as 'at least as good as' them, i.e. parity on CPU. The '1.65x on two nodes' figure in the search record did not appear in any summary I saw.
hardware: Summit (ORNL): IBM POWER9 CPUs and NVIDIA V100 GPUs, up to 24,576 POWER9 cores and 6,144 V100 GPUs, per the ICCS 2020 paper as summarized in search results; no hardware is stated in the repo.
stars_or_usage: 59 stars; DOE Exascale Computing Project library (ICL UTK / ORNL)
tradeoffs: MPI-based distributed FFT; local 1-D/2-D kernels are delegated to FFTW, MKL, oneMKL, cuFFT or rocFFT backends, so heFFTe is a communication/decomposition layer and does not beat FFTW on a single core. Needs MPI and a backend library; also Fortran and Python bindings. Optional GPU-aware MPI.
caveats: The paper (Springer, iccs-meeting.org, icl.utk.edu, netlib.org copies) was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so all figures come from search-result summaries, not from the paper text; compiler, flags and the exact competitor configurations are unverified. The headline 2x over fftMPI and SWFFT compares heFFTe on V100 GPUs with CPU-only libraries (fftMPI and SWFFT have no GPU path), and the 40x compares GPU with CPU kernels, so both are mostly hardware gains; on CPU heFFTe reuses improved fftMPI/SWFFT kernels and is described only as at least as good as them. The FFTE comparison (>2x) is the cleanest software claim but its configuration is unverified. The repo's own benchmarks time heFFTe alone (no head-to-head harness). AccFFT GPU runs reportedly failed correctness on Summit (search-record claim, not re-checked). Docs site (icl-utk-edu.github.io/heffte) is blocked. README 'Getting Help' links to the SLATE issue tracker rather than heFFTe's.

name: JTransforms
baseline: FFTW 3 through the ezFFTW Java wrapper (single-threaded)
workload: Java JMH benchmark in the third-party FFTBench repo (JMH 1.21, JTransforms 3.1 vs ezFFTW 0.1.2): full real-to-complex forward FFT, zero the DC bin, then inverse FFT, for 1-D (1,024 to 10,000,000 elements), 2-D (1280x720 to 5000x5000) and 3-D (100x120x140 to 400x300x200) arrays, as single calls (arrayInput/singleArrayInput) and as parallel invocations.
claimed_speedup: FFTBench README (s/op, 3 JMH iterations; 2 for 3-D): 1-D arrayInput, JTransforms with its heuristic multithreading vs single-threaded ezFFTW/FFTW: 10,000,000 elements 3.205 vs 4.560; 1,024 about 1e-4 vs 0.006 (FFTW error +-0.053); FFTW faster at 98,304 (0.029 vs 0.033), 589,829 (0.815 vs 1.052) and 1,000,000 (0.175 vs 0.290). 2-D singleArrayInput with JTransforms threading disabled (snglthrd_JT) vs FFTW: 1280x720 0.137 vs 0.155, 1920x1080 0.331 vs 0.360, 3000x2000 1.100 vs 1.374, 5000x5000 6.033 vs 8.422, but 1087x1931 2.132 vs 0.998 (FFTW 2.1x faster); multithreaded JTransforms 0.058 at 1280x720 and 0.125 at 1920x1080. 3-D single-threaded: 256^3 2.272 vs 4.252, but FFTW faster at 100x120x140 (0.176 vs 0.311) and 400x300x200 (2.955 vs 4.277).
compiler_and_flags: JMH 1.21 on Oracle JDK 1.8.0_111 (HotSpot 64-Bit Server VM 25.111-b14); VM options none for the 1-D runs and -Xmx6g -Xms3g for the 2-D and 3-D runs (per the linked run log); native FFTW comes from the bytedeco JavaCPP preset via ezFFTW, build and version not stated
hardware: AMD Phenom II X4 955 on Ubuntu 16.04 (from the run-log file name runs/ubuntu_16.04_phenom_II_x4_955.txt)
stars_or_usage: 430 stars, 94 forks; version 3.2 on Maven Central
tradeoffs: Pure Java, multithreaded by default, DFT/DCT/DST/DHT derived from Ooura's FFT package; JVM warm-up and GC apply.

FFTW is reached through ezFFTW (GPL-2.0, written by the benchmark's author), which creates an FFTW_ESTIMATE plan, executes and destroys it on every call inside the timed operation, serializes planning behind a global lock, uses the split-array guru interface and copies data through JNI, so the baseline is far from tuned FFTW (the 1,024-point 0.006 s figure is overhead, not FFT time). The 1-D JTransforms rows have JTransforms' multithreading enabled while FFTW is single-threaded; in like-for-like single-threaded 2-D and 3-D runs the results split both ways. Hardware is a 2009-era AMD Phenom II on Java 8; each JMH row used only 2-3 iterations and some error bars exceed the score. The JTransforms README itself shows no FFTW numbers. Pure Java, not C++.

name: matchedfilter (formerly peak-fft)
language: C core with Python bindings; GPU kernels in Slang (Vulkan/Metal)
baseline: FFTW (inverse transform only, timed through pyFFTW); on GPU rocFFT / MLX FFT inverse-only references
workload: Batched matched filtering (frequency-domain product, inverse FFT and peak scan) of 16 data spectra x 512 templates x 4096-point complex64 transforms, one CPU thread, timed against FFTW doing only the inverse FFT of the same batch.
claimed_speedup: Milliseconds per batch (16 x 512 x 4096-point complex64, one thread), FFTW inverse-only vs matchedfilter full / peak-only / hierarchical fd=0.01 at SNR 5.5: Ryzen 9 5950X 63.63 vs 52.23 / 34.27 / 3.95; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 69.54 vs 35.12 / 20.68 / 3.12; Ryzen 5 5500U 87.45 vs 73.70 / 49.37 / 6.11; Core i5-13500H 44.96 vs 56.24 / 35.49 / 4.69; Apple M2 252.55 vs 68.75 / 57.84 / 6.28; Xeon Platinum 8260 (VM) 219.57 vs 155.19 / 79.18 / 6.24; Xeon E5-2698 v3 (contended) 178.90 vs 303.35 / 132.75 / 14.47. Peak-only is 1.86x, 3.36x, 1.77x, 1.27x, 4.37x, 2.77x and 1.35x faster than FFTW's inverse-only time (derived from page data); full output is slower than FFTW on the i5-13500H and the Haswell node. GPU (Radeon 8060S): rocFFT inverse-only 2.58 ms vs full 1.49, peak-only 0.71, hierarchical 0.20 ms; M2 GPU: MLX FFT-only 11.73 vs peak-only 3.92 ms.
compiler_and_flags: matchedfilter: setup.py builds with -O3 -fno-math-errno -std=c++17 (plus -msse4.2 -maes -mpclmul on x86) and Highway runtime dispatch (AVX2/AVX3 on the x86 hosts, NEON_BF16 on M2); compiler not recorded. FFTW baseline: pyFFTW-bundled FFTW 3.3.5 'sse2-avx' build (gcc -O2 with Fedora RPM hardening flags) on the x86 hosts, FFTW 3.3.10-neon through FFTW's C API on the M2; FFTW_PATIENT, 15 s planning limit, one thread.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X; Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Radeon 8060S); Ryzen 5 5500U; Intel Core i5-13500H; Apple M2; Xeon Platinum 8260 (VM); Xeon E5-2698 v3 (shared, contended node)
tradeoffs: Not a general-purpose FFT. It fuses the spectral product, inverse FFT and peak search for matched-filter searches. Peak-only sizes are powers of two from 64 to 1,048,576 on CPU; full-output sizes are powers of two from 1,024 to 4,194,304. Single precision (complex64) only, one CPU thread per filter. The main interface is a pip-installable Python package over a C core, so use from C++ means linking the C code directly. Hierarchical mode needs calibration files and trades a false-dismissal budget for speed. The README calls it alpha software with an unstable API.
caveats: First-party numbers from a young alpha repo (PyPI 0.1.0a5, 1 star). The page itself says the comparison is unequal work: FFTW and the rocFFT/MLX references time only the inverse transform, while matchedfilter also does the spectral product and peak scan and peak-only mode skips writing the output, so the gain comes from fusion and output reduction, not a faster FFT kernel; it is not a drop-in FFT. Full-output mode is slower than FFTW on the Core i5-13500H and on the Haswell node. The x86 FFTW baseline is the pyFFTW-bundled FFTW 3.3.5 built for SSE2/AVX only (no AVX2/FMA codelets), while matchedfilter dispatches to AVX2/AVX3. The M2 FFTW baseline (252.55 ms) is 3-6x slower than the x86 hosts' FFTW (44.96-87.45 ms), so the 4.37x M2 ratio likely reflects a weak arm64 FFTW build (derived from page data). The page flags the Haswell node as contended (full and hierarchical rows indicative only) and the Xeon 8260 VM as least stable. Hierarchical mode trades a false-dismissal budget for speed and these timings do not measure FDR. Compiler for matchedfilter not recorded; build flags taken from current setup.py, which may differ from revision eecb43c. Interactive pages at ahnitz.github.io were not opened (egress-blocked); repo was renamed from peak-fft and its docs mention agent handoffs, so treat claims as unreviewed.

name: MPSFT (Matrix Pencil Sparse Fourier Transform)
baseline: FFTW (FFTW_ESTIMATE and FFTW_MEASURE plans)
workload: Sparse Fourier transform of an N=2^22 signal with S nonzero frequencies, single core, Google Benchmark, FFTW built from source on the same machine.
claimed_speedup: At N=4194301 (prime near 2^22) MPSFT takes 19.4 ms at S=64, 75.8 ms at S=512, 140.8 ms at S=1024 and 263.4 ms at S=2048; FFTW at N=4194304 takes 225.3 ms with FFTW_ESTIMATE (benchmark arg 64) and 102.3 ms with FFTW_MEASURE (arg 0). The README and report say it is faster than FFTW when S is below about 1800, which is the FFTW_ESTIMATE crossover; the README also says S must be around 1000 to beat FFTW, matching FFTW_MEASURE. Derived from page data: 5.3x faster than FFTW_MEASURE and 11.6x faster than FFTW_ESTIMATE at S=64; break-even against FFTW_MEASURE between S=512 and S=1024.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated; the report discusses gcc autovectorization and .bazelrc uses the GCC-only -fopt-info-vec-optimized), Bazel --config=opt: -std=c++11 -O3 -ffast-math -mavx2 -mtune=native -fopenmp-simd -g0 -DNDEBUG; FFTW 3.3.6-pl2 compiled locally with -O3 -mtune=native -ffast-math (report section 4.1); CPU scaling disabled; single-threaded.
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700K, 4 GHz (report/report.pdf section 4.1)
tradeoffs: Only useful for signals that are exactly or nearly sparse in frequency; approximate output; depends on FFTW, Eigen and Boost.SIMD.
caveats: Wins hold only for sparse spectra (S below about 1000 against FFTW_MEASURE). MPSFT is timed at prime N=4194301 while FFTW runs at the power of two 4194304, FFTW's best case. The report says MPSFT is not competitive with sFFT1 or sFFT2 at N near 2^22 (they win there; MPSFT only overtakes them at larger N with S=50). The input model is a noisy sparse spectrum (sigma=0.1), and MPSFT returns approximate modes, not an exact DFT. The report is explicitly 'not a formal publication'. GPL-2.0 text is in src/COPYING.txt; whether 'or later' applies is not stated. The README says it plans to drop the FFTW dependency (KissFFT), which never happened. Last commit 2017.

name: gpuNUFFT
baseline: cuFINUFFT (3D, single-coil and 32-coil MRI data, as measured in cufinufft issue #126, Jan 2022); CPU NUFFT libraries only directionally via the MRI-NUFFT benchmark statement
workload: GPU gridding / NUFFT of arbitrary 2D and 3D non-Cartesian MRI k-space data (MATLAB mex and Python bindings). No benchmark workload found.
claimed_speedup: cufinufft issue #126 (paquiteau, Jan 28 2022), 3D 128x128x160: forward 73.42 +/- 1.119 ms vs cufinufft 279.36 +/- 0.552 ms (3.8x), adjoint 62.73 +/- 0.640 vs 132.27 +/- 0.697 ms (2.1x); 32 coils (32x128x128x160): forward 1582.74 +/- 3.853 vs 8952.54 +/- 2.771 ms (5.65x), adjoint 1739.30 +/- 10.767 vs 4159.96 +/- 5.939 ms (2.39x). The ratios are the reporter's own. The reporter adds that 'cufiNUFFT remains faster for 2D data' and gives no 2D numbers.
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit, CMake 2.8+; README notes it was tested with CUDA 5.0 and gcc 4.6; a later commit adds CUDA 11 support
hardware: Not stated in issue #126 (results produced in a Google Colab notebook, https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1IuOgwshEG04GVaZoinZNdbRkPmG-Kadp, not opened). The cuFINUFFT paper's harness (MelodyShih/cuFINUFFT-bench) builds with CUDA 10.0.130 and gcc 7.4.0 and runs gpuNUFFT through its MATLAB interface in single precision; per a WebSearch snippet, the paper's measurements were on a V100.
stars_or_usage: 85 stars, 37 forks; a gpuNUFFT backend of MRI-NUFFT (JOSS) and pysap-mri; the actively maintained fork chaithyagr/gpuNUFFT is what PyPI gpuNUFFT ships (0.10.8, released 2026-07-08)
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA; built primarily around MATLAB mex files (MATLAB required unless the Python bindings are used); NUFFT only (gridding with Kaiser-Bessel style kernels), not a general FFT replacement; single precision.
caveats: Tier D: no speed numbers anywhere I could open. README gives install steps only (tested with CUDA 5.0 and gcc 4.6; a 2022 merge adds CUDA 11 support). matlab/demo/run_demo.m and cgsense_phantom_recon_cpu.m time gpuNUFFT forward/adjoint against a CPU NUFFT operator with tic/toc, but no results are committed. The LICENSE cites Knoll et al., Proc ISMRM 2014 p4297 (conference abstract, not opened) and README points to Dropbox 'Supporting material' (not opened). mind-inria/mri-nufft-benchmark commits no results; the MRI-NUFFT JOSS paper source (docs/paper-joss/paper.md in mind-inria/mri-nufft, opened via raw.githubusercontent.com) states only that cufinufft and gpuNUFFT give the best performance in that benchmark, with no numbers; its authors include the gpuNUFFT Python-binding author (Chaithya G R), so it is not fully independent. Published third-party comparisons (for example the cuFINUFFT paper) were not checked; the direction against cuFINUFFT is unknown to me. The upstream repo's last commit is 2022-02-06 (abandoned), but MRI-NUFFT docs name chaithyagr/gpuNUFFT (a GitHub fork, 2 stars, 1,356 commits) as the active fork and PyPI gpuNUFFT 0.10.8 was released 2026-07-08. LICENSE is MIT plus a request to credit the authors and cite the ISMRM abstract in academic work. Baselines FFTW, MKL FFT and KissFFT in the assignment are not what gpuNUFFT is compared with; the relevant incumbents are CPU NUFFTs. [retier] Two sources conflict. (1) cufinufft issue #126 (Jan 2022, user paquiteau, who is not a gpuNUFFT author but works on MRI tooling that later wrapped gpuNUFFT in MRI-NUFFT) measured gpuNUFFT 2.1x to 5.65x faster than cufinufft in 3D. The GPU, the cufinufft eps and the gpuNUFFT kernel width, oversampling and sector width are not stated, so accuracy was probably not matched. Copy accounting is unequal: cufinufft times cover computation and D2H only, while gpuNUFFT times also include H2D, which biases against gpuNUFFT. The reporter says the result contradicts Figure 4 of arXiv 2102.08463 and that cufinufft is still faster in 2D. The issue was closed with no maintainer reply. (2) The peer-reviewed cuFINUFFT paper (Shih et al., PDSEC 2021, arXiv 2102.08463; PDF blocked here, figures from WebSearch snippets only) reports cuFINUFFT about 78x faster than gpuNUFFT on type 1 and 5x faster on type 2 at matched accuracy, with its harness in MelodyShih/cuFINUFFT-bench (gpuNUFFT run via MATLAB, CUDA 10.0, gcc 7.4.0; no results committed). The two may both hold: gpuNUFFT can win on fixed MRI trajectories with its precomputed sector operator and low-accuracy gridding, and lose at higher requested accuracy or on clustered points. Upstream gpuNUFFT is unmaintained since 2022-02; the maintained fork is chaithyagr/gpuNUFFT.

name: SFFT library (ETH Zurich optimized sparse FFT, versions 1-3)
baseline: FFTW
workload: Discrete Fourier transform of a signal whose spectrum has only k non-zero frequencies out of n (sparse spectrum), compared in the underlying sFFT work against a full dense FFT such as FFTW; this repository itself contains no benchmark.
claimed_speedup: No numbers anywhere in the repository or its docs. The docs call it a 'high-performance C++ implementation' of sFFT v1, v2 and v3 with SSE kernels. The underlying MIT sFFT algorithm is billed as faster than FFTW for sparse spectra (Hacker News thread 'The faster-than-fast Fourier transform'), but those figures were not opened this session.
tradeoffs: Only helps when the spectrum is sparse; it is not a general dense FFT. README states it is experimental and 'NOT intended to be used as a drop-in replacement for the FFT library of your choice'. Docs say v1 and v2 work only with a few specific input parameters and v3 cannot handle noisy signals. Targets x86 with SSE; Intel IPP is required by default (configure --without-ipp disables it). It calls FFTW internally for its sub-transforms (FFTW plan flags are a plan parameter), so FFTW is a dependency as well as the baseline. GPL-2.0-or-later (strong copyleft).
caveats: Tier D: no benchmark numbers in README.txt, CHANGELOG.txt or doc/*.rst (all read via raw.githubusercontent.com). The bundled dev tools (sfft-timing, sfft-timing_many, sfft-instruction_count, sfft-verification; built with --develop) time only the SFFT call and include no FFTW comparison. Numbers presumably live in J. Schumacher's ETH master thesis 'High Performance Sparse Fast Fourier Transform' (2013, supervised by M. Pueschel; PDF at spiral.ece.cmu.edu/pub-spiral/pubfile/Final_Thesis_SFFT_169.pdf) and in Schumacher and Pueschel, 'High-performance sparse fast Fourier transforms', IEEE SiPS 2014; spiral.net, spiral.ece.cmu.edu, research-collection.ethz.ch and arXiv were all egress-blocked, so none was opened. WebSearch snippets only (not verified): the thesis abstract reports the optimized library as two to five times faster than the MIT reference SFFT implementation, and one summary says the optimized SFFT is 'about equally efficient as' FFTW for large input sizes, so a win over FFTW is not established and at best holds for large, very sparse signals. The project's own README and docs say the implementation 'is in an experimental state', is 'NOT intended to be used as a drop-in replacement for the FFT library of your choice', and 'Be prepared to find bugs'. It depends on FFTW 3 (used internally) and by default on Intel IPP (configure --without-ipp to disable); kernels are SSE for x86. The GitHub repo is an import of the spiral.net 0.1.0 release ('Official download of version 0.1.0', 2015-06-01) plus a ctypes Python wrapper, example app and API cleanups by the importer (12 commits, last 2015-06-03); it is not a GitHub fork, and the canonical upstream is spiral.net/software/sfft.html. Notability is modest by stars (69), but the sFFT algorithm (Hassanieh, Indyk, Katabi, Price) is widely cited. Related sparse-FFT repos mpsft and Auto-MPFT are already catalogued.

name: SpFFT (sparse-input 3D FFT)
baseline: FFTW / MKL and cuFFT / rocFFT dense 3D FFT (implied; no comparison is published; SpFFT itself calls these libraries for its 1D/2D sub-transforms)
workload: No benchmarked workload. Design target: 3D FFT of sparse frequency-domain data with spherical cutoff, as in plane-wave electronic-structure codes, with MPI slab and pencil decomposition and CUDA or ROCm backends.
claimed_speedup: none: no numbers or speedup claim appear in the README, docs/source details.rst, index.rst, examples.rst or tests/programs/benchmark.cpp
stars_or_usage: 56 stars, 16 forks; conda-forge package; listed as a required dependency ('domain-specific FFT library') in the SIRIUS README, the electronic-structure library used by Quantum ESPRESSO and CP2K
tradeoffs: Not a new FFT kernel: the 1D transforms are done by FFTW, MKL or cuFFT underneath, and the gain comes from skipping z-columns that are all zero in frequency space and exploiting Hermitian symmetry for R2C and C2R. Needs a precomputed list of non-zero columns, sizes best of the form 2^a 3^b 5^c 7^d, optional MPI, OpenMP, CUDA 11+ or ROCm 5+; C++17, with C and Fortran interfaces; pre-allocated Grid objects are reused between transforms.

name: tinyfft
baseline: FFTW3 (FFTW_MEASURE planner)
workload: In-place power-of-two complex double FFT (AVX variant) at lengths 2^17 to 2^20; the README gives no further workload detail.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Empirically, for vectors of length between 2^17 and 2^20, Tiny FFT is faster than FFTW3 with FFTW_MEASURE. For other cases, Tiny FFT is slower than FFTW3.' No numbers are given anywhere in the repo.
compiler_and_flags: README build lines only: 'clang -O3 example.c tinyfft.c -lm' and 'clang -O3 example.c tinyfft_avx.c -lm -march=native'; the flags used for the FFTW comparison are not stated.
tradeoffs: Tiny code base (tinyfft.c 132 lines, tinyfft_avx.c 342 lines). Power-of-two lengths only, double precision complex only, output left in bit-reversal order (so the transform is meant for convolution-style use, not a drop-in FFTW replacement). The AVX variant uses split real/imaginary arrays and needs -march=native. Slower than FFTW3 outside 2^17-2^20 by the author's own statement.
caveats: No benchmark program, results file, CPU model, compiler version or FFTW version is in the repo (example.c only reads integers from stdin and runs fft/ifft/convolution); the claim is a qualitative author statement and the README itself says 'comparable to FFTW3 for some length' near the top. Not like-for-like: tfft_fft and tfft_fft_avx leave the output in bit-reversed order (README), whereas FFTW returns natural order, so the comparison skips the permutation; fine for convolution, not for a general FFT. Narrow range (2^17 to 2^20), FFTW_MEASURE rather than FFTW_PATIENT or MKL, slower than FFTW at all other sizes. Last commit 2018-07-24, single author, 15 stars, 0 forks.

name: detria
baseline: CDT (artem-ogre/CDT) and poly2tri; Triangle (CMU) is also in the comparison but is faster on random point sets
workload: Constrained Delaunay triangulation timing (set-up and result retrieval excluded) on Natural Earth country outlines, poly2tri test files, a cocircular fractal, and 1,000 to 1,000,000 random points inside a square; box plots of repeated runs.
claimed_speedup: Medians from the 23 per-case SVG result files embedded in BENCHMARKS.md (images/benchmark/*.svg), detria vs CDT vs Triangle in ms: world land outline (407,072 vertices) 502 vs 1431 vs 441; United States outline 24.4 vs 58.8 vs 27.2; Afghanistan (1,532 vertices) 0.74 vs 2.17 vs 0.87; 10,000-vertex debug2.dat 11.6 vs 28.7 vs 12.5. Over the 23 files, detria is faster than CDT in 21 (about 1.5x to 3.2x, derived from page data) and faster than poly2tri in all 14 cases poly2tri supports (about 1.05x to 2.2x, derived from page data). It is faster than Triangle in 16 of 23: the 13 country outlines, city.dat, debug2.dat and the depth-4 fractal (1.66 vs 1.73 ms), by about 1.04x to 1.3x (derived from page data). It is slower than Triangle on all four random-point sets (1,000,000 points: 1798 vs 946 ms) and on the world land outline (502 vs 441 ms). It is slower than both Triangle and CDT on the depth-6 and depth-8 cocircular fractals (depth 8: 3091 vs 1407 CDT vs 857 Triangle).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 17.0.3 (MSVC-like command line), release build with default compiler flags
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, Windows 10
tradeoffs: Single-header CDT with a C# port; no point insertion after triangulation, no Steiner or refinement (stated non-goal). CDT and poly2tri versions are not stated. Triangle is still faster for generic point sets.
caveats: Mixed result. The library beats CDT and poly2tri on most inputs. Against Triangle it wins only by 4-30% on country outlines, poly2tri test files and the small fractal, and it loses on random points (up to about 1.9x slower at 1M points), the world land outline and the deeper fractals (3.6x slower than Triangle at depth 8). 'Default compiler flags' means the CMake Release defaults for clang-cl, not explicit flags. Baseline versions are pinned in src/benchmark/CMakeLists.txt (CDT 58f34da, poly2tri 13d64e7, Triangle vendored), but no release numbers are given. The machine is a single 2019 Windows desktop. name: geo-utils-cpp
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 (spherical_equatorial strategy: bg::within and bg::area); also S2 Geometry 0.14.0 and GeographicLib 2.7
workload: Google Benchmark on seeded random lat/lng data: spherical point-in-polygon (polygons of 10, 100 and 1000 vertices, 1000 query points per iteration) and spherical polygon area (10/100/1000 vertices); native library types are built outside the timed loop.
claimed_speedup: contains (M queries/s, geo-utils-cpp vs Boost.Geometry): 16.2 vs 1.91 at N=10, 2.87 vs 0.234 at N=100, 0.329 vs 0.024 at N=1000 (about 8.5x, 12x and 14x, derived from page data). area (M polygons/s): 69.9 vs 45.0 at N=10, 67.2 vs 36.2 at N=100, 67.7 vs 36.6 at N=1000 (about 1.5-1.9x, derived from page data). heading is about 1.05-1.1x faster (24.9 vs 22.5 at N=1000, 15.5 vs 14.7 at N=100,000). distance_between (40.5 vs 39.8 and 28.2 vs 28.8) and path_length (54.0 vs 48.7 down to 41.7 vs 40.2) tie Boost.Geometry within noise.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17, -std=c++17 -O2 -DNDEBUG, Release, Google Benchmark 1.8.4, Boost 1.90.0
hardware: Apple M1, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM, macOS 15.7
tradeoffs: Header-only, no dependencies, lat/lng-native API. Spherical Earth only (mean radius 6371009 m), not WGS84 ellipsoidal; accuracy degrades near the poles and for antipodal pairs. Far smaller feature set than Boost.Geometry (no generic geometry types, no spatial index).
caveats: The contains comparison is not like for like. geo-utils-cpp uses an O(N) ray cast over rhumb-line edges by default, while bg::within with the spherical CS picks a great-circle winding strategy. So the two give different answers near the poles and on long edges, and the 8-14x gap partly reflects that choice (the docs say so). S2 beats it by a wide margin on contains (18.0 M/s at N=100), on path_length (about 2x) and on snap-to-route (about 3x). The benchmarks were run on one machine only (Apple M1, Apple clang), with no GCC, MSVC or x86 numbers. The library is a C++ port of the geometry utilities in Google's android-maps-utils (Java, Apache-2.0). The repo is young: the oldest visible commit is from May 2026.

Synthetic rows (parallel batch; ratio = GEOS/GeoRepair): valid polygon 4v 4.8x, invalid bowtie 4v 25x, invalid bowtie 1000v 8.0x, collapsed 1000v 5.5x, zero-length line 45x, zigzag ls 500v 43x, dense self ls 1000v 120x; star-burst and spoke rows reach 5632x-12573x. GEOS is faster on valid polygon 10000v (0.37x), spaghetti 500v (0.56x), large coord 1e12 1000v (0.08x), self-int ls 1000v (0.05x) and arrange valid 500v (0.25x). docs/BENCHMARKS.md (tables dated 2026-08-07): real-world validation 2.47 s vs 3.46 s (1.40x), full pass 4.05 s vs 3.49 s (0.86x). The rustc version used for the runs is not stated. Windows x86_64. The README's 2026-09-18 table still shows overlap mp 186-318x and dense grid 183-250x, while BENCHMARKS.md gives 6.85-10.34x and 4.23-13.63x for the same rows and calls ~200x figures an artifact. name: ArborX
baseline: Boost.Geometry.Index R-tree (packing/bulk-load algorithm, Boost 1.67.0) and nanoflann kd-tree (hash 3b2065e)
workload: Section 3.2 of the ACM TOMS 2020 paper: single-threaded tree construction, k=10 nearest search and radius (spatial) search with m = n source/target points from 10^4 to 10^7, for a filled case (filled sphere queries in a filled cube) and a hollow case (hollow sphere in hollow cube), ArborX BVH vs Boost.Geometry.Index packing R-tree and nanoflann; Google Benchmark median, run on one core of a CADES node.
claimed_speedup: Figures 5 and 6 plot speedup relative to nanoflann (bars read by eye, single thread). Filled case: construction ArborX about 0.85x-1.37x vs Boost about 0.87x-1.32x (similar); nearest search ArborX about 0.58x-0.78x at 10^4-10^6 and about 1.48x at 10^7, Boost about 0.55x-0.93x, so ArborX is about 1.6x faster than Boost at 10^7 (derived from page data). Hollow case: nearest search ArborX about 0.95x, 1.75x, 2.0x, 2.6x at 10^4-10^7 vs Boost about 0.62x-1.22x, so about 2.1x over Boost at 10^7 (derived from page data); construction ArborX about 0.87x-1.12x vs Boost about 1.02x-1.40x, i.e. Boost builds faster in the hollow case. Paper text: 'ArborX and Boost.Geometry.Index libraries perform similarly' for construction; for nearest search 'ArborX significantly outperforms both Boost.Geometry.Index and nanoflann libraries for larger numbers of objects, particularly for the hollow case.'
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2695 v4 (18 cores, 2.1 GHz; CADES node, one thread used for the library comparison); scaling runs on OLCF Summit (2x IBM POWER9, NVIDIA V100)
stars_or_usage: 242 stars; Trilinos/Kokkos ecosystem library; ACM TOMS papers (2020 and 2025 v2.0)
tradeoffs: Kokkos-based performance-portable C++ library (CPU threads plus CUDA/HIP/SYCL GPU backends) with optional distributed trees; the BVH is built for static or batch-rebuilt data rather than being a dynamic insert/delete R-tree; heavier build dependency than a header-only R-tree.
caveats: Wins are single-threaded and modest: construction is on par with Boost (Boost is faster in the hollow case), ArborX is slower than nanoflann for nearest search in the filled case up to 10^6 points, and the clear win (about 1.6x-2.1x over Boost, derived from bars read by eye) appears only for nearest search at 10^7 points; spatial search in the hollow case at 10^6-10^7 favors Boost over ArborX's 2P variant. Numbers are bar charts with no table. The paper states no compiler, flags or Kokkos version; Boost 1.67.0 and nanoflann 3b2065e are from 2018-2019. The repo's bvh_driver keeps a Boost R-tree backend but no nanoflann backend. ArborX's main value is multithreaded and GPU search (Kokkos), which Boost and nanoflann do not offer.

name: GeometryOps.jl
baseline: GEOS (through GeoPandas/Shapely in Python and the 'geos' package in R)
workload: kadyb/vector-benchmark: a synthetic set of 500,000 planar points plus one polygon. The distance task uses only the first 5,000 points (a 5,000 x 5,000 pairwise distance matrix). intersects tests all 500,000 points against the polygon. The other tasks are buffer, sampling points in the polygon, CRS transform, and GeoPackage load/write. Each value is the median seconds per task. Julia is timed with Chairmarks for 15 s (60 s for buffer) after warm-up; R uses system.time and Python uses timeit, 10 runs each.
claimed_speedup: Median seconds in timings.csv, GeometryOps.jl vs GEOS-backed packages, on tasks where GeometryOps runs its own pure-Julia code: distance 0.11 vs 0.9 (GeoPandas) and 5.37 (R geos); intersects 0.04 vs 0.12 (GeoPandas) and 0.08 (R geos, prepared geometry); sample 0.04 vs 0.9 (GeoPandas). Derived ratios (derived from page data): distance about 8x vs GeoPandas and about 49x vs R geos; intersects 3x vs GeoPandas and 2x vs R geos; sample about 22x vs GeoPandas. The other tasks are not GeometryOps-vs-GEOS comparisons: buffer is 5.75 vs 4.07 (GeoPandas) and 5.65 (R geos), but the GeometryOps buffer script calls GEOS itself through LibGEOS (GO.GEOS backend), so it is GEOS vs GEOS; transform 0.08 vs 0.23 (GeoPandas) runs PROJ through Proj.jl on both sides, and R sf-project also takes 0.08; load 0.36 vs 0.45 (GeoPandas) and write 1.38 vs 1.28 are GDAL file I/O, and terra loads faster (0.33).
compiler_and_flags: Interpreted/JIT packages (Julia, Python, R); no Julia, R or Python version stated. geometryops/Project.toml sets compat GeometryOps = 0.1.26; pixi.toml pins geopandas >=1.1.1,<2, pandas >=2.3.2, numpy >=2.3.2 and pyogrio >=0.11.1,<0.12; R package versions are not pinned.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X @ 3.7 GHz, 64 GB RAM, Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
tradeoffs: Pure Julia, GeoInterface.jl-based, mostly 2D/2.5D geometry; not callable from C++ without embedding Julia. README warns the package is under heavy development. Includes OGC predicates, clipping (intersection, union, difference), simplification and more.
caveats: Only distance, intersects and sample compare GeometryOps' own pure-Julia code against GEOS. In buffer, GeometryOps calls GEOS itself via LibGEOS. Transform is PROJ on both sides, and load/write are GDAL I/O, so none of those are GEOS comparisons. GEOS is reached through wrappers (GeoPandas/Shapely, R 'geos'), so per-call marshalling overhead is part of the baseline. The R geos distance time (5.37 s) comes from an sapply loop over geos_distance, one row at a time. The script's commented-out alternatives (a matrix loop and a fully vectorised call) are noted at about 11 s, so the R wrapper itself, not just the loop style, looks like the bottleneck. Julia is timed after JIT warm-up with Chairmarks, while R/Python take the median of 10 cold-start-inclusive runs. Each package's scripts were written by that package's developers: the Julia side by GeometryOps lead asinghvi17 (PR #12, 2024) and JuliaGeo's evetion (PRs #15-#17, 2025), and the GeoPandas side updated by GeoPandas maintainer martinfleis (PR #18). The suite owner kadyb re-ran everything on one machine. Suite repo: 23 stars, MIT. Its detailed report is on github.io and was not reachable. GeometryOps' README points at this suite and says 'More benchmarks coming soon', and the package warns it is under heavy development. Julia is outside the 'usable from C++' scope.

name: Pkd-tree (parallel kd-tree with batch updates)
baseline: CGAL kd-tree (Spatial_searching) and Boost.Geometry R-tree (also BHL-tree and Log-tree)
workload: Parallel kd-tree construction, batch insertion and deletion, k-nearest-neighbor, range query and range count on large point sets, compared with CGAL, Boost's sequential R-tree and other parallel kd-tree baselines (SIGMOD 2025 paper).
claimed_speedup: Repo raw results (script/data, times presumably in seconds, hardware unstated), all ratios derived from page data: build.csv, 10^9 3-D points: CGAL kd-tree 1082.4 vs Pkd-tree 3.91 (uniform, about 277x) and 381.3 vs 4.77 (Varden, about 80x). knn.csv, 10^9 3-D points, k=10: CGAL 0.223 vs 0.162 (uniform, about 1.4x) and 3.066 vs 1.713 (Varden, about 1.8x). summary.csv, 10^8 12-D points: build 112.18 vs 0.938 (uniform, about 120x) and 46.69 vs 1.07 (Varden, about 44x); 10% batch insert 171.2 vs 0.115 and 10% delete 29.99 vs 0.148 (uniform); range query 109.1 vs 17.4 (uniform, about 6.3x); kNN column 63.7 vs 51.4 (uniform) but 0.046 vs 0.048 on Varden (CGAL slightly faster). insert.csv/delete.csv: CGAL needs 709-2794 for any batch insert (it rebuilds the tree), and CGAL deletion of 0.1M points takes 0.347 vs 0.0054 (uniform) and 0.033 vs 0.0062 (Varden). Paper numbers seen only in search-result summaries, not checked: 17.4-40.7x faster insertions and 3.27-21.7x faster deletions than Log-tree; on 96 cores 91.9-115x faster construction than the sequential Boost R-tree, 10.4-14.8x faster kNN and 4.13-4.17x faster range report.
compiler_and_flags: -O3 -mcx16 -march=native (CMakeLists.txt Release build); README: tested with clang 17, also compiles with g++ 13; the compiler used for the paper runs was not confirmed
hardware: 96 cores (CPU model not seen)
stars_or_usage: 90 stars, 4 forks; SIGMOD 2025 (PACMMOD 3(1)) artifact; README says the code now lives in ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib (PSI-Lib)
tradeoffs: Built on ParlayLib (git submodule) for shared-memory parallelism, so wins need many cores; low-dimensional point sets (kNN, range, count queries), not general geometry or polygons. The repo README says Pkd-tree is now integrated into PSI-Lib (github.com/ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib, MIT, PPoPP 2026 'Parallel Dynamic Spatial Indexes') which adds orth-trees and space-filling-curve indexes.
caveats: The SIGMOD 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3709712, arXiv 2411.09275) could not be opened (arxiv.org and cs.ucr.edu blocked), so paper numbers and the CPU model (a search summary says four-way Xeon Gold 6252, 96 cores) are unverified. Comparisons are parallel Pkd-tree against CGAL built with Parallel_tag (TBB) and parallel TBB queries, which is fair for build and query, but CGAL's kd-tree has no batch insert (the harness inserts then rebuilds) and deletes one point at a time, so the huge update ratios reflect a missing CGAL feature. The Boost baseline at HEAD (tests/rtree.cpp) is a 2-D bgi::rtree with quadratic<2> node capacity (a very small node size) built and updated sequentially while Pkd-tree uses all cores; its kNN queries run in a parlay parallel_for. The repo CSVs name no hardware or date. CGAL is slightly faster for one 12-D Varden kNN row. The README says this repository will no longer be updated; the maintained code is ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib.

name: PSI-Lib / SpaceTreeLib (P-Orth tree, SPaC-tree; also contains the Pkd-tree)
baseline: Boost.Geometry bgi::rtree (quadratic, sequential); the repo also benchmarks CPAM and Zd-tree, and has a CGAL kd-tree harness (tests/cgal.cpp)
workload: Real-world point sets GeoLife (3-D), Cosmo50 (3-D) and OSM (2-D): whole-set build, all n points inserted or deleted in 10^4 batches of 0.01%, k-NN (k=1,10,100) on four query distributions, and range count/report (small/medium/large). Parallel PSI trees and the parallel Zd-tree are compared against a Boost bgi::rtree<quadratic<32>> that is updated one point at a time on one thread and queried in parallel with parlay::parallel_for (script/data/real_world/real_world.csv, from the PPoPP '26 scripts).
claimed_speedup: Ratios derived from page data (real_world.csv 'tot' column, seconds). Read the Boost rows carefully: script/merge_real_world.py maps Boost's '## incre insert full' to Insert/1.0, '## incre insert half' to Insert/0.0001 and '## incre delete half' to Delete/0.0001. So Boost 'Insert 1.0' is n sequential single-point inserts into a quadratic bgi::rtree, and Boost's '0.0001' rows are n/2 single-point inserts or deletes. PSI '1.0' is one parallel batch insert of all n points (a build), and PSI '0.0001' is all n points inserted, or deleted, in 10^4 parallel batches. Whole set: Cosmo50 Boost 414.38 vs P-Orth (OrthTree) 1.899 and SPaC-Z (PTree-Z) 0.8365 (about 218x and 495x); OSM 666.0 vs 4.960 and 2.122 (about 134x and 314x); GeoLife 0.2132 vs 0.00639 and PTree-H 0.00150 (about 33x and 142x). Deletes: Cosmo50 Boost 1482.7 s for n/2 single deletes vs OrthTree 17.85 and PTree-Z 8.463 for all n in batches (about 83x and 175x in total time, with Boost doing half the work); OSM 264.2 vs 14.93 and 7.368 (about 18x and 36x). On GeoLife, Boost's n/2 single deletes take less total time (0.064) than OrthTree (0.089) or PTree-H (0.137) deleting all n. Large range report (RRL), both sides parallel: Cosmo50 Boost 19.25 vs OrthTree 1.738, OSM 8.347 vs 1.128, GeoLife 7.829 vs 0.4466 (about 7-18x). Small range report (RRS) favours Boost: Cosmo50 0.00044 vs OrthTree 0.00082, OSM 0.00026 vs 0.00063, GeoLife 0.00028 vs 0.00086. Boost k-NN columns are not comparable (harness bug, see caveats). Against the third-party parallel Zd-tree in the same harness: SPaC-Z batch updates at 0.01% are about 2.1-3.2x faster (Cosmo50 insert 13.83 vs 5.631, delete 20.66 vs 8.463; OSM insert 16.50 vs 7.906, delete 23.86 vs 7.368), and P-Orth is roughly on par with Zd-tree (0.85-1.6x). The SPaC-Z build is about 2.0-2.8x faster than Zd-tree on Cosmo50 and OSM. On queries, P-Orth beats Zd-tree on large range report (Cosmo50 1.738 vs 2.197) and k=10 uniform k-NN (0.244 vs 0.301), while SPaC trees are much slower on k-NN (Cosmo50 IDU10 PTree-H 1.869, PTree-Z 11.55). Paper (search summary only): P-Orth and SPaC trees beat existing parallel kd-trees and Orth-trees on batch updates, with competitive queries, and SPaC-trees are 2-6x faster than Pkd-trees on updates.
compiler_and_flags: Clang >= 19 or g++ >= 14 (CMakeLists check); Release -O3; docs/ARTIFACT_EVALUATION.md says the paper numbers were measured with -march=native -mcx16 (PSI_NATIVE_ARCH=ON). The compiler used for the paper runs is not stated.
hardware: CPU model not stated in the repo; docs/ARTIFACT_EVALUATION.md asks for at least 512 GB RAM and preferably more than 128 cores; run scripts use numactl -i all. A search summary of the paper mentions 72 cores with 2-way hyperthreading (unverified, paper blocked).
stars_or_usage: 10 stars, 734 commits; PPoPP 2026 (doi 10.1145/3774934.3786412) and SIGMOD 2025 artifacts; successor repo of ucrparlay/Pkd-tree
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 on ParlayLib (submodule) and libmorton; needs many cores to win; points only (2-D to 16-D data generator), kd/orth/SPaC trees chosen per update-heavy vs query-heavy use. SPaC trees are built on a permanent fork of CPAM; vendored Hilbert code carries a Rice University notice requirement (THIRD_PARTY.md). A migration table from bgi::rtree is in docs/MANUAL.md. README notes the code was recently refactored with AI help and gives commit af67b82 for the original design.
caveats: The Boost baseline harness (tests/boost_rtree.cpp) has three problems. (1) Its k-NN loop (run_rtree_knn) ignores the query set it is given and queries wp[0..batch_size) for all four distributions, building each query point from only pnt[0] and pnt[1], so 3-D data sets (Cosmo50, GeoLife) get a query point whose third coordinate does not come from the data. The Boost k-NN times are therefore nearly identical across the IDS/ODS/IDU/ODU columns (Cosmo50 k=10: 0.2735, 0.2765, 0.2759, 0.2756) and are not comparable with PSI's. (2) Boost updates are sequential single-point insert/remove, while PSI and Zd-tree use parallel batches; Boost's bulk-loading (packing) constructor is timed as '## build tree half' but merge_real_world.py drops it, so the 134-495x 'build' ratios compare a parallel build with Boost's slowest construction path. (3) merge_real_world.py labels Boost's n/2 single-point insert/delete runs as ratio 0.0001, so those rows do half the work of the PSI rows with the same label. Boost queries run in parallel, so the range-query ratios are parallel against parallel; Boost wins small range reports on all three data sets. Numbers come from the paper-era code: the README says the library was later refactored with AI and some indexes are 'slightly affected' (original design at commit af67b82). The paper (dl.acm.org, cs.ucr.edu, conference-publishing.com) was blocked, so peer review is confirmed from the README citation and search results only. Pkd-tree (kd_tree.h, KdTree rows) is part of this library and is catalogued separately as ucrparlay/pkd-tree; on Cosmo50, Pkd-tree's 0.01% batch deletes total 800.3 s vs 8.46 s for SPaC-Z. include/psi/dependence/space_filling_curve/hilbert.hpp is under a Rice University notice license (attribution notice required); the CPAM fork and the submodules are MIT.

name: SPRK-tree (Sorted Projection Radius KD-tree)
baseline: Boost.Geometry R-tree (named among the paper's competitors in search snippets) plus KD-trees in several languages (Kiddo, nabo, Neighbourhood), a Rust VP-tree, scikit-learn BallTree, SNN and brute force. nanoflann and CGAL kd-tree are feature-gated backends in the rembed harness, but I could not confirm they appear in the paper.
workload: Radius queries (and nearest neighbor queries) on graph embeddings and other point sets, up to 10M points and 2 to 960 dimensions, from the ESA 2026 paper 'Benchmarking and Engineering Data Structures for Spherical Range Queries'.
claimed_speedup: No speedup numbers verified. The paper (Blaesius, von der Heydt, Kempf, Kobert, Maas, 'Benchmarking and Engineering Data Structures for Spherical Range Queries', arXiv 2607.07367, listed in search results as ESA 2026 LIPIcs) could not be opened, because arxiv.org and drops.dagstuhl.de are blocked. Neither the sprk nor the rembed README quotes results. According to its abstract, seen only in search snippets, the SPRK-tree achieves the fastest query times in almost all benchmarks and ranks second in the rest.
compiler_and_flags: The sprk README advises rustflags -Ctarget-cpu=native (AVX-512 compress when available). The rembed release profile is the Cargo default plus debug=true. The paper's compiler and flags were not read.
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; crate published as sprk on crates.io
tradeoffs: Radius queries in D-dimensional Euclidean space; SIMD leaf scans with lookup-table pruning, SVD projection for D > 16, parallel construction, update() rebuild that reuses allocations. Not a general spatial index (no rectangles or nearest-neighbor guarantees in the README).
caveats: Peer-reviewed (ESA 2026 LIPIcs) but numbers were not verified here: the paper and its tables were unreachable, and neither the sprk nor rembed README quotes speedups. Evidence tier B is on the strength of the paper plus public benchmark harness (rembed with reproducibility-cli). Verifier should open the paper for numbers, CPU and flags. Benchmarks target embeddings from graph drawing, with many high-dimensional cases. [retier] Peer review rests on search-result listings of the DROPS/LIPIcs ESA 2026 entry, whose page is blocked. name: tidwall/rtree.c
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 R*-tree
workload: Dynamic R-tree insert/erase/reinsert then range queries on point and box keys (GeoToolbox suite, 2D/3D synthetic and real datasets).
claimed_speedup: GeoToolbox README: tidwall R-tree is 'faster than Boost at insert/erase/reinsert and at querying afterwards'. Linked result TSVs (ikolev21.github.io, Insert-Erase-Query scenario, Boost time / tidwall time, geomean over 69 dataset/size/dim combinations): clang-cl insert 23.7x, erase 3.6x, reinsert 9.4x, range query 1.06x (range 0.30-2.54x), total 4.9x; MSVC insert 34.8x, erase 3.4x, reinsert 9.4x, query 1.08x, total 6.0x; at 10^6 elements total 10.9x (clang-cl) / 12.6x (MSVC) (derived from page data). Own README: 1M random points insert 151.3 ns/op, search-item 242.4 ns/op (clang-17 -O3, Ryzen 9 5950X), no Boost comparison.

hardware: GeoToolbox: ASUS ROG Strix G16 laptop, Windows 11 (CPU model not stated); own README: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X, Ubuntu 20.04

name: alpha-wrap (CGAL-free Alpha Wrapping)
baseline: CGAL 6.x CGAL::alpha_wrap_3 (Alpha_wrap_3), GMP-free build
workload: Alpha wrapping with offset of triangle soups (bundled meshes, a 100k-triangle sphere and a 236k-triangle Actaeon statue, alpha = diag/30), compared with the CGAL reference build for speed, topology and Hausdorff distance.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Speed: competitive to faster (ours ~2x faster on most inputs in this GMP-free CGAL environment)'. Same page: face count 0.6-1.0x CGAL's, symmetric Hausdorff distance to the CGAL wrap 0.1%-3.4% of the bbox diagonal. No per-model timing table.
compiler_and_flags: CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for the comparison build (RelWithDebInfo for the default build); optimization flags and compiler not stated

name: Arctern

name: Bonxai
baseline: Octomap (octree-based 3D occupancy map)
workload: Google Benchmark in bonxai_core/benchmark (benchmark_bonxai.cpp vs benchmark_octomap.cpp) on two PCD point clouds from data/: table_scene_mug_rgb.pcd at 0.01 voxel size and room_scan.pcd at 0.05. Create inserts every point into a new grid, Update re-sets the same cells in a filled grid, and IterateAllCells visits every leaf. The README does not say which dataset its numbers come from.
claimed_speedup: Create 1165 us vs 25522 us (about 21.9x, derived from page data); Update 851 us vs 3824 us (about 4.5x, derived from page data); IterateAllCells 124 us vs 698 us (about 5.6x, derived from page data). README also states Bonxai is 'much faster and, in some cases, even more memory-efficient than an Octree'.
tradeoffs: Hierarchical sparse voxel grid influenced by OpenVDB rather than a multi-resolution octree; sparse and unbounded with 32-bit indices (about 40,000 km at 1 cm voxels per the README); core is header-only.
caveats: The README labels the numbers 'preliminary' and says to take them with a grain of salt. It gives no compiler, flags, CPU or dataset; the default CMake build type is RelWithDebInfo. The two sides do not do the same work per point: Bonxai writes a uint32 value with accessor.setValue, while Octomap runs OcTree::updateNode(endpoint, true), a probabilistic log-odds occupancy update. That favors Bonxai in Create and Update. A fairer full-mapping comparison, bonxai_map/benchmark/benchmark_kitti.cpp (probabilistic map with ray casting vs Octomap on KITTI, prints a speed-up), exists, but no results from it are published. The README also says the project is built mostly for fun and education and is under development, and that very sparse clouds can use 20-40% more memory than Octomap. The Octomap baseline is a robotics-mapping incumbent rather than Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS, so the category fit is borderline.

name: Boost.Polygon (Voronoi diagram builder)
baseline: CGAL (Delaunay triangulation of points / segment Delaunay graph; CGAL-4.3-beta1 in the benchmark)
workload: Average construction time of the Voronoi diagram (Boost.Polygon) versus the Delaunay triangulation (CGAL, S-Hull) of random points and of random non-intersecting segments, uniformly distributed on a 32-bit integer grid, from 100 to 1,000,000 inputs.
claimed_speedup: Random segments, average construction time in seconds, Boost.Polygon vs CGAL: 100 segments 0.002284 vs 0.002985; 10,000 segments 0.2377 vs 0.3374; 1,000,000 segments 25.0 vs 39.09 (about 1.56x faster at 1M, derived from page data). Random points: Boost.Polygon is slower than CGAL (1,000,000 points 3.47 s vs 0.9023 s; S-Hull 6.603814 s). A second page in the repo (doc/analysis.htm) says Boost.Polygon's arbitrary-angle Booleans are 'roughly as fast as GPC at small scales, while algorithmically faster at large scales' and that a 2010 divide-and-conquer change gave 10X over its own older algorithm at 200,000+ rectangles; it gives no GPC numbers.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.7.3 with Boost 1.54.0, CGAL-4.3-beta1, GMP 5.1.4, MPFR 3.1.2; optimization flags are not stated (benchmark/Jamfile.v2 sets none)
hardware: Intel i5-7600 2.8 GHz, 16 GiB RAM, Ubuntu 13.04 64-bit (as printed on the page)
stars_or_usage: 70 stars; part of the Boost libraries
tradeoffs: Builds a Voronoi diagram (points and segments) with output coordinates at '128 machine epsilon' precision per the page, whereas the compared CGAL and S-Hull routines build a Delaunay triangulation with no output coordinates. No external dependencies (CGAL needs Boost, GMP, MPFR). The benchmark uses 32-bit integer input coordinates.
caveats: Mixed result: only segment input wins (about 1.3x to 1.56x vs CGAL's Segment_Delaunay_graph_2, derived from page data). For points, CGAL's Delaunay_triangulation_2 (Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions kernel) is about 3.8x faster at 1M points (derived from page data). Voronoi and Delaunay are different outputs; the page notes the Voronoi diagram carries more information. In the segments test, the time for generating segments and removing intersections is measured in a separate pass and subtracted, and timing is CPU time (user+system) from boost::timer::cpu_timer. benchmark/Jamfile.v2 hard-codes the author's local library paths and sets no optimization flags. b2's default variant is debug unless variant=release is passed, and the page does not say which was used. This is a first-party benchmark by the library author with an old setup (GCC 4.7.3, Boost 1.54, CGAL 4.3-beta1, Ubuntu 13.04). The page was last edited 2013-10-06 ('rerunning benchmarks'), so its CPU label 'Intel i5-7600 2.8 GHz' predates that CPU's 2017 release and is likely a typo; reported as printed. A WebSearch snippet of the boost.org copy summarised the result as complete dominance over the CGAL Delaunay graph, which the points table does not support. boost.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the repo copy was read. doc/analysis.htm separately says the 2010 divide-and-conquer Booleans are 'roughly as fast as GPC at small scales, while algorithmically faster at large scales', with no GPC numbers.

name: Contour-Coherent Hausdorff Distance
baseline: Boost.Geometry discrete_hausdorff_distance
workload: Exact discrete Hausdorff distance between all pairs of ordered image contours (21 related walking silhouettes, 210 pair evaluations), total package time.
claimed_speedup: Walking silhouettes: 50.48 ms total package (0.240 ms per HD) vs Boost discrete Hausdorff 12382.56 ms (58.96 ms per HD), stated as approximately 245x faster; also 16.3x faster than brute force with shuffling and 88.9x faster than brute force with early stop. Boost was only run on this package; on unrelated shape sets (Kimia216) the method is only about equal to shuffled brute force.
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build: Windows preset x64-release (Visual Studio 2026 toolchain, Ninja, vcpkg) or Linux -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with GCC/Ninja. Which toolchain produced the published numbers, and the explicit optimization flags, are not stated.
tradeoffs: Header-only, dependency-free; exact result; custom point types and L2/L1/Chebyshev policies; relies on ordered, coherent contours; worst case still O(n*m).
caveats: First-party benchmark; hardware not stated in the README or the article (docs/article.html). The speedup exploits contour ordering that Boost's general function cannot use, so it is a specialised-input comparison. Without BOOST_GEOMETRY_ENABLE_SIMILARITY_RTREE (not defined in this build), Boost's discrete_hausdorff_distance is a plain O(n*m) scan with no early break. The author's own shuffled brute force is already about 15x faster than Boost on the same package (821.73 vs 12382.56 ms, derived from page data), and the method beats that by 16.3x. The Boost timing includes converting contours to Boost linestrings on every call (CalcHausdorffDistanceBoost). Boost is reported only for the walking-silhouette package; the article says Boost was used mainly as a correctness reference. On Kimia216 the method only ties shuffled brute force (813.40 vs 812.02 ms). The README also lists an OpenCV FLANN kd-tree baseline, which the article says is not strictly exact. Very new repo (first commit 2026-05-14, 10 commits, 1 star).

Own Google Benchmark run dated 2018-09-29: 45K geojson nodes 22 ms; 2,000 uniform points 1 ms; 100,000 63 ms; 200,000 140 ms; 500,000 400 ms; 1,000,000 994 ms. hardware: 4 X 2300 MHz CPU (model not stated), run dated 2018-09-29

caveats: Its own evidence compares only against the JS original of the same algorithm (~10% at 1M points after the 6x claim was retracted in PR #8); bench/run.cpp benchmarks delaunator-cpp alone, and CGAL, Triangle and poly2tri are never measured in the repo (issue #34 'Comparison with CGAL?' got no numbers). The only C++ comparison is a competitor's table (Delaunay32 README, Apple M1, compiler and flags not stated): delaunator-cpp is about 1.08x faster than Triangle 1.6 but 4.1x slower than single-thread Delaunay32 and 1.7x slower than single-thread Fade2D, which contradicts the hedged 'probably the fastest' claim; Delaunay32 is already catalogued. name: DGtal QuickHull
baseline: CGAL convex_hull_3 (Cartesian and Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel)
