DGtal-only timings (MacBook Pro, 2.7 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7): 1e7 random lattice points in a ball of radius 1000 take 7913 ms in total, of which 4221 ms purge duplicates and 3214 ms is the QuickHull core.
tradeoffs: Part of the DGtal digital-geometry library, so using it pulls in DGtal and its dependencies. Facets are not necessarily triangles/simplices in the output, unlike CGAL's simplicial hull. Kernel is selectable, with an exact integral kernel for lattice points. Not tailored for incremental or dynamic hulls. LGPL.
caveats: The claim is a single qualitative sentence, repeated in the module docs, with no CGAL numbers, point distributions, flags or compiler. The only timings are DGtal's own, on a MacBook Pro i7 2.7 GHz quad-core. Only the 3D convex hull is claimed faster. The docs themselves say the Delaunay use is 5-10x slower than CGAL's Delaunay triangulation. Unlike CGAL, the hull is not simplicial (facets may be polygons). The exact lattice kernels are about 25x slower when BigInteger is used for the internal integers. The QuickHull module is part of the much larger LGPL DGtal library.

name: earcut.hpp
baseline: earcut.js, the original JavaScript implementation (~445 ms for the same set in its README); test/bench.cpp also times libtess2 v1.0.2 on 9 small fixtures but publishes no results; CGAL and libtess2 are called 'slower and larger' in the README without numbers.
workload: Triangulating 119,680 real-world polygons (1.9M vertices) cut from Mapbox Vector Tile windows at zooms 4-16, whole set timed.
claimed_speedup: README: 119,680 real-world MVT polygons (1.9M vertices, map-tile window at zooms 4-16) triangulated in ~276 ms on a MacBook Pro M1 Pro (2021), 'noticeably faster than the JS original'; optional Delaunay refinement adds ~98 ms. The earcut.js README states ~445 ms (refinement ~168 ms) for the same 119,680-polygon set on the same MacBook Pro M1 Pro (2021), so earcut.hpp is about 1.6x faster than earcut.js (refinement about 1.7x) (derived from page data across the two READMEs; Node version and C++ compiler/flags not stated).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 276 ms figure; CMakeLists.txt defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with C++17 for the bench and no -march (compiler unspecified).
hardware: MacBook Pro M1 Pro (2021)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++14 polygon triangulator (ear slicing with z-order curve and spatial hashing). Trades quality and guaranteed correctness for speed: assumes valid polygons, output is not conforming (T-junctions) and not Delaunay unless the opt-in mapbox::refine pass is used (that pass uses non-robust predicates). README points to CGAL or libtess2 when correctness on bad input is needed.
caveats: The only quantified baseline is the same-algorithm JS original (about 1.6x, derived across two READMEs on the same machine), a weak result. test/bench.cpp registers BM_LibtessTriangulation (libtess2 v1.0.2 fetched by CMake) only on 9 whitelisted fixtures (building, dude, water, water2, water3, water3b, water4, water_huge, water_huge2); the 119,680-polygon tile benchmark (BM_EarcutTiles) has no libtess2 or other C++ counterpart, and no libtess2 results are published, so the C++ comparison needs a local run. No CGAL, poly2tri or Triangle measurement. Compiler and flags for the 276 ms figure are not stated. By design earcut does not guarantee a correct triangulation: the README says that on invalid input (self-crossing or overlapping rings, holes outside the outer ring, duplicate or zero-length edges) the output can contain overlapping triangles, gaps or triangles outside the polygon; the output is not conforming (T-junctions), and refine() uses non-robust predicates.

name: fast_gicp (FastGICP / FastVGICP / FastVGICPCuda)
baseline: PCL pcl::GeneralizedIterativeClosestPoint (GICP); also PCL NormalDistributionsTransform (NDT)
workload: Registering one pair of point-cloud scans (target 17,249 points, source 17,518 points after a 0.1 m approximate voxel grid) with GICP-family methods; wall time of a single alignment and of 100 repeated alignments, with fitness score reported.
claimed_speedup: README table, i9-9900K + RTX 2080 Ti: pcl_gicp single 127.508 ms, 100 times 12549.4 ms (fitness 0.204892); pcl_ndt single 53.5904 ms, 100 times 5467.16 ms; fgicp_st (single thread) 111.324 ms / 10662.7 ms; fgicp_mt 20.1602 ms / 1585 ms (fitness 0.204412); vgicp_mt 18.1106 ms / 1381 ms; vgicp_cuda (parallel_kdtree) 15.9587 ms / 1451.85 ms; vgicp_cuda (gpu_rbf_kernel) 5.91508 ms / 590.725 ms (fitness 0.20557). Derived from page data versus pcl_gicp: fgicp_mt 6.3x (single) and 7.9x (100 runs); vgicp_mt 7.0x and 9.1x; vgicp_cuda rbf kernel 21.6x and 21.2x; single-threaded fgicp_st only 1.15x and 1.18x. README headline rates: FastGICP ~40 FPS, FastGICPSingleThread ~15 FPS, FastVGICP ~70 FPS, FastVGICPCuda ~120 FPS, NDTCuda ~500 FPS.
compiler_and_flags: CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Release (CMake default Release flags) and adds OpenMP flags; no -march option seen. Compiler name and version not stated (README says tested on Ubuntu 18.04/20.04 with CUDA 11.1).
hardware: Core i9-9900K, GeForce RTX 2080 Ti
tradeoffs: Drop-in PCL registration interface, but depends on PCL, Eigen, OpenMP, Sophus and (for CUDA) nvbio. VGICP is a voxelized approximation of GICP and the GPU rbf-kernel covariance mode is described in the source as 'extremely fast but maybe a bit inaccurate' (its fitness score 0.20557 is the worst in the table). README notes that using fewer threads than the maximum can be faster in some environments. The author's newer small_gicp (already on the known list) is stated in the README to be twice as fast as fast_gicp.
caveats: Tier would be A except that the compiler is never named and the flags come only from the CMake Release default plus OpenMP, so it stays C (own-repo benchmark with partial methodology). Benchmark code is public (src/align.cpp) but the README shows a single scan pair (data/251370668.pcd vs 251371071.pcd) on one machine. Most of the speedup comes from multithreading and GPU use against PCL's default single-threaded GICP/NDT: fgicp_mt and vgicp_mt both run with omp_get_max_threads() (FastGICP's constructor default; align.cpp leaves setNumThreads(8) commented out), and the thread count actually used on the 8-core/16-thread i9-9900K is not printed. Single-threaded fgicp_st is only about 1.15x faster than pcl_gicp. The PCL version is not stated; iteration and convergence settings are each class's defaults and were not verified to be identical; pcl_ndt reaches a worse fitness (0.2296) than the GICP variants (about 0.204), so it is a different algorithm rather than a like-for-like baseline. align.cpp also prints ndt_cuda rows that the README output omits. The ICRA 2021 VGICP paper was not opened. The README badges and install commands still point to SMRT-AIST/fast_gicp (the copyright holder), and the README now announces small_gicp (already listed as koide3/small_gicp) as the faster successor library. claimed_speedup: docs/benchmark.md (500,000 points, 500 queries): total time fastquadtree numpy path 0.068 s (build 0.052, query 0.017), list path 0.285 s (build 0.054, query 0.231), Shapely STRtree 0.309 s (build 0.200, query 0.110), Rtree 2.351 s (build 1.805, query 0.546), PyQtree 2.909 s. That is 42.52x vs PyQtree (numpy path) and 10.20x (list path). Derived from page data: about 34.6x faster total than Rtree on the numpy path and 8.2x on the list path; against Shapely STRtree, 4.5x total on the numpy path but only 1.08x on the list path, and STRtree's query time (0.110 s) beats the list path's (0.231 s). The drop-in pyqtree shim takes 1.127 s vs 11.647 s for the original pyqtree (10.333x).
compiler_and_flags: CPython 3.14.5. The Rust engine is built via PyO3/maturin with a Cargo.toml release profile of opt-level=3, lto=thin, codegen-units=1, panic=abort. The rustc version is not stated (MSRV 1.89).
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X (16 threads), 31.3 GB RAM, CachyOS Linux
tradeoffs: Python package with a Rust core; point and rectangle quadtree with numpy bulk paths, optional object tracking, serialization to bytes. Quadtree rather than R-tree: no balanced bulk-loading guarantees.
caveats: First-party Python benchmark. The best number uses the numpy return path; the list path, which is comparable to Rtree's list returns, is much slower and loses to Shapely STRtree on query time. The Shapely STRtree row uses numpy points and returns. Both sides include Python call overhead, and Rtree inserts go one at a time through ctypes. The rustc version is not stated. Only 500 queries are run, on uniform point data rather than extended geometries.

name: geo-index (packed immutable R-tree and k-d tree)
baseline: rstar (georust dynamic R-tree, bulk_load)
workload: Criterion benchmark on one bounding-box dataset (benches/bounds.raw): bulk construction of an R-tree from boxes, and a bounding-box search, geo-index (Hilbert-sorted packed tree) vs rstar::RTree::bulk_load.
claimed_speedup: README: construction is ~2x faster than rstar and search is ~33% faster. Numbers: construction geo-index hilbert 80.891 ms vs rstar bulk 159.34 ms; STRTree 116.52 ms; search 116.41 us (flatbush-style) vs rstar 153.62 us; with the rayon feature STRTree construction drops to 72.099 ms.
compiler_and_flags: cargo bench --bench rtree (Criterion); rustc version, profile and flags not stated
stars_or_usage: 200 stars, 18 forks; used under the hood in geoarrow-rs (per the README)
tradeoffs: Trees are immutable (no insert or delete after build), fully packed single-buffer layout with ABI-stable memory shared with Python and the flatbush/kdbush JavaScript libraries. Hilbert and STR sort methods. Also ships a k-d tree.
caveats: The author says it is just one benchmark and recommends benchmarking on your own data. Hardware, dataset size and compiler settings are not stated. A static packed index is compared against a dynamic R-tree's bulk load, which is not like-for-like on features (rstar supports updates). Search is one fixed bounding-box query (-112.007, 40.634, -111.921, 40.694) on one dataset, so the 33% figure rests on one query; the bench does assert that both return the same result count. The rstar construction closure clones the input Vec (rect_vec.to_vec()) inside the timed loop, while geo-index builds from a borrowed slice, which adds a copy to rstar's time. The rstar dev-dependency is 0.12. The bench labels geo-index runs 'flatbush' because the tree is a Rust port of mourner's flatbush and kdbush layouts. Derived from page data: construction 1.97x, search 1.32x.

name: GeoDesk (libgeodesk)
baseline: SQL-based geospatial databases (README says 'SQL'; PostgreSQL/PostGIS is implied but not named)
workload: Feature queries (tag and spatial) on OpenStreetMap data in an in-process GOL file, plus GOL build time and storage size, versus a SQL-based database; no workload, dataset or hardware is described in the README.
claimed_speedup: Queries 'typically 50 times faster than SQL'; converting .osm.pbf to a GOL is '20 times faster than an import into an SQL database'; GOL files are 20% to 50% larger than the source PBF, 'less than a tenth of the storage consumed by a traditional SQL-based database'.
tradeoffs: Read-mostly embedded query engine on its own GOL file format for OpenStreetMap data, not a general geometry library; optional GEOS integration for buffer, union and similar operations; C++20; the GOL tool needs Java; query engine adds under 250 KB per the README.

'SQL' and 'traditional SQL-based database' presumably mean PostGIS/osm2pgsql, but the README does not say so. benchmark/benchmark_main.cpp (inspected) has two Catch2 benchmarks that time only GeoDesk: 1,000 containing(Coordinate) queries on admin areas over Western Europe, and counting all buildings in the United States. They read hard-coded local Windows GOL paths (d:\geodesk\tests\*.gol) and contain no SQL comparison. The same three claims appear in the Java sibling repo clarisma/geodesk (201 stars, Apache-2.0), so the claim comes from the GeoDesk project as a whole, not from libgeodesk's C++ code specifically. geodesk.com was EGRESS_BLOCKED. name: Hob3l
baseline: OpenSCAD with CGAL rendering (CGAL Nef polyhedron 3D CSG) converting SCAD/CSG to STL
workload: Converting Prusa i3 MK3 part and personal SCAD models to STL by slicing into 0.2 mm layers (Hob3l) versus full 3D CSG rendering in OpenSCAD with CGAL.
claimed_speedup: README: x-carriage.csg to STL 45.208 s (openscad) vs 0.824 s (hob3l), about 50x faster; extruder-body.scad 2m42s vs 1.24 s, 130x; uselessbox+body 53.433 s vs 0.610 s, 85x. test31b.scad ($fn=99 ellipsoids) 4m30.198s vs 0.748s, 350x. Repo title says '100x Faster Slicing of SCAD Files'.
tradeoffs: Different pipeline, not a general CGAL replacement: it slices the model into 2D layers and does 2D boolean operations with integer arithmetic and snap rounding, so output is a layered STL (visible layering artifacts) rather than an exact 3D mesh. Reads flat .csg from OpenSCAD plus STL/SVG import. GPL-3.0.
caveats: Wall-clock `time` figures on unspecified hardware and flags, against an unstated OpenSCAD version. The speedups above 50x come from a different algorithm (slice first, then 2D booleans) with layered output, so they are not like-for-like with CGAL mesh booleans; the README shows the layered STL and says the final slicer result is the same. The baseline is OpenSCAD's CGAL rendering path, not CGAL used directly, and OpenSCAD's newer Manifold backend is not compared. The 85x uselessbox figure includes writing a 23 MB STL (loading and converting alone take 0.23 s). Only a subset of SCAD is read, so full SCAD needs OpenSCAD as a preprocessor. The author admits memory leaks ('Memory management has leaks. I admit I don't care enough'). The core 2D library was fuzzed with afl. Last commit June 2024.

name: ikd-Tree (incremental k-d tree)
baseline: Boost.Geometry R*-tree, PCL octree and nanoflann dynamic k-d tree, each integrated into FAST-LIO2 (FAST-LIO2, IEEE T-RO 2022, Table III); also a static k-d tree rebuilt every scan (FAST-LIO, and the ikd-Tree preprint's PCL comparison)
workload: LiDAR-inertial SLAM map maintenance (FAST-LIO2 style): incremental point insertion, box deletion and k-NN on a growing 3-D map.
claimed_speedup: FAST-LIO2 Table III (average ms per scan over 18 sequences, single-thread kNN; ratios derived from page data): total time (incremental update + kNN), ikd-Tree vs Boost.Geometry R*-tree 1.26-2.09x faster (e.g. nclt 3: 15.42 vs 32.29 ms; utbm 1: 18.42 vs 26.50), vs PCL octree 2.29-3.06x (utbm 1: 18.42 vs 45.00), vs nanoflann 1.03-1.34x (nclt 1: 15.64 vs 20.41). kNN search: R*-tree 1.25-2.09x slower, nanoflann 1.04-1.34x slower, octree 2.6-3.3x slower. Incremental update: the octree is fastest in most sequences (ikd-Tree up to 1.8x slower, e.g. utbm 1 3.23 vs 2.12 ms); ikd-Tree beats the R*-tree by 1.17-2.2x, and nanoflann is slightly faster on ulhk 1-3 and lili 2. Worst case: nanoflann's incremental-update peaks exceed 3 s on seven utbm sequences and 7 s on three nclt sequences, against an ikd-Tree maximum of 214.4 ms (nclt 2) and under 150 ms elsewhere. System level (Table VII): FAST-LIO, which rebuilds a static k-d tree each scan, spends 13.81 ms per scan on mapping vs 0.13 ms for FAST-LIO2 with ikd-Tree (Intel). The ikd-Tree preprint numbers (about 1.6 ms vs over 10 ms for PCL's static tree; 4% of static computation time) were seen only through search snippets.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the FAST-LIO2 paper. The ikd-Tree demo CMakeLists uses -std=c++14 -pthread -O3 and links PCL.
hardware: DJI Manifold 2-C: Intel Core i7-8550U (1.8 GHz, 4 cores), 8 GB RAM, for the data-structure comparison; FAST-LIO2 alone was also run on a Khadas VIM3 (2.2 GHz Cortex-A73, 4 GB RAM).
stars_or_usage: 810 stars, 219 forks; used inside FAST-LIO2 (IEEE T-RO 2022)
tradeoffs: GPLv2 (README: contact the authors for commercial use). Dynamic deletion is lazy: points are flagged deleted and removed during a background rebuild, so memory and k-NN cost depend on rebuild timing; threaded rebuild (-pthread). Supports box delete, box/radius search and on-tree downsampling; written for 3-D LiDAR points and later templated (README thanks a contributor for templating it). Demo build requires PCL.
caveats: The evidence is a peer-reviewed paper by the same group (first-party but reviewed). The baselines were wrapped into FAST-LIO2 by the authors, with downsampling emulated through range or radius search for the R*-tree, octree and nanoflann (nanoflann masks deleted points instead of removing them, so its tree grows); that integration code is not public. ikd-Tree is not uniformly faster: the PCL octree has the fastest incremental updates in most sequences, and nanoflann's updates are slightly faster on ulhk 1-3 and lili 2. The gain over nanoflann in total time is small (3-34%); the main advantage is bounded worst-case latency. The 13.81 vs 0.13 ms mapping figure compares two different SLAM pipelines (FAST-LIO rebuilds a static tree per scan), so it measures incremental vs rebuild, not tree speed. The repo's own demo (examples/ikd_Tree_demo.cpp) times only ikd-Tree. The header includes pcl/point_types.h, so PCL is a dependency. Last commit 2022-03-04. README says GPLv2 (links the GPL-2.0 text) with no 'or later' clause and asks commercial users to contact the authors; SPDX GPL-2.0-only is a reading of that.

name: iOverlay (Rust polygon boolean overlay engine)
baseline: Clipper2 (C++ polygon clipping library, v1.4.0); also Boost.Geometry (Boost 1.86.0)
workload: Checkerboard polygon boolean-operation test with up to 8,384,513 squares, iOverlay (Rust, multithreading feature on) versus Clipper2, as reported in the project's performance comparison page.
claimed_speedup: Performance Comparison page (seconds; 3 GHz 6-Core Intel Core i5; iOverlay Rust v1.9.0 multithreading on/off, iOverlay Swift v1.13.0, Clipper2 C++ v1.4.0, Boost C++ 1.86.0). Checkerboard test, 8,384,513 squares: Rust mt on 33.742 s, Rust mt off 38.640 s, Clipper2 644.338 s, about 19.1x (mt on) and 16.7x (mt off) faster (derived from page data); at 2,095,105 squares 7.94 s / 9.29 s versus 73.31 s. Not Overlap, 8,384,513 squares: 9.60 s / 13.51 s versus 167.97 s (17.5x / 12.4x, derived). Windows, 8,388,608: 12.06 s / 15.48 s versus 265.39 s (22.0x / 17.1x, derived). Spiral, 1,048,576: 3.23 s / 3.19 s versus 259.87 s (about 80x, derived). Lines Net 4096: 7.70 s / 7.51 s versus 45.93 s (about 6x, derived). Nested Squares 65,536: 2.20 s / 4.03 s versus 3502.23 s for Clipper2. Clipper2 is as fast or faster on small inputs (for example Checkerboard 481 squares 1.017 ms versus 1.117 ms; Lines Net up to 256; Spiral up to 1024). name: Kiddo (Rust k-d tree)
baseline: pykdtree, scipy.spatial.KDTree and sklearn KDTree (Python), nabo-rs and FNNTW (Rust); no C++ baseline (nanoflann, PCL, CGAL) is benchmarked
workload: Nearest-1/10/100, within-radius and construction on 100 to 10M points, 2-4 dimensions, f32/f64, 1,000 query points per Criterion iteration (companion repo sdd/kd-tree-comparison). The bench code generates uniform random points in the unit hypercube (rand::random, np.random.rand), although the Kiddo README says the points lie on a unit sphere.
claimed_speedup: Derived from page data (all-benchmarks.json, 3-D f64, 1,000,000 points, Criterion mean in ns per 1,000-query iteration): Query Nearest 1: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 49,798 (Kiddo_v3_immutable 44,366) vs nabo 71,993 (about 1.45x), pykdtree 77,187 (about 1.55x), FNNTW 80,818, scipy 907,836 (about 18x), sklearn 1,911,706 (about 38x). Query Nearest 10: Kiddo_v3_std 109,819 vs nabo 131,085 (about 1.2x), pykdtree 199,638 (about 1.8x), scipy 2,227,477 (about 20x). Query Nearest 100: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 550,945 vs nabo 677,895 (about 1.2x), pykdtree 1,789,125 (about 3.2x). Construction is not faster: Kiddo_v5_immutable_dynamic 161.4 ms and Kiddo_v3_std 124.6 ms vs pykdtree 92.3 ms (scipy 294.8 ms). The scipy and sklearn ratios compare parallel against single-threaded code (see caveats).
compiler_and_flags: cargo criterion; rustc version and RUSTFLAGS not stated. The comparison Cargo.toml builds kiddo_v5 with the nightly-only 'simd' feature.
hardware: Ryzen 5900X (12/24 core), 32 GB DDR4 3600 MHz (kd-tree-comparison Readme)
tradeoffs: Rust crate, not callable from C++ without FFI work, so it is outside the C++-first scope and flagged cross-language. Low-dimensional (2-4D) exact and approximate NN; ImmutableKdTree is best for static data, MutableKdTree has no dynamic rebalancing; batch queries multi-threaded by default (rayon); SIMD path needs nightly Rust.
caveats: Rust library with no C/C++ API, so it is outside the catalog's C/C++ scope. No published numbers against nanoflann or any C++ library: the comparison repo tests only Rust and Python libraries. The Kiddo repo does have an FFI harness for nanoflann, ALGLIB and Pkd-tree (benches/profile_cpp_competitors.rs, charted by scripts/chart_cpp_competitor_results.py), but no results were found on any reachable page; the results site sdd.github.io is blocked. Parallel against serial: the Kiddo, nabo and FNNTW benches run the 1,000 queries per iteration with rayon par_iter on a 12-core/24-thread CPU, while scipy's KDTree.query is called with the default workers=1 (the bench comments 'workers=-1 makes this slower?') and sklearn's is single-threaded, so the 18-38x over scipy and sklearn mostly measures threading. pykdtree (a C extension) may use OpenMP, so it is the closest like-for-like competitor (about 1.5-3x on queries, slower on construction). At 1,000 queries per iteration (about 50-80 microseconds), rayon dispatch and Python call overheads are a sizeable share of each sample. Published numbers cover Kiddo v1-v5 (last updated 2024-12-04); the current release is v6.3.0. The README says the data lie on a unit sphere but the bench code uses uniform cube data. The author benchmarks his own library (disclosed). all-benchmarks.json has duplicate 'Query within radius' rows for Kiddo_v1 and Kiddo_v2 with different values. kd-tree-comparison's Cargo.toml builds kiddo_v5 with the nightly-only 'simd' feature.

name: ParGeo (parallel 3D convex hull and kd-tree library)

claimed_speedup: From a search-result snippet of the ESA 2022 paper (paper not opened): fastest ParGeo convex hull up to 44.7x self-relative parallel speedup and up to 559x speedup against the best existing sequential implementation; Pseudohull up to 43.7x parallel speedup compared to Qhull and up to 5.05x over CGAL on 3-dimensional shapes. name: pgl (Pangolin plane geometry library)
baseline: CGAL 6.1.2 (Delaunay_triangulation_2, convex_hull_2, Kd_tree, AABB_tree, Arrangement_2, General_polygon_set_2, minkowski_sum_2; EPECK and EPICK kernels)
workload: Wall-clock time of 2D computational-geometry problems (triangulation, convex hull, kd-tree/AABB search, segment intersection, arrangements, polygon unions, Minkowski sum, visibility) on identical integer-coordinate inputs, pgl number type vs the comparable CGAL kernel, across input sizes up to the dataset limits (random data plus Salzburg polygon database).
claimed_speedup: Ratios are pgl time / CGAL time (below 1 = pgl faster), median over input sizes, range in parentheses, averaged over two machines. ERational vs EPECK, pgl faster: regularized union of triangles 0.23x (0.20-0.59), arrangement point-location query 0.46x (0.32-0.84), segment intersection 0.55x (0.19-1.8), arrangement point-location build 0.61x (0.46-0.87), segment search count in Rectangle 0.68x (0.55-0.91); near parity: nearest-neighbour query 0.82x (0.63-1.1), kd-tree build 0.88x (0.63-1.4), visibility 0.90x, two-polygon union 0.93x. int vs EPICK, pgl faster: point search count in Triangle 0.21x and segment search count in Triangle 0.21x, segment intersection 0.35x (CGAL's EPICK sweep is not exact; pgl's exact int version is 0.20x against EPECK), segment search count in Rectangle 0.51x, convex hull 0.51x, visibility 0.73x. CGAL faster: Delaunay triangulation (pgl 2.6x slower ERational/EPECK, 1.7x slower int/EPICK), point search count in Triangle with ERational (2.4x), convex hull with ERational (1.8x), Minkowski sum (1.7x), triangulation point location with ERational (1.7x), and with int/EPICK the kd-tree build (1.7x), nearest-neighbour query (1.8x), segment search build (1.8x) and triangulation point-location build (1.4x). Overall ERational/EPECK spans CGAL 2.6x faster to pgl 4.4x faster; int/EPICK spans CGAL 1.8x faster to pgl 4.8x faster.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16.2.1 (g++), -std=c++23 -O2 -DNDEBUG, CGAL 6.1.2
hardware: Two machines, one run each: AMD Ryzen 9 9900X 12-Core Processor and Intel Xeon w5-3433 (named in the meta block of gfonsecabr/pgl-benchmarks history/asymptotic-baseline/*.json; doc/cgal.md itself does not name them). Ratios are per-machine pgl/CGAL, then averaged over the two machines.
tradeoffs: Plane-only (2D) library; no higher dimensions, curved geometry, straight skeletons/offsets, alpha shapes or file formats. Header-only, needs C++20 or newer (tested GCC 13, Clang 18, MSVC). Fixed short list of number types, no filtered-kernel layer.
caveats: First-party comparison, but fully reproducible (code, compiler, flags and CPU models public), so tier A. doc/cgal.md says pgl is tuned against this very benchmark, so the comparison favours pgl. Some rows favour pgl by construction: CGAL Kd_tree has no triangle query, so the benchmark wrote one for the 'count in Triangle' rows, which is where pgl's int column looks best; CGAL's Range_tree_2 is deliberately not run. Mixed result: CGAL wins Delaunay triangulation, Minkowski sum, triangulation point location, and with int/EPICK the kd-tree build and nearest-neighbour query. Ratios are averaged over two machines, one run each. The table changes often (it was refreshed 2026-09-23 and re-averaged 2026-09-26), so re-read before quoting. Very young project (6 stars). Do not read it as a blanket CGAL replacement.

name: PH-tree (phtree-cpp)
baseline: Boost.Geometry R-tree (boost::geometry::index::rtree); libspatialindex R-tree also measured
workload: 3D points and boxes, CUBE (uniform) and CLUSTER datasets, 1K to 1M entries: insert, window query (about 3-15 results per query) and kNN, PH-tree vs Boost R-tree vs libspatialindex vs MCXME PH-tree.
claimed_speedup: Insert at 1M entries (CUBE / CLUSTER): points PhTreeMM 2.79M/s vs BoostRT 500k/s and 3.97M/s vs 781k/s (about 5.6x and 5.1x, derived from page data); boxes PhTree3D 1.44M/s vs BoostRT 406k/s and 3.18M/s vs 573k/s (about 3.5x and 5.6x, derived); libspatialindex is slower still. Window queries are mixed: point data at 1M, PhTree3D 314k q/s vs BoostRT 364k q/s on CUBE (Boost 1.16x faster) and 1.35M q/s vs 990k q/s on CLUSTER (PH-tree 1.36x faster), with about 3-4 results per query; with about 100 results per query BoostRT wins (121k vs 84k q/s for PhTreeMM2 on CUBE). Box data at 1M on CUBE: PhTree3D 56.3k q/s vs BoostRT 263.6k q/s (Boost about 4.7x faster). kNN clearly favours Boost: 3D, 1M points, k=1, BoostRT 736k/741k q/s vs PhTree3D 28.4k/54.9k q/s on CUBE/CLUSTER (Boost about 26x and 13x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 12.1 (insert and window-query runs, 2023-02-01/02) and Clang 14.0.0 (3D kNN run, 2023-03-09; the 10D block is labelled 'GCC 14.0.0'). Built with bazel --config=benchmark, which in the current .bazelrc means opt mode with -O3 -g -mavx -mbmi2 -std=c++17. The result files do not record the flags used at the time.
hardware: 8 x 4600 MHz CPU, L3 12 MiB (model not named in the result files)
tradeoffs: Z-order PH-tree: very fast insert/erase/relocate, scales to millions of entries and higher dimensions; not efficient when queries return 1000+ results; header-only C++17; coordinates go through converters; multimap variants exist.
caveats: Benchmark written and run by the PH-tree author in a separate repo (tzaeschke/phtree-cpp-perf, MIT, 0 stars). The phtree-cpp README does not link to it, and it vendors PH-tree C++ 1.4.0, while the library is now at 1.7.0. Results date from February-March 2023. The perf README notes that Boost RT was driven with std::array coordinates (a small slowdown), that the libspatialindex wrapper uses a buffering hack, and that an unexplained libspatialindex bug appears on the WEB dataset. The win is insertion (about 5x over Boost's R-tree). Window queries are mixed and box queries favour Boost; 3D kNN favours Boost by about 13-26x. CPU model not named (8 x 4600 MHz, 12 MiB L3), so not tier A. Fork of Improbable's unmaintained original, now maintained by the original PH-tree developer.

name: picoflann
baseline: nanoflann (also OpenCV FLANN)
workload: Exact kd-tree index build, knn and radius search on a small point set (README heading says 10,000 2D points, the speed-up block says 3D points).
claimed_speedup: Index building: 1.46x faster than nanoflann, 1.73x faster than OpenCV FLANN. Knn: 4.14x faster than nanoflann, 1.8x faster than OpenCV FLANN. Radius search: 1.25x faster than nanoflann, 3.21x faster than OpenCV FLANN.
stars_or_usage: 22 stars; part of the ucoslam project
tradeoffs: Minimal header-only exact kd-tree search with a small adapter API; picoflann2.h added in 2026; no license file in the repo.
caveats: First-party README numbers (2018) with no hardware, compiler, flags or k stated, and an internal inconsistency (heading says 10,000 2D points, block says 'Speed up in 3D points'). The repo has no nanoflann benchmark code: testperformance.cpp (added 2026-04-27, -O3 -march=native, KNN=10, 1,000 queries) compares picoflann v1/v2 only against OpenCV FLANN. An independent but small benchmark (LimHyungTae/OpenFLANN, 18 stars, PCL wrappers, 1,000 repeats, no hardware stated; numbers in its imgs/knn_*.png tables) found nanoflann faster at small K: 10,000 points K=1 0.00104 ms vs 0.00149 ms and K=10 0.00213 vs 0.00358 ms; 200,000 points K=1 0.00215 vs 0.00242 ms. Picoflann is much faster only at large K (200,000 points, K=5000: 0.84 ms vs 8.36 ms). Its author concludes 'For robotics application, NanoFLANN is better'. So the 4.14x knn figure does not hold at the small K most users need. No LICENSE file (LICENSE, LICENSE.txt, LICENSE.md, COPYING all 404) and no licence header in picoflann.h, so reference only. nanoflann is not a listed incumbent here.

name: PicoTree
baseline: nanoflann v1.7.1 (also OpenCV FLANN 4.11.0, SciPy KDTree, scikit-learn KDTree, pykdtree)
workload: Single-threaded kd-tree build over a 7,733,372-point LiDAR cloud and nearest-neighbour (knn=1) queries with a second 7,200,863-point cloud, max_leaf_size=10.
claimed_speedup: C++ build 0.54 s vs nanoflann 1.42 s (2.6x, derived from page data) and OpenCV FLANN 0.99 s; C++ knn 1.13 s vs nanoflann 1.40 s (1.2x, derived from page data) and OpenCV FLANN 2.30 s. Python knn 1.64 s vs SciPy KDTree 212.04 s, scikit-learn 11.90 s, pykdtree 2.95 s; Python build 0.54 s vs SciPy 1.37 s and scikit-learn 3.60 s, but pykdtree builds faster (0.43 s).
compiler_and_flags: README table (i9-14900HX run): compiler not stated; root CMakeLists.txt defaults CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE to Release. docs/benchmark.md (29-08-2021 run, PicoTree v0.7.4 vs nanoflann v1.3.2): MinGW GCC 10.3, flags not stated.
hardware: Intel Core i9-14900HX
tradeoffs: Header-only C++ kd-tree with Python bindings; Eigen, OpenCV and custom point types; sliding-midpoint build; range and knn search.
caveats: Author's own benchmark on one LiDAR dataset (Bremen Gaussian Point scans), single thread, max_leaf_size=10, knn=1. Benchmark code is public in examples/benchmark/ (Google Benchmark), but compiler and flags for the README table are not stated. docs/benchmark.md says nanoflann's build regressed by about 90% in v1.5.0, which inflates the build gap against nanoflann v1.7.1; the detailed C++ comparison there is a 2021 run (nanoflann v1.3.2) shown only as plots. pykdtree beats PicoTree on Python build time. nanoflann is not a listed incumbent for this category. [retier] The 2.6x build ratio is inflated: bm_nanoflann.cpp builds the nanoflann index twice in the timed loop (since nanoflann 1.4 the constructor already calls buildIndex()). The real build gap is about 1.3x (estimate). kNN numbers are unaffected. An independent suite, Lawson/Gropp/Lofstead 'Exploring Spatial Indexing for Accelerated Feature Retrieval in HPC' (arXiv 2106.13972; CCGrid 2022 per search results; code at github.com/mlawsonca/benchmarking_suite_range_searching_libraries, Release build), benchmarks 20 C/C++ libraries including pico_tree (TEST_PICO_TREE) and nanoflann (TEST_NANOFLANN). Its results are only in the paper, which was not opened (arxiv.org, osti.gov and researchgate are blocked), so a retier to B is pending paper access.

name: Polylidar3D
baseline: CGAL 2D Alpha Shapes (also PostGIS ST_ConcaveHull 2.5.2 and Spatialite ST_ConcaveHull, which the README treats as GEOS-based)
workload: Non-convex (concave hull) polygon extraction from random point sets sampled inside the California state outline, 2,000 to about 64,000 points, with and without holes; execution time in ms (concavehull-evaluation repo).
claimed_speedup: concavehull-evaluation README chart (California shape, read by eye): at about 64,000 points Polylidar about 30-40 ms, CGAL alpha shapes about 200 ms, PostGIS about 3,150 ms (no holes) and 4,100 ms (holes), Spatialite about 11,300 ms. The same README lists 30 raw sub-timing runs on caholes_64000 (64,000 points with holes): Polylidar about 36 + 4.4 + 1.0 = about 41 ms per run, CGAL triangulation plus alpha shape about 44.4 + 153 = about 197 ms, Spatialite about 235 + 135 + 10,900 = about 11,300 ms; i.e. about 4.8x faster than CGAL and about 270x faster than Spatialite (derived from page data). Robust predicates were on; disabling them gives a further 30% speedup per the README.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (C++14 compiler; Polylidar built with PL_USE_ROBUST_PREDICATES=1; CGAL 4.12, PostGIS 2.5.2)
tradeoffs: C++ with pybind11 Python bindings; multi-threading (marl) and optional GPU path in the 3D mode; polygons with holes. It extracts planar-region polygons from Delaunay-triangulated data, so the hull is defined differently from an alpha shape or PostGIS concave hull; CGAL returns unordered boundary edges rather than a polygon.
caveats: The benchmark measured the original 2D Polylidar (submodule thirdparty/polylidar at commit 6e25d1f, now the polylidar2d branch, tied to the RA-L 2020 paper), not the current Polylidar3D code on master, whose API differs. Evidence is a chart image and raw timing lists in a separate 4-star benchmark repo, with no hardware, compiler or flags stated. CGAL timing covers alpha shape construction plus unordered boundary edge extraction only (no polygon assembly) but also computes alpha intervals for the whole family of shapes. CGAL 4.12 and PostGIS 2.5.2 are old; PostGIS timing includes client/server round trip. The RA-L paper (doi 10.1109/LRA.2020.3002212, arXiv 2002.01886) reportedly claims more than 4x speedup over other concave polygon extraction methods but was not opened. Repo unmaintained since 2023-03.

name: qdgeo
baseline: GEOS 3.13.1 (via Shapely 2.1.2): union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and buffer
workload: 26 boolean/buffer workloads over a 4,040-parcel, 135,080-coordinate public county parcel dataset (GeoMoose demo data); each figure is median of three suite runs of 11 repeats.
claimed_speedup: README Union table (median of three suite runs of 11 repeats): 4,040 parcels qdgeo wasm 160 ms, qdgeo native 130 ms vs GEOS 426 ms; 1,000 parcels 20.3 / 16.8 ms vs 65.7 ms. Derived from page data: 2.7x (wasm) and 3.3x (native) on the full union; the README's Design goals section rounds this to '3.1x native GEOS'. Geometric mean over the 26 workloads: GEOS native 1.5x slower than qdgeo wasm (range across runs 1.36-1.62). Buffer of 100 parcels +2 m: 1.30 ms vs GEOS 4.54 ms. GEOS is faster on the single 19,208-coordinate parcel buffer (+2 m 8.25 ms vs 33.2 ms; -2 m 13.0 ms vs 31.9 ms).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0, zig build native -Doptimize=ReleaseSafe (shipped build keeps safety checks); WASM build run in Node 22+
hardware: One idle machine; CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Only five operations (four booleans and rounded buffer). Rejects invalid geometry instead of repairing it, and valid input can occasionally fail (4 of 3,946 cluster unions) because it declines to snap coordinates. WASM artifact 135 KB raw, 50.8 KB gzipped, no C or C++ dependency; Zig native build has a C-compatible ABI.
caveats: Application-level comparison, and the README admits the boundaries are not equal. GEOS gets shapely.union_all over geometries that are already GEOS objects (no parse or encode), while qdgeo native rows include a WKB parse/encode round trip and the wasm rows a flat-ABI copy. That favors GEOS, though GEOS is native and qdgeo wasm is not. The harness notes GEOS measured 417 ms and 356 ms for the same workload an hour apart, and the README says to treat gaps under 20% as unresolved. GEOS is faster on very large single polygons. The shipped build keeps safety checks (ReleaseSafe; ReleaseFast is 11% faster). qdgeo rejects invalid input instead of repairing it, and it errors on 4 of 3,946 valid cluster unions it cannot node exactly. The project is days old (first commit 2026-09-14), only one dataset (GeoMoose parcels) is tested, and it is not a general GEOS replacement. The CPU model is missing, so tier C.

name: benchmark-rngs PhiloxSIMD (AVX Philox4x32-10)
baseline: xoshiro256**, PCG64 and std::mt19937 (also an at::mt19937 implementation shipped in the repo)
workload: Wall time in seconds to generate 134,217,728 random numbers with 1 to 1024 threads (and 8 to 8.6e9 numbers on 1 thread), global vs thread-local generators.
claimed_speedup: results/README.md, 1 thread, 134217728 numbers (best average): philox_simd (global) 0.176 s and philox_simd (thread local) 0.188 s vs xoshiro256** 0.651 s, pcg64 0.659 s, std::mt19937 1.609 s, at::mt19937 0.393 s, scalar philox 0.439 s; about 3.7x vs xoshiro256** and pcg64 and 9.1x vs std::mt19937 (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GNU 7.4.0; CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS '-std=c++11 -Wall -pthread -march=native -lm' and the README builds with -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake's default Release flags for GCC add -O3 -DNDEBUG)
hardware: 16 x Intel Xeon E5-1660 v4 @ 3.20 GHz (1 socket), Ubuntu 18.04, turbo boost off, performance governor
tradeoffs: x86-only SIMD (x86intrin.h, built with -march=native); a counter-based Philox generator, so streams and statistical properties differ from xoshiro/PCG/MT; PhiloxSIMD.h has an UNSHUFFLE switch to match the non-SIMD output order. The repo is a benchmark harness with the headers inside, not a packaged library.
caveats: No LICENSE file (none in the top-level listing, and the GitHub sidebar shows no license), so usability is reference; Philox.h and PhiloxSIMD.h say the engine was 'Originally implemented in PyTorch's fusion compiler' (PyTorch is BSD-3-Clause), but the repo itself grants nothing. PhiloxSIMD.h defaults to UNSHUFFLE 0, which skips the transpose ('set to 1 to match non-SIMD ordering'), so the benchmarked SIMD stream is a block-wise reordering of standard Philox4x32-10 output and the timings exclude the cost of restoring standard order. The SIMD variants consume outputs with vector adds while scalar engines are called one value at a time. Counts are in 32-bit units for every engine (64-bit engines count two per call), so the comparison is per bit. At tiny counts (8 numbers) xoshiro256** is faster (1.58e-7 s vs 1.79e-7 s). 2019 results on GCC 7.4, single machine.

name: pure-rand (fast-check PRNG library for JavaScript/TypeScript)
baseline: JavaScript native Math.random() (Xorshift128+ in Node 16.19.1) and the seedrandom, random-js, chance and faker Mersenne Twister libraries
workload: Shuffle of an array of 1,000,000 items; mean time in ms, with separate non-uniform and uniform (unbiased range) sections.
claimed_speedup: Non-uniform: pure-rand Xoroshiro128+ 24.5 ms versus native Math.random 33.3 ms (native 1.4x slower), seedrandom Xorshift128 28.8 ms (1.2x slower), seedrandom Alea 28.1 ms (1.1x slower), chance Mersenne Twister 142.9 ms (5.8x slower), faker Mersenne Twister 109.1 ms (4.5x slower). Uniform: pure-rand 53.5 ms versus random-js Mersenne Twister 119.6 ms (2.2x slower).
compiler_and_flags: Node 16.19.1 (V8 JIT, default flags), pure-rand 6.0.0; benchmark script perf/compare.cjs (permalinked from COMPARISON.md at commit 556ec331) uses tinybench with 1,000 iterations and about 50 warmup iterations
hardware: 2 x x64 Intel Xeon Platinum 8272CL @ 2.60GHz on GitHub Actions default runners, Ubuntu 22.04 container, 5.88 GB RAM
stars_or_usage: 117 stars; the PRNG behind fast-check (usage claim not checked)
tradeoffs: Pure functional API: generators are immutable and return a new generator on every call, which costs allocation but enables rollback and purity. Offers congruential32, Mersenne Twister, xorshift128+ and xoroshiro128+ with built-in unbiased uniform ranges and jump support.
caveats: JavaScript only, not usable from C++. Measured on shared GitHub Actions runners (noisy), with old versions (pure-rand 6.0.0, Node 16). The workload is a Fisher-Yates shuffle, so it measures range reduction as well as the generator. The non-uniform pure-rand rows call the mutating unsafeNext() API rather than the pure next() API the library is named for. The native Math.random baseline appears only in the non-uniform section; the uniform section compares only against random-js. COMPARISON.md's prose calls the non-uniform section 'known to be slower' (rejection resampling), which describes the uniform section; the tables themselves are consistent. Run by the project author. The 'Congruential' generator (congruential32 in the code) is listed as 1.1x faster than the recommended Xoroshiro128+ in the non-uniform table.

name: pXart
baseline: std::mt19937 (libstdc++, GCC 9.2.0); also Boost.Random mt19937
workload: Bulk generation of 16 GiB of 32-bit random numbers through a 16 KiB cache buffer, plus a 10^8-sample Monte Carlo pi benchmark, comparing std::mt19937, Boost mt19937 and pXart scalar/SSE4.1/AVX2 MT19937 and Xoroshiro128+.
claimed_speedup: Thesis Table 9.1 (i7-7700K, 4.51 GHz, 16 GiB generated through a 16 KiB buffer): STL MT19937 9.29 s, Boost MT19937 5.79 s, pXart scalar MT19937 7.61 s, pXart SSE MT19937 2.11 s, pXart AVX MT19937 1.15 s (AVX about 8.1x faster than STL and 5.0x faster than Boost, derived from page data). Thesis text: scalar pXart beat the STL version but not Boost's; SSE/AVX are 'more than three times' / 'more than six times' faster than pXart scalar. Monte Carlo pi, 10^8 samples (Table 9.2): STL MT19937 with pXart's uniform function 0.53 s (0.72 s naive with std::uniform_real_distribution), Boost 0.33 s; pXart AVX MT19937 used as a drop-in through a cache ('AVX cache') 0.15 s, about 3.5x faster than STL (derived from page data); the 0.07 s 'AVX' figure also vectorizes the pi loop itself with AVX intrinsics in single precision, so it is not an RNG-only gain.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 9.2.0, -O3 -march=native
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700K (Kaby Lake, 4.51 GHz measured); second machine Intel Core i5-8250U laptop
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; build2 package (cppget.org badge in README)
tradeoffs: Needs an Intel CPU with SSE4.1/AVX2 for the vectorized engines. The SIMD engines interleave independent streams, so output differs from std::mt19937 and state is larger; own API (pxart::uniform, pxart::simd256::mt19937), not a drop-in std engine.
caveats: Numbers come from a December 2019 master's thesis (Friedrich-Schiller-Universitat Jena) stored in the repo, not peer reviewed; results appear only in the thesis PDF, not in the README. GCC 9.2 / libstdc++ only, Kaby Lake hardware, single run per configuration with no variance reported. The 0.07 s Monte Carlo figure rewrites the whole pi loop in AVX intrinsics; the drop-in RNG gain ('AVX cache') is 0.15 s vs 0.53 s. The benchmark code at HEAD (2021) may differ slightly from the 2019 thesis version. Last commit 2021-01-18.

name: randp (AES-CTR Random Pool)
baseline: glibc arc4random / arc4random_buf / arc4random_uniform (glibc 2.36+ getrandom-based); also getentropy, RDRAND, RDSEED
workload: Median Google Benchmark time to fill a 4 GiB buffer with random bytes, and median time per call for one uniform uint32_t and one uniform uint32_t below a bound in [1..0x100000].
claimed_speedup: 2026-09-22 run: randp_bytes 247 ms vs arc4random_buf 5211 ms for 4 GiB (page says 21.1x faster); randp_u32 7.00 ns vs arc4random 14.0 ns (2.0x); randp_lt_u32 7.19 ns vs arc4random_uniform 23.6 ns (3.3x); rdrand32 291 ns and rdseed32 1825 ns are much slower than randp_u32.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (GCC) 16.2.1 20260810, glibc 2.44, libbenchmark 1.9.5. Results page does not print flags; repo build files set -O3 -flto=auto -march=x86-64-v2 -maes (config.mk) and benchmarks/Makefile adds -march=x86-64-v3 -maes -mvaes -mrdrnd -mrdseed.
hardware: 13th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i9-13980HX, Linux 7.2.6-arch2-1 x86_64
tradeoffs: Linux-only (MADV_WIPEONFORK, getentropy), needs a CPU with AES instructions (VAES variant for 256-bit), GCC 14+ for C23 thread_local (clang explicitly unsupported), glibc 2.34+. Thread-local pool of at most one page, reseeded from getentropy every 1024 refills by default. Author states it makes no CSPRNG claim. C API with a generated single header (make randp-single.h), usable from C++.
caveats: Despite the name, randp's PRNG is not AES-128-CTR: src/aes_ctr_128_prng-defaults.h sets 3 keys x 1 round, and aes_enc_128 in src/aes-128-utils.h applies one _mm_aesenc_si128 per key, so each 16-byte block gets 3 AES rounds with independent random round keys (no key schedule, 3 rounds instead of 10). The README's FAQ disclaims CSPRNG status but still calls the output 'practically unpredictable', which 3-round AES does not support; glibc arc4random is backed by the kernel's ChaCha20 getrandom, so the 21x/2x/3.3x gaps compare a reduced-round generator against a cryptographic one, not like for like. Baseline is glibc arc4random (a getrandom() wrapper, sped up by the getrandom vDSO since glibc 2.41), not std::mt19937, PCG or xoshiro. First-party benchmark on one laptop CPU; flags come from the HEAD Makefiles, not printed with the results. Older runs on the same page (2024-10-04, glibc 2.40 before the vDSO) showed 27x-43x; the current figures are the 2026-09-22 ones. No LICENSE file at the root (raw LICENSE returns 404); MPL-2.0 comes from SPDX headers in every source file, so confirm before copying. Very young project, 1 star, changing daily.

name: simd-rand (SIMD Xoshiro256+ / Xoshiro256++ and frand generators for Rust)
baseline: Scalar Xoshiro256+ (benchmark label 'rand/Xoshiro256+', from the rand crate ecosystem)
workload: Criterion benchmark that generates and accumulates batches of u64x8 values (64 u64 values per iteration according to the page's Gelem/s figures) with scalar versus portable-SIMD and AVX-512 vectorised generators.
claimed_speedup: Scalar rand_xoshiro Xoshiro256+ 33.10 ns per batch of 64 u64 (1.93 Gelem/s) versus portable Xoshiro256+X8 7.51 ns (8.52 Gelem/s) and AVX-512 Xoshiro256+X8 7.08 ns (9.04 Gelem/s): about 4.4x and 4.7x (derived from page data). For the author's frand generator, the scalar upstream frand crate (autovectorised by the compiler) runs 3.18 ns and FrandX8 2.53 ns, only about 1.26x (derived from page data). The 13x figure in the earlier record compared FrandX8 with scalar Xoshiro256+, which is a different generator. README text: vectorised PRNGs 'may perform anywhere from 4-6 times faster'.
compiler_and_flags: cargo +nightly (rustc version not stated; MSRV 1.89). .cargo/config.toml sets -C target-cpu=native; bench-top adds RUSTFLAGS -C target-feature=+avx2,+avx512f,+avx512dq,+avx512vl; release profile opt-level 3, lto = true, codegen-units = 1; pinned to one SMT pair with taskset and the performance governor
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-core desktop
tradeoffs: Rust crate (not callable from C++ without FFI work); the 8-lane generators produce eight independent streams per call, so the sequence differs from the scalar generator; lane jumps are not implemented (TODO in README); AVX-512 specific paths need avx512f and avx512dq, and the portable module needs nightly Rust.
caveats: The speedup compares the same algorithm scalar versus lane-parallel, so it measures vectorisation, not a better algorithm. Checked: the portable and AVX-512 Xoshiro256+X8 lanes run the standard xoshiro256+ step (s0+s3 output, s1<<17, rotl 45), and FrandX8 lanes match the upstream frand crate (the crate's tests assert this), so the SIMD paths compute the named generators as 8 independent streams. FrandX8::seed_from_u64 copies one seed into all 8 lanes, so the lanes emit identical streams. Seed with distinct from_seed bytes for independent lanes; the timed FrandX8 rows used seed_from_u64. Benchmarks accumulate batches into u64x8 to keep the work observable, which favours wide registers. frand is the author's choice of a small generator, and the README says he is no expert in statistical testing (PractRand only). The latest commit is 'fix frand implementation (#34)'. README warns that older AVX-512 CPUs may throttle.

name: simdrng
baseline: std::mt19937_64 and std::uniform_real_distribution; also scalar xoshiro256++
workload: Google Benchmark runs (CI, GitHub-hosted runner) of per-call u64, per-call double and buffer fill for Xoshiro256++, ChaCha and Philox, scalar versus xsimd-dispatched SIMD, against std::mt19937_64.
claimed_speedup: gcc-15 benchmark JSON (2026-07-22): XoshiroSIMD fill_u64 1645 ns per 4096 values (2.49e9 values/s) vs scalar Xoshiro fill_u64 3835 ns (1.07e9 values/s), about 2.3x (derived from page data); SIMD Philox4x32 fill 7970 vs scalar 27502 ns (about 3.5x) and ChaCha20 21555 vs 61019 ns (about 2.8x) (derived from page data). Scalar Xoshiro uniform() 1.32 ns vs the same engine through std::uniform_real_distribution 4.65 ns (about 3.5x) and vs std::mt19937_64 + std::uniform_real_distribution 8.01 ns (about 6x) (derived from page data); std::mt19937_64 single u64 call 1.60 ns vs scalar Xoshiro 0.94 ns. docs/benchmarks.rst: Xoshiro bulk 'reaches ~2.3x its scalar loop'; uniform() ~1.6 ns vs ~5.2 ns, 'roughly 3x' (a different run).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 15, CMake Release, CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS=-march=x86-64-v3 (bench preset in CMakePresets.json); also clang-19/20 and gcc-14 result sets on the same branch
hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 (GitHub-hosted runner, 4 vCPUs, 2.445 GHz; cpu_model.txt in results)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 with xsimd runtime dispatch and numpy.random.Generator-compatible Python bindings (nanobind); the SIMD engines are faster only in bulk fills (single-call SIMD xoshiro is 2.81 ns vs 0.94 ns scalar) and produce lane-interleaved streams.
caveats: The gain is for bulk fills only: single-value SIMD calls cost 2.82 ns vs 0.94 ns for scalar Xoshiro (buffered read overhead, per the docs), so one-at-a-time use should stay scalar. The SIMD stream interleaves SIMD_WIDTH xoshiro256++ lanes, lane i being the scalar generator after i jump() calls (tests/test_xoshiro_simd.cpp checks each lane against the scalar engine, which tests/test_xoshiro.cpp checks against Vigna's xoshiro256plusplus.c), so it is the same generator but a different output order than one scalar stream for the same seed. The std::mt19937_64 figure is a per-call time, not a bulk fill. Shared GitHub-hosted runner; cpu_model.txt is rewritten on each publish run. libstdc++ inferred from gcc-15 on ubuntu-24.04. License is BSD-3-Clause with an added acknowledgement clause (SPDX BSD-3-Clause-Attribution, not OSI-approved), so marked reference although permissive. Pre-1.0, no tagged release, 3 stars.

The AVX2 machine's CPU model is not given. Correctness: despite the 'vectorized Xoshiro256++' label, src/xoshiro.jl outputs rotate_right(s0+s3, 23) without the '+ s0' term (left commented out), and it updates s3 with rotate_right(s3, 45), which equals a left rotation by 19, not xoshiro's left rotation by 45. VectorizationBase defines rotate_right as a true right funnel shift. So the engine is a nonstandard xoshiro-like variant, and the standard xoshiro256 jump constants it uses to space streams 2^128 apart are not valid for that engine; full period and stream separation are not established. It passes SmallCrush in CI and BigCrush per the README. Baseline is not std::mt19937.

name: VMT19937 (V-family and X-family vectorized Mersenne Twister)
baseline: std::mt19937 and std::mt19937_64 (STL-MT19937 / STL-MT19937-64 rows); also the original reference MT19937 / MT19937-64 / SFMT19937 and Intel MKL MT/SFMT
workload: Throughput in million samples/s of 32-bit (MT19937, SFMT19937) and 64-bit (MT19937-64) random numbers, about 1.6e10 numbers per CPU (30 runs of 8.19e6 samples), in scalar (one value per call) and vectorial (block of 10,240) query modes, on five CPU targets (SSE4.2, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON, SVE256).
claimed_speedup: README table, M samples/s, vectorial mode: V-MT19937-64 2865 (AVX-512) / 1161 (AVX2) vs STL-MT19937-64 590 / 317 (about 4.9x and 3.7x, derived from page data); V-MT19937 2392 (AVX2) vs ORIG-MT19937 259 (about 9.2x, derived from page data); V-SFMT19937 10943 (AVX-512) vs ORIG-SFMT19937 4445 (about 2.5x, derived from page data). Scalar mode: X-MT19937-64 1095 (AVX-512) vs STL 590 (about 1.9x, derived from page data). doc/main.tex also has a 32-bit std::mt19937 row: V-MT19937 vectorial 2391.8 (AVX2) / 5841.4 (AVX-512) vs STL-MT19937 305.7 / 598.6 (about 7.8x and 9.8x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 16 per doc/main.tex; Makefile default (NBITS=native) is -O3 -std=c++20 -march=native (plus -msve-vector-bits=256 on SVE); explicit NBITS builds use -msse4.2/-mavx2/-mavx512f -mavx512vl -mavx512bw -mavx512dq with -mpclmul, or -march=armv8-a+simd / -march=armv8-a+sve -msve-vector-bits=256. Which variant produced the tables is not stated. Harness: perf.exe from src/perf.cpp.
hardware: Intel Celeron J4125 2.0 GHz (SSE4.2), Intel Xeon E5-2686 v4 2.3 GHz (AVX2), Intel Xeon Platinum 8375C 2.9 GHz (AVX-512), Neoverse-N1 2.5 GHz (NEON), Neoverse-V1 2.6 GHz (SVE256) (from doc/main.tex).
tradeoffs: The V-family changes the output sequence: it interleaves several MT19937 states de-phased by polynomial jump-ahead, and the sequence depends on the chosen register width (VRegBitLen). The X-family is bit-identical to the original MT19937/MT19937-64/SFMT sequences. Needs jump-polynomial data files (dat/poly) for the V-family, C++20, and SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 or NEON/SVE hardware for the large gains. Large block-fill API (block of 16 or state-size blocks) is where the speedup is.
caveats: Big speedups are in vectorial (block fill of 10,240) mode; scalar single-value V-MT19937 is about 1.7-2.1x the original reference. Intel MKL-MT beats V-MT19937 at AVX-512 vectorial (6479 vs 5742 M/s README; 6578.9 vs 5841.4 in main.tex). The README omits the 32-bit STL-MT19937 row that doc/main.tex and perf.cpp include; std::mt19937 beats the original reference from AVX2 up. On SVE256 STL-MT19937-64 (573) beats V-MT19937-64 scalar (513). README and main.tex disagree on the AVX-512 MT19937 scalar figures (README X 1341 / V 729; main.tex X 929.5 / V 1354.0) and slightly on other AVX-512 MT19937 cells, so they come from different runs. V-family output interleaves jump-separated MT states (src/test.cpp checks each against the reference at the jumped index), so it is a different sequence from one MT19937 for the same seed; the X-family is bit-identical to the reference. libstdc++ inferred from GCC 16 (main.tex credits GCC auto-vectorization of the STL MT). Single author, first-party; arXiv 2309.16682 could not be opened (egress blocked).

name: vphilox
baseline: std::mt19937 (also compared with xoshiro256++ and PCG64)
workload: Cycles per byte of bulk random-byte generation (generate_n) and per-call operator() for a counter-based Philox4x32-10 engine with scalar/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON backends versus std::mt19937, xoshiro256++, PCG64 and unspecialised Philox on five machines.
claimed_speedup: docs/benchmarks/README.md cost per byte relative to std::mt19937 (lower is faster), vphilox generate_n: Pi 5 0.75x, Sapphire Rapids 0.38x, Skylake-SP 0.22x, Cascade Lake 4v 0.24x, Cascade Lake 32v 0.33x (README: '1.3x to 4.6x the throughput of std::mt19937'). For comparison xoshiro256++ is 0.17-0.30x and PCG64 0.32-0.83x; vphilox operator() is 0.51-1.15x.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 24.04) for every x86 matrix run and GCC 12.2.0 (Debian 12) for the Pi 5 NEON run (docs/benchmarks/raw/machines.csv); CMake 'bench' preset = CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC), with kernel TUs adding -mavx2 or -mavx512f -mavx512dq -mavx512vl (CMakeLists.txt); runs through scripts/benchmarks/run_matrix.sh, pinned to one CPU, 9 repetitions with random interleaving and a 1% CV bar.
hardware: Raspberry Pi 5 (Cortex-A76, NEON, performance governor); Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C @ 2.70GHz (Sapphire Rapids, cloud vCPU); Intel Xeon @ 2.00GHz (Skylake-SP, GCP vCPU); Intel Xeon @ 2.80GHz Cascade Lake (family 6 model 85 stepping 7) on a 4-vCPU slice and on a whole 2-socket host.
tradeoffs: Counter-based (seekable in constant time, bit-identical across machines, thread-count independent output) with C++20 header-only SIMD backends chosen at runtime; the bulk generate_n path is needed for the speed (operator() goes through a refill buffer).
caveats: Very new (first runs 2026-08), one author, not yet tagged, 0 stars. All numbers are first-party. Cycles per byte uses RDTSC reference cycles (perf_event on the Pi) and only compares within one machine. Per-value operator() on the Pi 5 is 0.87x the speed of std::mt19937; operator() through the refill buffer is 1.5-2.4x slower than generate_n. xoshiro256++ is cheaper per byte on four of the five machines (vphilox wins only on Skylake-SP, 0.4210 vs 0.4703 cycles/byte). Four archived harness-validation runs (unpinned governor, 2-vCPU VM) are excluded from the figures by the project. SIMD backends are checked bit-for-bit against the scalar Random123 reference vectors (tests/test_reference_vectors.cpp, tests/test_kernel_parity.cpp). The accompanying paper is a preprint (TechRxiv/Zenodo), not peer-reviewed. libstdc++ inferred from GCC on Ubuntu/Debian.

name: vpxyz/xorshift (Go xorshift*, xorshift+, xoroshiro and splitmix64 generators)
baseline: Go math/rand (rand.NewSource Int63 source, and rand.New(source).ExpFloat64())
workload: go test -bench: nanoseconds per call of a raw Uint64 from each source versus rand.NewSource(...).Int63, and per rand.New(source).ExpFloat64() call for the wrapped variants.
claimed_speedup: Raw source ns/op: math/rand BenchmarkRandSource 4.93 versus XorShift128Plus 2.42, XorShift1024Star 2.40, Xoroshiro128Plus 2.66, Xoroshiro256PlusPlus 3.86, Xoroshiro256StarStar 3.93, Xoroshiro512Plus 6.15, Xoroshiro512StarStar 6.34, SplitMix64 1.61. Wrapped in rand.Rand (ExpFloat64): BenchmarkRand 10.2 versus XorShift128Plus 8.42, Xoroshiro128Plus 8.10, SplitMix64 8.66, but Xoroshiro256PlusPlus and Xoroshiro256StarStar 11.7, XorShift1024Star 9.61, Xoroshiro512Plus 13.2 and Xoroshiro512StarStar 13.6. Raw speedup is about 2.0x for XorShift128Plus and 3.1x for SplitMix64; once wrapped it is only about 1.2x, and the 256- and 512-bit-state xoroshiro variants are slower than math/rand (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.14, go test -bench=. with default flags; benchmark code is xorshift_test.go in the repo (includes the math/rand baseline)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3840QM, Fedora 31, Linux 5.6.9
tradeoffs: Generators are not concurrency-safe (README says to wrap with a monitor goroutine). Generators with state larger than 64 bits are seeded via SplitMix64 as Vigna suggests. Implements Vigna's generators, so it carries their known linearity weaknesses in low bits for the + scramblers.
caveats: Go package, not callable from C++. Numbers are from 2020 on a 2012-era laptop CPU with Go 1.14, run by the repo author. The raw rows are asymmetric: the generators' Uint64() is called on the concrete type returned by NewSource (static dispatch, inlinable), while the baseline calls Int63() through the rand.Source interface (dynamic dispatch), so part of the raw 2-3x gap is call overhead. The wrapped rows go through rand.Rand on both sides and show only about 1.2x, with the 256/512-bit-state variants slower than math/rand. The baseline is Go's default math/rand source, not a C++ standard facility. Go's standard library has since added math/rand/v2 (PCG, ChaCha8), so the gap against current Go is likely smaller (background knowledge, not tested). [retier] xoroshiro512starstar's update complements s7 ('s6 ^ ^s7 ^ s3'), so it is not Vigna's xoshiro512** and its Jump is invalid; xoroshiro128plus Jump uses xorshift128+ constants; packages named xoroshiro256/512 are actually xoshiro; most Int63 implementations keep the weak low bits; no reference-output tests (issue #2); the README example does not compile. Once wrapped in rand.Rand, Xoroshiro256 (11.7 ns/op) and Xoroshiro512 (13.2/13.6) are slower than math/rand (10.2); the raw rows compare a concrete-type Uint64 call against Int63 through the rand.Source interface. Last commit 2020-05-02.

name: FastShuffleExperiments (nearly divisionless bounded random integers)
baseline: std::shuffle (same underlying PRNG), plus OpenBSD-style and Java-style bounded-integer generation
workload: Random shuffles of arrays of 5 to 10^9 elements, ns per element, with 32-bit and 64-bit random words, comparing Lemire's nearly divisionless bounded-integer method against OpenBSD-like, Java-like, floating-point and std::shuffle approaches.
claimed_speedup: README sample output (arrays of 1000 elements, ns per element): nearly divisionless 1.88 (32-bit) and 1.86 (64-bit) vs std::shuffle 18.66 and 15.28, vs OpenBSD-like 5.40 and 14.36, vs Java-like 3.08 and 7.96 (about 10x and 8x faster than std::shuffle, derived from page data); the README notes 'the exact numbers will vary'.
compiler_and_flags: g++ or clang++ with -std=c++11 -O3 (from cpp/Makefile)
stars_or_usage: 41 stars; technique adopted by libstdc++ std::uniform_int_distribution, Abseil, Swift, Go, Julia, Zig, NumPy per README
tradeoffs: Needs 128-bit multiplication (__uint128_t) for 64-bit words; the buffered/precomputed variants trade memory for speed; unbiased, nearly divisionless rejection method.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (ACM TOMACS 2019, 'Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval') with a replication package, but the numbers on the page are an illustrative sample run ('the exact numbers will vary') with no CPU, compiler version or standard library stated. The std::shuffle baseline reflects libstdc++ before it adopted this very technique in std::uniform_int_distribution, so the gap against a current libstdc++ is smaller. The benchmark generator is lehmer64, not std::mt19937, so the std::shuffle column isolates the range-reduction and shuffle cost. In the RCR gnuplot script, Figure 3a (shuffle32.pdf) plots the std::shuffle series from the 64-bit rows ('every 2::1'), which understates std::shuffle's 32-bit cost in that figure. The repo Makefile uses -O3 without -march. Last commit 2024-03-12.

name: MELG-64 (MELG19937-64)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference C code (algorithmically std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 10^9 64-bit unsigned integers with MELG19937-64, MT19937-64, MT19937-64 (ID3), SFMT19937-64 without SIMD and SFMT19937-64 with SIMD.
claimed_speedup: README table, CPU seconds for 1e9 64-bit outputs: MELG19937-64 4.2123 (Intel Core i7-3770) / 6.2920 (AMD Phenom II X6 1045T) vs reference MT19937-64 5.1002 / 6.6490 (about 1.21x and 1.06x, derived from page data). SFMT19937-64 without SIMD is about level (4.2654 / 5.6123, faster on the AMD part) and with SIMD much faster (1.8457 / 2.8806). The README and paper describe the speed as 'equivalent to' / 'competitive with' MT19937-64; the claimed advantage is equidistribution (Delta=0 vs 7820 for MT19937-64).
compiler_and_flags: gcc with -O3 on Linux (README Platforms section); compiler version not stated; build line 'gcc melg19937-64.c -o melg19937-64 -O3 -Wall'. No timing program is in the repo.
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 (3.40GHz) and AMD Phenom II X6 1045T (2.70 GHz)
tradeoffs: Plain C, 312-word state like MT19937-64; jump-ahead for disjoint streams; recommends using most significant bits; no SIMD path.
caveats: Speed is parity-class, not a speedup: about 6-21% faster than the reference mt19937-64.c and slower than SFMT19937-64 without SIMD on the AMD part. name: SFMT (SIMD-oriented Fast Mersenne Twister)
baseline: MT19937-64 reference implementation (mt19937-64.c from the MT homepage; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64)
workload: CPU time to generate 1e9 64-bit unsigned integers, SFMT19937-64 (with SIMD) vs MT19937-64, measured by a third party (Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 2018) in the README of sharase/melg-64.
claimed_speedup: Intel Core i7-3770: SFMT19937-64 with SIMD 1.8457 s vs MT19937-64 5.1002 s per 1e9 numbers (about 2.8x, derived from page data); AMD Phenom II X6 1045T: 2.8806 s vs 6.6490 s (about 2.3x, derived from page data). SFMT19937-64 without SIMD: 4.2654 s and 5.6123 s (about 1.2x on both, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 on Linux (stated in the melg-64 README)
hardware: Intel Core i7-3770 3.40 GHz; AMD Phenom II X6 1045T 2.70 GHz
stars_or_usage: 96 stars; widely used reference generator (also dSFMT for doubles in the same org)
tradeoffs: Produces a different sequence from MT19937, so it is not a drop-in for std::mt19937 output. Designed for 32-bit output; for 64-bit output the high-dimensional equidistribution is worse (Harase's table gives Delta=14095 vs 0 for MELG), and dSFMT is the variant meant for doubles. 128-bit SIMD blocks with SSE2, AVX2/AVX512 (added in 1.5.2), NEON (1.5.3) and Altivec backends; README warns big-endian and Altivec are not tested. C API with the state in a struct.
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party table in the melg-64 README (companion repo of Harase and Kimoto, ACM TOMS 44(3) 2018), measured on 2012-era CPUs with an unstated gcc version; the melg-64 repo holds only the MELG generators, not the timing harness for SFMT or MT19937-64. The baseline is the original mt19937-64.c, not libstdc++ std::mt19937_64. The SFMT README itself has no numbers, and the authors' homepage claim ('about twice as fast as MT') could not be opened (egress blocked). The SIMD path computes the same generator as the scalar one: the repo's check.sh diffs the std, sse2, avx2 and altivec test builds against the same reference outputs (SFMT.<MEXP>.out.txt). Quality trade-off noted on the same page: for 64-bit output SFMT19937 has a large equidistribution defect (Delta 14095 vs 7820 for MT19937-64), since SFMT is tuned for 32-bit output; dSFMT is the recommended variant for doubles. SFMT also produces a different sequence than MT19937, so it is a replacement generator, not a faster std::mt19937.

The repo has no benchmark source (only AVX512-VAES2-PRNG.h, README.md, LICENSE and throughput_chart.png, whose bars omit mt19937), and no CPU model, compiler or flags are given. name: cauldron random.h (ziggurat normal distribution)
baseline: std::normal_distribution (driven by std::minstd_rand in the benchmark's cpp11random entry)
workload: Generating 1,000,000 standard-normal float or double samples per trial (minimum over 10 trials) in miloyip/normaldist-benchmark, camel-cdr's 128-block ziggurat with a single condensed lookup table and an LCG as the uniform source versus the benchmark's other implementations.
claimed_speedup: Issue #3 in miloyip/normaldist-benchmark (author camel-cdr), ns per sample, float: ziggurat_new 4.018, cpp11random (std::normal_distribution) 8.852, existing ziggurat 7.289, marsagliapolar 6.133, inverse 6.017, boxmuller 7.484; double: ziggurat_new 4.081, cpp11random 17.009, existing ziggurat 7.817, marsagliapolar 8.711, inverse 7.222, boxmuller 16.546. Derived from page data: 2.2x faster than std::normal_distribution for float and 4.2x for double; 1.8x and 1.9x faster than the benchmark's existing ziggurat. The issue says its implementation is 60% faster than the existing ziggurat.
tradeoffs: Single-file C header (usable from C++) with the ziggurat entry points dist_normalf_zig and dist_normal_zig that need an init call and a lookup table (128 entries, float or double) and a caller-supplied RNG function; the slow path uses log and exp. The library also offers a lower-accuracy dist_normalf_fast that was not part of this evidence. Output quality of the issue's code was not verified here (the benchmark harness has a correctness check, but the issue does not report its result).
caveats: First-party claim in a GitHub issue comment with no CPU model, compiler or flags, so tier C. The std::normal_distribution baseline is driven by std::minstd_rand, not std::mt19937 (confirmed in the benchmark's src/cpp11random.cpp), and the standard library implementation is not stated; the ziggurat uses a cheap LCG, so the gap partly reflects RNG cost (the benchmark's null entry is 1.049 ns float, 1.149 ns double). In the same tables the benchmark's clt4 entry (sum of 4 uniforms, an approximation) runs at 4.064 ns float and 4.088 ns double, essentially tied with ziggurat_new. The code in the issue is the author's proposed template, not literally the current cauldron function: random.h's dist_normal(f)_zig is described as based on Doornik's implementation with a single lookup table, and in the current random.h the float version defaults to 128 blocks while the double version defaults to 256 blocks (DIST_NORMAL_ZIG_COUNT), so the link is by author and design, not identical code. The double version builds a 64-bit value from two 32-bit LCG outputs per the issue. The cauldron repo has tools/random/bench.c (referenced from random.h) but publishes no results. Issue dated 2020-12-19; last repo commit 2025-02-01. The lead's '4.0 ns versus 7.3-7.8 ns' compares against the benchmark's existing ziggurat, while the std::normal_distribution figures are 8.852 ns and 17.009 ns.

name: fastrand (PCG32 and xorshift128+ with nearly-divisionless bounded integers for Python)
baseline: CPython random.randint (Mersenne Twister)
workload: python3 -m timeit of a single bounded integer draw in [0,1001) or [100,1000] with fastrand versus random.randint(0,1000) and numpy.random.randint(0,1000).
claimed_speedup: fastrand.pcg32bounded(1001) 23.6 ns and fastrand.pcg32randint(100,1000) 24.6 ns versus random.randint(0,1000) 216 ns (about 9.2x and 8.8x, derived from page data) and numpy.random.randint(0,1000) 955 ns (about 40x, derived). README headline: 'up to 10x faster than random.randint'.
tradeoffs: Python extension with module-level generator state; pcg32 gives 32-bit output only and xorshift128+ is available only on some 64-bit platforms; not cryptographically secure; the C core (PCG32 plus Lemire's multiply-shift bounded draw) is small enough to reuse in C/C++.
caveats: One-line timeit measurements with no CPU, Python version or compiler stated. The gap is dominated by random.randint's Python-level call overhead and its slower bounded-integer path rather than by raw generator speed. The baseline is CPython, not std::mt19937. Checked in fastrandmodule.c: PCG32 (XSH-RR) and Lemire's nearly-divisionless bounded method are implemented correctly. Correctness issues seen by code reading (not executed): pcg32randint takes signed long bounds but returns n1 + value through Py_BuildValue("I"), an unsigned 32-bit format, so ranges with a negative lower bound (e.g. pcg32randint(-10, 10)) should come back wrapped to values near 2**32 instead of negatives. The error paths set ValueError and then return None, which CPython 3 turns into a SystemError.

workload: bench/Mt19937_bench.d: 100 million Mt19937 outputs summed in a loop, Gb/s, mir Mt19937_32/Mt19937_64 vs Phobos std.random.Mt19937 (32-bit). bench/randindex_bench.d: 800 million bounded-integer calls with moduli 6..105 per engine, modulo-with-rejection (randIndexV1) vs Lemire multiply-shift (randIndexV2), both implemented in the bench file. README 'Comparison with Phobos' bullets summarize both.
claimed_speedup: README: Mt19937 +100% initialization and +54% generation versus Phobos (merged to Phobos); randIndex with Lemire's method on x86-64 with LDC 1.6.0: 1.40x uint Mt19937_64, 1.73x uint Xoroshiro128Plus, 2.36x ulong Mt19937_64, 4.25x ulong Xoroshiro128Plus. bench/Mt19937_bench.d comment: mir 32-bit Mt19937 6.80851 Gb/s vs Phobos 32-bit 4.41989 Gb/s (1.54x), mir 64-bit Mt19937 12.5984 Gb/s (2.85x vs Phobos 32-bit; Phobos 64-bit noted as having wrong initialization and tempering). bench/randindex_bench.d sample results on i7-7920HQ: ulong Xoroshiro128Plus 4.40044 vs 1.0195 x 10^8 calls/s (4.32x, derived from page data), ulong Mt19937_64 1.87091 vs 0.796416 (2.35x, derived from page data). No benchmark found for the +100% initialization figure.
compiler_and_flags: LDC via ldmd2, dub --build=release-nobounds (bench file shebangs); README names LDC 1.6.0 for the randIndex figures
hardware: Intel Core i7-7920HQ @ 3.10GHz for the randIndex sample results in bench/randindex_bench.d; not stated for bench/Mt19937_bench.d
tradeoffs: D language with a Better C mode and no DRuntime dependency; provides Mt19937, PCG (Apache-2.0), SplitMix, XorshiftStar, Xoroshiro128Plus and Xoshiro256** engines plus ndslice-based random arrays and distributions; the new API uses opCall rather than a range interface. Not for cryptography.
caveats: D only, not callable from C++ without bindings. Benchmarks date from the LDC 1.6.0 era (about 2017-2018). The Mt19937 generation and initialization improvements were merged back into Phobos, so the gap against current Phobos has probably closed; the Mt19937 bench states no CPU or LDC version. The randIndex 1.40x-4.25x figures compare Lemire's reduction against a modulo reduction written in the same bench file on the same engine, not mir-random against Phobos's uniform. No benchmark source found for the +100% initialization claim. No root LICENSE file (LICENSE returns 404); license comes from dub.sdl ('BSL-1.0 (default), Apache License, Version 2.0 for PCG') and per-file Boost License 1.0 headers.
found_via: Not surfaced by a Hacker News search; recalled from prior knowledge of non-C++ RNG libraries. Opened README, repo page and commits page on github.com, and read dub.sdl via raw.githubusercontent.com for the license.

name: miranda (coolbutuseless/miranda, R package with C PRNGs: romu trio, xoshiro256+, lehmer64, splitmix64)
baseline: R base runif()
workload: bench::mark of generating 1 million uniform random numbers with each package function versus runif(N).
claimed_speedup: README text: up to 20x faster than R's built-in PRNGs; 'At their best, these PRNGs are about 20x faster than runif()'. Chart (log-scale beeswarm, values read approximately from the image): runif(N) about 30 ms for 1e6 doubles vs about 1.5 ms romutrio, 1.7 ms xoshiro256p, 1.8 ms lehmer64 and 2.5 ms splitmix64 (roughly 12x-20x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: R package with C source in src/, lifecycle marked experimental; includes jump-ahead for xoshiro256+; romu trio has a probabilistic period and xoshiro256+ has weak low bits; all four generators are listed as passing or having no systematic failures in BigCrush.
caveats: R package, usable from C++ only by reusing its small C sources (MIT). No CPU, R version, compiler or flags stated; the chart is an image and the millisecond values above are approximate readings off a log axis. Both sides are vectorized R calls that allocate a 1e6-double result, so the gap reflects R's runif path (Mersenne-Twister through R's RNG dispatch) versus inlined small-state generators, not raw generator speed against std::mt19937 or PCG. Lifecycle badge: experimental.

name: MRG32k3a branchless implementation (Vigna)
baseline: L'Ecuyer's reference double-based MRG32k3a.c (also the equivalent 64-bit integer implementation)
workload: Time to emit one double in (0,1) from MRG32k3a using the author's standard PRNG timing harness; output stream is identical to the original when seeded through MRG32k3a_init6().
claimed_speedup: Header comment: double-based reference about 17.5 ns per double, equivalent 64-bit integer implementation about 7.9 ns, this implementation about 4.1 ns (about 4.3x and 1.9x faster, derived from page data). README: 'roughly four times faster than the double-based implementation and two times faster than the trivial 64-bit integer implementation'.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 9.2.1 with the author's standard harness; optimisation flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700 @ 3.60GHz
tradeoffs: Single stream only (no stream or jump support yet); returns doubles in (0,1); emits the output from the current state, so one value must be discarded to line up with L'Ecuyer's original stream; state is six 64-bit integers.
caveats: First-party header comment with CPU and gcc version but no flags. The timing harness is the author's external prng.di.unimi.it/harness.c (not opened, host blocked), and the 64-bit integer comparison code is not published. Checked: the branchless combination step matches the reference output rule, and MRG32k3a_init6() discards one output to align with L'Ecuyer's stream, as the README says. No multiple-stream support yet (the header says so). The README notes that for batch generation nothing beats Intel MKL's vectorised MRG32k3a. The repo has no LICENSE file; the CC0 dedication is in each source header (no patent grant). Baseline is the reference MRG32k3a, not std::mt19937.
found_via: GitHub: https://github.com/topics/pseudorandom-number-generator topic page (vigna/MRG32k3a); README, MRG32k3a.h and MRG32k3a.c opened via raw.githubusercontent.com
