name: NumPy numpy.random Generator (PCG64, PCG64DXSM, SFC64 bit generators)
baseline: MT19937 (legacy RandomState and MT19937 under Generator)
workload: Time in ns per random value (32-bit and 64-bit unsigned ints, uniforms, normals, exponentials, gammas, binomials, laplaces, poissons) per bit generator under numpy.random.Generator versus legacy RandomState, measured by doc/source/reference/random/performance.py with timeit (each call draws 1,000,000 values, min of 3 repeats), on Linux with an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X; plus relative tables (MT19937 = 100) for 64-bit Linux, 64-bit Windows and 32-bit Windows.
claimed_speedup: Uniforms: PCG64 3.1 ns, PCG64DXSM 2.9, SFC64 2.6 versus MT19937 5.9 and legacy RandomState 6.0; 64-bit unsigned ints: PCG64 3.2, SFC64 2.5 versus MT19937 5.6. Overall geometric mean relative to RandomState: PCG64 219%, PCG64DXSM 225%, SFC64 251%, MT19937 under Generator 159%. 64-bit Linux table normalised to MT19937=100: PCG64 161, PCG64DXSM 168, SFC64 192 overall.
compiler_and_flags: Linux tables: GCC 9.3.0 on Ubuntu 20.04; Windows tables: Microsoft C/C++ Optimizing Compiler Version 19 (Visual Studio 2019) on Windows 10; optimization flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 3900X for all tables (Linux and Windows timings)
tradeoffs: Python-first API; using the generators from plain C++ means embedding Python/NumPy or copying the C sources. SFC64 lacks jump-ahead (per the same page); PCG64DXSM is recommended for heavily parallel use.
caveats: First-party docs. The script is public (doc/source/reference/random/performance.py) and the page names GCC 9.3.0 (Linux) and MSVC 19 / VS2019 (Windows) on an AMD Ryzen 9 3900X, but optimization flags are not stated. Values are drawn in bulk (1,000,000 per call), so the per-value times amortize Python call overhead and do not represent one-at-a-time draws. The win depends on the platform: on 32-bit Windows the new generators are slower than MT19937 (overall PCG64 25, PCG64DXSM 39, SFC64 77 versus 100), and Philox scores 28 on 64-bit Windows. Not every distribution improves: Laplaces take 76.1 ns with PCG64DXSM versus 73.2 ns with MT19937 under Generator, and Laplace and Poisson gains are 3-27 percent. Much of the normals and exponentials gap versus RandomState comes from the algorithm (ziggurat versus Box-Muller and log inversion), not from the bit generator. PCG64 is the PCG family already catalogued as pcg-cpp, and SFC64 comes from PractRand, so those rows are partly evidence for the underlying algorithms. The baseline is NumPy's own C MT19937, not std::mt19937.

name: OpenRAND (Philox, Threefry, Squares, Tyche counter-based generators)
baseline: std::mt19937 (libstdc++) on CPU and NVIDIA cuRAND on GPU
workload: CPU: Google Benchmark (benchmarks/raw_speed_cpu.cpp) constructing a fresh engine each iteration and drawing 10 to 100,000 uint32 values, against std::mt19937. GPU: 2D Brownian dynamics, 1M particles x 10,000 steps, timed with `time` on each whole executable (brownian-dynamics/runfile.sh) for cuRAND (curandStatePhilox4_32_10_t kept in global memory), Random123 Philox4x32 and OpenRAND Philox.
claimed_speedup: Paper Fig. 4b, Brownian dynamics wall time (1M particles, 10,000 steps, Philox in every library): A100 SXM cuRAND 3.20 s vs OpenRAND 1.78 s (1.80x, derived from page data), Random123 1.81 s; Tesla V100 PCIe cuRAND 4.23 s vs OpenRAND 2.48 s (1.71x, derived from page data), Random123 2.46 s. Text: 'OpenRAND outperformed cuRAND by 1.8x, while saving ~64 MB of GPU memory per million particles, and performed on par with Random123.' CPU (Fig. 4a, log-scale chart without printed values, read by eye) against libstdc++ std::mt19937 on a Xeon Platinum 8260: all four generators are far faster for 10-100 draws per freshly constructed engine. At 10K draws, Tyche (~1.6e4 ns) and Squares (~1.4e4 ns) are roughly 3.5-4x faster than mt19937 (~5.5e4 ns), while Philox (~6.6e4 ns) is slightly slower and Threefry (~3.3e5 ns) is about 6x slower.
compiler_and_flags: GPU benchmark: nvcc -Xcompiler -Wall -O3 -std=c++17 -arch=sm_80 (brownian-dynamics Makefile; CUDA version not stated; the README says to change -arch for other GPUs, so the V100 build used a different arch flag). CPU micro-benchmark: compiler and flags not stated (Google Benchmark via CMake; the repo CMakeLists sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE).
hardware: Intel Xeon Platinum 8260 (CPU micro-benchmark); NVIDIA Tesla V100 PCIe and A100 SXM (Brownian dynamics benchmark).
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17, works on CPU and GPU (CUDA) device code; counter-based design needs a (seed, counter) pair per work unit and gives reproducibility independent of thread count; the std-compatible engine interface lets it drive standard distributions.
caveats: The GPU win over cuRAND comes from the counter-based API, which avoids loading and storing per-thread cuRAND state in global memory. It is not a faster algorithm: every library uses Philox, Random123 is on par, and the authors say they do not expect the margin to hold in real kernels where RNG cost is smaller. Timing is whole-process wall time (including CUDA context setup and cuRAND state initialization). The benchmark repo vendors an early copy of the library (namespace rnd) rather than the current openrand headers, and its Makefile targets sm_80 (A100); the V100 build flags are not published. CPU micro-benchmark: compiler and flags unstated, and the repo CMake sets no build type. The engine is constructed inside the timed loop, so mt19937's 624-word seeding dominates small streams (the paper says so). At 10K draws only Tyche and Squares beat mt19937; Philox and Threefry are slower. CPU values exist only as a log-scale chart. The paper is first-party.
found_via: WebSearch: 'github OpenRAND counter-based random number generation library Philox Tyche Squares CUDA C++ performance vs curand'; opened the repo page, README.md, benchmarks/raw_speed_cpu.cpp, benchmarks/raw_speed_cuda.cu and commits page.

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from C. The paper (SoftwareX 27 (2024) 101773; preprint in the repo as docs/OpenRAND.pdf) gives Brownian-dynamics wall times against cuRAND on named GPUs (A100 SXM, Tesla V100 PCIe). The benchmark code is public in the paper's linked repo Shihab-Shahriar/brownian-dynamics (Curand.cu, Openrand.cu, r123.cu, runfile.sh), and its Makefile gives the compiler and flags (nvcc -Xcompiler -Wall -O3 -std=c++17 -arch=sm_80). That meets A for the cuRAND result; the nvcc version is not stated, the same gap the midint precedent accepted. The CPU comparison against std::mt19937 alone would only be B (chart only, compiler and flags unstated).

name: pgregory.net/rand (sfc64-based replacement for Go math/rand)
baseline: Go math/rand/v2 (PCG source and top-level functions), math/rand, golang.org/x/exp/rand
workload: Go benchmark suite (benchstat output) of Float64, Intn, Uint64, Shuffle, Perm, NormFloat64, ExpFloat64 and constructor cost, versus math/rand/v2 on a laptop and versus math/rand and x/exp/rand on a 48-thread Xeon.
claimed_speedup: Versus math/rand/v2 on i7-10510U: Rand_Float32 7.67 ns to 3.61 ns (-52.93%), Rand_Int31n 10.2 to 4.2 ns (-59.15%), Rand_Uint64 6.86 to 3.93 ns (-42.64%), Rand_Shuffle 711 to 412 ns (-42.12%), but top-level Uint64 3.06 to 3.20 ns (+4.75%, slower) and Float64 3.29 to 3.55 ns (+7.92%, slower). Versus math/rand on Xeon E5-2680 v3 with 48 threads: top-level Uint64 193 ns to 1 ns (-99.72%), Rand_Uint32 7.82 to 1.72 ns (-77.98%).
compiler_and_flags: Go toolchain, linux/amd64; Go version and flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i7-10510U @ 1.80GHz (versus math/rand/v2) and Intel Xeon E5-2680 v3 @ 2.50GHz (versus math/rand and x/exp/rand)
tradeoffs: Go-only; deliberately omits the Source interface and top-level Seed(); generator is sfc64; Rand_New costs 48 bytes and seeding (Rand_Seed 46.09 ns versus 0.57 ns) is much slower than in math/rand/v2.
caveats: README benchmarks run by the author (benchstat, n=8-10) with CPU stated but no Go version or flags; the benchmark code is public in rand_bench_*_test.go. The win over math/rand/v2 is mixed: top-level Uint64 (+4.75%), Float64 (+7.92%), Intn (+2.58%) and Intn_Big (+15.35%) are slower than v2, and Rand_Seed goes from 0.57 ns to 46.09 ns (+7995%). The headline gains are in *Rand methods (float conversion, bounded ints, shuffle, perm) and against the legacy math/rand package. The roughly 99% gains against math/rand and x/exp/rand top-level functions on 48 threads come from lock contention on the global source; this package's top-level functions use goroutine-local runtime generators (wyrand via runtime.fastrand64 on most platforms), not sfc64. Go's own PCG source in math/rand/v2 is the closest named baseline. Go-only: not callable from C++. Files derived from Go's standard library are under BSD-3-Clause (LICENSE-go); the rest is MPL-2.0.

name: prng-test-bench (aes_ctr_128 and clmulrand PRNG headers)
baseline: std::mt19937 (also std::mt19937_64, pcg64, xoshiro256**, wyrand in the same table)
workload: Google Benchmark loop calling next() once per iteration on a randomly seeded generator, 7 threads, per-thread average, 5 repetitions, reported as GiB/s of generator output.
claimed_speedup: Results file prng-next-benchmark.txt (per-thread GiB/s, 7 threads, median of 5): aes_ctr_128 37.22, aes_compress_ctr2_128 28.60, clmulrand 21.03, wyrand 16.88, xoshiro256starstar 8.53, xoshiro256plusplus 8.10, std::mt19937_64 5.24, pcg64 5.17, std::mt19937 4.67, pcg32 3.73, std::philox4x32 3.56. aes_ctr_128 vs std::mt19937 is about 8.0x in GiB/s, but aes_ctr_128 returns a 128-bit value per call and mt19937 a 32-bit one, so calls per second differ by about 2.0x (derived from page data and header). clmulrand returns uint64_t: about 4.5x mt19937 in GiB/s, about 2.25x per call vs std::mt19937 and about 4.0x per call vs std::mt19937_64 (derived from page data and header).
compiler_and_flags: Makefile defaults: g++ -std=c++26 -O3 -flto=auto -march=native with Google Benchmark 1.9.5 (release build); g++ version not recorded in the results.
hardware: CPU model not stated in results/prng-next-benchmark.json: host arch-vm (a VM), 8 CPUs at 2419 MHz, L1D 32 KiB, L1I 64 KiB, L2 4 MiB, L3 36 MiB, run dated 2026-09-18. The PractRand summaries built from the same Makefile record -march=raptorlake, so the host is a Raptor Lake part (the author's randp page names an i9-13980HX), but the L1/L2 sizes look like the E-core clusters, not P-cores, so the exact core type is unconfirmed.
tradeoffs: AES-based generators need AES-NI (and __int128) and g++ (clang++ unsupported per README). The headers expose each generator as a std::uniform_random_bit_generator. aes_ctr_128 runs only 3 AES rounds and is not claimed to be a CSPRNG. The same table includes many other generators (romu, sfc64, wyrand, squares, biski64) that may be separately catalogued.
caveats: Author-run, first-party numbers on an unnamed CPU inside a VM, so tier C. GiB/s favours generators with wide outputs (aes_ctr_128 returns 128 bits per call vs 32 for mt19937), so per-call gains are about 2x, not 8x. aes_ctr_128 is not AES-128-CTR: include/aes_ctr_128.hpp applies 3 _mm_aesenc_si128 rounds with one key to a Weyl-sequence counter, so it is a fast non-cryptographic generator and must not be used where unpredictability matters. The README does not itself claim to beat mt19937; the comparison is read from the results table. Statistical quality: aes_ctr_128 and clmulrand pass PractRand to 256 MB with all four seed types (results/prng-results.tlmax-256MB.summary.txt, GCC 16.2.1); clmulrand and an older 'aes128_ctr_128' pass to 512 GB in results/prng-results.tlmax-512GB.summary.txt, but that run predates the current code (GCC 15.2.1 build), while std::mt19937 fails at 256 MB. No LICENSE file; MPL-2.0 comes from SPDX headers in source files. Very active (several commits a week), so numbers change between runs.

name: randomgen (NumPy-compatible bit generators: SFC64, Romu, Xoshiro256, PCG64, SFMT)
baseline: MT19937 as used by NumPy's legacy RandomState (also compared against MT19937, MT64, DSFMT inside randomgen)
workload: Time in ns per random value (uint32, uint64, uniform double, exponential, normal, gamma) from each bit generator through numpy.random.Generator versus NumPy's legacy RandomState, measured by doc/source/performance.py with timeit (each call draws 25,000 values, 100 calls, min of 10 repeats), on Linux with an Intel Cascade Lake CPU (Family 6, Model 85, Stepping 7) at 3.1GHz.
claimed_speedup: uint64: Romu 2.6 ns, SFC64 2.6, Xoshiro256 2.8, SFMT 2.8, PCG64 3.2 versus MT19937 4.2 ns and NumPy RandomState 5.2 ns; uniform double: Romu 2.4, SFC64 2.5, Xoshiro256 2.7, PCG64 2.9 versus MT19937 4.0 and RandomState 5.2. The page's own overall geometric-mean score relative to RandomState: Romu(trio) 276%, Romu 268%, SFC64 259%, Xoshiro256 243%, SFMT 242%, PCG64 227%, MT19937 (via Generator) 191%.
hardware: Intel Cascade Lake (Family 6, Model 85, Stepping 7) at 3.1GHz, Linux
tradeoffs: Python/Cython package that needs NumPy; the C generator sources live in the repo and can be lifted into C/C++ projects, but the package itself is not a C++ library. SFC64 lacks jump-ahead (per the NumPy docs), so parallel streams rely on distinct seeds or Weyl increments; Philox, AES and other counter-based generators are available when many streams are needed.
caveats: First-party documentation table. The script is public (doc/source/performance.py; also a top-level benchmark.py), and the CPU family is stated without a model name, but compiler and flags are not stated. Values are drawn in bulk (25,000 per call), so Python call overhead is amortized and the numbers do not represent one-at-a-time draws. On gammas, MT19937 under Generator (20.8 ns) beats PCG64 (23.2), PCG64DXSM (23.8), Xoshiro256 (22.1) and SFMT (21.5); only Romu variants and SFC64 (20.6) are faster there. The RandomState gap on normals and exponentials is inflated by Box-Muller and log-based inversion versus ziggurat in the newer code. The page itself recommends against all Mersenne Twister variants unless backward compatibility is needed. The baseline is NumPy's C MT19937, not std::mt19937. Dual-licensed NCSA or BSD-3-Clause; component licenses are stored with each component's source.

name: RANLUX++ (sibidanov/ranluxpp)
baseline: std::ranlux (GCC libstdc++ RANLUX) in the repo README and tests/std_random_test.cxx; ROOT's TRandom1 (James' RANLUX implementation) in the independent ROOT measurement
workload: Generation of single-precision floats from the RANLUX family: an LCG formulation of RANLUX (modulus 2^576 - 2^240 + 1, 576x576-bit modular multiplication in x86-64 assembly) versus GCC's std::ranlux and a SIMD-optimized conventional RANLUX.
claimed_speedup: Independent (ROOT blog, AMD Ryzen 9 3900, GCC 8.3.1): Sibidanov's implementation 'comes in at around 8ns per number' vs TRandom1 RANLUX 'around 62ns per number' (single-precision only), about 7.8x (derived from page data); ROOT's own portable RANLUX++ reaches about 9 ns after tuning. First-party README: 'generation speed achieved (20 clock/float) is order of magnitude faster than the usual approach, for example, GCC C++ RANLUX implementation where 198 clock/float is measured at Haswell CPU'; the optimized conventional RANLUX reaches 40 clock/float, and 'The SSE2 and AVX2 versions is approximately 4 and 8 times faster correspondingly' (README does not name the reference; the SIMD classes run 4 or 8 independent RANLUX lanes, so this is aggregate throughput).
compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile: g++ -O3 -Iinc -mavx2 -DASMSKIP (compiler version not stated). Independent ROOT measurement: GCC 8.3.1 on CentOS 8.2.2004 (flags not stated).
hardware: README: Haswell (GCC RANLUX 198 clock/float) and Skylake (155 clocks per 576-bit modular multiplication), microarchitectures only; the CPU for the 20 clock/float figure is not named. ROOT blog: single core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900.
stars_or_usage: 11 stars, 4 forks; the algorithm was adopted in ROOT 6.24 as TRandomRanluxpp/RanluxppEngine through a portable C++ reimplementation (not this x86-64 assembly code); described in Computer Physics Communications 2017 (arXiv 1705.03123)
tradeoffs: x86-64 assembly (mulx/adcx/adox variants chosen by GCC function multiversioning), so not portable to other architectures; LGPL-3.0 (COPYING and COPYING.LESSER in repo). The win is inside the RANLUX family: RANLUX is itself far slower than mt19937/PCG/xoshiro, so this does not beat the category baselines.
caveats: The README's 10x figure mixes CPUs: GCC's 198 clock/float was measured on Haswell, the 155-cycle modmul on Skylake, and the CPU for 20 clock/float is not named. The README does not say whether std::ranlux24 (p=223) or std::ranlux48 (p=389) gave 198 clock/float, while ranluxpp defaults to p=2048 (higher luxury, so the comparison is conservative on quality). ranluxpp's float/double output is unpacked directly from the 576-bit LCG state, not the RANLUX base-2^24 sequence, so the numbers differ from std::ranlux even though the state is provably equivalent; tests/ranluxpp_test.cxx modes 0 and 1 check the LCG state against the conventional RANLUX for 1e8 steps. The SIMD (SSE2/AVX2) conventional-RANLUX classes run 4 or 8 independent RANLUX lanes; their claimed 4x/8x is aggregate multi-stream throughput, and the same-seed consistency check (ranlux_test mode 7) only prints values for visual comparison. RANLUX++ is x86-64 assembly only (mulx/adx variants via GCC function multiversioning). It is faster than other RANLUX implementations but slower than Mersenne Twister: the ROOT blog measures TRandom3 at about 3 ns per number on the same machine. The CPC 2017 paper could not be opened (arxiv.org blocked). License: LGPL-3.0-or-later per source headers, with COPYING (GPLv3) and COPYING.LESSER (LGPLv3) texts at the repo root (there is no LICENSE file).
found_via: WebSearch 'fast random number generator C++ library benchmark faster than std::mt19937 vcpkg OR conan' surfaced arXiv 1705.03123; repo opened from a follow-up search
WebSearch: 'github RANLUX++ ranluxpp Sibidanov faster than ranlux48 C++'; opened the repo page, README.md and commits page.

name: ROOT RanluxppEngine (portable RANLUX++)
baseline: ROOT TRandom1 (RANLUX); ROOT TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is faster than RANLUX++ in the same benchmark
workload: Average time per generated random double from a Google Benchmark microbenchmark (BM_Rndm calling Rndm() once per iteration, rootbench TRandomBenchmarks.cxx) for TRandom1, TRandom3, TRandomMixMax and TRandomRanluxpp, 10 repetitions with standard deviation under 1 percent.
claimed_speedup: ROOT blog 'Implementing and tuning RANLUX++ for ROOT' (2020-11-30): initial portable version about 30 ns per double, Sibidanov's assembly version about 8 ns, TRandom1 (RANLUX, single precision) about 62 ns, after tuning about 9 ns per number ('very close to the assembly version'), slightly slower than TRandom3 at about 3 ns. Derived from page data: about 6.9x faster than TRandom1 (62 ns versus 9 ns); 2x faster than TRandom1 already at the untuned 30 ns. Tuning gains reported: loop unrolling up to 30 percent, overflow handling up to 15 percent, native __int128 multiplication over 40 percent, carry propagation over 20 percent on GCC 7.5.0.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 8.3.1 (default); graph also covers Clang 9.0.1 and GCC 7.5.0 built from source; optimisation flags not stated in the post.
hardware: Single core of an AMD Ryzen 9 3900, CentOS 8.2.2004
stars_or_usage: ROOT: 3.3k stars; used across high-energy physics; RANLUX++ shipped in ROOT 6.24
tradeoffs: Portable C++ (uses unsigned __int128 where available, with unrolling pragmas) instead of Sibidanov's x86 assembly; 576-bit LCG state stored as 9 x 64-bit words, and the generator advances in blocks via a multiply and modulo. It gives 48 random bits per double and passes TestU01 per the blog, but it is about 3x slower than ROOT's Mersenne Twister and the code sits inside ROOT (mathcore) with ROOT dependencies (TRandomEngine base class), so extracting it needs the src/ranluxpp helper headers. Provides RanluxppEngine24 and RanluxppEngine2048 plus compatibility engines for James/Luescher RANLUX.
caveats: The benchmark compares against TRandom1 (original RANLUX) and does not beat std::mt19937, PCG or xoshiro: in the same post TRandom3 (Mersenne Twister) is about 3 ns per number, about 3x faster. TRandom1 yields only 24-bit single-precision numbers while RANLUX++ yields 48-52 bits per double, so the work per number differs. The post itself notes that Luescher's newer RANLUX (ranlxd) was measured at 30 ns for double values in a cited review, so against modern RANLUX the tuned 9 ns is about 3.3x faster (derived from page data), not 6.9x; std::ranlux24/std::ranlux48 from <random> were not measured. The measured code predates correctness changes in June 2021 (commits '[mathcore] Ensure full modulo operation in mod_m', 'RANLUX++: Convert LCG state to RANLUX numbers', 'RANLUX++: Extract only 48 bits per number', per the RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx history page; the blog says 52 bits per double), so the 9 ns figure was not re-measured for the shipped implementation and the tier is capped at C. Optimisation flags are not stated; the benchmark source is public (root-project/rootbench PR #200, merged 2020-12-15, root/math/mathcore/TRandomBenchmarks.cxx) but no results are checked in. The last commit shown for RanluxppEngineImpl.cxx was 2021-06-23 (the June 2021 commit 'Move RANLUX++ implementation to directory' split helpers into a subdirectory not covered by that file history); last_commit above is the overall ROOT repo (large project, judged only for math/mathcore RanluxppEngine*).

name: seiran (seiran128 PRNG)
baseline: Reference mt19937-64.c (Matsumoto-Nishimura C code; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64, but std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed), pcg64_xsh_rr and xoshiro256**
workload: 64-bit values generated per ns using the xoshiro/xoroshiro speed harness (harness.c), compared against ten other 64-bit generators.
claimed_speedup: README table (64-bit values/ns): seiran128 1.20 vs sfc64 1.21, xoroshiro128+ 1.13, xoshiro256** 0.99, pcg64_xsh_rr 0.38, mt19937_64 0.32. README says 'About 3.7 times faster than Mersenne Twister(64-bit version)'. That is 1.20/0.32 = 3.75x, and 3.2x over pcg64_xsh_rr (both derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 7.3.0 (flags not stated; xoshiro harness.c)
hardware: Intel Core i7-7700HQ @ 2.80 GHz
tradeoffs: Two-word (128-bit) LFSR state with an add/rotate/multiply output scrambler, period 2^128-1, jump of 2^64; no 32-bit variant; not cryptographically secure (the author recovered state from three outputs with Z3). Portable, no 128-bit multiply. CC0 dedication, so no patent grant.
caveats: First-party measurement with compiler flags unstated. The speed edge over xoshiro256** is only about 1.2x and seiran128 ties sfc64 (1.21), so the clear wins are over the reference MT19937-64 C code and PCG64 only; std::mt19937_64 was not timed. The author says that, being new, it has not been investigated by others. The PractRand 32 TB, BigCrush, gjrand and hwd results are the author's own. Not cryptographic: the author recovered the full state from 3 consecutive outputs with Z3 in a few minutes. seiran128.c uses a global static state and exports bare next()/init() symbols, so it must be wrapped before use as a library. CC0 dedication gives no patent grant. The last commit (2021) only added a C# port.

name: shioi128 (Shioi PRNG)
baseline: Reference mt19937-64.c (Matsumoto-Nishimura C code; same algorithm as std::mt19937_64, but std::mt19937_64 itself was not timed), pcg64_xsh_rr and xoshiro256**

It relies on arithmetic right shift of a negative int64_t (the README says 'MUST use arithmetic right shift'), which is implementation-defined in C before C23 and in C++ before C++20. Single-CPU gain over math/rand Int31n is small (29.7 vs 31.8 ns/op); the larger single-CPU gain is per-goroutine RNG.Uint32n 6.50 vs rand.New(...).Int31n 17.9 ns/op.

The README states that Romu2jr (RomuDuoJr with a NASAM-based seeding wrapper, xromu2jr.h) wins overall for game development, that the fixed-point (Lemire) range mapping beats biased modulo and unbiased masking, and that results are charts of relative speed per console (for example '2.2 implies the test was 2.2 faster than the slowest test that ran in this game console'). stars_or_usage: 3 stars, 0 forks (re-host of the rhet.dev post by account Almightygir, three commits on 2023-06-25); the original post is cited by the ulfben/cpp_prngs README ('Winner of Rhet Butler's RNG Battle Royale (2020) and second fastest engine in the lineup')
tradeoffs: RomuDuoJr has a 128-bit state and no guaranteed minimum period, so some seeds can end in short cycles; the README mitigates this with a NASAM-based initializer and brute-force checks (no cycles for 32-bit seeds within 2^24 bytes, 16-bit seeds within 2^36 bytes) but it is not a proof. Chaotic generators give low-quality first outputs unless seeded through a mixer. The README charts report some PractRand failures, and the author himself suggests xoshiro256++ or sfc64 when a guaranteed period matters. The header uses reinterpret_cast type punning in as<>() and either __uint128_t or __umulh for 64-bit ranges.

name: Cache-Aware and GPU-Accelerated SpMV (VSJ001)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpMV (CSR_ALG2)
workload: CSR SpMV effective memory bandwidth (GB/s) of a hand-written one-warp-per-row CUDA kernel versus cuSPARSE on four SuiteSparse matrices (cant, consph, pdb1HYS, webbase-1M) on an A100.
claimed_speedup: 'beats NVIDIA's cuSPARSE library by 24-56 percent on regular real-world matrices': cant 1531 vs 1172 GB/s (+30.6%), consph 1557 vs 1252 GB/s (+24.4%), pdb1HYS 1718 vs 1102 GB/s (+55.8%); cuSPARSE wins on webbase-1M (847 vs 203 GB/s).
compiler_and_flags: src/Makefile: nvcc (CUDA 12.3 per README) -O3 -arch=sm_80 -lineinfo -std=c++14 --ptxas-options=-v -Xcompiler -O3, linked with -lcusparse -lcublas; CPU build gcc -O3 -march=native -ftree-vectorize.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 80GB (README also quotes a 1555 GB/s HBM2 peak) on the Northeastern University Explorer cluster; Intel Xeon Gold host CPUs
tradeoffs: Simple CSR-vector kernel (one warp per row, warp-shuffle reduction) with an ELL variant and a selector that skips ELL on irregular rows; CPU side adds cache tiling and AVX2 with software prefetching. Loses to cuSPARSE on irregular web-graph matrices.
caveats: Coursework-style project with four real matrices, one A100 run, 1 warm-up plus 10 timed single-call iterations. Bandwidth figures use a formula that counts every x[col] read as DRAM traffic, which is why they exceed the 1555 GB/s peak (98-110 percent); the CSR arrays themselves are about 48-72 MB (derived from page data), so this is x-vector reuse in L2, not the whole matrix fitting in cache. Only cuSPARSE CSR_ALG2 was compared, and each timed cuSPARSE call uses a freshly created handle and descriptors with no reuse or preprocessing. In results/gpu/timings.csv cuSPARSE takes about 0.021-0.025 ms on the 10K-row synthetic matrices where the custom kernels take about 0.007-0.010 ms, and the absolute gaps on cant, consph and pdb1HYS are 0.016, 0.019 and 0.028 ms (derived from page data), so much of the 24-56 percent win may be cuSPARSE per-call overhead rather than kernel efficiency. cuSPARSE is 4.2x faster on webbase-1M. No LICENSE file, so reference only.

name: sparsam
baseline: GTSAM 4.2.1 (PyPI wheel driven through its Python bindings) on 2D pose graphs; Ceres 2.2 on BAL bundle adjustment
workload: End-to-end Gauss-Newton/LM optimization of the 2D M3500 pose graph using sparsam's own block-sparse Cholesky with AMD ordering, versus GTSAM 4.2; bundle adjustment on BAL Ladybug versus Ceres 2.2.
claimed_speedup: docs/benchmarks/m5.md: on M3500 (3500 poses) with both stacks converging to final chi-squared within 0.009%, sparsam GN (7 iterations) takes 0.078 s vs GTSAM GN (8 iterations) 0.133 s as in-sweep medians of 5, and 0.066 s vs 0.141 s standalone after cooldown; the author states the defensible claim as 1.7-2.1x faster end to end. Against Ceres 2.2 on BAL Ladybug (README), sparsam is slower in wall clock (1.74 s vs 0.67 s on ladybug-49, 1.57 vs 0.48 s on ladybug-73, 9.9 vs 4.9 s on ladybug-138, 26.5 vs 24.0 s on ladybug-318) but 552 vs 1091 ms per iteration on ladybug-318.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3 -O3, single-threaded, Eigen 3.4.0 dense fixed-size kernels (docs/benchmarks/m4.md, m5.md); GTSAM side is the prebuilt gtsam==4.2.1 PyPI wheel (numpy<2), build flags not stated
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX
tradeoffs: SLAM and estimation backend written from scratch in C++20 using only the standard library and Eigen dense fixed-size types; own CSR-of-blocks storage, AMD/RCM ordering and simplicial block Cholesky. Not a general sparse solver API. Benchmarks need GTSAM and Ceres built behind an off-by-default CMake flag.
caveats: Mixed result that the README itself states: Ceres wins wall clock on bundle adjustment (1.1-3.3x, mostly from fewer iterations), and on fill-heavy 3D pose graphs GTSAM's per-iteration linear algebra is about 3-5x faster than sparsam's simplicial block Cholesky. The M3500 speedup is end to end GN (7 vs 8 iterations), not a like-for-like factorization time, and the author notes laptop boost-clock state moves both numbers by about 15%. GTSAM was timed through its Python wheel (optimize() call only, median of 5) with wheel build flags unknown. sparsam's own LM plateaus on M3500 where GTSAM's LM converges. Author-run on one laptop; project created July 2026 with 1 star. Category fit is loose: a nonlinear least-squares/SLAM backend whose core is a from-scratch block-sparse Cholesky; baselines are GTSAM and Ceres, not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc.

README per-matrix table (Xeon Gold 6242 dual socket, GFlops): rma10 ALBUS 94.52 vs CSR5 42.05 vs CVR 65.84; mac_econ_fwd500 68.56 vs 25.33 vs 40.79; webbase-1M 34.14 vs 21.92 vs 22.13; ALBUS loses to CVR on cant, ins2 and pdb1HYS.
compiler_and_flags: Both Makefiles (ALBUS(OpenMP) and ALBUS(OpenMP+AVX2)): icpc -g -w -fno-alias -qopt-report -qopt-report-phase=all -mbranches-within-32B-boundaries -falign-double -inline-calloc -falign-loops=8 -xCORE-AVX2 -fopenmp -O3. The README's example shows an older 'icpc -xCORE-AVX2 -qopt-prefetch=3 -fopenmp -O3'. A commented g++ alternative uses -march=native -mavx -mavx2 -fopenmp -O3. The icpc version is not stated.
hardware: README table: dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6242 (2x16 cores). Abstract numbers: dual-socket Xeon E5-2670 v3. The README also lists a dual-socket Xeon Silver 4110 test platform.

tradeoffs: Research code (main.cpp plus headers, not a packaged library); needs a conversion/preprocessing step into the ALBUS format; AVX2-oriented and built with the Intel compiler; OpenMP and OpenMP+AVX2 variants.
caveats: Peer-reviewed paper but the authors' own benchmark. The MKL column of the README table is empty, so the MKL ratios appear only in the paper abstract (the paper itself was not reachable: sciencedirect.com is blocked here). The README table (Xeon Gold 6242) and the abstract (E5-2670 v3) use different CPUs. ALBUS loses to CVR on cant, ins2 and pdb1HYS in the README table. main.cpp runs the albus_balance preprocessing outside the timed loop, after a warm-up of the same number of iterations, so the GFlops exclude preprocessing. No comparison harness for MKL, CSR5 or Merge is in the repo. MKL is not one of SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc. Hardware is 2014-2019 era and the repo has been idle since April 2022 (README edits). [retier] ALBUS uses plain CSR with no format conversion; preprocessing is only a thread partition. Kernel reads one double past rows of length 3 mod 4; repo bench runs cache-warm and ignores the iterations argument.

name: AmgT (tensor-core AMG)
baseline: HYPRE (GPU build calling cuSPARSE)
workload: Algebraic multigrid solves on SuiteSparse matrices where AmgT replaces HYPRE's SpGEMM (setup phase) and SpMV (solve phase) with tensor-core kernels over a new mBSR storage format, in FP64 and mixed precision; the repo builds three executables (AmgT_FP64, AmgT_Mixed, and cuSPARSE = HYPRE baseline).
claimed_speedup: Paper (SC'24): AmgT outperforms the original GPU version of HYPRE by a factor of on geomean 1.46x, 1.32x and 2.24x (up to 2.10x, 2.06x and 3.67x) on NVIDIA A100, H100 and AMD MI210 GPUs, respectively. (Numbers taken from the WebSearch result text; which phase or total time they cover is not stated there.)
compiler_and_flags: compile.sh: CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-12.0; HYPRE configured with --with-cuda --enable-unified-memory and --with-gpu-arch='80 80' (A100) or '90 90' (H100); -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80 (or compute_90); README advises CUDA 12.2+ and OpenMPI 4.0+. No explicit CXX optimization flags are visible in compile.sh.
hardware: NVIDIA A100, H100 and AMD MI210 (per the paper text returned by search); repo recommends compute capability 8.0; host CPU not verified
tradeoffs: Implemented inside a modified copy of HYPRE (AmgT_HYPRE/), not a standalone library: using it means taking that fork or porting the mBSR data structure (seq_mv.h), SpGEMM (csr_spgemm_device.c) and SpMV (csr_matvec_device.c). The variant is chosen at build time by copying config_files/<variant>.h over seq_mv.h. Needs tensor-core GPUs (compute capability 8.0 or newer) for the main gains; the mixed-precision mode changes numerics. The embedded HYPRE code carries its own license files, which I did not inspect.
caveats: Numbers are from a WebSearch snippet of the SC '24 abstract (ACM DL record of DOI 10.1109/SC41406.2024.00058, the DOI the repo README cites); the paper itself could not be opened here (dl.acm.org, doi.ieeecomputersociety.org, ieeexplore are egress-blocked), so which phase (setup, solve or total) the geomeans cover and the FP64 versus mixed-precision split are unverified. The repo has no result tables. Its harness (AmgT_test/test_new.c) runs HYPRE PCG with a BoomerAMG preconditioner (tolerance 1e-5, max 300 iterations) and times BoomerAMGSetup and the solve separately with gettimeofday; compile.sh builds three variants (AmgT_FP64, AmgT_Mixed, cuSPARSE = unmodified HYPRE calling cuSPARSE) for A100 (sm_80) or H100 (sm_90) only, on embedded HYPRE 2.31.0 (2024/02/14) configured with --with-cuda --enable-unified-memory. There is no MI210/HIP build path in compile.sh, so the 2.24x MI210 figure is not reproducible from the repo. Host CPU model and per-matrix problem set not verified. Not a GitHub fork, though it embeds modified HYPRE. [retier] 2026-10-03 retier attempt: the SC '24 paper body is still unreachable (dl.acm.org, ieeexplore.ieee.org and ssslab.cn are egress-blocked; no GitHub-hosted PDF found). name: DASP (dense-tensor-core SpMV)
baseline: cuSPARSE CSR SpMV (CUSPARSE_SPMV_ALG_DEFAULT); also CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR and cuSPARSE BSR in the paper
workload: General sparse matrix-vector multiplication (y = Ax) on SuiteSparse matrices in FP64 and FP16 on NVIDIA A100 and H800 GPUs, using tensor-core MMA units; the repo's harness times cuSPARSE and DASP for 1000 iterations after 100 warm-ups for a given .mtx file.
claimed_speedup: Paper (SC'23) FP64 on A100: DASP outperforms CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR, cuSPARSE BSR and cuSPARSE CSR by a factor of on average 1.46x, 2.09x, 3.29x, 2.08x and 1.52x (up to 12.64x, 17.48x, 90.59x, 283.92x and 6.94x), respectively. FP16 versus cuSPARSE: on average 1.70x and 1.75x (up to 26.47x and 65.94x) on A100 and H800. (Numbers taken from the WebSearch result text for the paper; see caveats.)
compiler_and_flags: From the repo Makefile: nvcc from CUDA 12.0 with host gcc 12.2, -O3 -m64 -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80, -Xcompiler -fopenmp-simd, linked with -lcusparse -lcublas
hardware: NVIDIA A100 and H800 GPUs (per the paper text returned by search); the repo recommends a GPU with compute capability 8.0. Host CPU model not verified.
tradeoffs: Needs NVIDIA GPUs with MMA tensor-core support (compute capability 8.0 or newer; FP64 and FP16 variants built from separate mains: make double, make half). Research code driven by Matrix Market files, not a library API. Rows are grouped into long, medium and short categories and repacked into MMA-sized blocks, which adds preprocessing and padding (fill-zero) data. AGPL-3.0 network copyleft applies to anything built on the code.
caveats: The paper could not be opened here (dl.acm.org and other publishers are egress-blocked); the speedups come from a WebSearch snippet of the SC '23 abstract (ACM DL record of DOI 10.1145/3581784.3607051, the DOI the repo README cites), including the A100-only list of FP64 averages. The repo holds no result tables. Its harness (src/main_f64.cu) times cuSPARSE CSR SpMV (CUSPARSE_SPMV_ALG_DEFAULT) and DASP over 1000 iterations after 100 warm-ups, times cuSPARSE setup separately, and checks the DASP result against cuSPARSE; the DASP row reordering/format conversion is not in the timed loop, so gains pay off only when one matrix is multiplied many times. The repo has no scripts for the CSR5, TileSpMV, LSRB-CSR or BSR baselines, so only the cuSPARSE comparison is reproducible from it. cuSPARSE version used in the paper and host CPU not verified. Large 'up to' ratios (283.92x vs cuSPARSE BSR) are outliers; averages are the meaningful figures. [retier] Harness has no result check (verify_new commented out in both mains); all matrix values and x are 1.0; y is returned in permuted row order; FP16 rows accumulate in f16 against an FP32 cuSPARSE baseline. Open issues #1 (wrong result with 1 iteration), #3 (wrong result on mip1), #4 ('Speedup are mostly fake data?', A100 user slower than cuSPARSE on many matrices including bibd_20_10). Independent: CB-SpMV (ICS '25, FP64, 2,843 matrices) is 1.21x faster than DASP on A100 and 2.76x on RTX 4090; arXiv 2502.16851 (snippet) finds cuSPARSE beats DASP on average for matrices larger than L2. SC '23 paper numbers remain snippet-only.

name: PIQP
baseline: OSQP
workload: Convex QP solve time on the Maros-Meszaros test set (138 problems; 76-problem sparse subset), shifted geometric mean of runtime over four accuracy settings, run through the qpsolvers Python wrappers.
claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0 (2024-09-07), Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean with PIQP = 1.0: OSQP 12.7 (default), 16.1 (high accuracy), 52.8 (low), 51.9 (mid); sparse subset (76 problems): OSQP 9.5 / 17.4 / 30.0 / 56.0. Success rates on the full set: PIQP 95.7 / 73.2 / 97.1 / 94.2% vs OSQP 43.5 / 26.1 / 21.0 / 24.6%. First-party piqp_benchmarks on Maros-Meszaros (shifted geometric means, PIQP = 1.0): OSQP 7.55 at low accuracy (eps_abs 1e-3, eps_rel 1e-4) and 42.66 at high accuracy (eps_abs 1e-8, eps_rel 1e-9).
hardware: qpbenchmark run: Intel Core i7-6500U @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs). First-party piqp_benchmarks: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 3990X 64-core @ 4.3GHz.
tradeoffs: Convex QPs only. Header-only C++14 built on Eigen, with dense, sparse and multistage backends; C/C++, Python, Matlab/Octave and R interfaces. Proximal interior-point method, so it needs sparse/dense LDL factorizations per iteration.
caveats: Category fit is loose: PIQP is a convex QP optimization solver (header-only C++14 on Eigen), not a sparse linear-system solver, and OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc baseline list; there is no optimization-solver category in this wave. The qpbenchmark run used prebuilt Python wheels (piqp 0.4.1, osqp 0.6.7.post0, qpsolvers 4.3.3, Python 3.12), so no compiler or flags apply, runtimes include a sliver of wrapper time, and the versions are two years old (PIQP is now 0.6.x). The suite's known limitations include CPU thermal throttling (issue 88) on a 2-core laptop CPU. Only solves that return no solution are counted at the 1000 s time limit (qpbenchmark/results.py not_found_value); solutions returned as solved but failing the tolerance check keep their measured runtime. Rankings depend on the suite: ProxQP's own benchmark (different problem classes) shows ProxQP ahead of OSQP instead.

name: AMGCL
baseline: PETSc (GAMG); Trilinos ML; CUSP
workload: 3D Poisson problem on shared memory, AMG setup and solve times
claimed_speedup: docs/benchmarks.rst (first-party), shared-memory 3D Poisson with 150^3 = 3,375,000 unknowns on dual Xeon E5-2640 v3, CG with smoothed-aggregation AMG: AMGCL sets up the solver about 20-100% faster than Trilinos ML and 4-7x faster than PETSc, and overall CPU performance is on par with Trilinos. Medians computed from the published raw data in docs/smem_data/poisson/{amgcl,trilinos,petsc}.txt (derived from page data): setup on 1 core 3.97 s, against 6.81 s for Trilinos (1.7x) and 27.87 s for PETSc (7.0x); on 16 cores 0.92 s against 1.00 s (1.09x) and 3.57 s (3.9x). Total setup+solve on 1 core 11.58 s against 15.28 s (1.32x) and 49.72 s (4.3x); on 16 cores 2.33 s against 2.48 s (1.06x) and 5.87 s (2.5x). GPU (Tesla K80): AMGCL/CUDA is slightly better than CUSP, and its total time is only about 30% better than CPU AMGCL or Trilinos. Distributed memory: about 3x slower than Trilinos AMG in MareNostrum 4 weak scaling (2.5x faster than Trilinos DD-ML), and 2.5x slower than Trilinos/AMG at 384 cores on SuperMUC.

No CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or -O level, compiler name or version, or PETSc, Trilinos or CUDA version is recorded in the repo or in docs/benchmarks.rst.

name: CKTSO (parallel sparse direct solver for circuit simulation)
language: C (prebuilt shared libraries with a C header; source not published)

README (first-party, no hardware): more than 3x over sequential KLU and more than 25x with 16 threads; the 2022 results PDF shows about 2.8x and 14.6x over KLU.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.8.5 on CentOS 7.9 for the version-202205 comparison PDF; flags not stated; prebuilt binaries are shipped per platform (centos6 gcc482, centos7 gcc485, rocky8 gcc850, win7)

tradeoffs: x86-64 binaries only (CentOS 6/7, Rocky 8, Windows 7 x64); needs a license key file (license/cktso.lic) next to the library; specialised for SPICE-style circuit matrices; races 10 reordering methods, so analysis is slow by design.
caveats: Binary-only: the repository ships compiled libraries, a header, demos and docs, not source, so it cannot be audited or copied. The library needs license/cktso.lic, a signed key file with EXPIRE = 2028-12-31, so a pinned binary can stop working when the key expires. The README averages (>3x, >25x) are first-party without hardware or method; the 2022 PDF is from an old version ('results are from an old version') and shows lower KLU ratios (about 2.8x and 14.6x), in part because KLU there used NICSLU's ordering. Its scatter plots show MKL PARDISO factorizing several of the largest matrices (over 1M rows) faster than CKTSO, so the averages hide losses on big cases. The GPU-solver comparisons reuse numbers from other papers rather than running those solvers. The IEEE TCAD 2025 paper was not opened.

name: GLU (GPU-accelerated sparse LU solver for circuit simulation)
baseline: KLU and UMFPACK (SuiteSparse)
workload: Sparse LU numeric factorization of circuit-simulation and general matrices from the University of Florida (SuiteSparse) collection plus self-generated RLC mesh networks, GPU versus CPU direct solvers (KLU 1.2.0, UMFPACK 5.6.2, PARDISO 5.0.0); preprocessing and symbolic analysis excluded from timings.
claimed_speedup: TVLSI 2016 (GLU 1.0): on typical UFL circuit matrices about 19.56x over KLU and 47.13x over UMFPACK (also 5.71x / 1.46x over single- / 16-threaded PARDISO and 1.47x over a GPU left-looking solver); on general UFL matrices 39.39x over KLU and 24.04x over UMFPACK (geometric mean). Times are numeric factorization only, excluding preprocessing and symbolic analysis. GLU3.0 (IEEE D&T 2020, docs/Peng_DT_2020.pdf Table I): 3.51x arithmetic / 2.81x geometric mean over 32-thread NICSLU on 15 circuit matrices, numeric factorization time.
compiler_and_flags: TVLSI 2016: CUDA 5.0, compiler flags not stated; GLU3.0 paper: C++ and CUDA C compiled with -O3
hardware: TVLSI 2016: NVIDIA Tesla K40 (all GPU results), host with two 8-core Xeon E5-2670 and 64 GB DDR3-1600; GLU3.0 paper: NVIDIA GTX TITAN X (Maxwell) with Xeon E5-2698 v3 and 128 GB
tradeoffs: Needs CUDA (nvcc); README says the solver runs in single-precision float32 on the GPU, with float64 inputs/outputs converted at the boundary; CSC input; Python bindings (pyglu) and scipy-style splu wrapper; aimed at low-fill circuit matrices.
caveats: The 19.56x / 47.13x figures are from the TVLSI 2016 GLU 1.0 paper (docs/He_TVLSI_15.pdf); baselines are old (KLU 1.2.0, UMFPACK 5.6.2, PARDISO 5.0.0) and timings cover numeric factorization only, so symbolic analysis and preprocessing (where KLU is cheap) are excluded. GLU is slower than the CPU solvers on very small circuits (circuit_2, rajat15), and on the self-generated RLC meshes 16-threaded PARDISO is the best CPU solver. The repo now holds GLU3.0, which the 2020 paper measured in single precision against 32-thread NICSLU (2.81x geometric mean); pyglu also runs float32 on the GPU, so precision differs from the double-precision CPU baselines. Recent commits (Feb 2026) fixed a CUDA __syncthreads() deadlock on a divergent path and unchecked CUDA calls, so published numbers were measured on code with those issues. The repo bundles NICSLU (src/nicslu) under LGPL-2.1-or-later alongside the BSD-3-Clause GLU code. README has no benchmark numbers.

name: GraphBLAST (GraphBLAS on the GPU)
baseline: SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS through LAGraph (CPU)
workload: BFS, SSSP, PageRank and triangle counting on graph adjacency matrices; GraphBLAST on one NVIDIA GPU against SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS (directly in the paper; through LAGraph in the spla chart) on a multi-core CPU.
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed ACM TOMS paper (Yang, Buluc, Owens, 'GraphBLAST: A High-Performance Linear Algebra-based Graph Framework on the GPU', doi 10.1145/3466795), per its abstract as quoted in search results: 43.51x geometric mean and 1268x peak speedup over SuiteSparse GraphBLAS on multi-threaded CPUs, and on average at least an order of magnitude over SuiteSparse and GBTL. Third-party check in the spla README chart (docs/stats/rq1_rel.png, log scale, GTX 1070 against LAGraph on a 4-core i7-6700, read by eye): PageRank roughly 13x to 75x, triangle counting roughly 5x to 13x, BFS roughly 0.4x to 4.5x and SSSP roughly 0.2x to 2.6x (slower than LAGraph on some graphs).
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 3.40 GHz 4-core, 64 GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: NVIDIA CUDA only, Boost dependency, tested on CUDA 9.1/9.2 with g++ 4.9.3/5.4.0 per the README, so it may need porting to build on current toolchains.
caveats: GPU against CPU in both sources, so not like for like; the paper's numbers were seen only as an abstract quote in search results (paper blocked), so its GPU, CPU, SuiteSparse version, compiler and flags are unverified, and the 43.51x geometric mean is an aggregate over its own algorithm and graph mix. In the spla chart (made by a competing project, no flags or harness for GraphBLAST in the repo) GraphBLAST has no bar for comOrkut and i2004 in BFS/SSSP and none for comOrkut, socLvJr, rggn223s0 and rdcent in PageRank, which suggests it failed or was not run on those larger graphs on the 8 GB GPU; it is slower than LAGraph on several BFS and SSSP graphs. Last commit 2021-06-18; CUDA build era of 2019-2021.

name: GSS (GRUS Sparse Solver, trial binaries)
baseline: Intel MKL PARDISO (Intel Composer XE 2013 SP1), CPU only
workload: Numerical factorization time only (not symbolic analysis or solve) on 12 SuiteSparse/UF matrices (msdoor, inline_1, apache2, boneS10, audikw_1, bone010, StocF-1465, nd24k, Fault_639, Flan_1565, Emilia_923, nd12k), both solvers at default parameters; GSS 2.4 runs CPU-GPU hybrid, PARDISO runs CPU only.
claimed_speedup: README: 'For many large matrices, GSS is about 2-3 times faster than PARDISO and other CPU based solvers.' User guide Table 1 (numerical factorization time, s, GSS 2.4 CPU-GPU hybrid vs PARDISO): total 315.114 vs 904.244 over 12 matrices, about 2.9x (derived from page data); per matrix up to 5.4x on nd24k (15.880 vs 85.519) and 4.3x on Fault_639 (43.633 vs 186.405), but GSS is slower on msdoor (1.061 vs 0.424), inline_1 (3.385 vs 2.605) and boneS10 (5.585 vs 4.636). The guide itself says 'For matrices need short time computing, PARDISO is faster than GSS.'
hardware: Intel Core i7-4770 (3.4 GHz), 24 GB RAM, ASUS GTX 780 GPU (compute capability 3.5), CUDA Toolkit 5.5, Windows 7 64-bit (user guide section 7, dated 2014).
tradeoffs: Closed-source commercial solver; the repo contains only 'GSS 2.4.1 x64 TRIAL' binaries with C and Fortran samples and a user guide PDF. Claims hybrid CPU+GPU (CUDA) execution with a Q-learning scheduler.
caveats: Closed-source trial distribution: the repo holds only Windows x64 DLLs (GSS_Dl.dll, GrusLic_de.dll, cublas64_55.dll), a trial license file (gss_spd.lic), headers, C/Fortran samples and a PDF guide; no license grant, no source. The speedup compares a CPU+GPU hybrid run against CPU-only PARDISO on 2013-era hardware, covers numerical factorization only, and GSS loses on 3 of 12 matrices (smaller/shorter jobs). No benchmark harness or compiler flags are published, so the numbers cannot be reproduced. Built against CUDA 5.5. Last commit 2021-10-05; the benchmarked release (GSS 2.4) dates from 2014. The linked arXiv paper (2109.14929, Q-learning for sparse Gaussian elimination) is a preprint; it could not be opened from this environment.

baseline: cuSPARSE 12.2 SpMM (CSR ALG2, CSR ALG3, CSR default, COO) and GE-SpMM
workload: FP32 sparse-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM) in GFLOPS, averaged over K = 32, 64 and 128 dense columns, on 17 GNN datasets (Yelp, Flickr, AIFB, BGS, AM, MUTAG, AmazonCoBuyComputer, arxiv, collab, ddi, ppa, products, protein, reddit, ...) on an NVIDIA H800.

No exact numbers are printed.
compiler_and_flags: NVCC >= 11.8 (stated as a minimum; the toolkit actually used is not given beyond 'cuSPARSE-12.2') via CMake. CMakeLists.txt builds Release with host -O3. cmake/public/CUDA.cmake adds -gencode arch=compute_80,code=sm_80, -gencode arch=compute_90,code=sm_90, -std=c++11 and --expt-extended-lambda.
hardware: NVIDIA H800 for the README figure (host CPU not stated); code requires Ampere (A100, A800) or Hopper (H100, H800) GPUs
license: Apache-2.0 via per-file headers on the HP-SpMM sources (spmm/mm/spmm_kernel.cu, spmm/mm/spmm_common.cpp, include/spmm/mm/*, test/*.cpp). The repo has no LICENSE file. The bundled starml framework headers (e.g. include/starml/basic/matrix.h, allocator.h) and include/spmm/utils/timer_cuda.h carry no license. The integrated GE-SpMM baseline code is MIT upstream.
stars_or_usage: 8 stars, 0 forks (an identical copy at https://github.com/HPMLL/HP-SpMM has 5 stars, 1 fork)
tradeoffs: FP32 only, Ampere and Hopper GPUs only, CUDA 11.8+. Targets the sparsity patterns of GNN training graphs rather than scientific matrices. Companion code to 'Fast Sparse GPU Kernels for Accelerated Training of Graph Neural Networks' (IPDPS 2023); this repo is described as the updated version.
caveats: Results are only a chart image, and the README calls the code an updated version of the IPDPS 2023 method; the paper (DOI 10.1109/IPDPS54959.2023.00057) was not opened. Not like-for-like input: HP-SpMM (LBSpMM in spmm/mm/spmm_kernel.cu) runs on a COO matrix whose rows are permuted by a precomputed '.cugraph_reorder' file, while cuSPARSE and GE-SpMM get the original order. The reorder cost is excluded, and the reorder files exist only as downloads from a personal SharePoint (dataset/download.sh); no generator script is in the repo. The correctness check (CHECK_RES) is commented out in test/test_all.cpp by default. Values are unweighted (all 1.0). No LICENSE file: the kernel sources carry Apache-2.0 headers but the bundled starml framework does not. cuSPARSE is a vendor library, not one of the listed incumbents. CUDA_ARCHITECTURES is set to 80 on the target while CUDA.cmake also adds sm_90 gencode.

name: HYLU
language: C (C API header with extern "C", closed-source prebuilt library)
baseline: Intel MKL PARDISO
workload: Parallel sparse LU solve (preprocessing, numerical factorization, forward-backward substitution) of 37 SuiteSparse Matrix Collection matrices with dimensions 525,825 to 5,558,326, wall time with 16 threads.
claimed_speedup: One-time solve: 1.70X faster than Intel MKL PARDISO on geometric mean in total time (preprocessing + factorization + solve); 2.36X faster in numerical factorization, 1.48X faster in preprocessing, but forward-backward substitution 18% slower. Repeated solve with identical sparsity pattern: 2.90X faster in numerical factorization, 2.53X faster in factorization + solve total, forward-backward substitution 20% slower. Also claims an order of magnitude higher accuracy (residual) on geometric mean.
compiler_and_flags: Test code compiled with gcc 13.3.0 (flags not stated); HYLU library compiled with gcc 8.5.0 on Rocky Linux 8.10 (flags not stated); MKL 2025.3; HYLU version 20260331
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6130 @ 2.1GHz, 256GB memory, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, 16 threads
license: None stated: no LICENSE file, and the README, include/hylu.h and doc/ug_en.pdf give no terms; prebuilt binaries only (unlike CKTSO, no license key file is required)
tradeoffs: Closed source: the repo ships one C header (include/) plus prebuilt x64 libraries (centos7_x64_mkl, centos7_x64_openblas, win7_x64_mkl, win7_x64_openblas) and a demo; no solver source. Needs an x64 CPU with AVX2 and FMA; Windows or Linux only (README names Windows 7/10/11 and CentOS 7/8, other mainstream Linux said to work). Supports unsymmetric, symmetric indefinite and symmetric positive-definite matrices, real and complex, 32-bit and 64-bit index APIs. Forward-backward substitution is slower than MKL PARDISO (18-20% on geometric mean), so the win comes from preprocessing and factorization.
caveats: First-party evidence only: README and doc/results.pdf by the author, plus the author's arXiv preprint 2509.07690 (not opened; arXiv is unreachable here, and no copy of the paper is checked into the repo: doc/ holds only results.pdf, ug_cn.pdf and ug_en.pdf). A WebSearch snippet of the preprint abstract gives older figures: 34 SuiteSparse matrices, numerical factorization 1.95X (one-time) and 2.40X (repeated) faster than MKL PARDISO, versus 2.36X and 2.90X on 37 matrices in results.pdf (version 20260331). No benchmark code is public (demo/ only builds examples with gcc -O3 -std=gnu11 and solves sample .mtx files), compiler flags for the timed builds and the MKL PARDISO settings (ordering, iparm) are not stated, and all results are 16-thread wall time on one Xeon Gold 6130 with no sequential numbers. No license file or terms anywhere, and only binaries are provided (Linux .so built for CentOS 7 and Windows DLLs, MKL or OpenBLAS variants, x64 with AVX2/FMA), so it can be neither audited nor copied; usability is reference and has_code is false. Baseline is Intel MKL PARDISO, not SuiteSparse, Eigen sparse or PETSc. Per-matrix charts in results.pdf (read visually, approximate): in one-time total time HYLU is slower than PARDISO on af_shell10 (about 0.8x) and roughly even on CurlCurl_4 and a few others, while off-scale wins on ASIC_680k, ASIC_680ks, circuit5M and nlpkkt80, where PARDISO creates huge fill-in, lift the geometric mean; forward-backward substitution is slower on most matrices. The residual chart shows HYLU relative residuals near or above 1 on CurlCurl_2, CurlCurl_4 and dgreen (PARDISO worse still) and about 0.1 on nv2, so those timings come from runs that did not produce accurate solutions; the text acknowledges only Hamrle3. The matrix set is limited to 37 large SuiteSparse matrices (n from 525,825 to 5,558,326), and results.pdf (created 2026-04-01) uses version 20260331 while the latest is 20260930. Repo history runs from 2025-09-12 (initial release) to 2026-09-30 (39 commits). A sibling project by the same author, CKTSO, is already catalogued (https://github.com/chenxm1986/cktso); HYLU is a separate general-purpose solver, not a duplicate.
found_via: Hacker News: WebSearch 'Show HN sparse Cholesky LU solver faster than SuiteSparse' with allowed_domains news.ycombinator.com returned the arXiv paper HYLU 2509.07690, not an HN thread; no Hacker News thread about HYLU was found. A follow-up WebSearch 'HYLU hybrid parallel sparse LU factorization github' led to the repo.

KLU is a sequential solver, so the 1.87X is likely multithreaded NICSLU against one-thread KLU. The README says NICSLU 'will no longer be updated or maintained' and points users to its successor CKTSO (already on the known list), which 'provides better performance and scalability'. claimed_speedup: Ratios to PARDISO time (below 1 is faster): solve 0.34 / 0.43 / 0.37 / 0.30 on the four classes (about 2.3x to 3.3x faster, derived from page data); factor 1.35 / 3.97 / 0.95 / 4.76 and refactor 1.38 / 4.28 / 0.90 / 1.83 (faster only on MoM near field); one-shot analysis+factor+solve 1.05 / 1.06 / 0.74 / 1.12 (faster only on MoM near field).

caveats: Mixed result: the win is the solve phase; factorization and one-shot time are slower than PARDISO on three of four classes. The corpus is exported from production codes and the benchmark scripts take a corpus path, so the table cannot be reproduced from the README alone. CPU model, Rust version and flags are not given. name: sparse_dot_topn
baseline: SciPy sparse CSR matrix multiplication (scipy.sparse A.dot(B), SciPy 1.12.0)
workload: Sparse matrix product A.dot(B) of two TF-IDF CSR matrices of shape (20,000 x 193,190) by (193,190 x 20,000) built from SEC EDGAR company names, with and without keeping only the top-n values per row; 30 repeats.
claimed_speedup: Apple M2 Pro, 8 threads: plain sp_matmul 5.1x faster than SciPy (0.032 s vs 0.165 s min time); sp_matmul_topn with top_n=10 and 8 threads 6.9x faster (0.024 s). Intel i9 2.3 GHz 8-core, 8 threads: sp_matmul 3.4x. Single-thread plain product about 1.0x on M2 Pro.
hardware: Apple MacBook Pro M2 Pro (32GB RAM); MacBook Pro 2.3 GHz 8-core Intel Core i9 (16GB RAM)
tradeoffs: Python package with a C++17 extension (OpenMP vendored); uses a max-heap to keep memory low when only the top-n entries per row are needed. Result type and API differ from plain SciPy products. Not a general SpGEMM replacement.
caveats: First-party benchmark (tier C): bench code is public and hardware is named but compiler and flags are not. SciPy's sparse matmul is single-threaded, so almost all of the speedup comes from multithreading; single-thread plain product is about 1.0x. The top-n variant is slower than SciPy for large n (for example 6.2x slower at top_n=1000 on one thread on the M2 Pro). SciPy CSR matmul is not SuiteSparse, Eigen or PETSc, so baseline_in_list is false and the category fit is partial.

name: SparseX (CSX-format SpMV library with LLVM runtime code generation)
baseline: Intel MKL CSR SpMV (and pOSKI, ViennaCL in the TOMS paper)
workload: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on multicore CPUs; the Compressed Sparse eXtended (CSX) format stores dense substructures compactly to cut memory bandwidth and emits specialised kernels per matrix.
claimed_speedup: No verified numbers. SparseX TOMS 2018 abstract (search-result quote): superior performance over competitive libraries on large-scale problems, comparable performance to Intel MKL and ViennaCL. The earlier '19.5x over MKL inspector-executor (1.6x average) for HPC matrices' belongs to a different paper by the same group (arXiv 1711.05487, a CSR-based optimizer), not to SparseX.
tradeoffs: Needs LLVM/Clang >= 4.0, Boost >= 1.48 (regex, serialization, system), numactl and gcc >= 4.8 (README); autotools build; format conversion and tuning step before the first multiply, so it pays off only for repeated SpMV (iterative solvers).
caveats: No numbers for SparseX itself could be verified: the TOMS paper (dl.acm.org) and the SparseX home page are blocked here, and its abstract as quoted only claims superior performance on large-scale problems and comparable performance to MKL and ViennaCL. The figure the search agent recorded (up to 19.5x, 1.6x average over MKL inspector-executor for HPC matrices) comes from a different paper by the same authors (arXiv 1711.05487) about a CSR-based optimization selector, so it does not apply to SparseX. A 2025 third-party paper (DIV, ICS 2025; snippet only) says SparseX mainly speeds up SpMV for large matrices, median 13 percent, geometric mean 7.7 percent, baseline not visible. The repo ships a benchmark driver (src/bench, bench_spmv with --enable-bench and --with-mkl / pOSKI) but no results. Requires LLVM/Clang >= 4 for its JIT and notes every LLVM release breaks the JIT module; last commit 2018 (LLVM 6 support), so it likely does not build against current LLVM.

name: spECK (lightweight-analysis GPU SpGEMM)
baseline: cuSPARSE SpGEMM
workload: Sparse general matrix-matrix multiplication (SpGEMM) in CSR on NVIDIA GPUs over a large SuiteSparse-derived matrix set (PPoPP '20 evaluation; matrix count and GPU not seen), compared with other GPU SpGEMM libraries.
claimed_speedup: PPoPP '20 abstract (search-result quote): outperforms all currently available GPU SpGEMM solutions in 79 percent of cases over all matrices with more than 15k products and is second best in 15 percent, on average 83 percent faster than the second-best approach and up to 25x faster. A later third-party study ('Optimizing General Sparse Matrix-Matrix Multiplication on the GPU', ACM, doi 10.1145/3774654) reportedly gives spECK 5.67x average over cuSPARSE (OpSparse 4.91x, TileSpGEMM 3.47x) (snippet only, not verified here).
tradeoffs: CUDA GPU only (CUDA 10.1+; cuda11 branch for CUDA 11+), CMake build; per-device static/dynamic shared-memory sizes must be set by hand in include/Multiply.h; also builds as a library (spECKLib) with an .mtx reader and a config.ini for benchmarking.
caveats: Numbers come from abstract quotes in search results; the PPoPP '20 paper (dl.acm.org, tugraz.at PDF) is blocked here, so GPU, CUDA version and the exact baseline list were not seen, and the quoted abstract does not single out cuSPARSE (the repo's harness checks results against cuSPARSE via externals/cusparse and config.ini CompareResult). Newer peer-reviewed work beats spECK: OpSparse (IEEE Access 2022) reports 1.52x average over spECK, and TileSpGEMM (PPoPP '22) is faster on 94 of 142 large matrices (spECK wins on 48). The 5.67x average over cuSPARSE comes from a third-party snippet the search agent saw and was not re-verified. Builds need per-GPU shared-memory constants set by hand in include/Multiply.h; CUDA 11+ needs the cuda11 branch. Last commit 2022-07-29, which fixed a readOperations kernel bug on matrices whose last row is empty.

PageRank about 7.5x (coAuthorsCiteseer) to about 50x (coPapersDBLP, com-Orkut) on 12 graphs. SSSP about 1.4x (indochina-2004) to about 23x (road_central). Triangle counting about 4x to 12x. BFS about 0.7x to 3.7x, slower than LAGraph on coAuthorsCiteseer, belgium_osm, com-Orkut and indochina-2004. In PageRank spla beats Gunrock on every graph but trails GraphBLAST on several (e.g. belgium_osm, roadNet-CA, cit-Patents). The second chart (docs/stats/rq3_int.png) runs spla on the integrated GPU of the same machine as LAGraph. name: TACO (Tensor Algebra Compiler)
baseline: Eigen (sparse), Intel MKL, OSKI and pOSKI, uBLAS and Gmm++ for sparse linear algebra; SPLATT and the MATLAB Tensor Toolbox for sparse 3rd-order tensor kernels
workload: OOPSLA 2017 paper, Section 8. SpMV on six SuiteSparse matrices (rma10, cant, cop20k, scircuit, mac-econ, pwtk). Blocked SpMV against tuned OSKI/pOSKI. Compound kernels: SDDMM, PLUS3 (A = B + C + D), MATTRANSMUL (y = alpha A^T x + beta z) and RESIDUAL (y = b - Ax), the last two also on webbase-1M. 3rd-order tensor kernels TTV, TTM, MTTKRP, PLUS and INNERPROD on the Facebook, NELL-2 and NELL-1 tensors. Average cold-cache times, serial unless marked -par (12 threads on one socket).
claimed_speedup: The paper's headline is parity: performance 'competitive with best-in-class hand-optimized kernels in popular libraries' (abstract). SpMV (Fig. 14): 'competitive with Intel MKL and matches, if not slightly exceeds, single-threaded performance of all of the other libraries'; Eigen's bars sit at about 1.0x to 1.1x taco's time, and MKL is slightly faster on rma10 and cant. Compound operations (Fig. 16, bars read off the chart, so approximate): Eigen takes about 0.93x to 1.4x taco's time (largest on webbase-1M for MATTRANSMUL and RESIDUAL, where MKL and OSKI are also about 1.2x to 1.4x slower). Fig. 16 labels its off-scale bars: uBLAS 2,411.81x to 73,404.75x slower on SDDMM; PLUS3 bars at 4.88x to 5.79x (uBLAS) and 9.16x to 16.75x (Gmm++, 'about an order of magnitude slower'). Table 2 (serial unless noted): the MATLAB Tensor Toolbox is 9.329x to 1856x slower. MTTKRP against SPLATT: SPLATT takes 1.218x taco's time serial and 1.266x parallel on Facebook, but 0.7157x and 0.8371x on NELL-2 and NELL-1, and 0.6542x parallel on NELL-1, i.e. taco is up to 1.53x slower. Blocked SpMV: 'OSKI outperforms taco in almost all cases.'
compiler_and_flags: GCC 5.4 (paper). taco-bench/CMakeLists.txt builds the harness and the header-only baselines with -O3 -ffast-math -std=c++11. taco JIT-compiles its generated C kernels with TACO_CFLAGS, which defaults to '-O3 -ffast-math -std=c99' in src/codegen/module.cpp at HEAD; the 2017 default was not checked. Baseline library versions (Eigen, MKL, OSKI, Boost uBLAS, Gmm++, SPLATT) are not stated.
hardware: Two-socket 12-core/24-thread 2.4 GHz Intel Xeon E5-2695 v2, 32 KB L1d, 30 MB L3 per socket, 128 GB RAM; parallel runs use 12 threads pinned to one socket with numactl
tradeoffs: Usable as a C++ library to load tensors and compute expressions, or as a code generator that emits C functions for a given expression and format. The README links the OOPSLA 2017 paper and two technical reports (arXiv 1802.10574 on optimization, 1804.10112 on formats) for details.
caveats: The README and paper claim parity, not a broad win. Against Eigen sparse, the incumbent, taco is roughly equal on SpMV and up to about 1.4x faster on fused compound operations; Eigen is slightly faster on some SDDMM and PLUS3 matrices. MKL is slightly faster on some SpMV matrices, tuned OSKI beats taco on blocked SpMV in almost all cases, and SPLATT's MTTKRP is up to 1.53x faster on NELL-1/NELL-2. The very large ratios have algorithmic causes: uBLAS SDDMM does Theta(n^3) dense work, and the Tensor Toolbox matricizes in MATLAB. The taco-bench harness covers only the linear-algebra libraries (no SPLATT or Tensor Toolbox code). Its last commits (2017-08-31 and 2017-09-01) disabled result validation for MKL SpMV, Gmm++ PLUS3 and uBLAS SDDMM/PLUS3. Baseline library versions are not stated. The measurements are from 2017 on an Ivy Bridge-EP Xeon with GCC 5.4 and -ffast-math on both sides; taco HEAD has changed since. Stale: last taco commit 2025-04-14, taco-bench last commit 2017-09-01.

name: TileSpMV
baseline: Merge-SpMV (Merrill and Garland), CSR5 and BSR SpMV on NVIDIA GPUs, as named in the IPDPS 2021 abstract. The BSR implementation is presumably cuSPARSE bsrmv, but the snippets do not say so, and whether cuSPARSE CSR was also compared is unconfirmed.
workload: SpMV (y = Ax) on NVIDIA GPUs over all 2757 matrices of the SuiteSparse Matrix Collection (per abstract snippets). The matrix is split into 16x16 sparse tiles, and seven warp-level kernels (CSR, COO, ELL, HYB, dense, dense row, dense column) are chosen per tile; nonzeros of very sparse tiles go to a separate matrix, which the repo computes with an embedded CSR5 (src/external/CSR5_cuda). FP64 by default (MAT_VAL_TYPE=double).
claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed paper (Niu, Lu, Dong, Jin, Liu, Tan, 'TileSpMV: A Tiled Algorithm for Sparse Matrix-Vector Multiplication on GPUs', IPDPS 2021, pp. 68-78). According to its abstract as quoted in search results, TileSpMV is faster than Merge-SpMV, CSR5 and BSR on most matrices of the full SuiteSparse Matrix Collection, with up to 2.61x, 3.96x and 426.59x speedups respectively. These are maxima only; average or geomean speedups were not visible. The paper body was not opened, and the repo README has no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: From src/Makefile: nvcc, CUDA 11.1 path, -O3 -w -arch=compute_61 -code=sm_86 -gencode=arch=compute_61,code=sm_86, -Xcompiler -fopenmp -O3, MAT_VAL_TYPE=double
hardware: Paper, per search-result snippets: NVIDIA A100 (Ampere) and NVIDIA Titan RTX (Turing), all 2757 SuiteSparse matrices; host CPU unknown. README: GPU with compute capability >= 3.5 ('NVIDIA Tesla K40 as tested'), CUDA 11.1, Ubuntu 18.04/20.04.
tradeoffs: NVIDIA GPUs only (compute capability 3.5 or newer). Matrices are first converted to a tiled format (csr2tile), and very sparse tiles are split into a separate matrix; conversion cost and the extra format memory are tradeoffs. Research code driven by a Matrix Market file (./test -d 0 matrix.mtx). Bundles the CSR5 CUDA code under src/external/CSR5_cuda.
caveats: Paper not opened: IEEE, doi.org, ResearchGate, Semantic Scholar and the lab's PDF at ssslab.cn are blocked from this container. Speedups are 'up to' maxima from the abstract, and the 426.59x maximum against BSR is an outlier typical of matrices that do not suit BSR. Precision per figure, average speedups and the cuSPARSE version are unverified. The repo does not reproduce any comparison: src/main.cu checks one TileSpMV run against a CPU CSR reference, and the CSR5 code is part of TileSpMV, not a baseline. In the current HEAD harness (src/tilespmv_cuda.h), the timed loop has the CSR5 call for the extracted very-sparse nonzeros commented out. Reported runtime and GFlops (computed from all nnzA) therefore leave that work out whenever coototal != 0, and the y checked afterwards would lack those contributions. Whether the paper's numbers came from this harness is unknown. The Makefile builds only sm_86 SASS plus compute_61 PTX, a target that matches neither the README's K40 nor the paper's GPUs. Same-lab follow-up DASP (SC'23) reports beating TileSpMV by 2.09x on average in FP64 on A100 (search-result text only), so this is no longer the lab's fastest SpMV. Last commit 2022-08-12. [retier] Independent measurement (Cong, Sun, Chen, Xie, Liu, Qian, 'CB-SpMV', ICS '25, Salt Lake City; opened): on 2843 SuiteSparse matrices in FP64, with CUDA 12.4 and driver 550.135, each kernel was run 1000 times. cuSPARSE v12.4 bsrmv used the best block size of 2x2, 4x4, 8x8 or 16x16 per matrix, and TileSpMV used 16x16 tiles. CB-SpMV averaged 2.95x over cuSPARSE-BSR and 3.06x over TileSpMV on the RTX 4090, and 2.99x over cuSPARSE-BSR and 3.95x over TileSpMV on the A100. That suggests TileSpMV was on average no faster, and on the A100 slower, than best-block-size cuSPARSE BSR on current GPUs. The ratio of those averages, about 0.96x on the RTX 4090 and 0.76x on the A100, is derived from page data and is only indicative, since averages of per-matrix speedups do not divide exactly. The original IPDPS 2021 paper body (average speedups, cuSPARSE version, precision) remains unopened.
